1:1.headline: אשרי is always plural: happiness is many goods together
1:1.body: The word for 'happy is' always comes in a plural form. Radak and Meiri say a person is not called happy for one good thing, only for many.

sources.quote: מלת אשרי היא לעולם בלשון רבים
sources.says: Radak says the word is always plural because a person is called happy only for many good things, not one.

sources.quote: מפני שהיא אמורה על קבוץ הצלחות
sources.says: Meiri says it is plural because it speaks of a gathering of many successes.

1:1.headline: Walking, standing, sitting: which step is the worst?
1:1.body: The sages read the three verbs as a slide: whoever walks with the wicked ends up standing, then sitting with them. Meiri reads הלך as fully taking up their way of life, not walking on foot, so for him it is the strongest of the three.

sources.quote: כִּי מִתּוֹךְ שֶׁלֹּא הָלַךְ לֹא עָמָד
sources.says: Rashi says that because he did not walk with them, he did not come to stand, and so he did not come to sit.

sources.quote: שלשון הליכה לא נאמ׳ על הליכת הרגל אבל על אחיזת הדרכים והנהגות לגמרי
sources.says: Meiri says walking here is not walking on foot but taking up ways of life completely, a stronger hold than standing.

1:1.headline: Scoffers, or gossips who carry secrets?
1:1.body: Ibn Ezra links לצים to מליץ, a go-between, so these are people who pass on other people's secrets. Metzudat Zion links it to מליצה, the polished speech that mockers use.

sources.quote: מגזרת: כי המליץ בינותם שהוא יגלה סוד ראובן לשמעון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from מליץ, the go-between, someone who reveals Reuven's secret to Shimon.

sources.quote: מלשון מליצה כי המלעיג בבני אדם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from מליצה, because a mocker dresses up his words to make them sink in.

1:2.headline: First it is God's Torah, then it becomes 'his'
1:2.body: The verse says 'the Torah of the LORD' and then 'his Torah'. Rashi says that once a person toils in it, the Torah is called by his own name.

sources.quote: וּמִשֶּׁעָמַל בָּהּ הִיא נִקְרֵאת תּוֹרָתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is first called the Torah of the LORD, and once he has toiled in it, it is called his Torah.

sources.quote: שאלו היתה מלת ובתורתו חוזרת על האל היה לו לומר ובדתו
sources.says: Meiri argues that if 'his' meant God, the verse would have used another word, so 'his' means the learner.

1:2.headline: Thinking about the Torah, or saying it aloud?
1:2.body: הגה can mean to think or to speak. Rashi says it always means thought in the heart, while Metzudat Zion says it is sometimes thought and sometimes speech.

sources.quote: כָּל לְשׁוֹן הֶגֶה בַּלֵּב הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says every use of this word means something in the heart.

sources.quote: פעם תשמש ענין מחשבה כמ״ש והגיון לבי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it sometimes means thought and sometimes speech.

1:3.headline: Even the leaves count: scholars' small talk is worth study
1:3.body: A tree's leaves are not its fruit, yet here they do not wither. Rashi and Radak, following the sages, say even the everyday talk of Torah scholars is worth studying.

sources.quote: שִׂיחָתָן שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים לְצֹרֶךְ הִיא
sources.says: Rashi says even the waste of the tree has a use: the talk of scholars needs study.

sources.quote: אפילו שיחת חולין שלהם יכול אדם ללמוד ממנה מוסר העולם
sources.says: Radak says, after the sages, that one can learn good conduct even from scholars' everyday talk.

1:3.headline: Its leaf will not wither, or will not rot?
1:3.body: Rashi reads יבול as wither. Meiri reads it as wear out and rot, from בלה: a tree by water could rot, yet this one does not.

sources.quote: לֹא יִבּוֹל. לְשׁוֹן כָּמוֹשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says the word means to wither.

sources.quote: ואצלי לפרשו מענין בלוי ורקב מלשון בלה בשרי ועורי
sources.says: Meiri says some read it as 'fall', but he reads it as wearing out and rotting, as in Lamentations 3:4.

10:3.headline: A 'blessing' that is really an insult to God
10:3.body: ברך means 'bless', and the commentators ask who blesses whom. Radak: the wicked man blesses greed and scorns God. Meiri: a robber who thanks God for his success insults God by that very blessing.

sources.quote: הרשע מברך ומשבח הבצע ומי שאוחז דרכו ומנאץ האל
sources.says: Radak says the wicked man blesses and praises greed and those who follow it, and scorns God.

sources.quote: כי הגזלן המברך את האל על הצליחו בגזלותיו הוא מנאץ האל
sources.says: Meiri says a robber who blesses God for the success of his robberies is insulting God.

sources.quote: והבוצע אשר הוא מברך השם מנאצו ויהי ברך, כמו: ברך נבות אלהים ומלך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a reading where the robber who 'blesses' God is reviling him, like the false charge that Naboth 'blessed' God and king.

10:5.headline: He blows his enemies away, or lays a trap for them
10:5.body: Rashi reads יפיח as 'blows': with one puff the wicked man knocks his enemies down. Radak gives that reading and another, from פח, a trap: he sets snares to catch them.

sources.quote: בְּהַפָּחַת רוּחַ הוּא מֵפִיחַ בָּהֶם, וְהֵם נוֹפְלִים לְפָנָיו
sources.says: Rashi says he blows a breath at them and they fall before him.

sources.quote: או הוא מענין פח ומוקש, כלומר שישים בהם פח ללכדם
sources.says: Radak says it may come from פח, a trap: he sets a trap to catch them.

10:7.headline: Deceit named for what is hidden 'inside'
10:7.body: תך is a rare word for deceit. Radak and Metzudat Zion connect it to תוך, 'inside': the liar keeps one thing inside his heart and says another with his mouth.

sources.quote: ותך היא כמו מרמה, לפי שאין בתוך לבו מה שמראה בפיו
sources.says: Radak says תך means deceit, because what is inside his heart is not what he shows with his mouth.

sources.quote: ותוך. ענין מרמה הנסתר בתוך הלב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means deceit hidden inside the heart.

10:8.headline: Spying on 'your army', or on the helpless
10:8.body: חלכה is a rare word. Rashi reads it from the Masorah as חילך, 'your army', meaning Israel. Menachem, whom Rashi quotes, and Radak read it as the poor and weak.

sources.quote: לָמַדְנוּ מִמְּסוֹרֶת שֶׁחֵלְכָה כְּמוֹ חֵילְךָ חֵיל שֶׁלְּךָ
sources.says: Rashi says the Masorah teaches that חלכה is like חילך, 'your army'.

sources.quote: עֵינָיו שֶׁל עֲמָלֵק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהֵם חֵילְךָ, יֶאֱרֹבוּ
sources.says: Rashi says the wicked one's eyes lie in wait for Israel, who are God's army.

sources.quote: לחלכה כמו חלך והה"א נוספת; ופרושו: לעני
sources.says: Radak says חלכה is חלך with an added letter, and means the poor man.

10:10.headline: Written as one word, read as two: 'a band of the broken'
10:10.body: חלכאים is written as one word but read as two, חל כאים. Rashi and Radak read 'a band of the broken and weak'. Meiri adds another reading of חיל: 'the wealth of the downtrodden'.

sources.quote: והוא כתיב מלה אחת וקרי שתי מלות חל כאים, ופרושו: עדת הנכאים והחלושים
sources.says: Radak says it is written as one word and read as two, meaning the company of the dejected and weak.

sources.quote: וְנָפַל בַּעֲצוּמָיו חֵלְכָּאִים. חֵיל נִשְׁבָּרִים
sources.says: Rashi says it means a band of broken people, and notes it is one of fifteen words written as one and read as two.

sources.quote: או נפרש חיל כאים ממון הנדכאים והיא כתובה מלה אחת ונקראת בשתים
sources.says: Meiri offers a reading of 'the wealth of the downtrodden', and notes the word is written as one and read as two.

10:10.headline: The robber crouches low, or pretends to be weak
10:10.body: ידכה means 'he crouches' or 'he is crushed'. Rashi says the ambusher makes himself small so no one notices him. Radak says the robber pretends to be sick and weak, so travelers let him join them.

sources.quote: כָּךְ דֶּרֶךְ הָאוֹרֵב, שֶׁמְּדַכֶּה וּמַשְׁפִּיל וּמַקְטִין עַצְמוֹ, כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יְהֵא נִכָּר
sources.says: Rashi says an ambusher crouches and makes himself small so he will not be seen.

sources.quote: הוא וחבורתו יעשו עצמם חולים ומדוכאים כדי שלא ישמרו בני אדם מהם
sources.says: Radak says the robber and his band pretend to be sick and crushed so people will not guard against them.

10:10.headline: By his winks, his strong men, or his strong limbs
10:10.body: Rashi gives two readings of בעצומיו. It may be his winks, from עצם עיניו, 'shutting the eyes'. Or it may be his strong men. Ibn Ezra reads it as his powerful hands and feet.

sources.quote: וְנָפַל בַּעֲצוּמָיו שֶׁל רָשָׁע זֶה בִּרְמִיזוֹתָיו וּבִקְרִיצוֹתָיו
sources.says: Rashi says the poor fall by the wicked man's hints and winks, and also offers 'by his strong men'.

sources.quote: בעצומיו - ידיו ורגליו שיש להם כח עצום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word means his hands and feet, which have great strength.

10:18.headline: No more crushing the weak, or no more fear of men
10:18.body: ערץ can mean 'crush' or 'terrify'. Rashi reads it as crushing the weak and sick. Ibn Ezra reads it as fear: no one will need to fear a mere man again. Meiri gives both.

sources.quote: לַעֲרֹץ אֱנוֹשׁ. לְכַתֵּת וְלִשְׁבֹּר אֶת הָאֲנוּשִׁים וְחוֹלִים
sources.says: Rashi says it means to crush and break the weak and sick.

sources.quote: והנה לערוץ אנוש לירא אנוש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means to fear a man.

sources.quote: או הוא לשון מורא כדרך אל נערץ
sources.says: Meiri says it means breaking, or else fear, as in 'a God feared' in Psalm 89.

100:2.headline: Serve with joy here, but 'serve with fear' in Psalm 2
100:2.body: Psalm 2 says to serve God with fear, and this verse says with joy. The midrash settles it: when you stand in prayer, let your heart be glad, because you serve the God above all.

sources.quote: בשעה שאתה עומד ומתפלל יהא לבך שמח כי לאלקים עליון אתה עובד
sources.says: The midrash notes the clash with 'serve with fear' and says that in prayer the heart should be glad, since one serves the highest God.

sources.quote: שלא תהיה עבודתו למשא אלא בשמחה וטוב לבב
sources.says: Radak says serving God should not feel like a burden, but be done with joy and a good heart.

100:3.headline: Know God first, then serve him
100:3.body: Maimonides cites 'know that the LORD is God' among verses showing that knowing comes first. In his view the deepest service of God, the service of the heart, can only begin after a person understands.

sources.quote: אלא ראוי להתחיל במין זה של עבודה רק לאחר תפיסה שכלית
sources.says: Maimonides says this kind of service should begin only after one grasps God with the mind, and quotes this verse.

100:3.headline: He made us: created us, or made us great
100:3.body: 'He made us' can mean God created us when we did not exist. Radak and Metzudat David read it as 'he raised us up', as Samuel says God 'made' Moses and Aaron.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁלֹּא הָיִינוּ בָּעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says God made us when we were not yet in the world.

sources.quote: הוא גדלנו ורוממנו כמו אשר עשה את משה ואת אהרן
sources.says: Radak says it means God made us great and raised us, as he 'made' Moses and Aaron.

100:4.headline: Every offering will end except the thanks-offering
100:4.body: The midrash reads 'enter his gates with thanks' as the thanks-offering. All other sacrifices will one day stop, it says, but the thanks-offering never will.

sources.quote: כל הקרבנות בטלים וקרבן תודה אינו בטל לעולם
sources.says: The midrash says all offerings will cease, but the thanks-offering will never cease.

sources.quote: ולא יהיה עניינו אלא הודאה ותהלה
sources.says: Meiri explains that in the end time people will lack nothing to ask for, so only thanks and praise will remain.

101:1.headline: Singing for kindness and for hard judgment alike
101:1.body: Rashi reads משפט as God's harsh judgment on David: he will sing whether God is kind or strict. Radak and Meiri read it as the justice David himself does as king.

sources.quote: וּכְשֶׁאַתָּה עוֹשֶׂה בִּי מִשְׁפָּט, אֲנִי אָשִׁיר: בָּרוּךְ דַּיַּן הָאֱמֶת
sources.says: Rashi says that when God judges him harshly, he will still sing the blessing "Blessed is the true Judge".

sources.quote: על החסד והמשפט שאני עושה לישראל אשירה
sources.says: Radak says David sings about the kindness and justice he himself does for Israel.

sources.quote: והראשון נוח יותר לענין המזמור
sources.says: Meiri gives both readings and says the first, David's own justice as king, fits the psalm better.

101:2.headline: "When will you come to me": God, or the right path?
101:2.body: The verse does not say who is coming. Radak says it is God, coming to David with the holy spirit. Ibn Ezra and Rashi say it is the right path itself.

sources.quote: ואצפה מתי תבא אלי. כלומר תבא אלי ברוח הקודש
sources.says: Radak says David waits for God to come to him with the holy spirit.

sources.quote: וכאילו הדרך תבא אליו מאליה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says David trains himself so well that the path seems to come to him on its own.

sources.quote: הַדֶּרֶךְ הַיְשָׁרָה לְהִתְהַלֵּךְ בָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi says what comes is the straight path to walk in.

101:3.headline: A rare word for turning off the straight road
101:3.body: סטים appears only twice. Rashi and Metzudat Zion tie it to a verb for straying, as in a wife who goes astray. The midrash hears in it Shittim, where Israel sinned.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן ״כִּי תִשְׂטֶה אִשְׁתּוֹ״ (במדבר ה:יב), לָסוּר מִן הַדֶּרֶךְ
sources.says: Rashi says it is from "if a man's wife goes astray", meaning to turn from the road.

sources.quote: ענינו דברים הסרים מדרך הנכוחה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means things that turn away from the proper path.

sources.quote: עשה שטים שנאתי. ממה שעשה בשטים
sources.says: The midrash reads the phrase as aimed at the tribe of Shimon, for what it did at Shittim.

101:5.headline: A "wide heart": greedy, or very wise?
101:5.body: Radak and Metzudat David read רחב לבב as greed, a heart with room for every desire. Ibn Ezra reads it as great wisdom, so David cannot catch such a man.

sources.quote: ורחב לבב. החומד ומתאוה לכל דבר
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is one who craves and desires everything.

sources.quote: ולבו רחב בהם כלומר ירחיב להם מקום בלבו
sources.says: Radak says his heart makes wide room for worldly desires.

sources.quote: רק מי שהוא רחב לבב, והטעם חכם מאד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says a wide heart means very wise: such a man guards himself, so the king cannot cut him off.

101:8.headline: "Every morning", or the oxen of the Tabernacle
101:8.body: Plainly לבקרים means every morning: David removes the wicked day after day. The midrash also hears בקר, cattle, the oxen given for the Tabernacle. The Targum reads the morning as the world to come.

sources.quote: מִדֵּי יוֹם יוֹם אַכְרִית מְעַט מְעַט
sources.says: Rashi says it means every day: I will cut off the wicked little by little.

sources.quote: עד לעתיד לבוא הן מתוקנות להפרע מן הרשעים בהם שנאמר לבקרים אצמית
sources.says: The midrash cites a view that the oxen the princes gave for the Tabernacle are kept for the future, to punish the wicked, and quotes this verse.

sources.quote: לְעָלְמָא דְאָתִי דְאִמְתִיל לִנְהוֹר צַפְרָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it "in the world to come, which is likened to the light of morning".

102:1.headline: The poor man grows faint, or folds himself up in prayer?
102:1.body: יעטף can mean 'grows faint' or 'wraps himself'. Ibn Ezra and Rashi read it as fainting, the way people faint from hunger. Radak reads it as wrapping: a person praying in deep trouble bends over, as if folding himself up.

sources.quote: ומלת יעטוף – כמו: העטופים ברעב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word is like 'those who faint from hunger'.

sources.quote: בְּהִתְעַטֵּף נַפְשָׁם בְּצָרָה
sources.says: Rashi says it means when their soul grows faint in trouble.

sources.quote: כי המתפלל מתוך צרה גדולה כופף עצמו כאילו מתעטף קצתו בקצתו
sources.says: Radak says one who prays in great trouble bends himself, as if wrapping part of himself in another part.

102:7.headline: Like a desert bird in grief, not in feathers
102:7.body: 'I am like the קאת of the desert', a wild bird. Maimonides says this does not mean he looks like the bird, with its wings and head. His sorrow is like its sorrow. Radak says the likeness is the bird's wailing cry.

sources.quote: לא באו לומר שהוא דומה לה בכנפיה ובראשה, אלא שיְגונו דומה ליגונהּ
sources.says: Maimonides says the verse does not mean he resembles the bird in its wings and head, but that his grief is like its grief.

sources.quote: וקולו כקול נהי לפיכך אמר דמיתי לקאת מדבר ורוצה לומר לקולו
sources.says: Radak says the bird's voice sounds like wailing, and the likeness is to its voice.

102:9.headline: Those who mock me, or those I once praised?
102:9.body: מהוללי can come from הלל, praise, or from הוללות, madness and mockery. Rashi reads it as those who mock me. Ibn Ezra reads it as people who were praised in his eyes. Radak says they rage at him like madmen.

sources.quote: הַמִּתְלוֹצְצִים בִּי
sources.says: Rashi says it means those who mock me.

sources.quote: פעולים שהיו בעיניו מהוללים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means people who were praised in his eyes.

sources.quote: עד שישובו מהוללים ומשתגעים עלי
sources.says: Radak says they mock him until they rave like madmen against him.

102:9.headline: Enemies turn Israel's suffering into a curse
102:9.body: How do enemies 'swear by me'? Radak says they use the Jew as a curse: 'may I end up like the Jew if I do this'. Rashi says they saw Israel's misery and swear by it.

sources.quote: אומרים אהיה כמו היהודי אם אעשה כך וכך
sources.says: Radak says they say: may I be like the Jew if I do such and such.

sources.quote: רָאוּ בְרָעָתִי וְנִשְׁבָּעִים בִּי
sources.says: Rashi says they saw my misery and swear by me.

102:11.headline: Lifted up only to be thrown down harder
102:11.body: Why lift me up before throwing me down? Rashi says a fall from greatness brings more shame. Radak says that a person who wants to throw something hard first lifts it high.

sources.quote: וְאִם לֹא נְשָׂאתַנִי תְּחִלָּה, לֹא הָיְתָה חֶרְפָּתִי רַבָּה כָּל כָּךְ
sources.says: Rashi says that if God had not raised him first, his disgrace would not be so great.

sources.quote: כי הרוצה להפיל דבר בארץ נושא אותו למעלה ומפיל אותו בחזקה
sources.says: Radak says one who wants to throw something to the ground lifts it up and throws it down hard.

102:13.headline: God 'sits' forever: he never changes
102:13.body: God does not literally sit. Ibn Ezra says תשב, sit, means God does not change, since all movement is change. Metzudat David reads it as 'you endure forever'.

sources.quote: הטעם שאתה בלא שנוי, על כן מלת תשב כי כל תנועה שנוי הוא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the point is that God is without change, which is why it says 'sit', because every movement is a change.

sources.quote: אבל אתה לעולם תשב ותתקיים
sources.says: Metzudat David says: but you sit forever and endure.

102:14.headline: God 'rises' by keeping his word, not by standing
102:14.body: God does not stand up from a seat. Maimonides gives two readings of תקום here. You will keep your promise to have mercy on Zion. Or, you will rise against her enemies.

sources.quote: תקיים מה שהבטחת לה שתרחם עליה
sources.says: Maimonides says it means God will fulfill what he promised Zion, to have mercy on her.

sources.quote: כלומר: תקום על אויביה
sources.says: Maimonides gives another reading: God will rise against Zion's enemies.

102:15.headline: Exiles carried Jerusalem's stones to Babylon
102:15.body: God's servants 'want' Zion's stones. Rashi says they loved even its stones and dust. He brings a midrash: the exiles carried stones and earth from Jerusalem to build a synagogue in Babylon.

sources.quote: אָהֲבוּ אַף אֶת אֲבָנֶיהָ וְאֶת עֲפָרָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says they loved even its stones and its dust.

sources.quote: נָשְׂאוּ עִמָּהֶם מֵאַבְנֵי יְרוּשָׁלַיִם וַעֲפָרָהּ לִבְנוֹת לָהֶם בְּבָבֶל בֵּית הַכְּנֶסֶת
sources.says: Rashi brings a midrash that the exiles took stones and dust of Jerusalem with them to build a synagogue in Babylon.

102:19.headline: A people created anew when it goes free
102:19.body: How can a people already alive be 'created'? Rashi says redemption makes them a new creation, going from slavery to freedom and from darkness to great light. Meiri says they will be as if newly made.

sources.quote: שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה בְּרִיָּה חֲדָשָׁה, לָצֵאת מֵעַבְדוּת לְחֵרוּת, מֵאֹפֶל לְאוֹר גָּדוֹל
sources.says: Rashi says the people became a new creation, going from slavery to freedom, from darkness to great light.

sources.quote: שיהיה אז כאילו נברא מחדש
sources.says: Meiri says Israel will then be as if created anew.

102:25.headline: Dying is 'going up': the soul returns to heaven
102:25.body: Why say 'do not take me up' for 'do not let me die'? Ibn Ezra says the body is a vessel for a soul that comes from the heavens. When it leaves the body, it goes back up to its place.

sources.quote: הוא כלי לנשמה העליונה שהיא משמי השמים ובהפרדה מעל הגוף תשוב למקומה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the body is a vessel for the higher soul, which comes from the heavens and returns to its place when it leaves the body.

sources.quote: וזה טעם אל תעלני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this is the meaning of 'do not take me up'.

102:28.headline: 'You are He': the one who simply exists
102:28.body: 'You are He' sounds unfinished: He what? Rashi and Metzudat Zion say הוא here means the one who exists and lasts. Ibn Ezra says it means you truly are, and there is no other.

sources.quote: הָעוֹמֵד וְקַיָּם
sources.says: Rashi says it means the one who stands and endures.

sources.quote: ר״ל דבר העומד בהויתו ומתקיים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means something that stands in its being and endures.

sources.quote: הוא באמת ואין זולתך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means you truly exist and there is none besides you.

103:1.headline: Why David blesses God with his soul
103:1.body: The Midrash says the soul is like God: it fills the body as God fills the world, and it sees without being seen. Rashi adds that 'bless the Lord, my soul' comes five times, for the five worlds a person lives in, starting in the womb.

sources.quote: מה הנפש ממלאה את הגוף כך הקב"ה ממלא את עולמו
sources.says: The Midrash says that as the soul fills the body, so God fills his world.

sources.quote: חֲמִשָּׁה בָּרֲכִי נַפְשִׁי יֵשׁ כָּאן, כְּנֶגֶד חֲמִשָּׁה עוֹלָמוֹת שֶׁאָדָם דָּר בָּהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says there are five 'bless, my soul' here, matching five worlds a person lives in.

sources.quote: לדוד ברכי נפשי את ה' - היא הנשמה העליונה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the soul here is the higher soul.

103:2.headline: His benefits: good paid back, or good given first
103:2.body: Meiri notes that גמול can mean paying someone back, and also starting to do good for someone. The Midrash counts the body's hidden wonders among these gifts, such as a baby kept safe in the womb while its mother walks upright.

sources.quote: וידוע כי לשון גמול בא לשון תשלום, הוא התחלת הטוב
sources.says: Meiri says the word גמול is used for repayment, and also for beginning to do good.

sources.quote: והאשה הזאת פיה למטה ומהלכת על שתי רגליה והולד שמור במעיה ואינו נופל
sources.says: The Midrash says a woman walks upright on two legs, yet the baby is kept safe inside her and does not fall.

sources.quote: גמול טובה שגמל עמך
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means the good that God has done for you.

104:1.headline: Does God's robe of glory show him or hide him?
104:1.body: Radak says the heavens are like a king's robe: a stranger sees it and knows a king is there. Ibn Ezra says the robe hides: God's glory is so bright that the mind cannot see past it.

sources.quote: כמו הלובש לבוש מלכות יכירו אדם שאינו יודעו כי הוא מלך
sources.says: Radak says the heavens show God's greatness the way royal clothes tell a stranger that the wearer is a king.

sources.quote: רוב הודך והדרך ילאו עיני הנשמה החכמה לראות כבודך, כאשר ימנע המלבוש לראות עצם הלובש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God's great splendor tires the soul's eyes, the way a garment keeps you from seeing the body under it.

104:4.headline: Here God's 'angels' are the winds that carry out his will
104:4.body: מלאך means 'messenger'. Rashi reads the verse as God making the winds his messengers. Maimonides uses this verse to show that even natural forces like wind and fire are called angels.

sources.quote: עוֹשֶׂה מַלְאָכָיו רוּחוֹת. עוֹשֶׂה אֶת הָרוּחוֹת שְׁלוּחָיו
sources.says: Rashi says God makes the winds into his messengers.

sources.quote: ידוע לך שמשמעות "מלאך" היא שליח, ואם כן כל מבצע ציווי הוא מלאך
sources.says: Maimonides says מלאך means a messenger, so anything that carries out a command is a מלאך, and he cites this verse for the elements.

104:5.headline: This 'forever' means truly forever, says Maimonides
104:5.body: עולם can mean a long time or forever. Maimonides says it means forever only when joined to עד, as it is here. So David is saying the earth will never fall.

sources.quote: ש"עולם" אינו מצביע על נצחיות אלא כאשר מצטרף אליו "עד
sources.says: Maimonides says עולם points to eternity only when עד is joined to it, and he cites this verse.

sources.quote: ובשאר הדברים פעם לדבר נצחי ופעם לכל ימי התמדת העולם הזה פעם לכל ימי האדם
sources.says: Meiri says that, said of things other than God, these words sometimes mean forever, sometimes as long as this world lasts, and sometimes a person's lifetime.

104:11.headline: The wild donkeys 'break' their thirst, meaning they are fed
104:11.body: ישברו looks like 'they break'. Meiri reads it as 'they are nourished'. He says the word covers any food or drink taken when hungry or thirsty.

sources.quote: וישברו פי׳ יזונו כלומ׳ ירוו עצמם מצמאם כי הוא כלל למזון מאכל ומשתה הבא בתאבון
sources.says: Meiri explains ישברו as 'they are fed': they drink their fill, since the word covers both food and drink.

104:12.headline: A word read from Aramaic: the birds sing among the leaves
104:12.body: עפאים appears only here. The commentators read it from the Aramaic in Daniel, where עפיה is a tree's foliage. Rashi says branches. Ibn Ezra and Meiri say leaves.

sources.quote: מִבֵּין עֳפָאיִם. עַנְפֵי אִילָנוֹת, וְכֵן ״עָפְיֵּהּ שַׁפִּיר
sources.says: Rashi says עפאים are the branches of trees, as in Daniel 4:9.

sources.quote: עפאים - יש אומרים: שעיפים. והנכון בעיני: כמו עלים, ועפיה שפיר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that some say branches, but he thinks it means leaves, as in Daniel.

sources.quote: והעלים יקראו עפאים והוא לשון ארמי עפיא בדניאל
sources.says: Meiri says leaves are called עפאים, an Aramaic word found in Daniel.

104:16.headline: Why are the cedars called God's trees?
104:16.body: Rashi says these are the trees of the Garden of Eden. Radak and Maimonides read it differently: wild trees are called God's because no person planted them.

sources.quote: עֲצֵי ה׳. בְּגַן עֵדֶן
sources.says: Rashi says 'the trees of the Lord' are those in the Garden of Eden.

sources.quote: וסמך העצים אל השם כי דעתו על העצים הרמים והנישאים לפי שאין בצמיחתם ובגדילתם תפיסת ידי אדם
sources.says: Radak says the tall forest trees are linked to God because no human hand helped them grow.

sources.quote: כיוון שקיומם טבעי ולא מלאכותי אמר שה' נטע אותם
sources.says: Maimonides says that because the cedars exist by nature and not by human craft, the verse says God planted them.

104:26.headline: Who plays: God with Leviathan, or Leviathan in the sea?
104:26.body: בו, 'with it' or 'in it', can point two ways. Rashi says God plays with Leviathan three hours a day, as the Talmud teaches. Radak says Leviathan plays in the sea, ruling over all the fish.

sources.quote: לְשַׂחֶק בּוֹ. שָׁלֹשׁ שָׁעוֹת בַּיּוֹם, כָּךְ אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ בְּמַסֶּכֶת עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
sources.says: Rashi says God sports with Leviathan three hours a day, citing the Talmud in Avodah Zarah.

sources.quote: ואמר לשחק בו פי' בים כלומר בכל נבראי הים הוא משחק כי כולם באים ברשותו
sources.says: Radak says 'in it' means in the sea: Leviathan plays with all sea creatures, since they are in its power.

104:27.headline: All creatures look to God in hope for food
104:27.body: ישברון here means 'they hope, they wait'. Metzudat Zion shows the same sense in another psalm. Radak adds that animals wait this way by instinct, without knowing who feeds them.

sources.quote: ישברון. ענין תקוה כמו שברו על ה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ישברון means hope, as in 'whose hope is in the Lord' in Psalm 146.

sources.quote: ואע"פ שאין בהם דעת מי הנותן והמכין, לפי הטבע הנתון בהם ישברו אל חוקם
sources.says: Radak says the animals do not know who provides for them, but by their nature they wait for their portion.

104:30.headline: New life: the dead rising, or new generations born
104:30.body: Rashi reads 'they are created' as the dead rising again. Radak gives that reading too, and another: new creatures are born to take the place of those who died.

sources.quote: תְּשַׁלַּח רוּחֲךָ. בִּתְחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים
sources.says: Rashi says the verse speaks of the resurrection of the dead.

sources.quote: כי יבראון אחרי', כי ימותו אלה ויולדו אחרים תחתיהם
sources.says: Radak says it can also mean that these die and others are born in their place.

105:4.headline: ועזו: God's strength, or the Ark, or the Torah?
105:4.body: Radak and Ibn Ezra say עוז here is the Ark, as in 'he gave his strength into captivity'. Metzudat David reads it as God's power, and the Targum as his Torah.

sources.quote: הארון נקרא עוז כלומר דרשו משכן הארון
sources.says: Radak says the Ark is called עוז, so the verse means: seek the place where the Ark rests.

sources.quote: ודרשו עזו, כמו: ויתן לשבי עזו והוא הארון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'seek his strength' is like 'he gave his strength into captivity', and it means the Ark.

sources.quote: ועוזו. דרשו להראות לכם עוזו ויכלתו
sources.says: Metzudat David says: ask him to show you his strength and power.

sources.quote: תְּבַעוּ אוּלְפָנָא דַייָ וְאוֹרַיְתֵהּ
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'seek the teaching of the Lord and his Torah'.

105:8.headline: לאלף: a thousand generations, or the 'chief' of a generation
105:8.body: Read plainly, לאלף דור means a thousand generations, which Meiri says just means a very long time. The Midrash reads אלף as אלוף, a chief: the covenant was made with the greatest man of his generation, Abraham.

sources.quote: אמר רבי חייא בר אבא לאלוף שבדור. למעולה שבדור
sources.says: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba reads it as 'to the chief of the generation', the finest of the generation.

sources.quote: ורבותי׳ דרשו לאלף דור אלוף שבדור וזהו אברהם
sources.says: Meiri says the sages read it as 'the chief of the generation', meaning Abraham.

sources.quote: ואלף דור לא בא בדיוק אלא להוראת זמן ארוך
sources.says: Meiri says 'a thousand generations' is not an exact number but means a long time.

105:8.headline: דבר צוה: the 'word' is the Torah, meant for generation one thousand
105:8.body: Rashi and the Midrash read 'the word he commanded' as the Torah. God meant to give it after a thousand generations, but saw the world could not last without it, so he left out 974 of them.

sources.quote: הַתּוֹרָה, אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה לְהוֹדִיעָהּ בָּעוֹלָם לְאַחַר אֶלֶף דּוֹר; וְרָאָה שֶׁאֵין הָעוֹלָם מִתְקַיֵּם בְּלֹא תּוֹרָה, וְהֶעֱבִיר מֵהֶם תְּשַׁע מֵאוֹת וְשִׁבְעִים וְאַרְבָּעָה דּוֹרוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it is the Torah, which God commanded to make known after a thousand generations; he saw the world could not last without Torah and removed 974 of those generations.

sources.quote: דבר צוה לאלף דור זו התורה ואין דבר אלא תורה
sources.says: The Midrash says the 'word' commanded for a thousand generations is the Torah.

sources.quote: וְיֵשׁ לִפְתֹּר כִּפְשׁוּטוֹ: זָכַר לְיִשְׂרָאֵל בְּרִיתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi adds that it can also be read plainly: God remembered his covenant with Israel.

105:16.headline: ויקרא: God 'summons' the famine, as if calling a servant
105:16.body: Radak says God calls the famine and it comes, since every decree comes from him. The Midrash says Jacob deserved to go down to Egypt in chains, so God brought the famine and sent Joseph first, as you lead a calf so the cow follows.

sources.quote: וטעם ויקרא כאלו קרא לרעב ויבא על הארץ, כי הגזירות הבאות לארץ מאתו הם
sources.says: Radak says it is as if God called the famine and it came upon the land, since the decrees that come to the land are from him.

sources.quote: ראוי היה יעקב לירד למצרים בשלשלאות של ברזל ובקולרין
sources.says: The Midrash says Jacob deserved to go down to Egypt in iron chains and collars.

sources.quote: משל לפרה אחת שהיו רוצין למשוך אותה למקולין שלה ולא היתה נמשכת. מה עשו משכו בנה תחלה והיתה רצה אחריו
sources.says: The Midrash compares it to a cow that would not be led, so they led her calf first and she ran after it.

105:18.headline: נפשו: iron in his soul, or a spike under his chin
105:18.body: Radak says the chains were on Joseph's body, but the verse says 'soul' because the soul suffers with the body. Rashi cites a midrash that a spike was set under his chin, so it would stab him if he bowed his head.

sources.quote: ואמר נפשו. כי הנפש מעונה בעינוי הגוף
sources.says: Radak says the verse says 'his soul' because the soul is pained when the body is pained.

sources.quote: שַׁרְתּוֹעַ עָשְׂתָה לוֹ תַּחַת זְקָנוֹ, שֶׁאִם יַרְכִּין פָּנָיו הַשַּׁרְתּוֹעַ מַכֵּהוּ
sources.says: Rashi cites a teaching that a spike was set under his chin, so that if he lowered his face the spike would strike him.

sources.quote: או נפשו הוא כמו גופו
sources.says: Metzudat David says נפשו may simply mean his body.

105:20.headline: שלח: Pharaoh sent to free Joseph, but whose act was it?
105:20.body: Rashi reads it simply: Pharaoh sent messengers to release Joseph. Maimonides lists this verse among things done by human choice that Scripture still speaks of as God's doing.

sources.quote: שָׁלַח פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרַיִם שְׁלוּחָיו וַיַּתִּירֵהוּ
sources.says: Rashi says Pharaoh, king of Egypt, sent his messengers and released him.

sources.quote: וכן נאמר על מה שסיבתו היא בחירות אנושיות
sources.says: Maimonides says Scripture speaks this way also about things whose cause is human choice.

sources.quote: ועל היחלצות יוסף הצדיק מן הכלא נאמר
sources.says: Maimonides gives Joseph's release from prison as one example.

sources.quote: ויוסף הצדיק אמר: "לֹא אַתֶּם שְׁלַחְתֶּם אֹתִי הֵנָּה כִּי הָאֱלֹהִים"
sources.says: Maimonides also cites Joseph: 'it was not you who sent me here, but God'.

105:22.headline: לאסר: to bind officials to Joseph in love, or to jail them?
105:22.body: Rashi reads 'to bind' as affection, like Jonathan's soul bound to David's: once Joseph read the dream, all the officials loved him. Radak reads it as power: Joseph could imprison Pharaoh's officers at will.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן חִבָּה הוּא זֶה, כְּמוֹ ״וְנֶפֶשׁ יְהוֹנָתָן נִקְשְׁרָה בְּנֶפֶשׁ דָּוִד״
sources.says: Rashi says this is a word of affection, as in 'Jonathan's soul was bound up with David's soul'.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁפָּתַר הַחֲלוֹם חִבְּבוּהוּ כֻּלָּם
sources.says: Rashi says that when Joseph interpreted the dream, everyone loved him.

sources.quote: שיהיה כח בידו לאסור שריו וגדוליו כמו שהיה כח ביד פרעה
sources.says: Radak says Joseph had power to imprison Pharaoh's officers and nobles, as Pharaoh did.

sources.quote: דבר אחר לאסור שריו שרו כתיב זה פוטיפר
sources.says: The Midrash notes the word is written שרו, 'his officer', and says this is Potiphar.

105:22.headline: בנפשו: here נפש means will, says Maimonides
105:22.body: נפש usually means soul or life. Maimonides lists 'will' as one of its senses and gives this verse as his example: Joseph could bind officials as he wished, and Radak and Metzudat Zion read it the same way.

sources.quote: והוא שם הרצון: "לֶאְסֹר שָׂרָיו בְּנַפְשׁוֹ" (תהילים קה,כב), כלומר ברצונו
sources.says: Maimonides says נפש is also the name for will, as in 'to bind his officials בנפשו', meaning by his will.

sources.quote: ופי' בנפשו. ברצונו
sources.says: Radak says בנפשו means by his will.

sources.quote: בנפשו. ברצונו כמו אל תתנני בנפש צרי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means by his will, as in 'do not hand me over to the will of my foes'.

105:25.headline: הפך לבם: did God turn Egypt's heart, or did it turn?
105:25.body: Radak and Meiri give two readings: God turned their heart, or their heart turned on its own. The Midrash marks how fast it came: yesterday Pharaoh welcomed Joseph's family, and now they were hated.

sources.quote: הפך במעשיו פעל יוצא ופירוש האל יתברך הפך לבם כי הוא גזר זה ואמר ועבדום וענו אותם או יהיה הפך פעל עומד כאלו אמר נהפך לבם
sources.says: Radak says it may mean God turned their heart, since he had decreed 'they will enslave and oppress them', or it may mean their heart turned by itself.

sources.quote: ואמ׳ הפך לבם ר״ל נהפך או יהיה פועל יוצא לשם
sources.says: Meiri says it means their heart was turned, or that God turned it.

sources.quote: אתמול (שם מה טז) והקול נשמע וגו' וייטב בעיני פרעה. ועכשיו הפך לבם לשנוא
sources.says: The Midrash says: yesterday 'the news was heard and it pleased Pharaoh', and now their heart was turned to hate.

105:39.headline: למסך: a cloud as a roof overhead, or a curtain in front?
105:39.body: מסך can mean a covering above or a curtain in front. Radak and Metzudat Zion say the cloud went before Israel like a curtain as they traveled, and Metzudat Zion adds that it covered them from above when they camped.

sources.quote: כן יקרא הסכך אשר ממעל גם המחיצה לפנים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word names both a roof above and a screen in front.

sources.quote: והענן בלכתם הלך לפניהם ובנוחם סככם ממעל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the cloud went before them on the march and covered them from above when they rested.

sources.quote: אינו סכך למעלה אלא כמו יריעה לפניהם כי הענן לפניהם היה בלכתם
sources.says: Radak says it is not a roof above but a curtain in front, since the cloud went before them as they traveled.

105:41.headline: בציות: rivers through dry land, or deep enough for ships?
105:41.body: Rashi and Radak read ציות as dry desert land: the water ran there like a river. Meiri cites a midrash that reads it from צי, a ship: the water was so deep they needed boats.

sources.quote: הָלְכוּ נְהָרוֹת מִן הַבְּאֵר בְּאֶרֶץ צִיָּה
sources.says: Rashi says rivers flowed from the well in a dry land.

sources.quote: במקום ציה וחורב הלכו המים כמו נהר
sources.says: Radak says the water ran like a river in a dry, parched place.

sources.quote: ובדרש פירשוהו מענין צי אדיר כלומ׳ שהיו צריכין לעבור בספינות מרגל לרגל
sources.says: Meiri says the midrash reads it from 'a mighty ship', meaning they had to cross by boat from one step to the next.

107:2.headline: צר: 'trouble', or 'enemy'
107:2.body: Radak and Ibn Ezra read צר as the noun for trouble, like צרה. The Targum renders it as an oppressor.

sources.quote: מיד צר. שם, כמו צרה
sources.says: Radak says צר is a noun, like צרה.

sources.quote: על כן אחריו יאמרו: מיד צר, כמו: צר ומצוק בצר לי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says מיד צר is like 'trouble and distress' in 'in my trouble'.

sources.quote: מִן יַד מְעִיקָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'from the hand of the oppressor'.

107:3.headline: ומים: the south, or those from across the sea
107:3.body: The Targum reads ומים as the fourth direction, the southern sea. Radak says the south is left out because it is thinly settled, and that ומים means those who cross the sea.

sources.quote: וּמִן יַמָא דָרוֹמָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'and from the southern sea'.

sources.quote: וזכר עם הפיאות מזרח ומערב וצפון ולא זכר דרום כי הוא מעט היישוב מכל הפיאות מפני חום השמש
sources.says: Radak says the verse names east, west and north but not south, which is the least settled because of the sun's heat.

sources.quote: ופי' ומים. אותם שעוברים דרך ים מארץ לארץ ישיבם לארצם בשלום
sources.says: Radak says ומים means those who cross by sea from land to land, whom God will bring back to their land in peace.

sources.quote: ומים. מאיי הים
sources.says: Metzudat David says ומים means from the islands of the sea.

107:5.headline: תתעטף: fainting from hunger, or bent over in distress
107:5.body: Ibn Ezra compares it to people fainting from hunger. Metzudat David says a person in trouble is bent and crushed, as if wrapped up in himself.

sources.quote: תתעטף - כמו: העטופים ברעב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like 'those who faint from hunger'.

sources.quote: כשאדם הוא בצרה הוא מדוכא וכפוף וכאלו הוא עטוף קצתו בקצתו
sources.says: Metzudat David says that when a person is in trouble he is crushed and bent over, as if part of him were wrapped in another part.

107:11.headline: המרו: 'rebelled', or 'changed his words'
107:11.body: Metzudat Zion ties המרו to rebellion. Meiri says it means they changed God's words and defied them, since if it meant 'angered' the verse would say הכעיסו.

sources.quote: המרו. מלשון מרי ומרד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says המרו comes from the words for defiance and rebellion.

sources.quote: ר״ל ששנו דבריו ומרו בהם ואלו היה לשון הכעסה היה לו לומר כי הכעיסו אל
sources.says: Meiri says it means they changed his words and defied them, and if it meant angering, the verse would have said 'they angered God'.

107:11.headline: אמרי אל: God's commandments, or the voice in the heart
107:11.body: Radak says אמרי אל are the commandments given to all humankind, not only to Israel. Ibn Ezra says they are the heart's own commands, which God planted in every speaking person.

sources.quote: והם המצות שצוה לבני אדם כי לא לישראל לבדם נאמרו המצות
sources.says: Radak says they are the commandments God gave to all people, since the commandments were not said to Israel alone.

sources.quote: פיקודי הלב, שהשם נטעם בלב כל מדבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are the commands of the heart, which God put in the heart of every speaker.

107:20.headline: דברו: his command, his will, or the causes he sets going
107:20.body: Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra say God heals by his word alone, not by a doctor's drugs. Radak says דברו means his will, and Meiri says he arranges the causes that heal.

sources.quote: לא כרפואת הרופאים שהמה בסממנים כ״א מרפא במאמרו
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is not like a doctor's cure, which uses drugs, but God heals by his word.

sources.quote: שיגזור ומיד יתרפא לא על ידי משקה ומעשה בן אדם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God decrees, and the sick are healed at once, not by a drink or any human act.

sources.quote: ודברו הוא רצונו
sources.says: Radak says his word is his will.

sources.quote: ישלח דברו וירפאם ר״ל יסבב סבותיו וירפאם
sources.says: Meiri says 'he sends his word and heals them' means he arranges his causes and heals them.

107:23.headline: Why people who sail are said to 'go down' to the sea
107:23.body: Radak gives two reasons: the shore stands higher than the water, or a ship is deep and one goes down into it, which was his father's view. Ibn Ezra says anyone who goes to sea is 'going down'.

sources.quote: לפי שהיבשה גבוה על שפת הים וכנגד השפה יקרא יורד
sources.says: Radak says one who goes to sea is called 'going down' because the land is high at the sea's edge.

sources.quote: פירש כי יקרא יורד כנגד האניה שהיא עמוקה ויורד בה
sources.says: Radak reports his father's view that he is called 'going down' because of the ship, which is deep and one goes down into it.

sources.quote: יורדי - כל הולך אל הים יורד הוא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says everyone who goes to the sea is going down.

107:24.headline: מעשי ה': Maimonides says it means nature
107:24.body: Maimonides says 'the works of God' means natural things, and cites this verse. Radak says sailors see these works in the great fish and the roaring sea.

sources.quote: כי כל הדברים הטבעיים מכונים "מעשה ה'": "הֵמָּה רָאוּ מַעֲשֵׂי ה'" (תהילים קז,כד)
sources.says: Maimonides says all natural things are called 'the work of God', and cites this verse, 'they saw the works of God'.

sources.quote: שם יראו מעשה ה' ונפלאותיו כי בדגים הגדולים וברעש הים
sources.says: Radak says there in the deep they see the works and wonders of God, in the great fish and the roaring of the sea.

107:25.headline: ויאמר: God 'said' means he willed it
107:25.body: Maimonides lists this verse among natural events that Scripture describes as God speaking, like the sea heaving in a storm. Radak reads 'he said' as 'he willed and decreed'.

sources.quote: על ענייני הטבע הנוהגים תמידית, א) כמו התמוססות השלג כשהאוויר מתחמם, וגעישת מי הים כשהרוח סוערת, נאמר
sources.says: Maimonides says that of the steady things of nature, like snow melting when the air warms and the sea heaving when the wind storms, it is said that God commanded them.

sources.quote: "וַיֹּאמֶר וַיַּעֲמֵד רוּחַ סְעָרָה וַתְּרוֹמֵם גַּלָּיו" (שם קז,כה)
sources.says: Maimonides cites this verse, 'he said, and a storm wind stood up and lifted its waves', as one of his examples.

sources.quote: ויאמר. האל כלומר רצה וגזר ויעמוד רוח סערה בים
sources.says: Radak says 'he said' means God willed and decreed, and a storm wind stood up in the sea.

107:27.headline: יחוגו: break apart, or reel and shake
107:27.body: Rashi says it is a word of breaking. Radak, Metzudat Zion and Meiri say it means moving, reeling or dancing, and Meiri ties it to the shaking of fear.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן שֶׁבֶר הוּא, וְכֵן ״בְּחַגְוֵי הַסֶּלַע״
sources.says: Rashi says it is a word of breaking, like 'in the clefts of the rock'.

sources.quote: יחוגו. ענין תנועה
sources.says: Radak says יחוגו means movement.

sources.quote: ענין רקוד ותנועה חזקה כמו המון חוגג
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means dancing and strong movement, like 'a festive crowd'.

sources.quote: יחוגו הוא ענין תנועה ג״כ מלשון והיתה אדמת מצרים לחגא (ישע׳ יט יז) שפירושו תנועת פחד
sources.says: Meiri says יחוגו means movement, like לחגא in Isaiah 19:17, which means the shaking of fear.

107:29.headline: יקם: 'raise', or 'return'
107:29.body: Radak says some read יקם as 'return' and some as written, 'raise'. Ibn Ezra reports Ben Balaam's view that it should have said ישב, and Metzudat David reads it as 'the storm he raised he will turn back to stillness'.

sources.quote: יש מפרשים יקם כמו ישוב ויש לפרשו כמשמעו
sources.says: Radak says some explain יקם as meaning 'return', and it can also be explained as it sounds.

sources.quote: אמר רבי יהודה בן בלעם: היה ראוי להיות תחת יקם ישב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports Rabbi Judah ben Balaam's view that it should have been ישב in place of יקם.

sources.quote: הסערה שהקים ישיבנה לדממה וגלי הים לא יהמו עוד
sources.says: Metzudat David says the storm he raised, he will return to stillness, and the sea's waves will not roar again.

107:32.headline: 'In the congregation': a group of ten
107:32.body: Rashi, following the Talmud, says the one who was saved must give thanks in front of ten people. He reads 'seat of the elders' as two of those ten being scholars.

sources.quote: צָרִיךְ לְאוֹדוֹיֵי בְּאַפֵּי בֵּי עֲשָׂרָה
sources.says: Rashi says one must give thanks in front of ten people.

sources.quote: וְתָרֵין מִנַּיְיהוּ צוּרְבָא מֵרַבָּנָן
sources.says: Rashi says two of them must be Torah scholars.

107:39.headline: מעצר: rule over them, holding back, or a closed womb
107:39.body: Radak and Meiri say עוצר is the rule of others over them. Metzudat Zion says it means holding back, and Ibn Ezra reads it as a closed womb, the opposite of 'they multiplied'.

sources.quote: ועוצר הוא ממשלת אחרים שהיה עליהם
sources.says: Radak says עוצר is the rule of others over them.

sources.quote: ועוצר מענין יורש עצר (שופטי׳ יח ז) זה יעצור בעמי (ש״א ט יז)
sources.says: Meiri ties עוצר to 'one who holds rule' and 'this one shall rule my people'.

sources.quote: מעוצר. ענין העכבה כמו נעצרה נא אותך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means holding back, like 'let us hold you here'.

sources.quote: מעוצר - רחם, כדרך כי עצר עצר ה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says מעוצר means the womb, as in 'the Lord closed up every womb'.

107:41.headline: וישם כצאן: who makes the families like flocks?
107:41.body: Radak reads it as God making the poor man's families many. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it as the poor man himself making his family like a flock.

sources.quote: משים האל יתברך לאביון משפחות לרוב כמו הצאן
sources.says: Radak says God gives the poor man many families, like a flock.

sources.quote: וַיָּשֶׂם הָאֶבְיוֹן מִשְׁפַּחַת זַרְעוֹ כַּצֹּאן
sources.says: Rashi says the poor man makes the family of his offspring like a flock.

sources.quote: הפועל הוא האביון, כמו ישימו בנים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the one acting is the poor man, as in 'they set up sons'.

108:5.headline: Kindness 'above the heavens' here, but 'up to' them in Psalm 57
108:5.body: Psalm 57 says God's kindness reaches up to the heavens; this repeat says above them. The Talmud, cited by Rashi, explains: above for those who serve God for its own sake, up to for others. Radak says this psalm is about Israel's redemption, a greater kindness.

sources.quote: כָּאן בְּעוֹשִׂין לִשְׁמָהּ, כָּאן בְּעוֹשִׂין שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says one verse is for those who act for its own sake, the other for those who do not.

sources.quote: וזהו שאמר על ישועת ישראל אמר מעל שמים כי החסד יותר גדול
sources.says: Radak says this psalm speaks of Israel's rescue, so it says 'above the heavens', a greater kindness.

108:8.headline: Shechem the city, or a word for 'portion'
108:8.body: שְׁכֶם is the city of Shechem, and Meiri reads it as one city standing for all. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as 'a portion', as when Jacob gives Joseph 'one portion above your brothers'.

sources.quote: שְׁכֶם חֵלֶק כְּמוֹ (בראשית מח:כב) ״שְׁכֶם אַחַד עַל אַחֶיךָ״
sources.says: Rashi says the word means a portion, as in Genesis 48:22.

sources.quote: שכם. ענין חלק
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means a portion.

sources.quote: שכם וסכות וגלעד ד״מ כהזכרת פרט במקום כלל
sources.says: Meiri reads Shechem, Succoth and Gilead as places named to stand for all the cities.

108:10.headline: Throwing my shoe on Edom, or my lock
108:10.body: נַעֲלִי usually means 'my shoe', and Rashi pictures Edom's kings taking off David's shoes like servants. Metzudat Zion instead reads it from מַנְעוּל, a lock or bolt.

sources.quote: שֶׁיִּהְיוּ מַלְכֵיהֶם נוֹטְלִין מִנְעָלַי בְּרַגְלִי
sources.says: Rashi says Edom's kings will take the shoes off David's feet, as servants.

sources.quote: נעלי. מלשון מנעול הסוגר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion reads the word as coming from a lock that shuts.

109:1.headline: God of my praise: the one I praise, or my pride
109:1.body: תהלתי can mean the praise I give, or the thing I am proud of. Meiri gives both readings, and the Midrash says each side is the other's praise: God is Israel's, and Israel is God's.

sources.quote: אלהי תהלתי ר״ל שאני מהלל תמיד או שאני מתהלל ומתפאר בעבודתו
sources.says: Meiri says it means either the God I always praise, or the God whose service I am proud of.

sources.quote: אין לישראל תהלה אלא הקב"ה ואין להקב"ה תהלה אלא ישראל
sources.says: The Midrash says Israel has no praise but God, and God has no praise but Israel.

109:6.headline: A satan at his right hand: an angel or a human enemy
109:6.body: Radak reads שטן as an accusing angel. Ibn Ezra reads it as a human enemy, as when God raised up a שטן against Solomon, and says it answers ישטנוני, 'they oppose me', in verse 4.

sources.quote: מלאך שטן יעמוד על ימינו לשטנו
sources.says: Radak says an accusing angel will stand at his right hand to oppose him.

sources.quote: ושטן כנגד ישטנוני והוא אדם כדרך ויקם ה' שטן לשלמה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word answers ישטנוני and means a man, as in 'God raised up a שטן against Solomon'.

109:7.headline: His prayer will count as sin, or simply miss the mark
109:7.body: חטא can mean to sin or to miss a target. Radak and Meiri say his prayer will miss, like the slingers in Judges who could hit a hair and 'not miss', and Radak adds it may also count as sin.

sources.quote: לא תחשב לו התפילה זכות אלא חטאה וחובה, או פירוש לחטאה כמו אל השערה ולא יחטיא כלומר שלא תקובל תפלתו
sources.says: Radak says either his prayer will count as sin and not merit, or it will miss, as in 'at a hair and not miss', meaning it will not be accepted.

sources.quote: ותפלתו תהיה לחטאה מלשון אל השערה ולא יחטיא
sources.says: Meiri takes the word from 'at a hair and not miss', so his prayer will not be accepted.

109:8.headline: What another takes: his office, his wealth, his wife, or soul
109:8.body: פקדתו comes from a root meaning to appoint or to entrust. Rashi reads it as his high office, Radak and Meiri as the wealth he only holds in trust, and Ibn Ezra reports 'his wife' and 'his soul'.

sources.quote: פְּקֻדָּתוֹ. גְּדֻלָּתוֹ, פְּרוֹבוֹשְׁטִיאָ״ה בְּלַעַ״ז, כְּמוֹ ״וְיַפְקֵד הַמֶּלֶךְ פְּקִידִים״
sources.says: Rashi says it means his high rank, as in 'let the king appoint officers'.

sources.quote: הדבר שיה פקיד עליו והוא ממונו או אשתו
sources.says: Radak says it is what he is in charge of: his money or his wife.

sources.quote: וקרא הממון פקודה שעל דרך האמת אין לאדם בו אלא כמי שהוא פקיד וממונה על איזה דבר לשמרו זמן אחד
sources.says: Meiri says money is called פקודה because in truth a person is only an officer put in charge of it for a while.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: כי פקודתו הוא נפשו, שהוא כמו פקדון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that some say it is his soul, which is like something left in his keeping.

109:11.headline: The lender sets a trap, or strains to grab everything
109:11.body: Radak ties the unusual verb ינקש to מוקש, a trap: the lender will lay a trap for all he owns. Rashi ties it to knees knocking together in Daniel, and reads it as someone straining and chasing after a thing.

sources.quote: וטעם מלת ינקש. ישים מוקש, כי נוקש ויקש ענין אחד
sources.says: Radak says ינקש means to set a trap, because the two forms of the root mean the same.

sources.quote: אָדָם הַטּוֹרֵחַ מְחַזֵּר וְלָהוּט לַעֲשׂוֹת דָּבָר, נוֹפֵל בּוֹ לָשׁוֹן מִתְנַקֵּשׁ, כְּלוֹמַר: מֻטְרָף וּמִתְלַבֵּט, כְּמוֹ ״וְאַרְכֻּבָּתֵהּ דָּא לְדָא נָקְשָׁן״
sources.says: Rashi says a person who toils and chases eagerly after something is said to be מתנקש, tossed and straining, like knees knocking in Daniel.

109:13.headline: 'His end' here means his children
109:13.body: אחרית usually means the end or the future. Ibn Ezra and Meiri read 'his אחרית' as his children, as in Daniel 11:4, and Radak says that is why the verse then says 'their name': father and son are both wiped out.

sources.quote: יהי - בנו כמו ולא אחריתו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means his son, as in 'and not to his אחרית' in Daniel.

sources.quote: ואחריתו ר״ל בניו כאמרו בדניאל (יא ד) ולא לאחריתו
sources.says: Meiri says אחריתו means his children, as in Daniel 11:4.

sources.quote: בדור שלישי ימח שם האב והבן לפיכך אמר שמם
sources.says: Radak says in the third generation the name of both father and son is erased, so the verse says 'their name'.

109:18.headline: Like oil soaking into his bones, or like marrow
109:18.body: Radak reads שמן as oil rubbed on aching bones that soaks into them, the way the curse sinks in. Meiri adds a second reading from שומן, fat, meaning the marrow inside the bone.

sources.quote: וכשמן בעצמותיו. שאדם מושח בו גופו לכאב העצמות
sources.says: Radak says it is the oil a person rubs on his body for aching bones.

sources.quote: או נפרש וכשמן מלשון שומן כאמרו למטה ובשרי כחש משמן ורומז על ענין המוח שבתוך העצם
sources.says: Meiri says it can also mean fat, as in verse 24, pointing to the marrow inside the bone.

109:20.headline: 'The work of my enemies' means the wages for that work
109:20.body: פעולה usually means a deed, but Radak and Meiri read it here as the pay for the deed, as in 'do not keep a worker's פעולה overnight'. Meiri explains that pay follows the work, so it takes the work's name.

sources.quote: זאת. תהיה שכר פעולתם שעשו לי, וכן לא תלין פעולת שכיר אתך שכר פעולתו
sources.says: Radak says this will be the pay for what they did to him, as in the law about a hired worker's pay.

sources.quote: ומפני שהשכר נמשך אחר הפעולה הוא קורא לו פעולה וכמוהו לא תלין פעולת שכיר
sources.says: Meiri says pay follows the work, so the verse calls the pay 'work', as in the law about a hired worker.

11:1.headline: Written 'flee' to many, read 'flee' to one
11:1.body: The word is written נודו, 'flee' said to many, but read נודי, said to one soul. Radak says the written plural speaks to body and soul together, and Rashi says it lets the verse speak of all Israel too.

sources.quote: נודו כתיב ונודי קרי. הכתיב כנגד הגוף והנפש
sources.says: Radak says it is written נודו and read נודי, and the written form speaks to the body and the soul.

sources.quote: נוּדוּ כְּתִיב, שֶׁהוּא נִדְרָשׁ אַף בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהָאֻמּוֹת אוֹמְרִים לָהֶם כֵּן
sources.says: Rashi says it is written נודו so that it is also read about Israel, to whom the nations say this.

sources.quote: נודי אין כתיב אלא נודו. א"ר אחא כלפי מעלה אמרו וכלפי מטה
sources.says: The Midrash says it is not written נודי but נודו, because it was said both toward heaven and toward earth.

11:1.headline: Why a wandering bird, and not a dove
11:1.body: Rashi says anyone driven from home is compared to a bird that wanders from its nest. The Midrash notes the verse does not say dove: a dove whose chicks are taken comes back to its nest, but this bird does not.

sources.quote: שֶׁכָּל אָדָם הַמִּטַּלְטֵל נִמְשָׁל לְצִפּוֹר הַנּוֹדֶדֶת מִן קִנָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi says every person who is driven about is compared to a bird that wanders from its nest.

sources.quote: ולא אמר כיונה אלא כצפור. היונה הזו נוטלין גוזליה והיא חוזרת למקומה שנאמר (הושע ז יא) כיונה פותה אין לב. אבל הצפור הזו אינו כן אלא ילדה במקומה ונוטלין את גוזליה אינה חוזרת למקומה
sources.says: The Midrash says the verse chose a bird, not a dove: a dove returns after its chicks are taken, but this bird does not.

11:2.headline: You 'tread' a bow, because a strong one needs a foot
11:2.body: Rashi says the verb for treading fits a bow, because to bend a strong bow you set your foot on it. He adds that the bow here is their tongue, as in Jeremiah: 'they bend their tongue, their bow, for lies'.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן דְּרִיכָה נוֹפֵל בְּקֶשֶׁת, שֶׁכְּשֶׁהוּא חָזָק, צָרִיךְ לִיתֵּן רַגְלוֹ עָלָיו כְּשֶׁרוֹצֶה לִנְטוֹתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says treading is used for a bow, because when it is strong one must put a foot on it to bend it.

sources.quote: קֶשֶׁת. לְשׁוֹנָם יִדְרְכוּ קַשְׁתָּם שֶׁקֶר
sources.says: Rashi says the bow is their tongue, as in 'they bend their tongue, their bow of lies'.

sources.quote: ודורכים קשת לשונם וחצי דבתם כוננו על יתר הקשת
sources.says: Meiri says they bend the bow of their tongue and set the arrows of their slander on the string.

11:3.headline: Foundations torn down, or nets torn apart
11:3.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion read השתות as foundations, and Rashi says they are the righteous priests, the foundations of the world. Ibn Ezra reads it first as nets or snares, and Radak gives that reading too.

sources.quote: עַל יֶדְכֶם נֶהֶרְגוּ כֹּהֲנֵי ה׳ הַצַּדִּיקִים, שֶׁהֵם שָׁתוֹת שֶׁל עוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says through them the righteous priests of God were killed, who are the foundations of the world.

sources.quote: השתות הם היסודות כמו והיו שתתיה מדכאים (ישעיהו יט י) וחשופי שת (שם כ ד). או פרושו: רשתות ומצודות
sources.says: Radak says השתות are foundations, as in Isaiah 19:10, or else nets and snares.

sources.quote: כי השתות - מצודות, כמו: והיו שתותיה מדוכאים. ויש אומרים: יסודות, כמו וחשופי שת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says השתות are snares, and reports that some say foundations.

11:4.headline: God's eyes see, but not with sight
11:4.body: Maimonides says that when eyes and seeing are said of God, as in this verse, they mean knowing with the mind, not seeing with the senses. Sensing means being acted on, and God acts but is not acted on.

sources.quote: משמעות הדבר הזה כולו היא השגה שכלית ולא השגה חושית, שהרי כל תחושה היא היפעלות והתרשמות, כידוע לך, והוא יתעלה פועל ולא נפעל
sources.says: Maimonides says this all means grasping with the mind, not with the senses, because sensing is being acted on, and God acts and is not acted on.

11:6.headline: Raining down coals, or raining down snares
11:6.body: Rashi reads פחים as coals, Radak reads it as snares, and the Midrash gives both. Ibn Ezra reads it as thin plates, like burning stones that fall with the rain.

sources.quote: פַּחִים. לְשׁוֹן פֶּחָמִים
sources.says: Rashi says פחים means coals.

sources.quote: ימטר על רשעים פחים מן פח יקוש
sources.says: Radak says פחים comes from 'the fowler's snare'.

sources.quote: דבר אחר פחים מצודים. כמה דאמר (משלי ז כג) כמהר צפור אל פח
sources.says: After reading פחים as coals, the Midrash gives another reading: snares, as in 'like a bird rushing into a snare'.

sources.quote: וחברו רקועי פחים והם כדמות אבנים שורפים, שהם יורדים עם המטר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra links it to 'beaten plates' and says they are like burning stones that come down with the rain.

11:7.headline: The upright see His face, or He sees theirs
11:7.body: פנימו can mean His face or their faces. Meiri reads it as His face watching over the upright, and Radak and the Midrash read it as the faces of the upright gazing at the Upright One of the world.

sources.quote: ישר יחזו פנימו כלומ׳ שפניו ישגיחו על הישר ופנימו כמו פניו
sources.says: Meiri says His face watches over the upright, and פנימו means 'His face'.

sources.quote: או פרוש פנימו: פניהם כמשמעו, כי מ"ם וא"ו לשון רבים. ופרושו: כי פני הצדיקים יחזו האל שהוא ישר
sources.says: Radak says פנימו may mean 'their faces', a plural, so the faces of the righteous will see God, who is upright.

sources.quote: לא היה צריך לומר אלא ישר יחזו פניו ומהו ישר יחזו פנימו
sources.says: The Midrash asks why the verse does not simply say 'His face', and answers that the faces of the upright will see the Upright One of the world.

110:1.headline: Who is 'my lord': Abraham, David, or Saul?
110:1.body: Rashi follows the sages: 'my lord' is Abraham, whom people called 'my lord.' Ibn Ezra says a singer wrote the psalm about King David, and Rashi's second reading has David speaking about 'my lord Saul,' who was hunting him.

sources.quote: נְאֻם ה׳ לְאַבְרָהָם, שֶׁקְּרָאוּהוּ הָעוֹלָם אֲדֹנִי
sources.says: Rashi says God spoke to Abraham, whom the world called 'my lord.'

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני: כי זה המזמור חברו אחד מהמשוררים על דוד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra thinks one of the singers wrote this psalm about David.

sources.quote: עַל עִסְקֵי אֲדוֹנִי שָׁאוּל, כְּשֶׁהָיִיתִי נִרְדָּף מִפָּנָיו
sources.says: Rashi offers a second reading: David speaks about his lord Saul, when Saul was chasing him.

110:1.headline: Sit at my right hand, or wait for my help?
110:1.body: Rashi says שב here means 'wait,' not 'sit,' as when Israel 'stayed' at Kadesh. Radak says David is told to wait a while longer for Saul's reign to end, and Ibn Ezra reads it as 'stay in my house and serve me.'

sources.quote: אֵין יְשִׁיבָה אֶלָּא עַכָּבָה, וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר: ״וַתֵּשְׁבוּ בְקָדֵשׁ״
sources.says: Rashi says 'sitting' here means waiting, as in 'you stayed in Kadesh.'

sources.quote: שב והמתין עוד זמן מה לשאול המלך
sources.says: Radak says David is told to wait a while longer for King Saul.

sources.quote: והטעם שב – בביתי ועבוד אותי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means stay in God's house and serve God.

110:3.headline: Born at dawn, dropped from the womb, or sought out?
110:3.body: משחר appears only here, and Radak hears שחר, 'dawn': the dawn of David's birth was a good one for him. Rashi reads it as 'dropped' from the womb, and Metzudat Zion as 'sought,' as in 'seeking prey.'

sources.quote: יום שיצאת מרחם ונולדת אותו השחר לך היה
sources.says: Radak says the dawn of the day you were born was for your good.

sources.quote: מִשֶּׁנָּפַלְתָּ מִן הָרֶחֶם, כְּמוֹ מְשִׁילִין פֵּרוֹת דֶּרֶךְ אֲרֻבָּה בְּיוֹם טוֹב
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'since you dropped from the womb,' comparing the Talmud's word for dropping fruit through a skylight.

sources.quote: משחר. ענין דרישה כמו משחרי לטרף
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means seeking, as in 'seeking prey' in Job 24:5.

110:4.headline: A priest forever, or a ruler forever?
110:4.body: כהן usually means 'priest.' Radak and Rashi note it can also mean a ruler, as in 'David's sons were כהנים,' and Ibn Ezra says every כהן is someone who serves.

sources.quote: אתה כהן. מלך ונגיד, כמו ובני דוד כהנים היו
sources.says: Radak says כהן here means king and leader, as in 'David's sons were כהנים.'

sources.quote: יֵשׁ בְּמַשְׁמָע כֹּהֵן – כְּהֻנָּה וּשְׂרָרָה
sources.says: Rashi says the word כהן can mean both priesthood and rule.

sources.quote: נשבע, אתה כהן - כל כהן משרת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says every כהן is a servant.

110:4.headline: Malki-tzedek the person, or 'a righteous king'?
110:4.body: Rashi takes מלכי צדק as the name Malki-tzedek, the priest-king who met Abraham. Radak and the Aramaic Targum read the name for its meaning, 'a righteous king': God chose David because he ruled justly.

sources.quote: עַל דִּבְרַת מַלְכִּי צֶדֶק – עַל פְּקֻדַּת מַלְכִּי צֶדֶק
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'by the charge of Malki-tzedek.'

sources.quote: ולמה בחרתיך מלך לעולם על דבר שאתה מלך צדק ויו"ד דברתי ויו"ד מלכי נוספות
sources.says: Radak says God chose David as king forever because he is a righteous king, and the final י in both words is extra.

sources.quote: בְּגִין זְכוּתָא דַהֲוֵיתָא מְלַךְ זַכַּי
sources.says: The Targum says it is because of the merit that you were a righteous king.

110:6.headline: A great land, or the city of Rabbah?
110:6.body: Metzudat Zion reads רבה as 'great,' a great land. Radak and Ibn Ezra report a reading that it is Rabbah, the Ammonite capital David conquered.

sources.quote: רבה. גדולה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means 'great.'

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים רבה. רבת בני עמון ועל אותה המלחמה אמר זה הפסוק
sources.says: Radak reports some who say it is Rabbah of the Ammonites, and the verse speaks of that war.

sources.quote: ורבי משה אמר: כי הטעם רבת בני עמון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that Rabbi Moshe read it as Rabbah of the Ammonites.

111:1.headline: "With all my heart": Meiri finds two hearts in לבב
111:1.body: The verse uses the longer form לבב for heart. Meiri says it hints at two hearts, the good urge and the bad, so that even the body's drives are bent to serving God.

sources.quote: אודה ה׳ בכל לבב רמז אל שתי הלבבות יצר הטוב ויצר הרע
sources.says: Meiri says "with all my heart" hints at two hearts, the good urge and the bad urge.

sources.quote: שאף הכחות הגופניות אני מכניע לעבודת האל
sources.says: Meiri says even the powers of the body are bent to the service of God.

111:1.headline: Praise in the council and the crowd: in private and in public
111:1.body: Ibn Ezra reads בסוד ישרים as praise in private and ועדה as praise in public. Metzudat Zion says סוד is counsel kept secret, or comes from יסוד, a foundation.

sources.quote: בסוד ישרים - בסתר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says "in the council of the upright" means in private.

sources.quote: ועדה - בגלוי וזה הוא שאודה לאמר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says "and the congregation" means in public.

sources.quote: ענין עצה כי נעשית בסוד לבל יגלה, או הוא מל׳ יסוד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says סוד means counsel, made in secret so it is not revealed, or it comes from יסוד, foundation.

111:3.headline: God's lasting "righteousness" is the world itself
111:3.body: Radak says this righteousness is the whole world, a gift of kindness from God to his creatures. Ibn Ezra reads it more simply: everything God does is just.

sources.quote: שהוא העולם כולו שהוא צדקה מאתו לנבראים עומדת לעד
sources.says: Radak says his righteousness is the whole world, which is a kindness from him to his creatures, and it lasts forever.

sources.quote: וטעם וצדקתו – שכל פעלו צדק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means that all his work is just.

111:5.headline: "Prey" for those who fear God: food, Egypt's spoil, or manna?
111:5.body: טרף is an animal's torn prey, and Metzudat Zion says it is borrowed here to mean food. Radak and Ibn Ezra say it is the wealth taken from Egypt, while Metzudat David says it is the manna.

sources.quote: והושאל ממזון החיה הבאה על ידי טרף
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means food, borrowed from the food a wild animal gets by tearing prey.

sources.quote: טרף. טרף ממון מצרים
sources.says: Radak says the prey is the wealth of Egypt.

sources.quote: טרף - דבר וינצלו את מצרים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra ties it to "they stripped Egypt".

sources.quote: טרף. זה המן שכלכל בו אנשי דור המדבר
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is the manna that fed the generation in the wilderness.

112:5.headline: Provide, measure, or bear: three readings of one verb
112:5.body: Metzudat Zion takes יכלכל as providing what is needed. Ibn Ezra links it to a verb for measuring, and also reports a view that it means to bear, as in 'a spirit bears his sickness'.

sources.quote: יכלכל. ענין ספוק הצורך כמו וכלכלו את המלך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means supplying what is needed, as in 'they provided for the king'.

sources.quote: ומלת יכלכל כפול כמו וכל בשליש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says יכלכל is a doubled form of the root in 'measured with a third-measure'.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: כי יכלכל כמו: יכלכל מחלהו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that some read it as in 'he will bear his sickness'.

sources.quote: שכל מתנותו ויציאותיו יעשה אדם במדה שוה בצדק ובמשפט
sources.says: Radak says the good man gives and spends in even measure, with fairness.

112:9.headline: He scatters gifts to many, without making himself poor
112:9.body: פזר means to scatter. Radak and Meiri say it means giving a little to many poor people, not giving away so much that the giver ends up poor.

sources.quote: וטעם פיזר שנותן לזה ולזה ולכל האביונים שיהיו לפניו, אבל אינו אומר שמפזר במתנות גדולות עד אשר ישאר הוא עני
sources.says: Radak says 'scattered' means giving to this one and that one, not giving such large gifts that he is left poor.

sources.quote: פי׳ בפזור הנה והנה ומעט מעט להרבות להיטיב הכל כפי שיוכל
sources.says: Meiri says it means giving here and there, a little at a time, to do as much good as he can.

113:1.headline: Why praise God with only half of His name
113:1.body: The psalm says הללויה, using the short name יה, not the full name. The midrash says this world is only worthy to praise God with half His name.

sources.quote: הללויה ולמה לא אמר הללו ה'. אמר רבי ירמיה בשם ר' אלעזר אין העולם הזה כדאי להלל בכל השם אלא בחציו
sources.says: The midrash asks why it says הללויה and not הללו ה', and answers that this world is fit to praise with only half the name.

113:1.headline: Servants of God, no longer servants of Pharaoh
113:1.body: The sages read "servants of God" as a contrast. On leaving Egypt, Israel stopped being Pharaoh's servants and became God's, so now they can sing this praise.

sources.quote: הַלְלוּ עַבְדֵי ה׳״ — וְלֹא עַבְדֵי פַרְעֹה
sources.says: Rava says the words mean servants of God and not servants of Pharaoh, which is why Hallel fits the Exodus.

sources.quote: לשעבר הייתם עבדי אבל עכשיו הרי אתם בני חורין הרי אתם ברשותכם והרי אתם עבדיו של הקב"ה
sources.says: The midrash has Pharaoh say: before you were my servants, now you are free and God's servants.

113:6.headline: God stoops to see the earth, or even the heavens?
113:6.body: Some split the two verses: God sits high in heaven and looks down on earth. Radak and Metzudat David read it that God stoops to see heaven and earth alike, since next to Him even heaven is low.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים מגביהי לשבת בשמים, ומשפילי לראות בארץ
sources.says: Radak brings a reading that God sits high in heaven and lowers Himself to see the earth.

sources.quote: ומשפיל לראות בתחתונים בין בשמים בין בארץ כי כולם שפלים לנגדו
sources.says: Radak's own reading is that God looks down on both heaven and earth, because all are low before Him.

sources.quote: כי למול רוממתו אף השמים תחשב לאין
sources.says: Metzudat David says that next to God's height even the heavens count as nothing.

113:9.headline: To sit at home, or to be made secure
113:9.body: Read plainly, the childless woman, who wandered outside to ease her grief, now sits at home with her children. Maimonides reads ישב here as being made firm and lasting: God gives her a settled place.

sources.quote: מוֹשִׁיבִי עֲקֶרֶת הַבַּיִת" (תהילים קיג,ט), כלומר: מעניק לה קביעות ויציבות
sources.says: Maimonides says ישב can mean anything fixed and lasting, and here means God gives her permanence and stability.

sources.quote: בעודה עקרה שבתה הבית מעט פעם בחוץ פעם ברחובות להפג צערה
sources.says: Metzudat David says that while childless she rarely stayed home and went out to ease her sorrow, and once she has children she sits at home.

114:3.headline: The sea fled the way Joseph fled
114:3.body: The midrash asks what the sea saw. It saw Joseph's coffin. Joseph "fled" (וינס) from Potiphar's wife, so the sea "fled" from him in turn.

sources.quote: ראה ארונו של יוסף יורד לים. אמר הקב"ה ינוס מפני הנס שנאמר (בראשית לט יב) וינס ויצא החוצה. אף הים יהיה נס מפניו
sources.says: The midrash says the sea saw Joseph's coffin; since Joseph fled outside, the sea would flee before him.

sources.quote: כי נבקעו המים כאילו פחד הים ונס מפניהם
sources.says: Radak says it is a figure of speech: the waters split as if the sea were afraid and fled.

114:4.headline: When did the mountains dance?
114:4.body: The verse does not say which event it means. Metzudat David says Mount Sinai shook at the giving of the Torah. Ibn Ezra and Meiri also point to rocks split open for water in the desert.

sources.quote: בשעת מתן תורה רקדו ההרים כאילים לגודל החרדה
sources.says: Metzudat David says the mountains skipped like rams at the giving of the Torah, from great trembling.

sources.quote: וטעם ההרים – הוא ההופכי הצור אגם מים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the mountains refer to the rock that God turned into a pool of water.

sources.quote: או רמז ברקידת ההרים והגבעות כענין יבקע צורים במדבר
sources.says: Meiri gives both: Sinai trembling, or rocks split in the desert for water.

114:7.headline: "Tremble, earth", or "the One who formed the earth"
114:7.body: חולי can be a command: "Tremble, O earth!" Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as "the One who forms the earth", from חול, to shape, with an extra yod.

sources.quote: הַמְּחוֹלֵל אֶרֶץ, יוֹ״ד יְתֵרָה בּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means the One who forms the earth, and the yod is extra.

sources.quote: ענין יצירה כמו באין תהומות חוללתי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means forming, as in "when there were no depths I was brought forth".

sources.quote: או חולי צווי, כמו קומי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it may be a command, like "arise": tremble, O earth.

sources.quote: אִתְחַלְחַלִי אַרְעָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it "tremble, O earth".

116:1.headline: 'I love': loving God, or longing to be heard
116:1.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra read אהבתי as 'how I long for God to hear my voice'. Metzudat David reorders the verse to say 'I love the Lord, because he hears my voice'.

sources.quote: תָּאַבְתִּי שֶׁיִּשְׁמַע ה׳ אֶת קוֹלִי
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'I longed for the Lord to hear my voice'.

sources.quote: כמה הייתי אוהב שישמע השם קולי בהתחנני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'how I would love for God to hear my voice when I plead'.

sources.quote: סרס המקרא אהבתי ה׳‎ כי ישמע את קולי
sources.says: Metzudat David says to reorder the verse: 'I love the Lord, because he hears my voice'.

116:2.headline: 'In my days': all my life, my hard days, or the holy days
116:2.body: Ibn Ezra reads ובימי as 'all my days', and Rashi as 'in my days of trouble I call, in my days of rescue I praise'. The Midrash reads it as the good days God gave, the Sabbath and the festivals.

sources.quote: טעם ובימי אקרא - כל ימי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'in my days I will call' means all my days.

sources.quote: בִּימֵי צָרָתִי אֶקְרָאֶנּוּ, וּבִימֵי גְּאֻלָּתִי אֲשַׁבְּחֶנּוּ
sources.says: Rashi says: in my days of trouble I will call him, and in my days of rescue I will praise him.

sources.quote: ובימי אקרא. בימים טובים שנתת לי
sources.says: The Midrash says 'in my days' means the good days you gave me, then lists the Sabbath, the Day of Atonement and Sukkot.

116:3.headline: Bands, pains, or pledges of death?
116:3.body: Rashi reads חבלי as bands of enemies, like 'a band of prophets', and Metzudat Zion reads it as pains, like the pains of giving birth. The Midrash reads it as a pledge: people are held as pledges to death.

sources.quote: כֻּלָּם לְשׁוֹן חֲבוּרוֹת הֵם, כְּמוֹ ״חֶבֶל נְבִיאִים״
sources.says: Rashi says all these uses mean groups, as in 'a band of prophets'.

sources.quote: חבלי. ענין מכאוב כמו צירים וחבלים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means pain, as in 'pangs and pains' in Isaiah.

sources.quote: אפפוני חבלי מות. בני אדם חבולים למות
sources.says: The Midrash says human beings are held in pledge to death.

116:3.headline: Troubles found me, and I find trouble
116:3.body: The verse uses 'find' twice: the straits of the grave 'found me', and 'I find' trouble and grief. Radak says troubles find a person who cannot run from them, and sometimes he goes out looking for good and finds bad.

sources.quote: אמר מצאוני ואמר אמצא כי המקרים ימצאו האדם לא יוכל לברוח וגם הוא ימצאם שילך אחריהם
sources.says: Radak says the verse says both 'found me' and 'I find', because events find a person who cannot escape, and he also finds them by walking toward them.

sources.quote: ופעמים ילך למצוא הטוב וימצא רע
sources.says: Radak adds that sometimes a person goes to find good and finds bad.

116:6.headline: God guards the simple, who have no tricks to save themselves
116:6.body: Radak says the simple person, who knows no clever way to escape harm, is guarded by God when he trusts in him. Ibn Ezra has David say he made himself one of the simple, and did not plot ways to escape.

sources.quote: אמר כי הפתי שאין יודע תחבולה להנצל מרעתו האל שומרו כשמשים עליו בטחונו
sources.says: Radak says God guards the simple person who knows no scheme to save himself, when he puts his trust in God.

sources.quote: הטעם שלא אחשוב תחבולות להמלט, כי שמתי נפשי כאחד הפתאים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the meaning is that David did not think up schemes to escape, but made himself like one of the simple.

116:9.headline: The lands of the living: Israel, this world, or the next
116:9.body: Rashi and Radak say 'the lands of the living' is the land of Israel, which David had been driven out of, and Radak adds that its air is the healthiest. Ibn Ezra says it means above the ground, not under it, and Meiri says it can mean the world to come.

sources.quote: אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁגֵּרְשׁוּנִי אוֹיְבַי וְרוֹדְפַי מִמֶּנָּה בִּימֵי שָׁאוּל
sources.says: Rashi says it is the land of Israel, which his enemies drove him out of in Saul's days.

sources.quote: כי ארץ ישראל אוירה טוב מכל הארצות
sources.says: Radak says the land of Israel is called the land of life because its air is better than any other land's.

sources.quote: שהם על פני הארץ ולא תחתיה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the lands of the living are on the face of the earth, not beneath it.

sources.quote: שאתהלך לפני ה׳ בארצות החיים לעולם הבא
sources.says: Meiri says it can mean walking before God in the world to come.

116:10.headline: 'I was afflicted', or 'I spoke up'
116:10.body: עניתי can come from עני, poor and suffering, or from ענה, to answer or speak. Metzudat David and Meiri read 'I was greatly afflicted', while Ibn Ezra, in his own view, reads 'I spoke', as in 'and Job answered'.

sources.quote: כי הייתי מדבר כאשר הייתי מעונה מאוד בתכלית הסכנה
sources.says: Metzudat David says David spoke while he was greatly afflicted, in the greatest danger.

sources.quote: עד שאני עניתי מאד כלומ׳ נכנעתי מאד
sources.says: Meiri says 'I was greatly afflicted' means 'I was brought very low'.

sources.quote: וככה עניתי כמו ויען איוב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says in his own view that עניתי means 'I spoke', as in 'and Job answered'.

116:11.headline: 'Every man is a liar', or every man lets you down
