116:11.body: Rashi says כזב means failing someone who relied on you, like a spring whose water runs dry; in one view David felt that even the prophet Samuel had failed him. Radak reads it as plain lying: anyone who said David would not be king was a liar.

sources.quote: כָּל לְשׁוֹן כָּזָב אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן חֶסְרוֹן מִבְטָח שֶׁבָּטְחוּ עָלָיו
sources.says: Rashi says every use of כזב means failing a trust that someone placed in you.

sources.quote: אַף שְׁמוּאֵל הַנָּבִיא שֶׁהוּא נֶאֱמָן לְנָבִיא אַף הוּא כּוֹזֵב, שֶׁמְּשָׁחַנִי לְמֶלֶךְ
sources.says: Rashi cites a view that David felt even Samuel, the trusted prophet who anointed him king, had failed him.

sources.quote: הייתי אומר כל אדם שאומר שלא תהיה לי המלוכה כוזב הוא
sources.says: Radak says David meant that anyone who said he would not become king was a liar.

116:13.headline: The cup of salvation: a real cup, or a person's lot
116:13.body: Some read כוס as a person's lot in life, as in 'my portion and my cup', while Radak allows a real cup of wine raised in thanks. Rashi says it is the wine poured with a thanksgiving offering, and the Targum says it is the cup of redemption in the world to come.

sources.quote: יש מפרשים כוס חלק כמו מנת חלקי וכוסי, ויתכן לפרש כמשמעו
sources.says: Radak says some explain 'cup' as a person's portion, as in 'my portion and my cup', but it can also be read plainly.

sources.quote: אָבִיא הַנְּסָכִים עַל הַתּוֹדוֹת שֶׁנָּדַרְתִּי
sources.says: Rashi says David will bring the wine offerings for the thanksgiving offerings he vowed.

sources.quote: כַּסָא דְפוּרְקָנַיָא אֲסוֹבַר לְעַלְמָא דְאָתֵי
sources.says: The Targum translates it as 'the cup of redemption I will bear for the world to come'.

116:14.headline: Not 'please' but 'now'
116:14.body: נא is often translated 'please', but Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say it means 'now'. Radak and Metzudat Zion say it goes with 'I will pay', so the verse says 'I will pay my vows now, before all his people'.

sources.quote: ומלת נא – עתה ככל נא שבמקרא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word נא means 'now', like every נא in scripture.

sources.quote: נא. כמו עתה וחוזר הוא על מלת אשלם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says נא means 'now' and goes back to the word 'I will pay'.

sources.quote: וטעם נא. דבק עם אשלם לא עם נגדה
sources.says: Radak says נא is joined to 'I will pay', not to 'before'.

116:16.headline: 'Ana' can plead, or can give thanks
116:16.body: Ibn Ezra says אנה sometimes pleads and sometimes thanks, and here it thanks, since David is not asking for anything. Radak notes that here too it is spelled with a ה instead of the usual א.

sources.quote: פעם לשון פיוס ופעם לשון תודה, כמו זה שהוא מודה לשם אנה ה' כי אני עבדך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word is sometimes a plea and sometimes thanks, and here it is thanks to God.

sources.quote: אנה. הוא כענין הודאה בין הודאה על החסד ובין הודאה ובקשה על חטא
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is used to give thanks for kindness, or to confess and ask forgiveness for a sin.

sources.quote: אנה. גם זה כתוב בה"א והוא בענין הודאה לאל יתברך
sources.says: Radak says this one is also written with a ה, and it means giving thanks to God.

116:16.headline: Son of your maidservant: a servant born in the house
116:16.body: Rashi says a servant born in the household is raised differently from one bought at the market. The Midrash adds that David is descended from Ruth, who called herself 'your maidservant' to Boaz.

sources.quote: אֵינוֹ דּוֹמֶה תַּרְבּוּת עֶבֶד הַלָּקוּחַ מִן הַשּׁוּק לִילוּד מִשְׁפָּחָה שֶׁבַּבַּיִת
sources.says: Rashi says the upbringing of a servant bought at the market is not like that of one born into the household.

sources.quote: אני בן בנה מן אותה שאמרה (רות ג ט) אנכי רות אמתך
sources.says: The Midrash has David say he is a descendant of the woman who said 'I am Ruth, your maidservant'.

116:16.headline: You loosened my bonds: ropes, or the bans on David's family
116:16.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read מוסרי as the ropes and straps that tie up a prisoner. The Midrash hears איסורי, 'my prohibitions', and says God released what bound David's line through Tamar and Ruth.

sources.quote: הִתַּרְתָּ מֵעַל צַוָּארִי מוֹסֵרוֹת וּמוֹטוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says God untied the ropes and yoke-bars from David's neck.

sources.quote: למוסרי. קשורי רצועי המאסר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means the tied straps of a prisoner's bonds.

sources.quote: פתחת למוסרי. פתחת איסורי מתמר התרתה אסורי מרות
sources.says: The Midrash says God opened David's prohibitions from Tamar and released his bonds from Ruth.

117:1.headline: Two words for nations: one group said twice, or two groups?
117:1.body: Radak says גוים and אמים say the same thing twice in different words. The midrash instead reads them as two groups, the nations that enslaved Israel and those that did not, and the second group reasons that if even the oppressors praise God, they surely should.

sources.quote: והוא כפל הענין במלות שונות
sources.says: Radak says the second half repeats the idea of the first in different words.

sources.quote: כל הגוים אלו העכו"ם ששעבדו בישראל. כל האומים אלו שלא שעבדו בהם
sources.says: The midrash says 'all the nations' are those that enslaved Israel, and 'all the peoples' are those that did not.

sources.quote: מה אם אלו ששעבדו בישראל מקלסין להקב"ה אנו שלא שעבדנו בהן על אחת כמה וכמה
sources.says: The peoples say: if those who enslaved Israel praise God, all the more so we who did not.

117:2.headline: The letters of אמת, truth, run from first to last
117:2.body: The midrash notes that אמת, truth, is spelled with the first letter of the alphabet, a middle letter, and the last letter. It ties this to God's words 'I am the first and I am the last'.

sources.quote: אמת ג' אותיות מעידות עליו שהוא אמת. א' ראשונה מ' תיכונה תי"ו אחרונה
sources.says: The midrash says the three letters of אמת testify that God is true: alef is first, mem is in the middle, tav is last.

sources.quote: אני ראשון ואני אחרון
sources.says: The midrash cites the verse 'I am the first and I am the last' to support the reading.

118:5.headline: From the narrow place to the wide place
118:5.body: מצר is a tight, narrow spot, and מרחב, open space, is its opposite, as Ibn Ezra notes. The Midrash reads the narrow place as Egypt, where life was made bitter, and the wide place as God spreading the wings of His kindness.

sources.quote: במרחב - הפך מצר כי בזה ענני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says מרחב is the opposite of מצר: God answered him with open space.

sources.quote: דבר אחר מן המצר מדבר במצרים (שמות א יד) וימררו את חייהם וגו'. ענני הקב"ה במרחב יה שהרחיב לי הקב"ה כנפי חסדו
sources.says: The Midrash says the narrow place speaks of Egypt, and the wide place is God widening the wings of His kindness.

118:5.headline: Called on as Yah, God answers as Yah
118:5.body: The short name יה comes twice in this verse. The Midrash says God answers by the same name He is called by, and Ibn Ezra calls the repeat a fine turn of style.

sources.quote: בכל לשון שישראל קוראין להקב"ה הוא עונה אותם
sources.says: The Midrash says that by whatever name Israel calls God, He answers them by it, and gives this verse as the case of the name יה.

sources.quote: והזכיר השם פעמים, דרך צחות בלשון הקדש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the name is said twice as a graceful style of the Hebrew language.

118:8.headline: Even thin shade from God beats a strong human prop
118:8.body: Rashi says חסות is only shelter in a shadow, a small thing, while מבטח is a firm, strong prop. Even so, the small shelter in God is better than full trust in people.

sources.quote: חֶסְיוֹן זֶה אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן חֶסְיוֹן צֵל, וְדָבָר מוּעָט הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says this kind of shelter is only the shelter of a shadow, and it is a small thing.

sources.quote: מִבְּטֹחַ. דָּבָר בָּרִיא וְסֶמֶךְ חָזָק, וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן לַחֲסוֹת בַּה׳ טוֹב מֵהַבְטָחַת בְּנֵי אָדָם
sources.says: Rashi says מבטח is a sound thing and a strong support, and still sheltering in God is better than what people promise.

sources.quote: שהחסיה מונחת על ההסתופף וההסתר תחת הכנפים כאמרו בצל כנפיך יחסיון
sources.says: Meiri says חסות means taking cover and hiding under wings, as in 'in the shadow of Your wings they take shelter'.

118:10.headline: 'I will cut them down', like grass that is mown
118:10.body: Rashi reads the unusual verb אמילם as 'I will cut them off', from the grass in Psalm 90 that 'is cut down and dries up'. Ibn Ezra agrees and calls a reading from אמלל, to wither, far-fetched.

sources.quote: אֲמִילַם. אַכְרִיתֵם, לְשׁוֹן ״יְמוֹלֵל וְיָבֵשׁ״
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'I will cut them off', the same word as 'it is cut down and dries up'.

sources.quote: ומלת אמילם – כמו: ימולל ויבש, כמו אכינם יכונן ובאה זאת הלמ"ד קמוצה, כדרך: ילבשם הכהן. ורבי משה אמר: כי אמילם מגזרת אמלל על משקל פקידה. והוא רחוק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word is like 'cut down and dries up', and that Rabbi Moshe's reading from אמלל is far-fetched.

118:12.headline: Swarming like bees around a jar of honey
118:12.body: Metzudat David pictures bees crowding around a jar full of honey. The Midrash turns the image around: as a bee brings honey to its owner, God will bring all the nations up to Jerusalem.

sources.quote: אף כי סבבו אותי כדבורים הללו אשר יסבבו כלי מלא מדבש
sources.says: Metzudat David says they surrounded him like bees that surround a vessel full of honey.

sources.quote: מה הדבורה הזו מכניסה דבש לבעליה כך עתיד הקב"ה לכנס כל אומות העולם ולהעלותם לירושלים
sources.says: The Midrash says as the bee brings honey in to its owner, so God will gather all the nations and bring them up to Jerusalem.

118:12.headline: A thorn fire: the flame leaps up as it dies
118:12.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion say the root of דעכו means leaping away, like a flame that jumps off the wick as it goes out. Radak adds that a thorn fire dies fast and leaves no coals.

sources.quote: כָּל לְשׁוֹן דְּעִיכָה נוֹפֵל עַל לְשׁוֹן קְפִיצָה וְנִתּוּר
sources.says: Rashi says every use of this root carries the sense of jumping and leaping away.

sources.quote: דעכו. ענין ניתור וקפיצה והוא כבוי האש שהשלהבת קופצת ממנה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means leaping: a fire going out, as the flame jumps away from it.

sources.quote: ואמר כאש קוצים. שהוא כבה במהרה ולא יעשה מהם גחלת
sources.says: Radak says a thorn fire goes out quickly and leaves no coals.

118:23.headline: Wondrous, or hidden from us
118:23.body: נפלאת usually means wondrous, and Ibn Ezra reads it that way. Metzudat Zion reads it as hidden, like the angel's name that is פלאי in Judges 13, and Metzudat David says we cannot know how the rescue came about.

sources.quote: ומלת נפלאת – מגזרת עושה פלא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from 'doing wonders'.

sources.quote: נפלאת. מכוסה ונעלם כמו והוא פלאי (שופטים יג)
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means covered and hidden, as in 'it is פלאי' in Judges 13.

sources.quote: ולא נוכל לדעת איך היתה גאולה שלמה
sources.says: Metzudat David says we cannot know how so complete a rescue happened.

118:27.headline: 'Bind the festival' means bind the festival's animal
118:27.body: חג usually means a festival, but Radak, Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra say here it means the offering, since most offerings came on festivals. So the verse means: tie the lamb with ropes and bring it to the altar.

sources.quote: וקרבן כבש או זולתו יקרא חג, לפי שבחגים נקריב אותם ברוב
sources.says: Radak says a lamb or other offering is called חג because most are offered on festivals.

sources.quote: חג. הקרבן נקרא חג על כי רוב הקרבנות באים בחג
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the offering is called חג because most offerings come on a festival.

sources.quote: אסרו חג הוא הכבש המוכן לזבוח כמו חגים ינקופו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the חג is the lamb ready to be offered, as in Isaiah 29:1.

119:2.headline: Why some commandments are called 'testimonies'
119:2.body: Metzudat Zion says עדות are the commandments that bear witness that God made the world, like the Sabbath and the festivals. Radak says they are a testimony and a reminder, and adds tzitzit and tefillin.

sources.quote: עדותיו. הם המצות שהם לעדות על חדוש העולם כשבת ומועדים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says they are the commandments that testify that the world was made, like the Sabbath and festivals.

sources.quote: המצות אשר הם עדות וזכר כמו שבת ומועדים ציצית ותפילין
sources.says: Radak says they are commandments that are a testimony and a reminder, like Sabbath, festivals, tzitzit and tefillin.

119:5.headline: אחלי is a wish: 'if only my ways were steady'
119:5.body: Rashi says אחלי voices a wish, like a person saying 'if only I were a prophet', and he gives the French word for a wish. Radak takes it from ויחל משה, 'Moses pleaded', with an extra א.

sources.quote: וְלָשׁוֹן אַחֲלִיּוּת שוהיי״ט בְּלַעַ״ז, כְּאָדָם הָאוֹמֵר: הַלְוַאי וְהָיִיתִי נָבִיא וְחָכָם
sources.says: Rashi says the word expresses a wish, gives the French for it, and compares a person saying 'if only I were a prophet and wise'.

sources.quote: ואחלי. מענין ויחל משה והאל״ף נוספת
sources.says: Radak says it comes from 'Moses pleaded', and the א is added.

119:9.headline: נער: a youth, a servant, or someone not yet wise
119:9.body: Meiri says נער can mean young in years, a servant of any age, or a person still lacking understanding. He thinks David calls himself a נער in the third sense, out of humility.

sources.quote: מלת נער מונחת על קטון השנים ולפעמים על יד שדרך קטן לשרת את הגדול נקרא המשרת נער
sources.says: Meiri says נער means young in years, and sometimes a servant, since the young serve the old.

sources.quote: נקרא מי שאינו שלם בדעת נער
sources.says: Meiri says a person who is not complete in understanding is also called נער.

sources.quote: ונראה שדוד השפיל עצמו וקרא עצמו על זה הצד נער
sources.says: Meiri says David humbled himself and called himself a נער in this sense.

119:17.headline: גמל here is not repaying, but doing a kindness first
119:17.body: Meiri says that when גמל comes without any sense of payment, it can mean starting a kindness. So David asks for life as a gift, not as a reward.

sources.quote: כבר ביארנו בענין גמול כשהיא נאמרת בלא לשון תשלום שהיא נאמרת גם על התחלת עשיית החסד
sources.says: Meiri says that when גמול is said without the sense of paying back, it also means beginning to do a kindness.

119:20.headline: לתאבה: longing, or breaking?
119:20.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion read לתאבה as longing, like תאוה. Rashi cites Menachem, who links it to מתאב in Amos 6:8 and reads both words as breaking.

sources.quote: לתאבה. מקור עניין תאוה וחשק
sources.says: Radak says the word means desire and longing.

sources.quote: לתאבה. כמו לתאוה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the same as 'for desire'.

sources.quote: וּמְנַחֵם חִבֵּר לְתַאֲבָה עִם ״מְתָאֵב אָנֹכִי אֶת גְּאוֹן יַעֲקֹב״ (עמוס ו:ח), וּשְׁנֵיהֶם לְשׁוֹן שֶׁבֶר
sources.says: Rashi says Menachem grouped this word with 'I abhor the pride of Jacob' in Amos, and both mean breaking.

119:22.headline: Roll away my shame: here גל does not mean 'uncover'
119:22.body: In verse 18 the same letters mean 'uncover my eyes'. Here Rashi and Meiri read גל as 'roll', like rolling the stone off the well, and Meiri says the 'uncover' reading does not fit.

sources.quote: גל. מלשון גלוי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says that in verse 18 the word means uncovering.

sources.quote: גַּל מֵעָלַי. לְשׁוֹן גִּלְגּוּל, כְּמוֹ ״וַיָּגֶל אֶת הָאָבֶן״
sources.says: Rashi says here it means rolling, as in 'he rolled the stone'.

sources.quote: ושורשו גלל כלומ׳ שנגול מעלי חרפתם
sources.says: Meiri says the root is גלל: their scorn is rolled off me.

sources.quote: וי״מ אותו מלשון גלוי מצד הדקדוק ואין לשון גלוי נופל יפה בענין
sources.says: Meiri says some read it as 'uncover' on grammar, but that meaning does not fit here.

119:23.headline: Speaking 'in' someone means speaking against them
119:23.body: Meiri says the verb for speaking joined to ב means speaking against, as when Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses. Ibn Ezra cites the same verse, so the princes sat and spoke against David.

sources.quote: ובי נדברו דרך גנאי כי כל לשון הדבור הנקשר עם בית מורה גנאי כמו ותדבר מרים ואהרן במשה
sources.says: Meiri says 'spoke in me' is disparaging, because speech joined to ב means disparagement, as with Miriam and Aaron and Moses.

sources.quote: בי נדברו - כמו: ותדבר מרים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares 'Miriam spoke against'.

119:28.headline: My soul drips away, drop by drop
119:28.body: Rashi says דלפה means 'dripped': my soul is wasting away bit by bit, and Metzudat Zion compares 'a steady drip' (דלף טורד) in Proverbs 27. Radak also offers 'shed tears'.

sources.quote: דָּלְפָה נַפְשִׁי. נָטְפָה, כְּלוֹמַר: נֶחְסֶרֶת וְהוֹלֶכֶת
sources.says: Rashi says it means dripped, that is, it keeps growing less.

sources.quote: דלפה. ענין הטפה כמו דלף טורד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means dripping, as in 'a steady drip'.

sources.quote: או פי׳ דלפה דמעה
sources.says: Radak says it may also mean 'shed tears'.

119:30.headline: I set your laws before me, or I found them even?
119:30.body: Meiri reports a reading that שויתי means 'I placed them before me' so as never to forget them. He prefers 'I held them even and straight', and Ibn Ezra reads 'I judged evenly'.

sources.quote: ומשפטיך שויתי י״מ שויתים לנגדי לבל אשכחם לעולם ולי נראה החזקתים כשוים וישרים מאין שום עוות
sources.says: Meiri says some read 'I set them before me so as never to forget', but he reads 'I held them even and straight, with nothing crooked'.

sources.quote: והטעם: עשיתי משפט שוה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the meaning is 'I did even justice'.

119:43.headline: Here תצל means 'take away', not 'rescue'
119:43.body: Rashi, Metzudat Zion and Meiri say it means to separate or remove, as when God 'took away' Laban's flocks for Jacob in Genesis 31. David asks: do not take the word of truth from my mouth.

sources.quote: וְאַל תַּבְדֵּל מִפִּי דְּבַר אֱמֶת, כְּמוֹ ״וַיַּצֵּל אֱלֹהִים אֶת מִקְנֵה אֲבִיכֶם״
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'do not separate the word of truth from my mouth', as in 'God took away your father's flocks'.

sources.quote: תצל. ענין הסרה וכן אשר הציל אלהים מאבינו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means removing, as in 'what God took from our father'.

sources.quote: ואל תצל פי׳ לשון הפרשה
sources.says: Meiri says it means separating.

119:54.headline: The house where I wander, or the house of my fear?
119:54.body: Meiri says בית מגורי can mean any place I lodge as a stranger, or it can come from מגור, terror, as in 'terror all around'. On the second reading, even when afraid, David sang your laws.

sources.quote: בבית מגורי ר״ל בכל מקום שאני מתגורר בו. או נפרש מגורי ענין פחד מלשון מגור מסביב
sources.says: Meiri says it means every place I lodge, or it can mean fear, from 'terror all around'.

sources.quote: אף בזמן שהייתי מפחד מאויבי הייתי מתעסק בתורתך
sources.says: Meiri says on that reading: even when I feared my enemies, I busied myself with your Torah.

119:61.headline: עודני: they robbed me, or they grew many around me?
119:61.body: Rashi cites Menachem, who reads it as 'plundered me', from 'he devours prey (עד)' in Genesis 49:27, and Rashi also reads it from עוד, 'more'. Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner in Scripture and rejects the 'prey' reading.

sources.quote: סִיעוֹת שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים שְׁלָלוּנִי, כְּמוֹ ״יֹאכַל עַד״
sources.says: Rashi says bands of wicked men plundered me, as in 'he devours prey'.

sources.quote: וְיֵשׁ לְפוֹתְרוֹ לְשׁוֹן עוֹד, כְּלוֹמַר: נוֹסְפוּ וְרָבוּ עָלַי
sources.says: Rashi says it can also come from עוד: they increased and grew many against me.

sources.quote: חבלי, עודוני - אין לו ריע והאומר שהוא מגזרת יאכל עד אין לו טעם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner, and deriving it from 'devours prey' makes no sense.

119:61.headline: Bands of the wicked, or the pains they cause?
119:61.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read חבלי as groups, like 'a band (חבל) of prophets' in 1 Samuel 10. Meiri reads it as their pangs and troubles.

sources.quote: חֶבְלֵי רְשָׁעִים עִוְּדוּנִי. סִיעוֹת שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים
sources.says: Rashi says it means bands of wicked men.

sources.quote: חבלי. ענין סיעה וחבורה כמו חבל נביאים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a group, as in 'a band of prophets'.

sources.quote: חבלי רשעים ר״ל ציריהם וצרותיהם
sources.says: Meiri says it means the pangs and troubles the wicked cause.

119:67.headline: Before I 'answered': before I studied, spoke, or suffered?
119:67.body: Rashi reads אענה as reciting in the house of study, and Radak and Meiri read it as speaking. Metzudat Zion reads it from עינוי, suffering, and Meiri also cites a reading of being humbled.

sources.quote: אֶעֱנֶה. לְשׁוֹן שׁוֹנֶה וְהוֹגֶה בְּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says it means repeating and reciting in the house of study.

sources.quote: אענה. כמו ויען איוב, וענית ואמרת
sources.says: Radak says it means speaking, as in 'Job answered'.

sources.quote: אענה. מלשון עינוי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from the word for suffering.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים בו לשון כניעה
sources.says: Meiri says some read it as being humbled.

119:70.headline: Their heart is 'fat', which is why a fool is called טפש
119:70.body: Ibn Ezra says טפש has no partner in Scripture. Metzudat Zion says it means fat, since the Targum renders 'make this people's heart fat' (Isaiah 6:10) with טפש, and from this a fool came to be called טפש.

sources.quote: טפש - אין חבר לו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner.

sources.quote: טפש. ענין שומן כי השמן לב העם הזה (ישעיהו ו׳:י׳) תרגומו טפש לבא ומזה קראו לכסיל טפש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means fat: the Targum translates 'make this people's heart fat' with טפש, and from this a fool is called טפש.

119:85.headline: שיחות here are pits the wicked dig, not talk
119:85.body: Elsewhere in this psalm שיחה is David's talk about the law, as in verse 99. Here Metzudat Zion says שיחות are pits, as in 'they dug a pit before me', and Meiri says it is a form of שוחות.

sources.quote: שִׂיחָה לִי. כָּל שִׂיחָתִי הָיְתָה בָּם
sources.says: Rashi says in verse 99 that all his talk was about God's testimonies.

sources.quote: שיחות. בורות כמו כרו לפני שיחה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שיחות are pits, as in 'they dug a pit before me'.

sources.quote: ושיחות ביו״ד ובחירק תחת השין כמו שוחות בוא״ו
sources.says: Meiri says שיחות, spelled with י, is the same as שוחות, pits, spelled with ו.

119:89.headline: Maimonides: God's word 'stands' in heaven means it is fixed forever
119:89.body: In the Guide, Maimonides says נצב can mean standing up, or being fixed and lasting. He cites this verse for the second sense: God's word is fixed and lasting.

sources.quote: א) לעתים משמעותו היא עמידה והתייצבות
sources.says: Maimonides says the word sometimes means standing up.

sources.quote: ב) ולעתים משמעותו היא קביעות ותמידות
sources.says: Maimonides says it sometimes means being fixed and lasting.

sources.quote: כלומר קבוע וקיים
sources.says: Maimonides explains this verse as 'fixed and lasting'.

119:96.headline: An end to every completion, or to every desire?
119:96.body: Rashi reads תכלה as completion: everything finished has a limit, but your commandment has none. Meiri reads it as desire, from כלתה: every desire ends once it is met, but the more one gets of wisdom, the more one wants.

sources.quote: לְכָל סִיּוּם דָּבָר יֵשׁ קֵץ גְבוּל, אֲבָל מִצְוָתְךָ אֵין קֵץ וּגְבוּל לְתַכְלִיתָם
sources.says: Rashi says every finished thing has an end and a limit, but your commandments have no end or limit.

sources.quote: ותכלה נראה שהוא לשון חמדה מענין ותכל דוד
sources.says: Meiri says תכלה seems to mean desire, as in 'David longed'.

sources.quote: וכל עוד שישיג האדם ממנה חושק ונכסף יותר להתעסק בה
sources.says: Meiri says the more a person gets of it, the more he longs to engage with it.

119:98.headline: Wiser from my enemies, or wiser than my enemies?
119:98.body: Radak's father read מאיבי plainly: I learn from my enemies, seeing they cannot take your Torah from me. Meiri reads it as 'more than': your Torah made me wiser than all my enemies.

sources.quote: אדוני אבי ז״ל פי׳ מאויבי כמשמעו מהם תחכמני ותלמדני מצותיך כאשר אראה שאינם יכולים להסיר תורתך מפי
sources.says: Radak says his father read it plainly: from my enemies you make me wise, when I see they cannot remove your Torah from my mouth.

sources.quote: מאויבי כלומ׳ יותר מכל אויבי חכמתני תורתך מאד
sources.says: Meiri reads it as 'more than all my enemies', your Torah made me very wise.

119:103.headline: Your words were sweet, or finely spoken?
119:103.body: Ibn Ezra calls נמלצו a strange word, not from מליצה, fine speech, and reads it as 'were sweet', as Rashi does. Radak links it to מליצה: Torah's words are said in the best language, so they are likened to honey.

sources.quote: מה נמלצו - מלה זרה ופרושו מתקו כי איננו מגזרת מליץ ומליצה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a strange word meaning 'were sweet', and it does not come from מליץ or מליצה.

sources.quote: נִמְלְצוּ. נִמְתְּקוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'were sweetened'.

sources.quote: והמליצה היא תוכן הדיבור לפיכך המשיל דברי התורה לדבש
sources.says: Radak says מליצה is the substance of speech, so he likened the words of Torah to honey.

119:107.headline: Brought low, or struck by an illness of the mind?
119:107.body: Rashi first reads נעניתי as 'I was made poor and low', and a poor man counts as dead, so he asks for life. He then gives a second reading: an illness that confuses the mind, called עניה in the Mishnah's Hebrew.

sources.quote: נַעֲנֵיתִי. נַעֲשֵׂיתִי עָנִי וְשָׁפָל
sources.says: Rashi says it means I was made poor and low.

sources.quote: וְעָנִי חָשׁוּב כְּמֵת, לְפִיכָךְ חַיֵּנִי כִדְבָרֶךָ
sources.says: Rashi says a poor man is counted as dead, so 'give me life'.

sources.quote: חֳלִי הוּא שֶׁמְּטָרֵף אֶת הַדַּעַת, וּשְׁמוֹ עֲנִיָּה בִּלְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is an illness that confuses the mind, called עניה in the language of the Mishnah.

119:113.headline: I hate סעפים: wavering thoughts, or people who scheme?
119:113.body: Rashi says סעפים are people who plot evil, and the same word read with other vowels means the thoughts. Radak and Meiri read it as the thoughts themselves, and Meiri means the wavering thoughts of a torn mind.

sources.quote: סֵעֲפִים שָׂנֵאתִי. חוֹשְׁבֵי מַחְשְׁבוֹת אָוֶן
sources.says: Rashi says it means people who think wicked thoughts.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁאַתָּה קוֹרֵא סְעִיפִים הוּא שֵׁם הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה, וּכְשֶׁאַתָּה קוֹרֵא סֵעֲפִים נוֹפֵל הַלָּשׁוֹן עַל הַחוֹשְׁבִים אוֹתָם
sources.says: Rashi says read as סְעִיפִים it names the thought, and read as סֵעֲפִים it names the people thinking them.

sources.quote: ולפי דעתי שהוא שם ולא תואר ופירושו כל שאר המחשבות שנאתי
sources.says: Radak says it is a noun, not a description of people: I hate all other thoughts.

sources.quote: כי סעפים הם לדעתי מחשבות אדם נבוך שמרבה מחשבות
sources.says: Meiri says סעפים are the thoughts of a confused person who has too many thoughts.

119:117.headline: ואשעה: keep busy with, tell over, or delight in your laws?
119:117.body: Rashi reads it as 'busy myself', or as 'tell and repeat', and Metzudat Zion explains the second from the Aramaic for telling. Ibn Ezra prefers to take it from שעשועים, delight.

sources.quote: וְאֶשְׁעָה בְחֻקֶּיךָ. וְאֶתְעַסֵּק
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'I will occupy myself'.

sources.quote: דָּבָר אַחֵר: וְאֶשְׁעָה לְשׁוֹן סִפּוּר וְשִׁנּוּן
sources.says: Rashi's other reading: it means telling and repeating.

sources.quote: ואשעה. ענין ספור כי ויספר תרגומו ואשתעי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means telling, since the Targum renders 'he told' as ואשתעי.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני: מגזרת שעשועים ונכפלה המלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the right reading is from שעשועים, delight, with letters doubled.

119:120.headline: My flesh bristles: סמר comes from the word for a nail
119:120.body: Metzudat Zion says סמר comes from מסמר, a nail, and means going stiff. Radak explains that a very frightened person's hairs stand up like nails.

sources.quote: סמר. מלשון מסמר ויתד ועניינו התקשות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from the word for a nail or peg, and means stiffening.

sources.quote: כי האדם המפחד מאד יעמדו שערותיו כמו מסמרים
sources.says: Radak says a very frightened person's hairs stand up like nails.

119:122.headline: Be my guarantor, or make things sweet for your servant?
119:122.body: Rashi reads ערב as standing surety for David against harm, and Metzudat Zion reads it as sweetness, as in 'your voice is sweet (ערב)'. Ibn Ezra notes this is the one verse in the psalm with no word for the law.

sources.quote: הֱיֵה עָרֵב בִּשְׁבִילִי לְנֶגֶד הָרָעָה
sources.says: Rashi says: be a guarantor for me against harm.

sources.quote: ערוב. ענין מתיקות כמו קולך ערב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means sweetness, as in 'your voice is sweet'.

sources.quote: כבר הזכיר בעל המסורה כי אין פסוק שאין שם זכר דרך או תורה או עדות או פקודים או אמירה או חוק או מצוה או משפט או דבר חוץ מפסוק אחד והוא ערוב עבדך לטוב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites the Masorah: every verse mentions way, Torah, testimony or a similar word, except this one.

119:128.headline: ישרתי: I found them right, or I called them happy?
119:128.body: Rashi reads ישרתי from ישר, straight: all your commands were right in my eyes. Ibn Ezra says the י stands for an א, as in אשרוני, 'they will call me happy'.

sources.quote: יִשָּׁרְתִּי. יָשְׁרוּ בְּעֵינַי
sources.says: Rashi says it means they were right in my eyes.

sources.quote: ישרתי - היו״ד תחת אל״ף כטעם כי אשרוני בנות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the י is in place of an א, with the sense of 'women will call me happy'.

119:129.headline: Your testimonies are 'wonders' because they are hidden
119:129.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion stop on פלאות and read it as hidden, as in 'if a matter is too hard (יפלא) for you'. Rashi gives an example: some light commands carry a great reward, like sending away the mother bird.

sources.quote: פלאות. מענין כי יפלא ממך דבר כלומר נסתרות יש בהם
sources.says: Radak says it is from 'if a matter is too hard for you': there are hidden things in them.

sources.quote: פלאות. מכוסה ונעלם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means covered and hidden.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ מִצְווֹת קַלּוֹת שֶׁהִרְבֵּיתָ בְּמַתַּן שְׂכָרָן, כְּגוֹן שִׁלּוּחַ הַקֵּן
sources.says: Rashi says some light commandments carry a great reward, such as sending away the mother bird.

119:130.headline: Which opening gives light: Sinai's first words, or creation's?
119:130.body: Rashi gives two readings of 'the opening of your words gives light'. It is the start of the Ten Commandments, 'I am the Lord who brought you out', or the first words of creation, 'Let there be light'.

sources.quote: תְּחִלַּת דְּבָרֶיךָ הֵאִירוּ אֶת לֵב יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says the start of your words lit up Israel's heart, with 'I am the Lord who brought you out'.

sources.quote: דָּבָר אַחֵר: פֵּתַח דְּבָרֶיךָ יָאִיר תְּחִלַּת דְּבָרֶיךָ בְּמַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית
sources.says: Rashi's other reading: the start of your words at creation, 'Let there be light'.

119:152.headline: I knew from the start, or I knew before it happened?
119:152.body: Radak reads קדם as 'at first': from the beginning I understood your testimonies. Rashi reads 'before': your laws told me things before they happened, like first fruits and tithes commanded before Israel had the land.

sources.quote: קדם. תחילה מה שידעתי ומה שהבינותי מעדותיך
sources.says: Radak says it means at first, what I knew and understood from your testimonies.

sources.quote: קוֹדֶם הֱיוֹת הַדָּבָר יְדַעְתִּיו מִתּוֹךְ עֵדֹתֶיךָ: קֹדֶם יָרְשׁוּ אֶת הָאָרֶץ צִוִּיתָ לָהֶם עַל הַבִּכּוּרִים
sources.says: Rashi says before a thing happened I knew it from your testimonies: before they inherited the land you commanded them about first fruits.

119:158.headline: I quarreled with the traitors, or I grew sick of life?
119:158.body: Radak reads ואתקוטטה as quarreling, from קטטה in the sages' Hebrew. His father and Ibn Ezra take it from נקטה נפשי, 'my soul is weary of my life': seeing traitors thrive, I grew sick of living.

sources.quote: ואתקוטטה. מענין קטטה בדברי רבותינו ז״ל
sources.says: Radak says it is from קטטה, a quarrel, in the words of the sages.

sources.quote: ואדוני אבי ז״ל פי׳ ראיתים מצליחים וקצתי בחיי כמו נקטה בחיי
sources.says: Radak says his father explained: I saw them succeed and I loathed my life, as in 'weary of my life'.

sources.quote: ואתקוטטה - מגזרת נקטה נפשי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from 'my soul is weary'.

119:160.headline: The 'head' of your word: from the start, or 'I am'?
119:160.body: Radak reads ראש as the start of the world: your word has been true from the beginning. Rashi cites the sages: the nations thought the first commands served God's own honor, until 'honor your father' proved the beginning true.

sources.quote: ראש. מראש העולם ולעולם כלומר כל ימי העולם היה דברך ומשפטך אמת
sources.says: Radak says from the start of the world and forever, your word has been true.

sources.quote: סוֹף דְּבָרְךָ הוֹכִיחַ עַל הָרֹאשׁ שֶׁהוּא אֱמֶת
sources.says: Rashi says the end of your word proved that the beginning is true.

sources.quote: כֵּיוָן שֶׁשָּׁמְעוּ ״כַּבֵּד״, ״לֹא תִרְצַח״, ״לֹא תִנְאָף״ (שמות כ:יב-יג), הוֹדוּ עַל רֹאשׁ דְּבָרְךָ שֶׁהוּא אֱמֶת
sources.says: Rashi says once the nations heard 'honor', 'do not murder', 'do not commit adultery', they admitted the head of your word is true.

119:162.headline: David rejoices over circumcision, given by 'saying', not 'speaking'
119:162.body: Rashi tells the sages' story: in the bathhouse David felt bare of all commandments, until he saw his circumcision and rejoiced. They read אמרתך, 'your saying', as circumcision, because it was given with ויאמר, not וידבר.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיָה דָוִד בְּבֵית הַמֶּרְחָץ וְרָאָה עַצְמוֹ בְּלֹא צִיצִית וּבְלֹא תְּפִילִּין וּבְלֹא תּוֹרָה
sources.says: Rashi says David was in the bathhouse and saw himself without tzitzit, tefillin or Torah.

sources.quote: הַמִּילָה שֶׁמִּתְּחִלָּה נִתְּנָה בְּמַאֲמָר וְלֹא בְדִבּוּר
sources.says: Rashi says circumcision was first given with 'saying', not with 'speaking'.

119:164.headline: Seven times a day: a real count, or just 'many times'?
119:164.body: Radak and Meiri say seven here simply means many times, as in 'a righteous man falls seven times'. Rashi counts seven real blessings: those said around the Shema each morning and evening.

sources.quote: שבע ביום. פעמים רבות כי שבע אינו דוקא
sources.says: Radak says it means many times, since seven is not exact.

sources.quote: ושבע ביום ר״ל הרבה פעמים הללתיך ואין מנין השבע בדיוק
sources.says: Meiri says it means I praised you many times, and the number seven is not exact.

sources.quote: שַׁחֲרִית שְׁתַּיִם לִפְנֵי קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע וְאַחַת לְאַחֲרֶיהָ, וּבָעֶרֶב שְׁתַּיִם לְפָנֶיהָ וּשְׁתַּיִם לְאַחֲרֶיהָ
sources.says: Rashi says: in the morning two blessings before the Shema and one after, and in the evening two before and two after.

119:171.headline: My lips will pour out praise, like a spring that never stops
119:171.body: Radak says תבענה means speech that keeps flowing, like a spring. Metzudat Zion compares 'day to day pours out speech' (יביע אומר) in Psalms 19.

sources.quote: ועל התמדת הדיבור אומר זה הלשון, כמו המקור שהוא נובע בלי הפסק
sources.says: Radak says this word is used for steady speech, like a spring that flows without stopping.

sources.quote: תבענה. ענין אמירה כמו יביע אומר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means speaking, as in 'pours out speech'.

119:172.headline: My tongue will speak, call out aloud, or sing praise?
119:172.body: Rashi says every ענייה is a loud voice, as when the Levites 'answered' aloud. Radak reads it as speaking, and cites the Masorah, which reads it as praise.

sources.quote: כָּל עֲנִיָּה לְשׁוֹן קוֹל רָם הוּא, וְאָב לְכֻלָּם ״וְעָנוּ הַלְוִיִּם וְאָמְרוּ״
sources.says: Rashi says every ענייה means a raised voice, and the model for all is 'the Levites shall answer and say'.

sources.quote: תען. ענין דיבור
sources.says: Radak says it means speaking.

sources.quote: ובעל המסרה פירש אותו לשון שבח
sources.says: Radak says the author of the Masorah explained it as praise.

12:2.headline: אמונים: the faithful people, or faithful words?
12:2.body: The Targum and Metzudat David read it as the faithful people, who have vanished. Meiri reads it as words of faith: nothing that people say can be trusted.

sources.quote: אֲרוּם סָפוּ מְהֵימְנַיָא מִן בְּנֵי נָשָׁא
sources.says: The Targum says the faithful ones have vanished from among people.

sources.quote: כלו אנשי אמונה
sources.says: Metzudat David says the men of faith are finished.

sources.quote: ואפסו אמונים ר״ל דברי אמונה מבני אדם
sources.says: Meiri says אמונים means words of faith have come to an end among people.

12:3.headline: "With a heart and a heart": they speak with two hearts
12:3.body: The doubled word means two hearts. Rashi says one heart shows peace and the other hides hatred. Ibn Ezra says the tongue acts as interpreter for one of them.

sources.quote: בִּשְׁנֵי לְבָבוֹת: לִי מַרְאִים שָׁלוֹם, וְיֵשׁ שִׂנְאָה טְמוּנָה בְּלִבָּבָם
sources.says: Rashi says they speak with two hearts: they show me peace, while hatred is hidden in their hearts.

sources.quote: כמו שיש לו שתי לבבות והלשון תליץ בעד האחד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is as if he has two hearts and the tongue acts as interpreter for the one.

sources.quote: כאלו הלשון מדבר בשליחות לב האחד והלב השני בל עמו
sources.says: Metzudat David says the tongue speaks as the messenger of one heart while the other heart is not with it.

12:5.headline: The extra ל in "ללשננו": "with", "for", or nothing?
12:5.body: Rashi and the Targum read it as "with our tongue we will prevail". Radak reads "for the sake of our tongue", and Meiri says the first ל is extra.

sources.quote: בִּלְשׁוֹנֵנוּ נִתְגַּבֵּר
sources.says: Rashi says it means with our tongue we will prevail.

sources.quote: בְּלִישָׁנָנָא נִתְגַבַּר
sources.says: The Targum renders it as with our tongue we will prevail.

sources.quote: ללשננו בעבור לשננו, כמו אמרי לי אחי הוא
sources.says: Radak says ללשננו means for the sake of our tongue, like אמרי לי אחי הוא.

sources.quote: והלמ״ד הראשונה יתירה כמו הרגו לאבנר
sources.says: Meiri says the first ל is extra, like הרגו לאבנר.

12:6.headline: "Now I will rise": keep My word, punish, or help?
12:6.body: Maimonides says קימה has four senses, and here God's "I will rise" means "I will keep My word", or perhaps "I will punish". Rashi and Radak read it as God rising to help the poor.

sources.quote: כלומר כעת אקיים את דברי והבטחתי ואיומי
sources.says: Maimonides says it means now I will keep My word, My promise and My threats.

sources.quote: עתה אגיב בענישה
sources.says: Maimonides says it may also mean now I will respond with punishment.

sources.quote: יֹאמַר ה׳ עַתָּה אָקוּם לְעֶזְרָתָם
sources.says: Rashi says the LORD says now I will rise to help them.

sources.quote: עתה אקום יאמר יהוה להושיעם
sources.says: Radak says now I will rise, says the LORD, to save them.

12:6.headline: יפיח: "speaks", "sets a snare", or "puffs"?
12:6.body: Rashi says it is a word for speech, as in Proverbs, while Menachem takes it as a snare. Radak reads it as setting snares, and Metzudat David reads a mere puff of breath.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן דִּבּוּר, הַרְבֵּה יֵשׁ בְּסֵפֶר מִשְׁלֵי
sources.says: Rashi says it is the language of speech, found often in Proverbs.

sources.quote: וּמְנַחֵם פָּתַר אוֹתוֹ לְשׁוֹן מוֹקֵשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says Menachem explained it as the language of a trap.

sources.quote: וכן יפיחו קריה (משלי כט ח) יציבו פח
sources.says: Radak says it is like יפיחו קריה, they set a snare.

sources.quote: אושיע את הבא לאבד את הרשע בהפחת רוח בעלמא
sources.says: Metzudat David says I will save the one who comes to destroy the wicked, with a mere puff of breath.

12:7.headline: "Sevenfold" means many times, or 49 ways to read the Torah
12:7.body: Radak, Ibn Ezra and Meiri say שבעתים means "many times over", since seven stands for many. Rashi gives a midrash: in David's day even children could explain the Torah in forty-nine ways, and that is the sevenfold.

sources.quote: כי מספר שבע ושבעה יבא בענין מספר רב
sources.says: Radak says the number seven comes to mean a large number.

sources.quote: שבעתים - פעמים רבות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says שבעתים means many times.

sources.quote: הָיוּ יוֹדְעִים לִדְרוֹשׁ אֶת הַתּוֹרָה בְּמ״ם טי״ת פָּנִים לְכָל צַד, וְזֶהוּ שִׁבְעָתַיִם
sources.says: Rashi gives a midrash: they knew how to expound the Torah in forty-nine faces on every side, and that is the sevenfold.

120:1.headline: "Song of Ascents": steps in the Temple, or exiles going up
120:1.body: Rashi says the Levites sang these fifteen psalms on the fifteen steps of the Temple court. Radak adds that the "ascents" may be the exiles going up to the Land of Israel, and Meiri cites those who say the singers' voices rose step by step.

sources.quote: שֶׁיֹּאמְרוּ הַלְוִיִּם אוֹתוֹ עַל חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה מַעֲלוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says the Levites sang it on the fifteen steps between the court of Israel and the women's court.

sources.quote: וי"ל עוד כי פי' מעלות הגלות שעתידים ישראל לעלות א"י
sources.says: Radak says it can also mean the ascents of the exiles, who will one day go up to the Land of Israel.

sources.quote: שהיו משוררים אותם תחלה בקול נמוך ומעלים אותו מעט מעט
sources.says: Meiri cites a view that these songs began in a low voice and were raised little by little.

sources.quote: שיר המעלה אין כתיב כאן אלא שיר המעלות
sources.says: The midrash notes the plural: when Israel rises, it rises not one step but many.

120:3.headline: What more could guard the tongue?
120:3.body: Rashi and Metzudat David read the verse as spoken to the tongue itself. God already set it behind two walls, the lips and the teeth. What more guarding could He add?

sources.quote: שְׁמִירָה וּמְחִיצּוֹת, הֲרֵי אַתְּ נְתוּנָה לִפְנִים מִשְּׁתֵּי מְחִיצּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it asks what more guards and walls God could give: the tongue is already placed inside two walls.

sources.quote: הלא כבר נתונה אתה לפנים מחומת השפתים והשינים
sources.says: Metzudat David says the tongue is already inside the wall of the lips and teeth.

120:4.headline: Why slander is an arrow, not a sword
120:4.body: The verse calls a lying tongue a warrior's arrows. Rashi says an arrow kills from far away. The midrash adds that a sword can be put back, but an arrow cannot be called back once shot.

sources.quote: וַהֲרֵי אַתְּ הוֹרֶגֶת בְּמָקוֹם רָחוֹק כְּחֵץ
sources.says: Rashi says the tongue kills from a distance, like an arrow.

sources.quote: אבל החץ כיון שירה אותו והלך אפילו מבקש להחזירה אינו יכול להחזיר
sources.says: The midrash says a sword can be returned to its sheath, but once an arrow is shot it cannot be brought back.

120:4.headline: Broom-wood coals look dead but still burn inside
120:4.body: רתמים is a rare word for the broom tree. Its coals seem cold on the outside but burn inside. Radak says lying talk is the same: it looks harmless and does harm.

sources.quote: כָּל הַגֶּחָלִים, כָּבוּ מִבַּחוּץ – כָּבוּ מִבִּפְנִים, וְאֵלּוּ כָּבוּ מִבַּחוּץ וְלֹא מִבִּפְנִים
sources.says: Rashi says other coals go out inside when they go out outside, but these go out outside and not inside.

sources.quote: ונכוו רגליהם מן הגחלים שתחת האפר לפי שאין נכבות
sources.says: The midrash tells of travelers who returned a year later and burned their feet on broom coals still alive under the ash.

sources.quote: כן דברי לשון רמיה שמראה בפני אדם שאין לבו רע עליו
sources.says: Radak says lying speech is like this: it shows a friendly face while speaking evil behind one's back.

120:5.headline: Meshech: a nation, or an exile dragged out
120:5.body: משך can be the nation Meshech, a son of Japheth. It can also mean "drawn out": an exile that has gone on too long. The midrash reads it as being dragged from one empire to the next.

sources.quote: הֲרֵי גַּרְתִּי מֶשֶׁךְ עִם בְּנֵי יֶפֶת
sources.says: Rashi says it is the nation Meshech, among the sons of Japheth.

sources.quote: בגלות משך, כלומר שנמשכה גלותי מאד
sources.says: Radak says it means my exile has been drawn out very long.

sources.quote: שהיו מוליכין אותי מבבל למדי וממדי ליון ומיון לאדום
sources.says: The midrash says it means being led from Babylon to Media, to Greece, to Edom.

121:1.headline: Only here: a song 'for' the ascents, not 'of' them
121:1.body: Every other song in this group opens שיר המעלות, but this one alone says שיר למעלות. Radak says the ל simply stands for 'the', while Rashi, citing the Sifrei, reads it as a song to the One who will build steps for the righteous to climb.

sources.quote: זה לבדו עם למ"ד והלמ"ד במקום ה"א הידיעה
sources.says: Radak says this psalm alone is written with ל, and the ל stands in place of 'the'.

sources.quote: שִׁיר הַמַּעֲלוֹת אֵין כָּתוּב כָּאן אֶלָּא שִׁיר לַמַּעֲלוֹת – שִׁיר לְמִי שֶׁעָתִיד לַעֲשׂוֹת מַעֲלוֹת לַצַּדִּיקִים לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא
sources.says: Rashi, citing the Sifrei, says the verse does not say 'song of ascents' but 'song for ascents': a song to the One who will make steps for the righteous in the time to come.

121:1.headline: Looking toward the hills, or standing on them to watch?
121:1.body: Radak, Metzudat Zion and Meiri read אל here as 'on'. The speaker is like a lookout on the hilltops, scanning for help to arrive, who then sees that help comes only from God.

sources.quote: ואל ההרים. כמו על ההרים
sources.says: Radak says 'to the hills' here means 'on the hills'.

sources.quote: כמו המצפה עזר מרחוק שעולה על ההרים ונושא עיניו אילך ואילך
sources.says: Radak compares it to someone waiting for help from far away, who climbs the hills and looks this way and that.

sources.quote: ומעמידים צופים על ההרים לראות מאין העוזרים באים
sources.says: Meiri says people at war post lookouts on the hills to see where their helpers are coming from.

121:3.headline: A wish, or a promise that you will not fall?
121:3.body: אל usually means 'may he not', which would make the verse a wish. Ibn Ezra and the Targum read it as 'he will not', a plain promise, while Rashi in the Talmud counts it as a request.

sources.quote: אל - כמו לא וככה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אל here means the same as לא, 'not'.

sources.quote: לא תפחד, כי לא יתן למוט רגליך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says: do not be afraid, for He will not let your feet slip.

sources.quote: לָא יִתֵּן לְאִתְמוֹטָטָא רִגְלָךְ
sources.says: The Targum translates with לא: He will not let your foot slip.

sources.quote: כגון (תהלים קכא) אל יתן למוט הרי לשון בקשה
sources.says: Rashi says words like אל can be a request or a statement about the future, and he gives this verse as a request.

121:4.headline: The guardian of Israel: Jacob, guarded while he slept
121:4.body: Ibn Ezra hears the patriarch Jacob, also named Israel, in this verse. God promised to guard Jacob wherever he went (Genesis 28:15), and Jacob was asleep when he heard it.

sources.quote: שומר ישראל - הוא יעקב אבינו: שמרתיך בכל אשר תלך, והוא היה ישן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Israel here is Jacob our father, to whom God said 'I will guard you wherever you go' while he was asleep.

121:6.headline: How can the moon strike you? Night chill, or night spirits
121:6.body: The sun's heat can hurt, but the moon? Radak and Metzudat David say the moon brings cold and damp that cause illness, while the Targum speaks of spirits that strike by day and by night.

sources.quote: שלא יככה חום השמש ביום וקור הירח בלילה
sources.says: Radak says God is a shade so the sun's heat by day and the moon's cold by night will not strike you.

sources.quote: ובלילה לא יזיק לך לחות הירח המביא תחלואים
sources.says: Metzudat David says at night the moon's dampness, which brings illness, will not harm you.

sources.quote: לָא יִמְחוּנָךְ צַפְרִירֵי וְלֵילֵי כַּד שַׁלִיט סִיהֲרָא
sources.says: The Targum says the morning spirits will not strike you when the sun rules, nor the night spirits when the moon rules.

121:8.headline: Going out and coming in: to war, to work, or home from exile
121:8.body: Ibn Ezra reads 'your going out and coming in' as going to war and coming back, and the Targum as going out to trade and coming in to study Torah. Meiri notes the order is the reverse of Moses' blessing in Deuteronomy 28:6 and reads it as leaving exile and coming home.

sources.quote: בצאתך למלחמה גם בבואך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means when you go out to war and when you come back.

sources.quote: מַפְקָךְ לִפְרַגְמַטְיָא וּמַעֲלָךְ לְמֶעֱסַק בְּאוֹרַיְתָא
sources.says: The Targum says: your going out to trade and your coming in to study Torah.

sources.quote: והקדים כאן היציאה לביאה ובדברי אדון הנביאים הקדים ביאה ליציאה
sources.says: Meiri notes that here going out comes first, while Moses put coming in first.

sources.quote: ודוד נבא על לשון הגלות ואמר ישמור צאתך מן הגלות ובואך לארץ
sources.says: Meiri says David spoke about the exile: God will guard your going out of exile and your coming into the land.

122:3.headline: A city joined together that makes all Israel friends
122:3.body: The midrash hears חברים, friends, in the word for 'joined together': Jerusalem makes all Israel companions. Rashi says the city 'joined' to it is Shiloh, the Tabernacle's earlier home, which scripture pairs with Jerusalem.

sources.quote: אמר רבי יהושע בן לוי עיר שהיא עושה כל ישראל חברים
sources.says: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says it is a city that makes all Israel friends.

sources.quote: כְּשִׁילֹה, שֶׁדִּמָּה הַכָּתוּב זוֹ לָזוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the city is like Shiloh, since scripture compares the two.

122:7.headline: Here חיל is the ring of defenses around the city wall
122:7.body: The word חיל often means strength or an army. Here Radak reads it as the ditch around the wall, Metzudat Zion as the low outer wall, and Ibn Ezra as the ground just outside the wall.

sources.quote: החפירה שהיא סביב החומה יקרא חיל
sources.says: Radak says the ditch around the wall is called חיל.

sources.quote: היא החומה הנמוכה אשר מחוץ להחומה הגבוהה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the low wall outside the high wall.

sources.quote: הוא הסובב מחוץ לחומה בארמנותיך, לפנים מן החומה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says חיל is what surrounds the outside of the wall, while the palaces are inside it.

123:4.headline: Written as one word, read aloud as two
123:4.body: The written text has one word found nowhere else, meaning "the very proud". It is read aloud as two words, לגאי יונים. Metzudat Zion hears both pride and oppression in it, and Rashi hears גיא היונים, "the valley of doves", meaning Jerusalem.

sources.quote: כְּתִיב חַד וְקָרִינָן תְּרֵין
sources.says: Rashi notes that it is written as one word and read as two.

sources.quote: שֶׁבָּזוּ אֶת גֵּיא הַיּוֹנִים, הִיא יְרוּשָׁלַיִם
sources.says: Rashi explains the scorn as that of people who scorned the valley of the doves, which is Jerusalem.

sources.quote: היא מלה מורכבת מלשון גאוה ומלשון אונאה וגזל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is built from two roots: pride, and oppression or robbery.

sources.quote: מלה אחת בכתוב והוא כמו גאים
sources.says: Radak says the written form is one word meaning the proud.

124:1.headline: "Let Israel say": the people, or Jacob himself
124:1.body: Radak reads Israel as the nation in exile. The midrash reads it as Israel the elder, Jacob, who it says recited the Songs of Ascents through twenty years at Laban's house.

sources.quote: כאן שכב הא כל עשרים שנה שהיה בבית לבן לא שכב. ומה היה אומר ט"ו שיר המעלות שבספר תהלים
sources.says: The midrash says this is Israel the elder: in twenty years at Laban's house Jacob never lay down, and he recited the fifteen Songs of Ascents.

sources.quote: יאמר נא ישראל. בהגלות
sources.says: Radak says it is Israel speaking in exile.

124:2.headline: One "man" standing for a whole enemy nation
124:2.body: The verse says "a man" rose against us. Ibn Ezra says the singular word means many. The midrash says this man is Egypt, since Isaiah calls Egypt "man and not God".

sources.quote: אדם - לשון רבים והעד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אדם here means many people, and the next verse proves it.

sources.quote: ואין אדם אלא מצרים שנאמר (ישעיה לא ג) ומצרים אדם ולא אל
sources.says: The midrash says "man" here is Egypt, as Isaiah says "Egypt is man and not God".

124:3.headline: Swallowed alive, or eaten raw
124:3.body: Radak reads חיים as raw: the enemy was so hungry it would not wait to cook its food. Ibn Ezra reads it as "while we were still alive", like those who went down alive to the grave.

sources.quote: כי אין דרך אדם לאכול הבשר כי אם מבושל והם מרוב תאותם לבלענו חיים היו בולעין אותנו
sources.says: Radak says people eat meat cooked, but the enemies wanted us so badly they would swallow us raw.

sources.quote: כאילו אמר בלעונו ואנחנו חיים, וירדו חיים שאולה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means they swallowed us while we were alive, as in "they went down alive to Sheol".

124:4.headline: A flooding stream, or a sickness
124:4.body: Radak reads נחלה as a stream, נחל, with an added ה. Rashi and the Targum read it as sickness, from חולי.

sources.quote: נחל שוטף, והמלה קריאתה מלעיל הטעם בנו"ן וה"א נוספת
sources.says: Radak says it is a flooding stream; the stress falls on the first syllable and the ה is added.

sources.quote: נַחְלָה. לְשׁוֹן חוֹלִי
sources.says: Rashi says the word means sickness.

sources.quote: מַרְעִית עָבְרָא עַל נַפְשָׁנָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it "sickness passed over our soul".

sources.quote: מלת נחלה – על שלש דרכים וכולם שונים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word נחלה comes in three different forms in the Bible, and explains how this one differs.

125:1.headline: Mount Zion does not 'sit' forever, it endures
125:1.body: ישב usually means to sit or to dwell. Radak and Meiri say that here it means to stand firm and last, and Meiri also offers 'it will be lived in again'.

sources.quote: ופי' ישב. יעמוד לעולם ויהיה קיים, וכן ואתה קדוש יושב
sources.says: Radak says ישב means it will stand forever and endure, as in 'You, holy one, are enthroned'.

sources.quote: ר״ל יעמוד קיים, או הוא כמו יתישב
sources.says: Meiri says it means it will stand and endure, or that it will be settled again.

125:5.headline: Those who turn aside, heard by the midrash as a bier
125:5.body: Plainly, המטים are those who turn aside onto crooked paths. The midrash hears מטה, a bier, in the word: whoever speaks ill of Torah scholars after their death falls into Gehinnom.

sources.quote: והמטים. מלשון נטיה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from 'turning aside'.

sources.quote: כל המספר אחר מטתן של תלמידי חכמים נופל בגיהנם שנאמר והמטים עקלקלותם יוליכם ה'
sources.says: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says whoever speaks ill after the bier of Torah scholars falls into Gehinnom, citing this verse.

126:1.headline: God brings Zion back, or comes back with it?
126:1.body: Radak and Metzudat David read בשוב as God bringing the exiles home, and Radak also offers 'giving them rest'. Meiri reads the next word, את, as 'with', so God returns together with them, since the sages taught that God shares Israel's suffering in exile.

sources.quote: בשוב. ענין הנחה כמו שיבה ה' רבבות וגומר או יהיה ענין תשובה ויהיה פעל יוצא
sources.says: Radak says בשוב may mean giving rest, as in Numbers 10:36, or it may mean bringing back.

sources.quote: כאשר ישיב ה׳‎ מן גלות בבל את בני ציון
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means when God brings the people of Zion back from Babylonian exile.

sources.quote: כמו שדרשו רז״ל בפסוק בכל צרתם לו צר
sources.says: Meiri ties the verse to the sages' teaching on 'in all their distress He was distressed' (Isaiah 63:9).

sources.quote: ולפי זה את כמו עם
sources.says: Meiri says that on this reading את means 'with'.

126:1.headline: Like dreamers, or like the sick made well?
126:1.body: Radak says the years of exile will feel like a bad dream once the joy comes, and Ibn Ezra says the return is a wonder you would only expect to see in a dream. The Targum reads it differently: like sick people who have been healed.

sources.quote: כחלום יעוף בעינינו צרת הגלות מרוב השמחה
sources.says: Radak, in his father's name, says the pain of exile will fly away like a dream because of the great joy.

sources.quote: אין אדם רואה בהקיץ הפלא הזה רק בחלום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says no one sees such a wonder while awake, only in a dream.

sources.quote: הֲוֵינָא הֵיךְ מַרְעַיָא דְאִתַּסְיָן
sources.says: The Targum translates: we were like sick people who have been healed.

126:5.headline: Sowing in tears stands for keeping the commandments in exile
126:5.body: A farmer sowing dry ground weeps, afraid nothing will grow. Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra say the sowing stands for Israel doing good deeds in exile, and the joyful harvest is the reward that comes with redemption.

sources.quote: והזריעה היא מעשה המצות ועושים אותם בדמעה מפני צרת הגלות
sources.says: Radak says the sowing is doing the commandments, done in tears because of the hardship of exile.

sources.quote: כָּךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל זוֹרְעִין לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא צְדָקָה בְּדִמְעָה בַּגָּלוּת
sources.says: Rashi says Israel sows charity before God in tears in exile, and will reap in joy when their reward is paid.

sources.quote: ודימה בני הגלות הזורעי. והטעם: שומרי התורה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the sowers stand for the people in exile who keep the Torah.

126:6.headline: The seed bag, or seed so precious it is worth weeping over
126:6.body: Ibn Ezra and Meiri say משך is the bag the sower carries his seed in. Radak reads it as 'precious seed': seed is costly in dry land, which is why the poor sower weeps as he carries it.

sources.quote: וטעם משך – הכלי שיש בו הזרע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says משך is the container that holds the seed.

sources.quote: והוא הכלי שהזורע נושא בו הזרע ונקרא כן על שהזרע נזרע במשך השדה
sources.says: Meiri says it is the container the sower carries seed in, named for the seed being sown along the length of the field.

sources.quote: פירוש יקר הזרע ונקרא הדבר היקר משך
sources.says: Radak says it means precious seed, and a precious thing is called משך.

sources.quote: נושא משיכת והולכת הזרע אל השדה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means carrying and drawing the seed out to the field.

127:2.headline: Sleep as the gift, or the gift that comes while you sleep?
127:2.body: שנא is 'sleep', spelled here with א instead of ה. Ibn Ezra reads sleep as the gift itself, the sweet rest of the worker, while Radak and Meiri say God gives His beloved what others toil for, without effort, as if in his sleep.

sources.quote: ושנא הכתוב באל"ף והוא כמו בה"א
sources.says: Radak says שנא is written with א but means the same as with ה.

sources.quote: שינה - על דרך מתוקה שנת העובד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means sleep, like 'sweet is the sleep of the worker' (Ecclesiastes 5:11).

sources.quote: כן נתן האל יתברך המלוכה בלא עמל לשלמה כאדם ההישן
sources.says: Radak says God gave Solomon the kingdom without toil, like a man asleep.

sources.quote: יתן לידידו שינה ר״ל לאשר חפץ בו בשינה ר״ל במנוחה ובלא עמל
sources.says: Meiri says God gives it to the one He loves 'in sleep', meaning at rest and without toil.

127:5.headline: Enemies at the gate, or scholars arguing over the law?
127:5.body: Radak reads it plainly: a man with many good sons need not fear his enemies at the city gate. Rashi and Meiri say the 'enemies' are scholars who argue hard over the law, look like enemies for the moment, and end up friends.

sources.quote: ויוכלו לדבר בשער לפני אויביהם ולא יבושו ולא יחתו מהם
sources.says: Radak says the father and sons can speak at the gate before their enemies without shame or fear.

sources.quote: תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים, שֶׁמְּנַצְּחִין זֶה אֶת זֶה בַּהֲלָכָה וְנִרְאִים כְּאוֹיְבִים זֶה לָזֶה
sources.says: Rashi says these are scholars who defeat each other in legal debate and look like enemies to each other.

sources.quote: נעשו אויבים זה לזה ולא זזו משם עד שנעשו אוהבים
sources.says: Meiri cites the sages: they become enemies to each other, and do not leave until they become friends.

sources.quote: עם אותם החולקים עמהם בדבר חכמת התורה הנראים כאילו היו אויבים להם
sources.says: Metzudat David says these are people who disagree with them about Torah and seem like enemies because of the dispute.

128:1.headline: "Everyone" here is there to include women
128:1.body: Other psalms say "happy is the man" (אשרי האיש). This one says "happy is everyone" (כל) who fears God, and Rashi says the word is there to include women.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁכָּתוּב ״אַשְׁרֵי הָאִישׁ״ (תהלים א:א), ״אַשְׁרֵי אִישׁ״ (תהלים קיב:א), לְכָךְ נֶאֱמַר כָּאן כָּל, לְרַבּוֹת אִשָּׁה
sources.says: Rashi says that since other verses say "happy is the man", this one says "everyone" to include a woman.

128:6.headline: Peace on Israel: a second blessing, or the result of grandchildren?
128:6.body: Ibn Ezra reads "see" twice: you will see grandchildren, and you will see peace on Israel. The Talmud links the two: if your sons have children, no widow must marry her husband's brother, so the family stays at peace.

sources.quote: ישרת בעבור אחר. וכן הוא וראה שלום על ישראל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word "see" serves a second phrase too: "and see peace on Israel".

sources.quote: כֵּיוָן שֶׁ״בָנִים לְבָנֶיךָ״ — ״שָׁלוֹם עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל״. דְּלָא אָתֵי לִידֵי חֲלִיצָה וְיִבּוּם
sources.says: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says that once there are grandchildren there is peace, because no one comes to the brother-in-law marriage or its release.

sources.quote: יִירְשׁוּ נַחֲלָה, וְאֵין אִשָּׁה זְקוּקָה לְיָבָם, אָז שָׁלוֹם בָּעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says the grandchildren inherit, no woman is bound to a brother-in-law, and then there is peace.

129:1.headline: Many enemies, or great suffering?
129:1.body: רבת can mean 'much' or 'many'. Radak reads great distress since the exile began, while Metzudat David reads many peoples attacking.

sources.quote: צררו אותנו האויבים צרה רבה
sources.says: Radak says the enemies caused great distress from the very start of the exile.

sources.quote: הן רבת עם צררו אותי מעת נעורי
sources.says: Metzudat David says many peoples have attacked me since my youth.

129:3.headline: The furrow: enemies plowed long rows across Israel's back
129:3.body: מעניתם is the row a plow cuts down a field. The longer the row, the longer the oxen pull without rest, so the enemies gave Israel no rest.

sources.quote: הוּא תֶּלֶם הַמַּחֲרֵשָׁה
sources.says: Rashi says it is the furrow of the plow, as in I Samuel 14:14.

sources.quote: וכל מה שיהיה ארוך המענית תהיה יגיע השוורים רבה
sources.says: Radak says a longer furrow means more work for the oxen, so the enemies never let Israel rest.

130:1.headline: Depths of trouble, or a low place to pray from?
130:1.body: Radak reads ממעמקים, "from the depths", as a picture: exile is like deep water. The midrash reads it as a rule: do not stand on a raised place to pray, because there is no room for pride before God.

sources.quote: דימה הגלות למעמקי מים
sources.says: Radak says the psalm compares exile to the depths of the water.

sources.quote: לעולם אל יעמוד אדם במקום גבוה ויתפלל משום שנאמר ממעמקים קראתיך
sources.says: The midrash learns from this word that a person should not stand on a high place to pray.

sources.quote: שאין גבהות לפני המקום
sources.says: It gives the reason: there is no haughtiness before God.

130:4.headline: Why would forgiving people make them fear God?
130:4.body: It seems odd that forgiveness leads to awe. Rashi says only God forgives, not an angel, so no one can count on someone else's pardon; Ibn Ezra says that without forgiveness, sinners would give up and stop fearing God at all.

sources.quote: לֹא נָתַתָּ רְשׁוּת לְשָׁלִיחַ לִסְלֹחַ
sources.says: Rashi says God did not give a messenger the power to forgive.

sources.quote: שֶׁלֹּא יְהֵא אָדָם בָּטוּחַ עַל סְלִיחַת אַחֵר
sources.says: Rashi says this is why God is feared: no one can rely on forgiveness from anyone else.

sources.quote: ואם לא תסלח - לא ייראוך ויעשו חפצם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that if God did not forgive, people would not fear him and would do as they please.

130:5.headline: "I hoped" twice: once for this life, once for after it
130:5.body: The verse says "I hoped" and then "my soul hoped". Radak and Meiri read two different hopes: rescue in this world, and a place with God after death. Metzudat David reads the repeat as one hope that does not let go.

sources.quote: אני קויתי אותו בעולם הזה שיראני הישועה וקיותה אותה גם כן נפשי במותי
sources.says: Radak says the first hope is to see rescue in this world, and the second is the soul's hope at death.

sources.quote: וקותה נפשי רומז לתקותו בעולם הבא
sources.says: Meiri says "my soul hoped" points to hope for the world to come.

sources.quote: כפל הדבר להתמדתו
sources.says: Metzudat David says the words are doubled to show the hope lasts.

132:1.headline: David's "hardships" are the self-denial of finding the Temple's place
132:1.body: עֻנּוֹתוֹ comes from עינוי, hardship you put on yourself. Rashi says it is David's self-denial as he labored to find a place for God, and the Targum has סגופיה, his self-denial.

sources.quote: עִנּוּי נַפְשׁוֹ אֲשֶׁר טָרַח וְעָמַל לִמְצֹא לְךָ מָקוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says it is the affliction of his soul, when he worked and toiled to find a place for You.

sources.quote: מגזרת עינוי והוא שם מהבנין שלא נקרא שם פועלו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from עינוי and is a noun of the form where the doer is not named.

sources.quote: יַת כָּל סִגוּפֵיהּ
sources.says: The Targum renders it as all his self-denial.

132:2.headline: "Mighty One of Jacob": what אביר means, and why Jacob
132:2.body: Metzudat Zion says אביר comes from a word for strength. Metzudat David says the vow is tied to Jacob because he was the first to make a vow.

sources.quote: ענין חוזק כמו ומשך אבירים בכחו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אביר is about strength, like ומשך אבירים בכחו.

sources.quote: ותלה ביעקב לפי שהוא היה תחילה להנודרים
sources.says: Metzudat David says the vow is hung on Jacob because he was the first of those who vowed.

sources.quote: למי שקראהו יעקב אבירו כמו שאמר מידי אביר יעקב
sources.says: Radak says it means the One whom Jacob called his אביר, as in מידי אביר יעקב.

sources.quote: לְתַקִיפָא דְיַעֲקֹב
sources.says: The Targum renders it as the Strong One of Jacob.

132:3.headline: אם here is an oath: "I will not enter my house"
132:3.body: אם usually means "if". Here Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra read it as the start of an oath, so "if I enter" means "I swear I will not". Radak adds that it is an exaggeration.

sources.quote: הוא ענין שבועה וגזם
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is an oath and an exaggeration.

sources.quote: נדר שלא יבא אל ביתו לירושלם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a vow not to come to his house in Jerusalem.

sources.quote: אם אעלה דרך הפלגה
sources.says: Radak says אם אעלה is said by way of exaggeration.

132:4.headline: שנת: regular sleep, a midday nap, or sleep for pleasure?
132:4.body: Radak says it means fixed, regular sleep. Ibn Ezra says it is the midday nap, and Metzudat David says it is sleeping for enjoyment, beyond what keeps a person alive.

sources.quote: רוצה לומר שינה קבועה
sources.says: Radak says it means regular sleep.

sources.quote: והנכון שהיא שנת צהרים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the right reading is that it is the midday sleep.

sources.quote: להיות ישן להתענג יותר מההכרח להחיות את הנפש
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means sleeping for pleasure, more than the need to keep the soul alive.

132:6.headline: "We heard of it": what is the "it"?
132:6.body: The ending ־ה means "it", but the verse does not say what. Rashi says it is the news, Radak says it is the divine presence, since the word is feminine, and Meiri says it is the place.

sources.quote: שְׁמַעֲנוּהָ. הַבְּשׂוֹרָה
sources.says: Rashi says what they heard is the tidings.

sources.quote: לשון נקבה רוצה לומר שכינת הכבוד
sources.says: Radak says the feminine form means the presence of the Glory.

sources.quote: ואמ׳ שמענו מאז דרך קבלה שהמקום ראוי להיות באיזה מקום שבאפרת
sources.says: Meiri says they heard from of old, by tradition, that the place should be somewhere in Ephrath.

132:6.headline: אפרתה: a distinguished place, or Bethlehem?
132:6.body: Rashi says אפרתה means a distinguished place, like the distinguished "Ephrathite" in Samuel. Metzudat David says it is Ephrath, Bethlehem, where David was born.

sources.quote: בְּמָקוֹם הֶחָשׁוּב וְהַמְעֻלֶּה
sources.says: Rashi says it means in the important and exalted place.

sources.quote: באפרת מקום מולדתי כי היא בית לחם
sources.says: Metzudat David says Ephrath is the place of David's birth, because it is Bethlehem.

sources.quote: קרוב הוא אל בית לחם אפרתה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the chosen place is near Bethlehem Ephrath.

132:6.headline: "Fields of the forest": a real forest, or the land of Benjamin?
132:6.body: Rashi says the "forest" is the territory of Benjamin, which was likened to a wild beast, a wolf. Radak and Metzudat David say it was a real place with forest trees, the threshing floor where Isaac was bound.

sources.quote: בִּגְבוּל בִּנְיָמִין שֶׁנִּמְשַׁל לְחַיַּת הַיַּעַר
sources.says: Rashi says it is the border of Benjamin, who was likened to a beast of the forest.

sources.quote: כי עצי יער היו שם
sources.says: Radak says there were forest trees there.

sources.quote: והיה גם שם עצי יער כי הוא המקום שנעקד עליו יצחק
sources.says: Metzudat David says forest trees were there too, because it is the place where Isaac was bound.

132:7.headline: The Temple is called God's footstool
132:7.body: הדום is a footstool. Metzudat David says the Temple is called God's footstool as a picture: He sits in heaven above and His feet come down to rest in the Temple. Radak says the Temple stands exactly opposite the throne of glory.

sources.quote: הוא שרפרף הכסא הנתון תחת רגלי האדם כשהוא יושב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says הדום is the stool of the chair placed under a person's feet when he sits.

sources.quote: ואחז דרך משל כאילו מושבו בשמים ממעל ורגליו יורדים לנוח
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is a picture, as if He sits in heaven above and His feet come down to rest.

sources.quote: הוא באמת שהוא מכוון כנגד כסא הכבוד
sources.says: Radak says it is truly set opposite the throne of glory.

132:8.headline: The Ark is called God's "strength"
132:8.body: Rashi says the Ark and the Temple are both called God's עז, "strength", as in "He gave His strength to captivity". Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion say it is because God showed His power through the Ark among the Philistines.

sources.quote: מִקְדָּשׁ וְאָרוֹן נִקְרְאוּ עֻזּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the Temple and the Ark are called His strength.

sources.quote: אשר הראת לכל את עוזך וכח זרועך בפלשתים
sources.says: Metzudat David says the Ark is where God showed everyone His strength and the power of His arm against the Philistines.

sources.quote: על שהראה בפלשתים עוז כח המקום
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is said of the Ark because God showed His power among the Philistines.

132:9.headline: "Clothed in righteousness" means the priests' own garments
132:9.body: Radak and Metzudat David say צדק here is the priestly garments. Metzudat David says they bring atonement and make sinners righteous, and Ibn Ezra says it is because priests teach the Torah and judge Israel.

sources.quote: בגדי כהונה נקראים בגדי צדק כי הם מכפרים ומצדיקים את החוטאים
sources.says: Metzudat David says priestly garments are called garments of righteousness because they atone and make sinners righteous.

sources.quote: וטעם לאמר על הכהנים בגדי צדק, כי הם מורים את התורה ושופטי ישראל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the priests' garments are called garments of righteousness because they teach the Torah and are judges of Israel.

sources.quote: לְבוּשִׁין דִזְכוּ
sources.says: The Targum renders it as garments of merit.

132:9.headline: חסידיך, "your devoted ones", means the Levite singers
132:9.body: חסידיך usually means "your devoted ones". Here Ibn Ezra, Meiri and the Targum say it means the Levites who sing, and Meiri cites "to Levi He said ... to your devoted man".

sources.quote: וחסידיך - הם הלוים המשוררים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says חסידיך are the Levites who sing.

sources.quote: וחסידיך ר״ל הלויים כמו שכתו׳ ללוי אמר תמיך ואוריך לאיש חסידך
sources.says: Meiri says חסידיך means the Levites, as written, to Levi He said your Tumim and Urim to your devoted man.

sources.quote: וְלֵוָאֵי חֲסִידָיִךְ יְשַׁבְּחוּן
sources.says: The Targum renders it as the Levites, your devoted ones, will praise.

132:10.headline: Who is the "anointed" the prayer asks God to answer?
132:10.body: Rashi and the Targum say משיחך is Solomon, bringing the Ark into the Temple. Ibn Ezra says it is David, the same person named twice in the verse.

sources.quote: שְׁלֹמֹה, בְּבוֹאוֹ לְהַכְנִיס שָׁם אֶת הָאָרוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says it is Solomon, when he comes to bring the Ark in there.

sources.quote: לָא תְּתֵיב אַפֵּי שְׁלֹמֹה מְשִׁיחָךְ
sources.says: The Targum renders it as do not turn away the face of Solomon, your anointed.

sources.quote: הוא דוד, כי הטעם כפול כמשפט
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is David, because the sense is doubled, as is the way.

132:12.headline: "I will teach them" does not mean a new Torah
132:12.body: Radak says אלמדם cannot mean a new law, since no later law is coming after Moses' Torah. It means God will keep rousing them through prophets so they do not forget. Meiri says the future tense stands for the past.

sources.quote: אלא פי' אלמדם אעורר אותם על ידי נביאים תמיד שלא ישכחו התורה
sources.says: Radak says אלמדם means I will rouse them through prophets always, so that they do not forget the Torah.

sources.quote: ואלמדם עתיד במקום עבר
sources.says: Meiri says אלמדם is a future form standing in the place of the past.

132:16.headline: The priests wear righteousness, and God dresses them in salvation
132:16.body: Verse 9 had the priests put on צדק. Here God dresses them in ישע, salvation. Radak says it repays them for wearing priestly garments in His service, and Ibn Ezra says the salvation will show on them like a garment.

sources.quote: תחת שהם לבושים בעבודתי בגדי כהונה אני אלבישם בגדי ישע
sources.says: Radak says that instead of their wearing priestly garments in My service, I will clothe them in garments of salvation.

sources.quote: שתהיה ישועה מפורסמת ונראה עליהם כבגד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says salvation will be well known and will show on them like a garment.

sources.quote: תבוא הישועה כי המה מכפרים
sources.says: Metzudat David says salvation will come through the priestly garments, because they atone.

132:17.headline: A "horn" for David means strength and kingship
132:17.body: קרן, "horn", stands here for strength and rule. Metzudat Zion says the word is borrowed because horned animals gain strength from their horns when they fight.

sources.quote: קרן. חוזק ומלכות
sources.says: Radak says קרן means strength and kingship.

sources.quote: המלה ההיא הושאל לממשלה והתחזקות ע״ש שבעלי הקרנים יתחזקו בהם בהלחמם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is borrowed for rule and strength, because animals with horns grow strong with them when they fight.

132:18.headline: יציץ: his crown will shine, blossom, or show itself?
132:18.body: Rashi says יציץ means to shine, like gleaming bronze. Ibn Ezra says it means to come out and be seen, and Radak adds a view that it comes from the gold ציץ, the priest's plate.

sources.quote: יָאִיר, כְּמוֹ ״וְנֹצְצִים כְּעֵין נְחֹשֶׁת״
sources.says: Rashi says יציץ means to shine, like וְנֹצְצִים כְּעֵין נְחֹשֶׁת.

sources.quote: כמו יצא ונראה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means to go out and be seen.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים יציץ מן ועשית ציץ זהב
sources.says: Radak says some explain יציץ as from ועשית ציץ זהב.

135:7.headline: God brings out the wind, or finds it ready in storehouses
135:7.body: Radak and Meiri read מוצא as 'brings out'. Rashi reads it from the word for 'find': God set up storehouses for the wind, where it is ready to hand when He sends it.

sources.quote: מוצא כמו מוציא
sources.says: Radak says מוצא is like מוציא, 'brings out'.

sources.quote: ומוצא רוח כמו ומוציא
sources.says: Meiri also reads it as 'and brings out wind'.

sources.quote: מוֹצֵא. לְשׁוֹן מְצִיאָה, כְּלוֹמַר: אוֹצָרוֹת תִּקֵּן לָרוּחַ, וְשָׁם הֵם מְצוּיִין לוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is from 'finding': God prepared storehouses for the wind, and there the winds are at hand for Him.

135:14.headline: God 'relents' over His servants, said only as a figure of speech
135:14.body: Meiri reads יתנחם as 'will relent', and says such words are used of God only as a manner of speaking. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as God thinking again, so as to do His servants good.

sources.quote: ועל עבדיו יתנחם ר״ל יתחרט מענין וינחם ה׳ על הרעה
sources.says: Meiri says יתנחם means he will regret, as in 'the LORD relented from the evil'.

sources.quote: וכלם אצל האל נאמרים דרך העברה
sources.says: Meiri says all such words are said of God in a borrowed, figurative way.

sources.quote: יִתְנֶחָם. יִתְעַשֵּׁת
sources.says: Rashi glosses it as 'he will reconsider'.

sources.quote: יחשוב מחשבה אחרת להיטיב להם
sources.says: Metzudat David says God will think a different thought, to do them good.

135:15.headline: Idols are called עצבים because they bring only sorrow
135:15.body: The word for idols, עצבים, shares its letters with the word for grief. Ibn Ezra says the name mocks them as useless sorrow, and Metzudat Zion says they grieve those who call to them and get no answer.

sources.quote: קראם עצבים דרך בזיון, שאין בהם תועלת רק עצבון חנם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are called עצבים in contempt, since they bring no benefit, only pointless sorrow.

sources.quote: כי מעצבת לב עובדיה קורא אליה ואינו נענה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the idol grieves the heart of its worshipper, who calls to it and gets no answer.

135:17.headline: Here אף means 'even', not 'nose' as in Psalm 115
135:17.body: Rashi notes that this אף is voweled differently from 'a nose they have' in Psalm 115, so here it means 'even': the idols do not even have breath. The Targum instead translates it as 'nostrils'.

sources.quote: גַּם רוּחַ אֵין בְּפִיהֶם אֲפִלּוּ כַּבְּהֵמָה זוֹ
sources.says: Rashi reads it as 'even': they have no breath in their mouths, not even like an animal.

sources.quote: אַף זֶה פַּתָּח, וְ״אַף לָהֶם וְלֹא יְרִיחוּן״ (תהלים קטו:ו) קָמַץ
sources.says: Rashi says this אף has a patach, while 'a nose they have but cannot smell' in Psalm 115 has a kamatz.

sources.quote: נְחִירֵי וְלָא אִית רוּחָא דְחַיֵי בְּפוּמְהוֹן
sources.says: The Targum translates: nostrils, and there is no breath of life in their mouths.

135:20.headline: Who are 'those who fear the LORD'? Rashi says converts
135:20.body: After Israel, Aaron and Levi, the verse adds 'those who fear the LORD'. Rashi says these are converts, Metzudat David says the pious of the nations, and Radak says the sages, or God-fearers from every people.

sources.quote: יִרְאֵי ה׳. אֵלּוּ הַגֵּרִים
sources.says: Rashi says those who fear the LORD are the converts.

sources.quote: אלו חסידי או״‎ה
sources.says: Metzudat David says these are the pious of the nations of the world.

sources.quote: הם החכמים בישראל המתבודדים בבית ה' ללמוד. או פירוש יראי אשר בכל עם
sources.says: Radak says they are the sages who study in the house of the LORD, or the God-fearers of every people.

136:2.headline: 'God of gods': the gods here are angels
136:2.body: אלהים can mean God, but here it means beings under God. Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David say they are the angels, who are like gods to those beneath them, while God rules over them.

sources.quote: הם המלאכים והם אלהים לאשר למטה מהם והוא אלהים עליהם
sources.says: Radak says these are the angels, who are gods to those below them, and God is God over them.
