sources.quote: המלאכים העליונים שאינם גופות ולא כגופות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says these are the higher angels, which are not bodies.

sources.quote: האלהים. הם מלאכי מעלה
sources.says: Metzudat David says the gods are the angels above.

136:3.headline: 'Lord of lords': the turning heavens, angels, or stars?
136:3.body: The commentators disagree on who these 'lords' are. Radak says the heavenly spheres that run the world below, Ibn Ezra says angels, and Metzudat David the stars and constellations, all ruled by God.

sources.quote: הם הגלגלים שהם אדונים על השפלים והמנהיגים אותם והוא אדון עליהם
sources.says: Radak says these are the spheres, which are lords over the lower world and guide it, and God is Lord over them.

sources.quote: המלאכים - הם אדוני הארץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says these are the angels, the lords of the earth.

sources.quote: הם צבא השמים וכסיליהם שהם אדונים למשול בארץ
sources.says: Metzudat David says these are the hosts of heaven and their constellations, which rule over the earth.

136:4.headline: 'Alone': no angel helped, because none existed yet
136:4.body: Rashi says that when God made heaven, earth, sun and moon, no angel had been created yet. Metzudat David says God needed no help from the angels, and Meiri says nothing at all existed beside Him.

sources.quote: בָּרִאשׁוֹנָה לֹא נִבְרָא מַלְאָךְ כְּשֶׁעֲשָׂאָן לַנִּפְלָאוֹת הַלָּלוּ
sources.says: Rashi says no angel had been created when God made these wonders.

sources.quote: ואינו צריך לעזר מלאכי מעלה
sources.says: Metzudat David says God does not need help from the angels above.

sources.quote: ואומ׳ לבדו שלא היה שם לא מלאך ולא גלגל ולא שום דבר
sources.says: Meiri says 'alone' means there was no angel, no sphere, and nothing else there.

136:6.headline: The earth hammered out flat like beaten gold
136:6.body: רקע is the word for beating metal into thin sheets, as a goldsmith does with gold, Rashi and Metzudat Zion say. Metzudat David adds the wonder: water naturally rises over land, yet God spread the land out above it.

sources.quote: לרוקע. ענין שטיחה ופרישה כמו וצורף בזהב ירקענו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means spreading out flat, like 'the smith beats it out with gold' (Isaiah 40:19).

sources.quote: וירקעו. כְּמוֹ לְרֹקַע הָאָרֶץ
sources.says: Rashi says the verb in Exodus 39:3 is the same as 'spreading out the earth' here.

sources.quote: טַסִּין הָיוּ מְרַדְּדִין מִן הַזָּהָב
sources.says: Rashi says it means hammering gold into thin plates.

sources.quote: והוא נגד הטבע כי טבע המים לעלות ממעל לארץ
sources.says: Metzudat David says this goes against nature, since water naturally rises above the land.

136:13.headline: Split into pieces: twelve paths, or a U-shaped road?
136:13.body: Why 'into pieces' and not just 'split'? Rashi says the sea split into twelve paths, one for each tribe, while Radak and Meiri say it was cut in sections so Israel walked in a curve and came out on the same shore they went in.

sources.quote: שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר קְרָעִים לִשְׁנֵים עָשָׂר שְׁבָטִים
sources.says: Rashi says it means twelve splits for the twelve tribes.

sources.quote: ויש לפרש כי לפיכך אמר לגזרים לפי שנגזר הים לרוחבו עד חציו או יותר ואחר כך לארכו ולרחבו
sources.says: Radak says it can also mean the sea was cut across its width to the middle, then along its length, then back across.

sources.quote: ונמצא שבאותו צד עצמו שנכנסו באותו צד יצאו
sources.says: Meiri says that this way they came out on the same side they went in.

136:21.headline: Why only Sihon and Og's land? It was a gift never promised
136:21.body: Canaan was already promised to Abraham, so giving it was keeping a promise. Radak and Ibn Ezra say the land of Sihon and Og, east of the Jordan, was never in that promise, so the psalm counts it as pure kindness.

sources.quote: שלא היה בברית לתתה להם, על כן הזכירה נחלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this land was not in the covenant to be given to them, so the psalm calls it an inheritance.

sources.quote: אבל ארץ סיחון ועוג שלא נתנה לאברהם ונתנה להם זה היה חסד
sources.says: Radak says the land of Sihon and Og was not given to Abraham, so giving it to Israel was kindness.

sources.quote: לפיכך לא זכר בזה המזמור ממלכות כנען
sources.says: Radak says that is why this psalm does not mention the kingdoms of Canaan.

136:24.headline: Rescued by being torn loose from our enemies
136:24.body: Metzudat Zion says פרק is the Aramaic word for rescue. Ibn Ezra ties it to the wind that 'tears apart mountains' (I Kings 19:11): God broke Israel loose from those who held it.

sources.quote: ויפרקנו. הוא תרגום של ישועה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is the Aramaic translation of 'rescue'.

sources.quote: פורק – כמו מציל, כמו ויפרקנו מצרינו (תהלים קלו כד), ושניהם מגזרת מפרק הרים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says פורק means rescuer, like ויפרקנו here, and both come from 'tearing apart mountains'.

137:1.headline: ישבנו: they sat down for the first time since Jerusalem
137:1.body: The Midrash says the captives were not allowed to sit at all from Jerusalem to the Euphrates. Ibn Ezra and Radak hear in the word the stunned stillness of people in grief.

sources.quote: מלמד שלא היה להם ישיבה משיצאו מירושלים עד שהגיעו לפרת
sources.says: The Midrash says they had no sitting down from the time they left Jerusalem until they reached the Euphrates.

sources.quote: וטעם ישבנו – כמו משתוממים, יושב משמים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ישבנו means sitting stunned, like one who sits desolate.

sources.quote: היינו שם מתבודדים יושבין ושוממין
sources.says: Radak says they were there alone, sitting and desolate.

137:2.headline: תלינו: hung the harps up, or tuned them tight?
137:2.body: Radak says the Levites hung their harps on the willows and sat crying. Meiri asks how captives could have carried harps at all, and reads 'hanging' as stretching the strings to play under force.

sources.quote: והיינו תולים אותו על ערבים והיינו יושבים ובוכים
sources.says: Radak says they hung the harp on the willows and sat crying.

sources.quote: ותמה אני לפירושם איך היו נושאים הכנורות
sources.says: Meiri says all the commentators explain that the harps were hung on the trees, and he wonders how they could have carried the harps.

sources.quote: ואותו הפשוט הוא קורא תליה כי כל שטיחת דבר ומתיחתו להעמידו על מתכונתו יאמ׳ בלשון תליה
sources.says: Meiri says the psalm calls stretching the strings 'hanging', because spreading and stretching a thing into its proper shape is called תליה.

137:4.headline: אדמת נכר: a foreign people's land, or a foreign god's?
137:4.body: Ibn Ezra says it can mean the land of a foreign nation or the land of a foreign god. Radak takes the second: a foreign god's land is the opposite of a song to God.

sources.quote: אדמת גוי נכר, או אדמת אל נכר הפך שיר ה'
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the land of a foreign nation, or the land of a foreign god, the opposite of God's song.

sources.quote: אדמת אל נכר הפך שיר לה'
sources.says: Radak says it is the land of a foreign god, the opposite of a song to God.

137:5.headline: תשכח: how can a right hand forget?
137:5.body: Radak says the hand forgets how to play, since the right hand plucks the harp. Ibn Ezra cites some who read it as 'wither', and Meiri says the hand loses all its skill.

sources.quote: תשכח הניגון כי הימין תנוע הכינור
sources.says: Radak says it means forget the tune, because the right hand moves the harp.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: שפירושו: תיבש – בלי חבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some explain it as 'dry up', a sense with no other example.

sources.quote: ולדעתי תשכח היכולת המצוי לה כלומ׳ יכלה כחה לגמרי עד שישכח ממנה מלאכת יד
sources.says: Meiri says the hand will forget its ability: its strength will end until it forgets all handiwork.

137:7.headline: ערו: tear it down, or pour it out?
137:7.body: Rashi reads ערו as 'destroy', a word used for ripping something out by its roots. In the Midrash, Rabbi Levi reads it as 'empty it', like Rebecca emptying her jar (ותער כדה).

sources.quote: וְאֵינוֹ נוֹפֵל אֶלָּא עַל דָּבָר שֶׁעוֹקְרִין שָׁרָשָׁיו מֵהָאָרֶץ
sources.says: Rashi says ערו means destruction and is only used for something whose roots are torn out of the ground.

sources.quote: ר' אבא בר כהנא אמר פגרו פגרו. כמה דאת אמר (ירמיה נא נח) חומת בבל ערער תתערער. רבי לוי אמר פינון פינון. כמה דאת אמר (בראשית כד כ) ותער כדה אל השוקת
sources.says: The Midrash gives two readings: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana says 'tear it down', like ערער תתערער, and Rabbi Levi says 'empty it', like ותער כדה.

sources.quote: והנה ערו מגזרת פתהן יערה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ערו comes from the same root as פתהן יערה, 'will lay bare'.

139:3.headline: Ringed around, or winnowed like grain?
139:3.body: Rashi reads זרית from זר, the gold rim around the table in the Tabernacle: God has fenced in all of David's ways. He also brings the sages, who read it as winnowing, sorting grain from chaff, said of how a child is formed.

sources.quote: זֵרִיתָ לְשׁוֹן ״זֵר זָהָב סָבִיב״ (שמות כה:כד), וְכֵן חִבְּרוֹ מְנַחֵם. וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ דָּרְשׁוּ (נדה לא.) עַל טִפַּת תַּשְׁמִישׁ שֶׁהַוָּלָד נוֹצָר מִן הַבָּרוּר שֶׁבָּהּ, וּפֵירוּשׁוֹ זֵרִיתָ לְשׁוֹן זוֹרֶה הַתְּבוּאָה לִבְרוֹר אֶת הַפְּסוֹלֶת שֶׁבָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi says זרית comes from "a gold rim all around," and the sages read it as winnowing grain, said of the child formed from the choice part.

sources.quote: זרית. ענין סבוב והוא מלשון זר זהב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says זרית means surrounding, from the gold rim.

139:3.headline: רבעי is my lying down, a word the Aramaic shares
139:3.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion say רבעי means lying down to rest. The Aramaic translation uses this root when Balaam's donkey lies down. With it, Radak says, the psalm names four ways a person moves: sitting, rising, walking, and lying down.

sources.quote: ורבעי והוא שכבי בלילה שהוא רובץ במטתו מתרגמינן ורבעת. והנה הזכיר ארבעה תנועות האדם
sources.says: Radak says רבעי is lying down at night, as the Aramaic renders רבץ, and that the psalm names four human movements.

sources.quote: ורבעי. ענין רביצה והוא השכיבה לנוח כמו ותרבץ תחת בלעם (במדבר כג) תרגומו ורבעת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רבעי means lying down to rest, as the Aramaic renders the donkey lying down under Balaam.

139:5.headline: You formed me, or You hemmed me in?
139:5.body: Radak gives his father's reading: צרתני comes from צורה, form, about God shaping the baby in the womb. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it as a siege: God has closed David in, behind and in front.

sources.quote: פירש א"א ז"ל ביצירת העובר בבטן אמו, ופי' צרתני ענין צורה
sources.says: Radak says his father read this as forming the fetus in the womb, with צרתני meaning to give form.

sources.quote: צרתני - מגזרת: וצרת עליה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says צרתני comes from the verb for laying siege.

sources.quote: צרתני. מלשון מצור וסבוב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says צרתני comes from siege and surrounding.

139:7.headline: Fleeing God's spirit, His anger, or His will?
139:7.body: Metzudat Zion reads רוח here as anger, as in Ecclesiastes 7:9. Meiri reads it as God's will and decree. Ibn Ezra says no one can walk at all unless God's spirit carries him.

sources.quote: מרוחך. ענין כעס כמו אל תבהל ברוחך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רוחך here means anger.

sources.quote: מרוחך ר״ל מרצונך וגזרתך עלי
sources.says: Meiri says it means from Your will and Your decree on me.

sources.quote: אין יכולת באדם ללכת אם לא יוליכהו רוח השם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says a person cannot walk unless God's spirit leads him.

139:11.headline: Here אור, "light," may mean darkness
139:11.body: Rashi reads אור in this verse as gloom: David imagines night darkening around him. He compares the cloud that "scatters its light" in Job 37:11. Ibn Ezra takes it as plain light.

sources.quote: אוֹר זֶה לְשׁוֹן אֹפֶל הוּא, כְּמוֹ ״יָפִיץ עָנָן אוֹרוֹ״ (איוב לז:יא)
sources.says: Rashi says this אור is a word for darkness, as in "the cloud scatters its light."

sources.quote: והנה ולילה ישוב אור בעדני וזה אור כמשמעו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says night will turn to light around him, and אור has its plain meaning.

139:13.headline: "Acquired" here means created
139:13.body: Metzudat Zion says there is a קנין, an acquiring, with no sale, as when God is called "maker (קונה) of heaven." Meiri says bringing into being what did not exist is called קנין.

sources.quote: קנית. יש קנין שאין שם מכירה כמו קונה שמים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says there is acquiring with no sale, as in "maker of heaven."

sources.quote: כי המצאת מה שאינו יקרא קנין
sources.says: Meiri says bringing into being what did not exist is called קנין.

139:13.headline: The kidneys, where thought begins
139:13.body: Rashi and Radak say the kidneys think a person's thoughts: the kidneys advise and the heart decides. If God made them, how could David's thoughts be hidden? Ibn Ezra reads them as the body's hidden inner parts.

sources.quote: כִּלְיוֹתָי. הַחוֹשְׁבִים כָּל מַחְשְׁבוֹתַי
sources.says: Rashi says the kidneys are what think all his thoughts.

sources.quote: הם תחילת המחשבה כי הכליות יועצות והלב גומר
sources.says: Radak says the kidneys are where thought begins: they advise and the heart decides.

sources.quote: וטעם כליותי – הם המקומות הנסתרות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the kidneys stand for the hidden places of the body.

139:15.headline: The depths of the earth: the womb, or Adam's clay?
139:15.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra say the "depths of the earth" are the hidden womb. Ibn Ezra notes that Rabbi Moshe read it as Adam, the first man, formed from the ground.

sources.quote: בְּתַחְתִּיּוֹת אָרֶץ. בַּמָּדוֹר הַתַּחְתּוֹן שֶׁבִּמְעֵי אִמִּי
sources.says: Rashi says it means the lower chamber of his mother's womb.

sources.quote: אמר רבי משה: כי דבר דוד כנגד האב הראשון שנברא מן האדמה, על כן אמר: רקמתי בתחתיות ארץ. ולפי דעתי: כי על עצמו ידבר ודימה סתרי הרחם כמו סתרי תחתיות ארץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Rabbi Moshe read this as the first man made from earth, but he thinks David speaks of himself and compares the womb to the earth's depths.

139:16.headline: My גולם: the unfinished shape before the limbs appear
139:16.body: Radak says גלמי is the early, unformed embryo before its limbs can be seen, as wood is called a גולם before it becomes a tool. Metzudat Zion says the sages use the word for unfinished wooden vessels.

sources.quote: הוא הטיפה הקפואה קודם שיוכרו האיברים בה כמו שנקרא העץ גולם בטרם שנעשה כלי
sources.says: Radak says it is the early drop before the limbs can be seen, as wood is called גולם before it is made into a vessel.

sources.quote: גלמי. ענין דבר שלא נגמרה מלאכתו ובדרז״ל גולמי כלי עץ
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says גלמי means something not yet finished, as the sages speak of unfinished wooden vessels.

139:17.headline: Your friends, or Your thoughts?
139:17.body: Rashi reads רעיך as God's friends: the people of Israel say how dear the righteous of every generation are to them. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as God's thoughts, from רעיון, His plans in forming a person.

sources.quote: כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל אוֹמֶרֶת: מַה נִּכְבְּדוּ בְּעֵינַי הַצַּדִּיקִים שֶׁבְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר
sources.says: Rashi says the people of Israel say how honored the righteous of each generation are in their eyes.

sources.quote: ופי' רעיך ומחשבויך כלומר כוונותיך ביצירה
sources.says: Radak says רעיך means God's thoughts, His intentions in creating a person.

sources.quote: רעיך. מל׳ רעיון ומחשבה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רעיך comes from רעיון, thought.

139:23.headline: Thoughts are the heart's branches
139:23.body: Radak says שרעפי, my thoughts, is like שעיפים. Both words are also used for a tree's branches, because thoughts are to the heart what branches are to a tree.

sources.quote: שרעפי ומחשבותי, כמו שעיפים שתי הלשונות בענין מחשבה כמו שהם באילן סרעפותיו סעפותיו כי המחשבות ללב כמו הבדים לאילן
sources.says: Radak says שרעפי and שעיפים both mean thoughts, and both are used for a tree's branches, since thoughts are to the heart as branches to a tree.

139:24.headline: A way of grief, or a way of rebellion?
139:24.body: Rashi reads עצב as a way of sorrow and ruin. Radak and Maimonides read it as rebellion and sin, as in Isaiah 63:10, "they rebelled and grieved His holy spirit."

sources.quote: אִם דֶּרֶךְ מַעֲצֵבָה וְקִלְקוּל בִּי
sources.says: Rashi says it means a way of sorrow and ruin in me.

sources.quote: דרך עצב. דרך מרי כמו המה מרו ועצבו את רוח קדשו
sources.says: Radak says דרך עצב is a way of rebellion, as in Isaiah 63:10.

sources.quote: והוא שמם של המרי והחטא
sources.says: Maimonides says one sense of עצב is rebellion and sin, and cites this verse.

14:1.headline: נבל: the Midrash hears disgrace and falling fruit in 'fool'
14:1.body: Ibn Ezra says a נבל is the opposite of a wise man. The Midrash reads the fool as Esau and plays on the sound: he filled the world with disgrace (נבלות), and God will shake him off like withered fruit (נובלות).

sources.quote: אמר נבל - הפך חכם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says נבל is the opposite of wise.

sources.quote: ולמה נקרא שמו נבל. ר' יהודה בשם ר' שמואל אומר על שמילא כל העולם כולו נבלות
sources.says: The Midrash asks why Esau is called נבל, and Rabbi Yehuda says it is because he filled the whole world with disgraceful things (נבלות).

sources.quote: ר' יעקב אומר שעתיד הקב"ה להשירו כנובלות שהן נושרות מן האילן
sources.says: Rabbi Yaakov says God will one day make him drop like withered fruit (נובלות) falling from a tree.

14:1.headline: אין אלהים: the fool says no one is judging
14:1.body: The commentators ask what the fool is denying. Radak says he means there is no judge to repay each person, the Targum says he denies God's rule on earth, and Metzudat David says he thinks all is chance.

sources.quote: כי אין אלהים ואין שופט ודין בעולם לשלם לאיש כמעשהו
sources.says: Radak says the fool thinks there is no God and no judge or justice in the world to repay a person for his deeds.

sources.quote: לֵית שׁוּלְטָנָא דֶאֱלָהָא בְאַרְעָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it: there is no rule of God on the earth.

sources.quote: אמר בלבו אין אלהים הכל לפי המקרה
sources.says: Metzudat David says he said in his heart there is no God and everything happens by chance.

14:3.headline: סר: turned aside, or gone bad?
14:3.body: Radak says it means they turned from the good path, and notes the twin psalm (53:4) has סג, 'drew back', instead. Others he cites read סר as 'went bad', linking it to ויבאש.

sources.quote: הכל סר סר מדרך הטובה. ויש מפרשים כמו סג כמו שאמר בספר השני (תהלים נג ד): כלו סג
sources.says: Radak says סר means turned from the good path, and some explain it like סג, as the second book says כלו סג.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים ויבאש וסרי
sources.says: Radak says some explain it from ויבאש, 'and it stank', and סרי.

14:3.headline: נאלחו: gone foul, from חלאה 'filth' with letters swapped
14:3.body: This rare verb means they turned rotten. Radak says it is חלאה, 'filth', with its letters turned around, as in the pot whose filth is inside it (Ezekiel 24:6).

sources.quote: נֶאֱלָחוּ. נֶהֶפְכוּ לְקִלְקוּל
sources.says: Rashi says נאלחו means they turned to ruin.

sources.quote: שענינו נתעבו ונבאשו; הפוך מן סיר אשר חלאתה בה (יחזקאל כד ו) שפרושו: זוהמא
sources.says: Radak says it means they became loathsome and stank, and it is reversed from 'a pot whose filth is in it', meaning dirt.

sources.quote: נאלחו. נבאשו כמו נתעב ונאלח
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says נאלחו means they stank, as in נתעב ונאלח.

14:7.headline: בשוב: when God brings back, or gives rest?
14:7.body: Radak gives two readings: 'bring back' the captives, or 'give rest', from בשובה ונחת, 'in stillness and quiet'. Metzudat Zion takes the second.

sources.quote: ופרוש בשוב: פעל יוצא, כמו בהשיב, או פרושו: בהניח, מן בשובה ונחת תושעון
sources.says: Radak says בשוב is an active verb like בהשיב, 'bring back', or it means 'give rest', from בשובה ונחת תושעון.

sources.quote: בשוב. ענין ההשקט כמו בשובה ונחת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בשוב means quieting, as in בשובה ונחת.

140:2.headline: חמס is wrong that need not involve stealing
140:2.body: Meiri says איש חמסים is a name for any wicked person, even one who steals no money. He still robs good people of justice by pressing them in some way.

sources.quote: ואיש חמסים הוא שם לכל רשע ובליעל אף בלא גזלת ממון כי הוא מכל מקום חומס משפט הטובים בהצר להם באיזה צד שיהיה
sources.says: Meiri says איש חמסים is a name for every wicked person, even without robbing money, since he in any case robs the justice of the good by pressing them in some way.

140:3.headline: יגורו: 'dwell', 'gather', or 'stir up' wars
140:3.body: Rashi reads it as 'wars will dwell in their homes'. Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra read it as 'gather', like יגורהו בחרמו, and the Targum has the wicked stirring up wars.

sources.quote: יִהְיוּ מִלְחָמוֹת בִּמְגוּרֵיהֶם וּבְמוֹשְׁבוֹתָם
sources.says: Rashi says wars will be in their dwellings and their homes.

sources.quote: יגורו. ענין אסיפה כמו יגורהו בחרמו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says יגורו means gathering, like יגורהו בחרמו.

sources.quote: יקבצו כמו יגורו יצפונו. ויש אומרים: שהוא כמו: אל תתגר בם, והם שנים שרשים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means they gather, like יגורו יצפונו, and some say it is like אל תתגר בם; they are two different roots.

sources.quote: כָּל יוֹמָא מְגָרְגִין קְרָבַיָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it: every day they stir up wars.

140:4.headline: חמת means venom here, not anger
140:4.body: Rashi says חמת is poison, as in חמת תנינים יינם, because 'anger' would not fit next to 'wine'. Radak and Metzudat Zion agree that it means venom.

sources.quote: שֶׁאִם תְּפָרְשֵׁהוּ לְשׁוֹן ׳אַף׳, וְכִי לְשׁוֹן ׳אַף׳ נוֹפֵל אֵצֶל ׳יַיִן׳? אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן ׳אֶרֶס׳
sources.says: Rashi says that if you read it as 'anger', would 'anger' fall next to 'wine'? Rather it means 'poison'.

sources.quote: חמת הוא הארס שמטיל הנחש
sources.says: Radak says חמת is the venom a snake injects.

sources.quote: חמת. ארס כמו חמת זוחלי עפר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חמת means venom, like חמת זוחלי עפר.

140:6.headline: סלה: read here as 'always, without a break'
140:6.body: Metzudat David and Meiri read סלה in this verse as 'without stopping'. The plotters keep setting snares, even after failing the first time.

sources.quote: רוצה לומר מבלי הפסק אף אם לא הצליחו בראשונה חזרו שוב לארוב
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means without a break: even if they did not succeed the first time, they went back to lie in wait.

sources.quote: שתו לי סלה ר״ל תמיד
sources.says: Meiri says שתו לי סלה means they set them for me always.

140:8.headline: סכותה: 'you covered' or 'you will cover' my head
140:8.body: Radak says the past form סכותה stands for the future: 'you will cover my head'. Metzudat David and Meiri read it as the past: 'you have always covered me'.

sources.quote: סכותה עבר במקום עתיד וכמוהו רבים
sources.says: Radak says סכותה is the past used in place of the future, and there are many like it.

sources.quote: מעולם סככת על ראשי בעת באו עלי בכלי נשק
sources.says: Metzudat David says: you have always covered my head when they came against me with weapons.

sources.quote: היית כובע ישועה לראשי כלומ׳ שהצלתני במלחמותי
sources.says: Meiri says: you were a helmet of salvation for my head, meaning you saved me in my wars.

140:9.headline: זממו: 'his plan', or a muzzle
140:9.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read זממו as 'his plan', like כאשר זמם. Rashi adds that our rabbis heard a muzzle: the bridle that muzzles a camel's mouth.

sources.quote: זְמָמוֹ אַל תָּפֵק. מַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ אַל תַּצְלִיחַ
sources.says: Rashi says זממו אל תפק means: do not let his plan succeed.

sources.quote: זממו. מחשבתו כמו כאשר זמם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says זממו means his plan, like כאשר זמם.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ פֵּרְשׁוּ (בראשית רבה עה:ט): זְמָמוֹ לְשׁוֹן רֶסֶן הַזּוֹמֵם אֶת פִּי הַגָּמָל
sources.says: Rashi says our rabbis explained זממו as a bridle, the one that muzzles a camel's mouth.

140:13.headline: Written 'You know', read 'I know'
140:13.body: The text is written ידעת, 'you know', and read ידעתי, 'I know'. Radak and Meiri say the written form speaks to God and the read form is David's own knowledge.

sources.quote: קרי וכתיב ידעת פירוש הכתיב כנגד האל אתה ידעת כי מחשבות הרשע עלי עשה לי דין ממנו, והקרי ידעתי פירושו אני ידעתי כי יעשה
sources.says: Radak says the written form ידעת is said to God: you know the wicked man's thoughts against me, so judge him for me; and the read form ידעתי means: I know that He will do justice.

sources.quote: זה הקרי אבל הכתיב ידעת בלשון נמצא ופירושו אתה ידעת כי האמת כדברי
sources.says: Meiri says ידעתי is the read form, but the written form is ידעת, meaning: you know that the truth is as I say.

sources.quote: ידעתי - אז אדע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ידעתי means 'then I will know'.

140:14.headline: ישבו את פניך: sit in prayer, or live on before Him
140:14.body: Metzudat Zion says את פניך means 'before You'. Ibn Ezra says the upright keep sitting before God in the house of prayer, and Meiri hears a hint of the next world.

sources.quote: את פניך. לפניך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says את פניך means 'before You'.

sources.quote: והישרים יתמידו לשבת את פניך - בבית התפלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the upright will keep sitting before You, in the house of prayer.

sources.quote: וישבו ר״ל יתקיימו ישרים לפניך תמיד רומז על חיי העולם הבא
sources.says: Meiri says וישבו means the upright will endure before You always, a hint of the life of the world to come.

141:2.headline: מנחת ערב: the evening offering, or an offering that pleases?
141:2.body: Radak reads ערב as evening, and says the same holds for the morning offering. Meiri adds that ערב may mean pleasing, as in וערבה לה׳ מנחת יהודה, so David's raised hands are an offering that pleases.

sources.quote: ואמר מנחת ערב. והוא הדין למנחת הבקר
sources.says: Radak says that saying evening offering applies just as much to the morning offering.

sources.quote: ואצלי במלת ערב היותה שם מענין וערבה לה׳ מנחת יהודה
sources.says: Meiri says that in his view the word ערב is a name from the sense of וערבה לה׳ מנחת יהודה, meaning pleasing.

141:3.headline: שמרה: a noun, 'a guard', or a command, 'guard!'
141:3.body: Radak says שמרה is a noun, shaped like חכמה, so the prayer asks God to set a guard on his mouth. Ibn Ezra reads it as a command, like שמרה נפשי.

sources.quote: שיתה ה' שמרה. שם בשקל חכמה עצמה
sources.says: Radak says שמרה is a noun in the pattern of חכמה.

sources.quote: ומלת שמרה – כמו: שמרה נפשי והצילני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word שמרה is like שמרה נפשי והצילני.

141:3.headline: דל שפתי: the lips as a door that opens and shuts
141:3.body: דל is found only here. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as דלת, a door, because the lips open and close. Rashi says it means the upper lip.

sources.quote: ונקראו שפתים דלת לפי שהם נפתחות ונסגרות
sources.says: Radak says the lips are called a door because they open and close.

sources.quote: ומלת דל – כמו דלת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word דל is like דלת.

sources.quote: היא שפה העליונה
sources.says: Rashi says דל means the upper lip.

141:6.headline: סלע: a heart hard as rock, or a real cliff?
141:6.body: Rashi reads the rock as a heart hard as stone, the evil urge, that the leaders were left in. Radak reads a real cliff the leaders are thrown from. Metzudat David ties it to the rock where David nearly fell into Saul's hands.

sources.quote: בְּיַד יֵצֶר הָרָע וְלֵב הָאֶבֶן וְקָשֶׁה כַּסֶּלַע
sources.says: Rashi says they were left in the hand of the evil urge and a heart of stone, hard as the rock.

sources.quote: שיפילו אותם מן הסלע
sources.says: Radak says they will be thrown down from the rock.

sources.quote: הוא סלע המחלקות שהיה דוד קרוב להיות נתפש ביד שאול
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is the Rock of Divisions, where David was close to being caught by Saul.

141:6.headline: נשמטו looks like the past, but is read as a curse
141:6.body: The verb is in the past tense. Radak and Meiri both read it as a wish for the future: may their leaders be flung down.

sources.quote: ישמטו בידי סלע שיפילו אותם מן הסלע, ואמר זאת הקללה על שופטיהם
sources.says: Radak says ישמטו, they will be thrown from the rock, and calls this a curse on their judges.

sources.quote: נשמטו עבר במקום עתיד והוא לשון קללה
sources.says: Meiri says נשמטו is past tense used for the future, and is the language of a curse.

141:8.headline: אל תער נפשי: do not pour out my soul
141:8.body: Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra all link תער to ותער כדה, 'she emptied her jug'. Radak says the soul leaving the body is like something poured out of it.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ ״וַתְּעַר כַּדָּהּ אֶל הַשֹּׁקֶת״
sources.says: Rashi compares it to ותער כדה אל השקת.

sources.quote: כמו ותער כדה, ענין שפיכה ויציקה, וכצאת הנפש מן הגוף כאילו נשפכת ממנו
sources.says: Radak says it is like ותער כדה, pouring, and that when the soul leaves the body it is as if it were poured out.

sources.quote: אל תער - כמו: ותער כדה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אל תער is like ותער כדה.

143:2.headline: כל חי: no one alive, or even the living creatures above?
143:2.body: Plainly, no living person is fully righteous before God. The Midrash asks whether that makes the dead righteous, and answers that כל חי means the living creatures (חיות) on high.

sources.quote: אם תשלם כפי הגמול אין מי בעולם שיהיה צדיק לפניך
sources.says: Metzudat David says that if God pays back exactly, no one in the world is righteous before Him.

sources.quote: מהו כל חי. כל חי לא יצדק לפניך הא המתים זכים. אלא על החיות של מעלן אינן יכולין להצדיק לפניך ביום הדין
sources.says: The Midrash asks whether 'no living one' means the dead are innocent, and says it refers to the living creatures above, who cannot be found righteous on the day of judgment.

143:3.headline: במחשכים: a real dark cave, or the darkness of grief?
143:3.body: Radak says it is the back of the cave where David hid, with no light. Ibn Ezra and Meiri also read it as the darkness of trouble, like a person sitting in the dark who cannot see.

sources.quote: במחשכים. ירכתי המערה שהיה יושב שאין שם אורה
sources.says: Radak says the dark places are the back of the cave where David sat, where there is no light.

sources.quote: וטעם במחשכים – שהוא נחבא מפניו, או ידמה צרת הלב ליושב חשך שאיננו רואה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means he was hiding from the enemy, or he likens a troubled heart to one sitting in the dark who cannot see.

sources.quote: הושיבני במחשכים ר״ל במחשכי הצרות
sources.says: Meiri says the dark places are the darkness of troubles.

143:6.headline: ארץ עיפה: a tired land is a thirsty land
143:6.body: A tired person is thirsty, so Metzudat Zion says 'tired' is borrowed here for land that had no rain. Radak says the soul longs for God as dry land longs for rain.

sources.quote: לפי שהעיף הוא צמא למים לזה אמר לשון עיפה בדרך שאלה על הארץ הצמאה שלא ירד בה המטר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says that since a tired person thirsts for water, the word 'tired' is borrowed for thirsty land on which no rain fell.

sources.quote: כמו הארץ הצמאה שהיא מתאוה ומיחלת אל המטר כן נפשי צמאה ומיחלת לך
sources.says: Radak says just as thirsty land longs and waits for rain, so my soul thirsts and waits for you.

143:7.headline: כלתה רוחי: the spirit 'runs out' from longing
143:7.body: Rashi says one who longs for something and cannot reach it is said to have his eyes or spirit run out. Metzudat David says the longing was so great his spirit almost left his body.

sources.quote: הַמִּתְאַוֶּה וְאֵינוֹ מַשִּׂיג קָרוּי ״כִּלְיוֹן עֵינַיִם״ (דברים כח:סה) וְכִלְיוֹן רוּחַ
sources.says: Rashi says one who longs and does not reach what he wants is called 'ending of eyes' and 'ending of spirit'.

sources.quote: לגודל התאוה כמעט כלתה רוחי מן הגוף ויצאה לה
sources.says: Metzudat David says from great longing his spirit almost ended from the body and left.

143:8.headline: בבקר: real morning, or the dawn of rescue?
143:8.body: Radak says trouble is called evening and rescue is called morning, and Rashi says it is when redemption sprouts. Ibn Ezra and Meiri also read it plainly: journeys start in the morning, or David wrote his psalms at night.

sources.quote: עת הצרה היא נקראת ערב, ועת הישועה בקר
sources.says: Radak says a time of trouble is called evening and a time of rescue is called morning.

sources.quote: בַּבֹּקֶר. בִּצְמֹחַ הַגְּאֻלָּה
sources.says: Rashi says 'in the morning' means when redemption sprouts.

sources.quote: וטעם בבקר – כי רובי ההליכות והמלאכות תחלתם בבקר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it says morning because most journeys and tasks begin in the morning.

sources.quote: או מצד שהמזמורים על הרוב היה מחברם בלילה היה אומר בבקר
sources.says: Meiri says another reason: David mostly wrote the psalms at night, so he said 'in the morning'.

143:8.headline: נשאתי נפשי: lifting the soul in prayer, or in hope?
143:8.body: Meiri gives both: lifting the soul in prayer, as in 'let us lift our hearts', or in hope. Radak reads it as hope, like the hired worker who 'lifts his soul' to his wages.

sources.quote: ואליך נשאתי נפשי ר״ל בתפלה כמו נשא לבבינו אל כפים (איכה ג מא) או הוא ענין תוחלת
sources.says: Meiri says it means in prayer, as in 'let us lift our hearts with our hands', or it means hope.

sources.quote: נשאתי נפשי. כמו ואליו הוא נושא נפשו, ענין התוחלת
sources.says: Radak says it is like 'and to it he lifts his soul', a word of hope.

143:9.headline: כסתי: I hid my troubles, or I took shelter?
143:9.body: Rashi says David hid his troubles from everyone, to tell them only to God. Rabbi Marinus, quoted by Ibn Ezra, reads כסתי like חסיתי, 'I took shelter', and Meiri says many struggled with this word.

sources.quote: תְּלָאוֹתַי, אֲנִי מְכַסֶּה מִכָּל אָדָם לְהַגִּידָם אֵלֶיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says I hide my troubles from every person, to tell them to you.

sources.quote: אמר רבי מרינוס ז"ל: כי אליך כסיתי, כמו: בך חסיתי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Rabbi Marinus read אליך כסיתי as 'in you I took shelter'.

sources.quote: הרבה טרחו המפרשים במלת כסיתי
sources.says: Meiri says the commentators worked hard over the word כסיתי.

143:10.headline: רוחך טובה: God's will, God's spirit, or a good wind?
143:10.body: Metzudat Zion reads רוח as will, and Radak as a power from the spirit above. Some cited by Ibn Ezra say David pictured himself at sea, asking for a good wind to bring him to land.

sources.quote: רוחך. ענין רצון כמו הנני נותן בו רוח
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רוחך means will, as in 'I will put a spirit in him'.

sources.quote: רוחך טובה. כח רוח העליונים
sources.says: Radak says it is the power of the spirit of the higher beings.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: כי דימה עצמו שהוא בתוך הים, על כן יבקש רוח טובה שתניחהו ויצא לארץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some explain that David pictured himself in the sea, so he asks for a good wind to set him down on land.

144:2.headline: הרודד is the Aramaic word for 'beats flat'
144:2.body: Rashi, Radak and Meiri tie it to the Aramaic translation of וירקעו, 'they hammered out', which is ורדידו. So the verb means to beat flat, or to lay low.

sources.quote: רוֹדֵד תַּרְגּוּם שֶׁל רוֹקֵעַ, כְּדִמְתַרְגֵּם ״וַיְרַקְּעוּ״ (שמות לט:ג): ״וְרַדִּידוּ״
sources.says: Rashi says רודד is the Aramaic translation of רוקע, as the Targum translates וירקעו as ורדידו.

sources.quote: הרודד פירושו כתרגומו מתרגמינן וירקעו ורדידו
sources.says: Radak says הרודד means what the Targum gives, translating וירקעו as ורדידו.

sources.quote: רודד הוא לשון ארמי וירקעו (שמות לט ג) תרגומו ורדידו
sources.says: Meiri says רודד is an Aramaic word, the Targum's rendering of וירקעו.

144:2.headline: עמי: 'my people', or 'peoples'
144:2.body: Some read עמי as 'peoples', and the Targum does too. Radak allows 'my people' as written, and Metzudat David says it means Saul's family, who were David's own people.

sources.quote: וְיֵשׁ פּוֹתְרִים: הָרוֹדֵד עַמִּים תַּחְתִּי, הַמַּחֲלִישׁ עַמִּים תַּחְתִּי
sources.says: Rashi reports that some explain it as 'who lays peoples low beneath me'.

sources.quote: מְרַדֵד עַמִין תְּחוֹתָי
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'who flattens peoples beneath me'.

sources.quote: כמו עמים ויתכן לפרשו כמשמעו בלא חסרון
sources.says: Radak says עמי is like עמים, but it may also be read as written, with nothing missing.

sources.quote: ועל משפחת בית שאול יאמר שהיו מבני עמו והיו לו לאויבים
sources.says: Metzudat David says it refers to the house of Saul, who were of David's own people but became his enemies.

144:3.headline: ותדעהו: 'know' here means 'care for'
144:3.body: Radak says 'know' means to notice and watch over for good, and Metzudat Zion says it means affection, as in 'I know you by name'. Maimonides cites the verse as wonder that God watches over each person.

sources.quote: ופי' ותדעהו כמו ותחשבהו כי פי' הידיעה במקום הזה ובכיוצא בו ההכרה וההשגחה לטובה
sources.says: Radak says ותדעהו means 'think of him', since knowing here means recognizing and watching over for good.

sources.quote: הוא ענין חיבה כמו ידעתיך בשם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means affection, as in 'I know you by name'.

sources.quote: הנביאים אף התפלאו על היות ההשגחה על פרטי בני האדם
sources.says: Maimonides says the prophets marvelled that God's care reaches individual people, and he lists this verse as an example.

144:8.headline: 'Their right hand': an oath, their strength, or their religion
144:8.body: Rashi and a view Ibn Ezra reports tie the right hand to swearing an oath. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as their strength, and Meiri as the core of their religion.

sources.quote: בָּאוּ לִפְשֹׁט יְמִינָם לִשְׁבוּעָה
sources.says: Rashi speaks of them coming to stretch out their right hand for an oath.

sources.quote: אמר בן בלעם כי וימינם לשון קדר שבועתם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports Ben Balaam's view that וימינם is a word from the language of Kedar meaning their oath.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני שהוא כמשמעו והטעם כחם וגבורתם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the right reading is as it sounds, meaning their strength and might.

sources.quote: וכן ימינם כלומר כחם וגבורתם
sources.says: Radak says their right hand means their strength and might.

sources.quote: וימינם ר״ל עיקר דתם ועצמות אמונתם שהוא כימין אצלם הוא שקר
sources.says: Meiri says their right hand means the core of their religion and belief, which they treat as their right hand, and it is false.

144:10.headline: הפוצה means 'rescues', from a word for 'opening'
144:10.body: Ibn Ezra ties הפוצה to ופצתה האדמה, 'the earth opened its mouth'. Meiri says it means that God opened him out of the prison of fear of the evil sword.

sources.quote: הפוצה - מגזרת ופצתה האדמה כדרך ויפרקנו מצרינו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says הפוצה comes from the same root as ופצתה האדמה, in the way of 'and he freed us from our enemies'.

sources.quote: שפתחו ממאסר אימת חרב רעה
sources.says: Meiri says it means that God opened him out of the prison of terror of an evil sword.

144:12.headline: Young trees: spotless, or well-watered and fast-growing
144:12.body: Rashi says the saplings have no blemish, so clean are they of sin. Radak and Meiri read the picture as trees growing quickly on rich, watered ground.

sources.quote: שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם מוּם, כָּל כָּךְ הֵם מְנֻקִּים מֵעֲבֵירָה
sources.says: Rashi says the saplings have no blemish, so clean are they of sin.

sources.quote: כנטיעים כמו הנטיעים שהם מגודלים על מים רבים, ובמקום דשן ושמן
sources.says: Radak says they are like saplings grown beside much water, in rich and fertile ground.

sources.quote: שנטועים בארץ לחה וטובה עד שבמעט זמן יהיו מגודלים בנעוריהם
sources.says: Meiri says they are planted in moist, good soil, so that in a short time they are fully grown.

144:12.headline: מחטבות: cut and shaped like stone, or praised
144:12.body: Metzudat Zion and Meiri read it as cutting, like stones hewn straight. Rashi reads it as 'praised by those who see them'.

sources.quote: מחוטבות. ענין כריתה וחתוך כמו מחוטב עציך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means cutting, like 'the hewer of your wood'.

sources.quote: ומחוטבות פי׳ לשון כריתה כמו מחוטב עציך
sources.says: Meiri says מחוטבות means cutting, like 'the hewer of your wood'.

sources.quote: מְהֻלָּלוֹת בְּפִי רוֹאֵיהֶן, וּמְדַמִּין אוֹתָם לְתַבְנִית קוֹמַת הַהֵיכָל
sources.says: Rashi says they are praised by those who see them, who compare them to the height of the Temple.

144:13.headline: מזוינו: corners of the storehouse, or the sages
144:13.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion tie it to זויות, corners, so the corners of our storehouses are full of good. Meiri also gives a reading where it points to the sages, corners full of wisdom.

sources.quote: זָוִיּוֹת אוֹצְרוֹתֵינוּ מְלֵאִים טוֹב
sources.says: Rashi says it means the corners of our storehouses are full of good.

sources.quote: מזוינו. מל׳ זויות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says מזוינו comes from the word for corners.

sources.quote: ומזוינו רומז על החכמים שהם הפנות מלאים חכמה
sources.says: Meiri says מזוינו hints at the sages, who are the corners full of wisdom.

144:14.headline: אלופינו: our oxen, or our leaders
144:14.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion say it means our oxen, as in שגר אלפיך. Rashi reads it as our great leaders, whom the smaller people listen to.

sources.quote: שורינו, וכן שגר אלפיך כבש אלוף
sources.says: Radak says אלופינו means our oxen, as in שגר אלפיך.

sources.quote: הם השוורים וכן שגר אלפיך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says they are the oxen, as in שגר אלפיך.

sources.quote: אַלּוּפִים גְּדוֹלִים שֶׁבָּנוּ נִסְבָּלִים עַל קְטַנֵּיהֶם, שֶׁהַקְּטַנִּים נִשְׁמָעִים לַגְּדוֹלִים
sources.says: Rashi says the great leaders among us are borne by their smaller people, because the small listen to the great.

144:14.headline: מסבלים: strong, fat, or carried by the small
144:14.body: Radak says the oxen are strong enough to carry their loads, or are loaded with flesh, and Metzudat David says fat. Rashi reads it of great leaders who are carried by the small, who listen to them.

sources.quote: ויכולים לסבול משא עבודתם בחרישה ובמשוך העגלות או פירושו ויש מסובלים בבשר
sources.says: Radak says they can carry the burden of their work in plowing and pulling carts, or else they are loaded with flesh.

sources.quote: יהיו שמנים ובעלי בשר כאילו יחשב עליהם למשא
sources.says: Metzudat David says they will be fat and fleshy, as if the flesh were a burden on them.

sources.quote: נִסְבָּלִים עַל קְטַנֵּיהֶם, שֶׁהַקְּטַנִּים נִשְׁמָעִים לַגְּדוֹלִים
sources.says: Rashi says the great ones are borne by the small, who listen to the great.

145:6.headline: Written 'your greatnesses', read 'your greatness'
145:6.body: The word is written as a plural but read aloud as a singular. Radak says God's great acts look like many to the people who receive them, but to God they are all one.

sources.quote: שהם רבות אצל המקבל, וקרי גדולתך כי הכל הם אחד אצלו יתברך
sources.says: Radak says the plural spelling shows the acts are many to those who receive them, and the singular reading shows they are one to God.

145:13.headline: A kingdom over all worlds, or through all ages?
145:13.body: עולם can mean the world or a long stretch of time. Radak reads 'all times', so God's rule never stops, while Metzudat David reads 'all the worlds'.

sources.quote: כי מלכותו מלכות כל העולמים כל הזמנים
sources.says: Radak says God's kingdom covers all times and never ends, unlike a human king's.

sources.quote: על כל העולמות
sources.says: Metzudat David says God rules over all the worlds.

145:16.headline: Does God give each creature enough, or what it wants?
145:16.body: רצון usually means will or desire, but Ibn Ezra reads it here as 'what is enough for them'. Metzudat David and Radak read it as each creature's own wish, which God fills.

sources.quote: וטעם רצון – מה שיספיק להם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says רצון here means what is enough for them.

sources.quote: ומשביע לכל חי לפי רצונו ותאותו
sources.says: Metzudat David says God satisfies every living thing according to its wish and appetite.

sources.quote: שישבעו רצון כל אחד לפי רצונו
sources.says: Radak says each one is satisfied according to its own wish.

145:17.headline: God is called חסיד: He gives more than He owes
145:17.body: צדיק means just, giving each what is fair. Radak and Ibn Ezra say חסיד adds more: God gives what He does not owe to those who have not earned it.

sources.quote: מזמין להם מה שהוא אינו מחוייב לתת והם אינם ראוים לקבל
sources.says: Radak says God provides what He is not obliged to give to those who do not deserve it.

sources.quote: כי השם כל מה שיתן בדרך חסד הוא, כי איננו חיוב עליו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says all God gives is kindness, since He owes nothing, and that is why the verse says חסיד.

145:20.headline: Those who love God rank above those who fear Him
145:20.body: Verse 19 speaks of those who fear God, and verse 20 of those who love Him. Radak says the lovers rank higher, because they love God without hope of reward or fear of punishment.

sources.quote: טובים מיראיו כי אהבוהו ללא תקות טובה ולא מפחד עונש
sources.says: Radak says those who love God are better than those who fear Him, since they love without hope of reward or fear of punishment.

sources.quote: רק אוהביו הוא ישמור אותם לא תבא להם רעה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God rescues those who fear Him from trouble, but guards those who love Him so that no harm comes at all.

146:3.headline: Do not trust in nobles: rulers, or your noble ancestors
146:3.body: Meiri reads נדיבים as princes and men of rank. The Midrash reads it as noble ancestors: a person cannot rely on his fathers' good deeds, as Ishmael could not rely on Abraham.

sources.quote: אל תבטחו בנדיבים ר״ל שרים ונכבדים
sources.says: Meiri says 'nobles' means princes and honored men.

sources.quote: כך אמר דוד אל תבטחו בנדיבים. לא יבטח אדם במעשה אבותיו
sources.says: The Midrash says 'do not trust in nobles' means a person should not rely on the deeds of his fathers.

sources.quote: לא יאמר ישמעאל אברהם אבי יש לי מחלקו והוא מצילני
sources.says: The Midrash says Ishmael cannot claim that Abraham, his father, will save him.

146:3.headline: A man with no salvation: he cannot save you, or even himself
146:3.body: Some read the verse as 'a man who has no real help to give you'. Ibn Ezra prefers 'a man who cannot even save himself', and Meiri agrees, since his breath will soon leave him.

sources.quote: יש אומרים: בבן אדם שאין לו תשועת אמת להושיעכם. והנכון בעיני: בבן אדם שלא יוכל להושיע נפשו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some read it as a man with no true help to save you, but he thinks it means a man who cannot save himself.

sources.quote: והכוונה שאף לעצמו לא יוכל להושיע כי תצא רוחו
sources.says: Meiri says the meaning is that he cannot even save himself, because his breath will leave him.

146:4.headline: A man is like a wineskin full of air
146:4.body: The Midrash compares a person to a puffed-up wineskin that frightens people until someone touches it and the air goes out. A body stands only by its breath, and when the breath leaves it turns to dust.

sources.quote: משל למה הדבר דומה לנאד שהוא נפוח ומלא רוח
sources.says: The Midrash compares it to a wineskin that is puffed up and full of air.

sources.quote: אינו עומד אלא על הרוח יצאת הרוח מיד נעשה עפר
sources.says: The Midrash says a person stands only by the breath, and once the breath goes out he becomes dust.

sources.quote: כי הנה יצאה רוחו המעמידה אותו
sources.says: Radak says the breath that kept him standing has gone out.

146:5.headline: Why 'the God of Jacob'? Jacob trusted God on the run
146:5.body: Radak says the verse names Jacob because he trusted God when he fled from his brother, who wanted to kill him. Rashi points to God's promise to Jacob: 'I am with you, and I will guard you'.

sources.quote: הזכיר יעקב אבינו כי הוא בטח באל כי אחיו היה מתנכל להמיתו וברח מפניו
sources.says: Radak says the verse mentions Jacob because he trusted God when his brother plotted to kill him and he fled.

sources.quote: שֶׁהִבְטִיחוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא ״הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי עִמָּךְ וּשְׁמַרְתִּיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says God promised Jacob, 'I am with you and will guard you'.

146:7.headline: Frees the prisoners, or permits what was forbidden?
146:7.body: אסורים means prisoners, but the same letters can mean forbidden things, and מתיר can mean 'frees' or 'permits'. Radak reads 'frees the prisoners', while the Midrash records a view that in the future God will permit animals now forbidden as food, a view others reject.

sources.quote: ה' מתיר אסורים. בכל דור ודור וכן עשה לישרא ממאסר גלותם
sources.says: Radak says God frees prisoners in every generation, as he freed Israel from the prison of exile.

sources.quote: יש אומרים כל הבהמה שנטמאת בעולם הזה מטהר אותה הקב"ה לעתיד לבוא
sources.says: The Midrash says some hold that every animal made impure in this world God will make pure in the future.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים אינו מתירן לעתיד לבוא
sources.says: The Midrash says others hold that God will not permit them in the future.

sources.quote: ומהו מתיר אסורים אסורי מות ואסורי שאול
sources.says: The Midrash also reads it as freeing those held by death and the grave.

146:8.headline: Opens the eyes of the blind: sick eyes, or people in the dark
146:8.body: Radak says the blind may be people with diseased eyes, or people blinded by trouble, since trouble is like darkness. The Midrash says the blind are those who study Torah like the blind: they read, but do not know what they are reading.

sources.quote: או פירושו עורים מרוב צרה כי הצרה דומה לחושך והישועה לאור
sources.says: Radak says it may mean blind from great trouble, because trouble is like darkness and rescue is like light.

sources.quote: שהם העורים מחולי העין הוא ירפאם
sources.says: Radak first says God heals those blinded by eye disease.

sources.quote: ומי הן העורים הדורות האלו שהולכות בתורה כעורים
sources.says: The Midrash says the blind are these generations, who walk in the Torah like the blind.

sources.quote: כולם קורין ואין יודעין מה הן קורין
sources.says: The Midrash says they all read but do not know what they are reading.

146:8.headline: Anyone can become righteous, whatever family they come from
146:8.body: The Midrash asks why God loves the righteous. A person cannot become a priest or a Levite unless he is born into the family, but anyone, even a non-Jew, can choose to become righteous.

sources.quote: אבל מבקש להיות צדיק אפילו היה גוי יכול להיות צדיק
sources.says: The Midrash says one who wants to be righteous can become righteous, even a non-Jew.

sources.quote: שאין הצדיקים באין מבית אב אלא מעצמן התנדבו ואהבו את הקדוש ברוך הוא
sources.says: The Midrash says the righteous do not come from a family line; they chose on their own to love God.

146:9.headline: The stranger: the convert God loves like a wild deer
146:9.body: Ibn Ezra says strangers need guarding because they come from another people and have no one to help them. The Midrash tells of a king who loved a deer that joined his flock, and says God loves the convert who left his family to come to him.

sources.quote: ה' שומר את גרים - שאין להם עוזר כי הם מגוי אחר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God guards strangers because they have no helper, coming from another nation.

sources.quote: טובה גדולה צריך אני להחזיק לגר שהניח משפחתו ובית אביו ובא אלי
sources.says: The Midrash has God say he owes great gratitude to the convert who left his family and father's house and came to him.

sources.quote: וכן שומר ישראל שהיו גרים בין האומות
sources.says: Radak says God also guards Israel, who were strangers among the nations.

146:9.headline: God bends the road of the wicked
146:9.body: Metzudat David says God makes the path of the wicked crooked so they stumble, and Ibn Ezra says he arranges events so they do not get what they want. The Midrash pictures the righteous and the wicked on the same road to Jerusalem, where God turns the wicked off toward Gehinnom.

sources.quote: עושה דרכם מעוות ומעוקם למען יכשל
sources.says: Metzudat David says God makes their way twisted and crooked so that they stumble.

sources.quote: ויתכן עלילות לעות דרכם, שלא ימלא שאלתם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God arranges events to twist their way, so their wish is not fulfilled.

sources.quote: הקב"ה מכניס הצדיקים לגן עדן ומעות דרכן של רשעים ומוליכן בדרך לגיהנם
sources.says: The Midrash says God brings the righteous into the Garden of Eden, and twists the path of the wicked and leads them to Gehinnom.

147:1.headline: נאוה: from 'beautiful', or from 'desire'?
147:1.body: Metzudat Zion ties נאוה to נאה, meaning fitting and beautiful. Ibn Ezra ties it to תאוה, desire, and says the word is in the niphal form.

sources.quote: מלשון נאה ויפה כמו לישרים נאוה תהלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is from the language of נאה, fitting and beautiful, like לישרים נאוה תהלה.

sources.quote: וכי נאוה - מגזרת תאוה כאשר פירשתי, שהמלה לבנין נפעל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says נאוה comes from the root of תאוה, as he explained, and that the word is in the niphal form.

147:3.headline: עצבותם: their sorrow, or something from another language?
147:3.body: Metzudat David reads it as their sorrow, which God bandages and takes away. Ibn Ezra quotes Rabbi Yitzhak the Spaniard, who ties it to the language of Ishmael, meaning Arabic, and gives his own reading, 'like their wounds'.

sources.quote: עושה תחבושת לעצבותם ר״ל מעביר העצבון
sources.says: Metzudat David says God makes a bandage for their sorrow, meaning He removes the sorrow.

sources.quote: ור' יצחק הספרדי אמר: כי לעצבותם כמו לשון ישמעאל וכמוהו: ידיך עצבוני. ולפי דעתי: שהוא כמו נגעם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Rabbi Yitzhak the Spaniard called לעצבותם like the language of Ishmael, as in ידיך עצבוני, and that in his own view it is like נגעם, their wounds.

147:5.headline: אין מספר: 'no count' cannot be right, so what does it mean?
147:5.body: Radak says wisdom is a quality and number is an amount, so the verse must mean there is no searching it out. Meiri offers that מספר may be like ספור, telling: no one can tell it.

sources.quote: כי תבא ממין האיכות ומספר ממין הכמות לפיכך צריך לפרשנו כך כי נשוא תבונה אין חקר
sources.says: Radak says that understanding comes from the kind of quality and number from the kind of quantity, so the verse must be explained this way: there is no searching out the subject of understanding.

sources.quote: או יהיה מספר כמו ספור כלומ׳ לא יוכל אדם לספרה
sources.says: Meiri says or מספר may be like ספור, that is, a person cannot tell it.

147:9.headline: בני עורב: cruel parents, and God feeds the chicks
147:9.body: Rashi, quoting the rabbis, says the raven is cruel to its young, and God feeds them. Radak says the chicks are born white, so the parents think they are not theirs and leave them.

sources.quote: שֶׁהוּא אַכְזָרִי עַל בָּנָיו, וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְרַחֵם עֲלֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi, quoting our rabbis, says the raven is cruel to its young, and the Holy One has mercy on them.

sources.quote: לפי שהם לבנים בהולדם ואמותיהם מניחים אותם כי יחשבו שאינם בניהם
sources.says: Radak says it is because they are white when born and their mothers leave them, thinking they are not their children.

148:3.headline: "Stars of light", or "stars of the night"?
148:3.body: אור usually means light, but in Aramaic אורתא means evening. Rashi reads "stars of the night"; the Talmud weighs that, then reads it as "stars that shine".

sources.quote: כּוֹכְבֵי אוֹר. כּוֹכְבֵי לַיְלָה
sources.says: Rashi says כוכבי אור means stars of the night.

sources.quote: אַלְמָא ״אוֹר״ אוּרְתָּא הוּא. הָכִי קָאָמַר: הַלְלוּהוּ כׇּל כּוֹכָבִים הַמְּאִירִים
sources.says: The Talmud first takes the verse to show אור means evening, then answers that it means the stars that shine.

sources.quote: הם חמשה כוכבי לכת המאירים יותר משאר הכוכבים
sources.says: Metzudat David says these are the five planets, which shine more than the other stars.

148:6.headline: The stars never break the law, or the law never ends?
148:6.body: Rashi reads it that sun and moon never cross the line of day and night that God set. Ibn Ezra adds a second reading, that the law itself never lapses, and Maimonides reads it that way too.

sources.quote: זֶה יְשַׁמֵּשׁ בַּיּוֹם וְזֶה יְשַׁמֵּשׁ בַּלַּיְלָה וְלֹא יַעֲבוֹר אוֹתוֹ חֹק
sources.says: Rashi says one serves by day and one by night, and neither crosses that law.

sources.quote: החק אחד מהם או החק לא יפסק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means either that none of them breaks the law, or that the law never stops.

sources.quote: כוונתו שהחוקים האלה שחקק לא ישתנו לעולם
sources.says: Maimonides says David means that the laws God set for the heavens will never change, though the heavens were created.

148:10.headline: "Winged bird": one creature, or two kinds?
148:10.body: Metzudat David reads צפור כנף as one phrase, every bird with wings. The Talmud suggests it names two groups: צפור is the kosher birds, and כנף is the non-kosher birds and locusts.

sources.quote: כל עוף בעלי כנפים
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means every bird with wings.

sources.quote: לָא, ״צִפּוֹר״ – טָהוֹר, ״כָּנָף״ – טָמֵא וַחֲגָבִים
sources.says: The Talmud answers that צפור means pure birds, and כנף means impure birds and locusts.

148:12.headline: Old men with the young, so they can teach them
148:12.body: The verse could have said "old and young". Radak says it says "with" on purpose: the young cannot yet praise God well alone, so the old stand with them and teach them how.

sources.quote: שהזקנים ילמדום היאך יהללו ה' זהו שאמר עם, כי אין בנערים לבדו דעת להלל
sources.says: Radak says the old will teach the young how to praise God, which is why it says "with", since the young alone lack the knowledge.

149:2.headline: 'His Makers': God spoken of in the plural, as with אלהים
149:2.body: עושיו is plural: 'his makers'. Ibn Ezra and Meiri say Scripture often speaks of God in the plural, as in אלהים, and Radak calls it a way of giving honor.

sources.quote: ישמח ישראל בעושיו - לשון רבים, כדרך: כי בועליך עושיך, כמלת אלהים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בעושיו is plural, like 'your husband is your Maker' and like the word אלהים.

sources.quote: ואמ׳ ישמח ישראל בעושיו לשון רבים כי ברוב מקומות כלל לשון אלהות ואדנות
sources.says: Meiri says בעושיו is plural because in most places words for God and for a master are plural.

sources.quote: ישמח, בעושיו. בלשון תפארת, וכן איה אלוה עושי
sources.says: Radak says the plural is a form of glory, like 'where is God my Maker'.

149:3.headline: מחול: a dance, or a musical instrument
149:3.body: The Targum renders מחול as dancing. Metzudat Zion lists it with the drum and the lyre as names of musical instruments.

sources.quote: יְשַׁבְּחוּן שְׁמֵיהּ בְּחִנְגִין
sources.says: The Targum says they will praise His name with dances.

sources.quote: במחול בתוף וכנור. שמות כלי נגון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says מחול, drum and lyre are names of musical instruments.

149:5.headline: בכבוד: in their honor, or in their soul
149:5.body: Radak reads בכבוד as the honor and rest God gives Israel. Meiri adds that כבוד can mean the soul, as in עורה כבודי, 'wake up, my soul' (Psalms 57:9).

sources.quote: ישראל שהם חסידים לאל על כבודם ומנוחתם שיעמדו לעולם
sources.says: Radak says Israel, who are devoted to God, will rejoice over their honor and rest, which will last forever.

sources.quote: ויש לפרש בכבוד בנפש כי הנפש יקרא כבוד כאמרו עורה כבודי
sources.says: Meiri says בכבוד can be explained as the soul, since the soul is called כבוד, as in 'wake up, my כבוד'.

149:5.headline: On their beds: alone at night, at rest, or after death
149:5.body: Ibn Ezra says they sing on their beds when alone at night. Metzudat David reads it as rest in their own land, and Meiri says it can mean after death, since lying down can stand for rest.

sources.quote: וטעם ירננו על משכבותם – בהתבודדם בלילה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'they sing on their beds' means when they are alone at night.

sources.quote: ור״ל ירננו לה׳ כשיהיו בארצם במנוחה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means they will sing to God when they are at rest in their land.

sources.quote: וירננו על משכבותם ר״ל אחר מנוחתם הוא אחר המות
sources.says: Meiri says 'they sing on their beds' means after their rest, that is, after death.

149:6.headline: Praise in the throat and a sword in hand, or praise as the sword
149:6.body: Radak reads two things at once: prayer in their mouths and a sword in their hands. Rashi and Metzudat David say the praise itself is the two-edged sword that beats the enemy.

sources.quote: והתפלה תהיה בפיהם וחרב בידם
sources.says: Radak says prayer will be in their mouths and a sword in their hands.

sources.quote: וְהֵם לְחֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת בְּיָדָם
sources.says: Rashi says the praises are a two-edged sword in their hands.

sources.quote: בגרונם יספרו רוממות האל וזה תהיה לחרב פיפיות בידם
sources.says: Metzudat David says they will tell God's praises with their throats, and this will be a two-edged sword in their hands.

sources.quote: אמר רבי משה: כי ישבחו השם בבואם למלחמה. ור' ישועה אמר: רוממות אל בגרונם, כמו: חרב פיפיות בידם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra brings two views: Rabbi Moshe says they praise God as they go to war, and Rabbi Yeshua says the praise in their throats is like a two-edged sword in their hands.

149:7.headline: תוכחות: punishments, or nations arguing with their own kings
149:7.body: Metzudat Zion reads תוכחות as judgment through suffering, as in 'he is rebuked with pain' (Job 33:19). Radak reads it as the nations arguing with their kings over why this came on them.

sources.quote: תוכחות. ענין משפט יסורים כמו והוכח במכאוב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says תוכחות means judgment by suffering, as in 'he is rebuked with pain'.

sources.quote: תוכחות שיתוכחו עם מלכיהם למה בא עליהם
sources.says: Radak says תוכחות means they will argue with their kings over why this came upon them.

149:9.headline: 'The written judgment' was not yet written in David's day
149:9.body: Rashi says the judgment is the one in Ezekiel 25:14, even though Ezekiel lived long after David. David was speaking of the final redemption, and by then it would long be written.

sources.quote: וְאִם תֹּאמַר עֲדַיִן לֹא נוֹלַד יְחֶזְקֵאל כְּשֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד זֹאת? נִתְנַבֵּא דָּוִד עַל קֵץ הַגְּאֻלָּה, וּכְשֶׁיָּבֹא הַקֵּץ, כְּבָר כָּתוּב הוּא הַמִּשְׁפָּט זֶה יָמִים רַבִּים
sources.says: Rashi asks how this can be, since Ezekiel was not yet born when David said it, and answers that David prophesied about the end, when the judgment will have been written for many days.

sources.quote: ואף שבימי דוד עדיין לא היה כתוב מ״מ אמר כתוב שבימי הגאולה כבר יהיה כתוב
sources.says: Metzudat David says that although it was not yet written in David's time, he says 'written' because in the days of the redemption it will already be written.

sources.quote: לְמֶעְבַּד בְּהוֹן דִין דִכְתִיב בְּאוֹרַיְתָא
sources.says: The Targum says it means to carry out on them the judgment written in the Torah.

150:1.headline: 'The sky of His strength': the heavenly spheres, or the Ark
150:1.body: Radak says it is the highest sphere around everything, where God's strength is seen. Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi, cited by Ibn Ezra, says it is the Ark, since the psalm speaks with the Levites who sang in the Temple.

sources.quote: ברקיע עוזו. הוא גלגל העליון מקיף הכל, לפיכך אמר עוזו שבו נראה עוז האל יתברך
sources.says: Radak says 'the sky of His strength' is the highest sphere, which surrounds everything, and it says 'His strength' because God's strength is seen in it.

sources.quote: וברקיע עזו הוא הארון וזה המשורר עם הלוים ידבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi, who says 'the sky of His strength' is the Ark, and the poet is speaking to the Levites.

150:5.headline: שמע here is a noun: cymbals of sound
150:5.body: Rashi says שמע here is a noun meaning sound, the same as שֶׁמַע, with its vowel changed by the pause in the verse. These are cymbals that make themselves heard.

sources.quote: שָׁמַע. שֵׁם דָּבָר הוּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמַע בְּסֶגוֹל, וּמִפְּנֵי הָאֶתְנַחְתָּא הוּא נָקוּד קָמַץ גָּדוֹל
sources.says: Rashi says שמע is a noun, like שֶׁמַע, and has a different vowel only because of the pause in the verse.

sources.quote: מְצִלְתַּיִם הַמַּשְׁמִיעִים קוֹל
sources.says: Rashi says they are cymbals that make a sound.

150:5.headline: The same word, now trumpets: צלצל means a rattling noise
150:5.body: Metzudat Zion and Meiri say the second צלצלי, 'of blasting', are trumpets, not cymbals. Metzudat Zion says צלצל means any rattling noise, as in צללו שפתי, 'my lips quivered' (Habakkuk 3:16).

sources.quote: בצלצלי תרועה. הם החצוצרות המשמיעים הרעשת קול תרועה כי צלצל הוא ענין הרעשת קול וכן לקול צללו שפתי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says 'cymbals of blasting' are the trumpets that make a loud blast, since צלצל means a rattling noise, as in 'my lips quivered at the sound'.

sources.quote: וצלצלי תרועה נראה שהם חצוצרות המשמיעות קול תרועה
sources.says: Meiri says 'cymbals of blasting' seem to be trumpets that sound a blast.

150:6.headline: נשמה: the musician's breath, or the soul
150:6.body: Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi, cited by Ibn Ezra, says music changes with the length of the player's breath, so the book ends 'every breath shall praise'. Radak says the highest praise is the soul's: thinking about what God has made.

sources.quote: בעבור היות המנגן אומר נעימות על הכינור וישתנו הנעימות כפי אריכות הרוח וקוצר הקול
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites Rabbi Yehuda, who says a musician plays tunes on the lyre and the tunes change with the length of the breath and the shortness of the voice.

sources.quote: ועל כל ההילולים הוא הילול הנשמה והוא התבונן במעשה האל יתברך
sources.says: Radak says above all the praises is the praise of the soul, which is thinking about the works of God.

sources.quote: כל מי שיש בו נשמה ונפש משכלת תהלל את יה
sources.says: Metzudat David says everyone who has a soul and a thinking mind should praise God.

17:1.headline: רנה can be a song, a shout, a prayer or weeping
17:1.body: Radak says רנה covers many things, and only the place in the text tells which. Midrash Tehillim hears 'murmuring' (רינונה) of Torah study in it.

sources.quote: וכל לשון רנה הוא לשון צעקה: ויש מהם לשירה ולשמחה, ויש מהם להכרזה, ויש לתפלה ולבקשה, ויש לבכי ואנקה
sources.says: Radak says רנה is a kind of outcry, and it can mean song and joy, proclaiming, prayer and request, or weeping and groaning.

sources.quote: רנתי - בקול גדול, כמו: ותעבר הרנה ותפלתי בלחש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says רנתי means in a loud voice, while תפלתי is whispered.

sources.quote: הקשיבה רנתי זו רינונה של תורה
sources.says: Midrash Tehillim says the רנתי here is the רינונה, the murmuring, of Torah study.

17:2.headline: משפטי: the verdict against me, or my case against my enemies
17:2.body: Rashi reads 'my judgment' as the sins that deserve punishment: let them leave God's presence. Radak prefers a different sense: God should take up David's case and rule for him against his enemies.

sources.quote: עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבְּיָדִי, שֶׁאֲנִי רָאוּי לְהִשָּׁפֵט עֲלֵיהֶם בְּיִסּוּרִין, יֵצְאוּ מִלְּפָנֶיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says the judgment is the sins in David's hands that deserve suffering, and they should leave God's presence.

sources.quote: והקרוב אלי כי הוא כמו כי עשית משפטי ודיני (שם ט ה) שפרושו: שתקח משפטי מאויבי
sources.says: Radak says it is like 'you have done my judgment and my cause': that God takes his case from his enemy.

17:3.headline: 'You visited me by night': which night?
17:3.body: Rashi says it was the evening of David's sin with Bathsheba. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David say it is simply the night, when a person is alone and his thoughts are clear.

sources.quote: לְעֵת הָעֶרֶב בַּעֲוֹן בַּת שֶׁבַע
sources.says: Rashi says the night was the evening of the matter of Bathsheba.

sources.quote: וטעם בלילה – בהתבודדו מבני אדם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the night means the time when a person is alone, away from people.

sources.quote: והוא עת שמחשבת האדם צלולה
sources.says: Metzudat David says night is the time when a person's thinking is clear.

17:3.headline: זמתי: thoughts that match my words, or regret for what I said
17:3.body: Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David read זמותי as 'my thoughts', which never go beyond what the mouth says. Radak reads it as regret that David once asked God to test him.

sources.quote: זמותי. ענין מחשבה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says זמותי means thought.

sources.quote: מחשבותי אינם עוברים דברי פי רצה לומר כמחשבותי כן אמרי פי
sources.says: Metzudat David says his thoughts do not go beyond the words of his mouth: as he thinks, so he speaks.

sources.quote: הלואי שלא יעבר פי ולא הייתי אומר אותו הדבר שנתגאתי בו ונכשלתי בו
sources.says: Radak says: if only my mouth had not passed, and I had not said the thing I was proud of and stumbled over.

17:4.headline: 'I guarded the paths of the violent': guarded against them
17:4.body: Read plainly, it sounds like David kept those paths. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David say he guarded himself or others away from them.

sources.quote: אֲנִי שָׁמַרְתִּי בִּשְׁבִיל דְּבַר שְׂפָתֶיךָ אָרְחוֹת פָּרִיץ לִנְטוֹת מֵהֶם, שֶׁלֹּא אֵלֵךְ בָּהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says David guarded the paths of the violent man so as to turn away from them and not walk in them.

sources.quote: מנעתי שלא ילך אדם בארחות פריץ ורשע. וכמוהו לשמר את דרך עץ החיים (בראשית ג כד), שלא ילך בה
sources.says: Radak says he kept people from walking those paths, as in 'to guard the way of the tree of life'.

sources.quote: אורח הפרוץ וההרוס המבטל אורח המצות הנה אני שמרתיו לבלי תת למי ללכת בו
sources.says: Metzudat David says David guarded the path of the breached and ruined so that no one would walk it.

17:5.headline: תמך: a command, 'uphold!', or a report, 'I held on'
17:5.body: Radak says תמך is a verb form used in place of a command. Meiri says it stands in for the past: 'I held my steps to your paths'.

sources.quote: תמך מקור במקום צווי כמו שמור את יום השבת
sources.says: Radak says תמך is an infinitive used in place of a command, like שמור את יום השבת.

sources.quote: והוא מקור במקום עבר כלומ׳ תמכתי אשורי במעגלותיך
sources.says: Meiri says it is an infinitive in place of the past: 'I held my steps in your paths'.

17:7.headline: הפלה: 'set apart' or 'make wonderful'
17:7.body: Rashi and Radak read הפלה as separating: set your kindness apart for those who trust you. Meiri hears great publicity, like פליאה, 'wonder'.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ ״וְנִפְלִינוּ אֲנִי וְעַמְּךָ״
sources.says: Rashi ties הפלה to ונפלינו אני ועמך, where God sets Moses and Israel apart.

sources.quote: הפלה הפרש, כמו והפליתי ביום ההוא
sources.says: Radak says הפלה means separate, like והפליתי ביום ההוא.

sources.quote: והפלה הוראת פרסום גדול כענין פליאה דעת
sources.says: Meiri says הפלה means great publicity, like פליאה דעת, 'wonderful knowledge'.

17:8.headline: The pupil is 'little man': you see a tiny man in it
17:8.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion say אישון is named for the small figure of a man (איש) seen in the eye, and the ון ending makes it small. Rashi instead links it to darkness, since the pupil is the black part.

sources.quote: ונקרא אישון לפי שנראת בו צורת איש. והוא"ו והנו"ן להקטין, לפי שהצורה היא קטנה
sources.says: Radak says it is called אישון because the shape of a man (איש) is seen in it, and the ו and ן make it small.

sources.quote: יקרא אישון על שנראה בו צורת איש קטן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the black of the eye is called אישון because a figure of a small man is seen in it.

sources.quote: וְעַל שֵׁם שַׁחֲרוּרִיתוֹ הוּא קָרוּי אִישׁוֹן, לְשׁוֹן חֹשֶׁךְ
sources.says: Rashi says it is called אישון for its blackness, from the word for darkness.

17:11.headline: Written 'surrounded me', read 'surrounded us'
17:11.body: The text is written with 'me' (סבבוני) but read aloud with 'us' (סבבונו). Radak says both fit: 'us' for David and the men with him, 'me' for David himself.

sources.quote: וקרי בוא"ו; והוא לשון רבים עליו ועל חבריו, שהתלקטו עמו בברחו מפני שאול, ולשון יחיד על עצמו, כי הוא העקר
sources.says: Radak says the reading is plural, for David and his companions who gathered to him, while the written form is singular, for David himself, the main one.

17:12.headline: Maimonides: 'likeness' here means likeness in character, not in shape
17:12.body: In the Guide, Maimonides lists this verse among uses where דמות means likeness in idea, not in form. Radak says the singular דמינו points to Saul, and Ibn Ezra says it means each one of the surrounding enemies.

sources.quote: כולם דומוּת בעניין, לא בתבנית ובמתאר
sources.says: Maimonides says these verses, including דמינו כאריה, all mean likeness in idea, not in form or outline.

sources.quote: דמינו לשון יחיד על שאול
sources.says: Radak says דמינו, in the singular, refers to Saul.

sources.quote: דמיונו - דמיון כל אחד מהסובבים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the likeness of each one of those surrounding.

17:13.headline: הכריעהו: make him kneel, or tip the scale against him
17:13.body: Rashi reads it as cutting his legs so he kneels and falls. Midrash Tehillim hears a scale: from the pan of merit to the pan of guilt, or else 'break him'.

sources.quote: קַפַּח אֶת רַגְלָיו וְיִכְרַע וְיִפּוֹל
sources.says: Rashi says it means strike his legs so that he kneels and falls.

sources.quote: מהו הכריעהו מכף זכות לכף חובה. דבר אחר שברהו
sources.says: Midrash Tehillim says הכריעהו means from the pan of merit to the pan of guilt, or else 'break him'.

17:13.headline: 'From the wicked, your sword': is he the sword, or the target?
17:13.body: Rashi says the wicked man is God's sword, which God lets loose on the guilty. The Targum says he is a man condemned to die by God's sword, and Meiri allows 'by your sword'.

sources.quote: מִכָּל רָשָׁע שֶׁהוּא חַרְבְּךָ, שֶׁאַתָּה מַשְׁלִיטוֹ לִיפָּרַע מִן הַמְחֻיָּבִים לְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says it means every wicked man who is God's sword, whom God lets take payment from the guilty.

sources.quote: מִן רַשִׁיעָא דְאִתְחַיֵיב קְטוֹל בְּסַיְפָךְ
sources.says: The Targum says: from the wicked man who is condemned to be killed by your sword.

sources.quote: או פירושו בחרבך
sources.says: Meiri also allows that it means 'by your sword'.

17:14.headline: חלד: the world, a lifetime, or rust
17:14.body: Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read חלד as the world or a span of time. Rashi hears חלודה, 'rust': people who die old, after they have gathered rust.

sources.quote: מֵאוֹתָם שֶׁמֵּתִים בְּזִקְנָה, מִשֶּׁהֶעֱלוּ חֲלֻדָּה
sources.says: Rashi says it means those who die in old age, after they have gathered rust (חלודה).

sources.quote: מחלד. ענין זמן כמו מה חלד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says מחלד means time, like מה חלד.

sources.quote: ממתים מחלד - שכל חפצם להיותם מבני זה העולם, כי חלד אינו דבר עומד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means those whose whole desire is to belong to this world, since חלד is not something that lasts.

17:14.headline: 'Your hidden store' fills bellies: whose, the righteous or the wicked?
17:14.body: Rashi says the hidden store is the good God keeps for those who fear Him. Radak says it is worldly goods that fill the wicked in this world.

sources.quote: וּמֵאוֹתָם אֲשֶׁר תְּמַלֵּא מְעֵיהֶם מִטּוּבְךָ אֲשֶׁר צָפַנְתָּ לִירֵאֶיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says it means those whose insides God fills from the good He hid for those who fear Him.

sources.quote: אלא שצפונך וטובך תמלא בטנם בעולם הזה
sources.says: Radak says it is your hidden store and your goodness that fill their bellies in this world.

17:15.headline: בהקיץ: 'when I wake', or 'when the dead wake'
17:15.body: Ibn Ezra says it means waking, not dreaming. Rashi and Metzudat David say it is the waking of the dead from their sleep, at the resurrection.

sources.quote: וזה איננו בחלום רק בהקיץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this is not in a dream but in waking.

sources.quote: אֶשְׂבְּעָה מֵרְאִיַּת תְּמוּנָתְךָ בְּהָקִיץ הַמֵּתִים מִשְּׁנָתָם
sources.says: Rashi says I will be satisfied from seeing your form when the dead wake from their sleep.

sources.quote: בעת בא זמן היקיצה הוא תחיית המתים
sources.says: Metzudat David says the waking is the time of the resurrection of the dead.

17:15.headline: תמונתך: the mind's grasp of God, or the likeness of God
17:15.body: Radak and Ibn Ezra say it is not seen with the eye but grasped by the mind. Rashi says the risen dead are in the likeness of God's form, since man was made in God's image.

sources.quote: והוא השגת השכל, מכבוד האל כפי כח הנשמה אחרי הפרדה מהגוף
sources.says: Radak says it is the mind's grasp of God's glory, according to the soul's strength after it separates from the body.

sources.quote: וזאת המחזה אינה במראה העין רק במראה שקול הדעת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this seeing is not with the eye but with the weighing of the mind.

sources.quote: שֶׁהֵם בִּדְמוּת תְּמוּנָתְךָ, שֶׁכֵּן נֶאֱמַר ״כִּי בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם״
sources.says: Rashi says that the dead are in the likeness of God's form, as it says man was made in God's image.

18:2.headline: ארחמך: I love you, or I beg your mercy?
18:2.body: Rashi and Radak read ארחמך as 'I love you', since the Targum renders 'you shall love' with רחם. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'I ask mercy of you', a reading Meiri calls strange.

sources.quote: אֶרְחָמְךָ. אֲאַהֶבְךָ, כְּדִמְתַרְגֵּם ״וְאָהַבְתָּ״ (ויקרא יט:יח): ״וְתִרְחַם״
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'I will love you', as the Targum translates 'you shall love' with this word.

sources.quote: ופרושו אאהבך
sources.says: Radak says it means 'I will love you'.

sources.quote: וזה אבקש רחמים ממך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'I ask mercy of you'.

sources.quote: וי״מ אבקש רחמים ממך כמו אתרחם ממך והוא זר
sources.says: Meiri says some read 'I ask mercy of you', and calls that strange.

18:3.headline: 'My rock' is the rock where David was nearly caught
18:3.body: Rashi reads סלעי as a real place: the 'rock of division' where Saul's men had David surrounded, in 1 Samuel 23. God helped him escape there.

sources.quote: שֶׁעֲזַרְתַּנִי בְּסֶלַע הַמַּחְלְקוֹת, כְּשֶׁהָיִיתִי מְצֻמְצָם בֵּין שָׁאוּל וַאֲנָשָׁיו לְהִתָּפֵס
sources.says: Rashi says: you helped me at the rock of division, when I was hemmed in between Saul and his men and about to be caught.

18:5.headline: Bands of enemies, or the pangs of birth?
18:5.body: Rashi reads חבלי מות as camps of enemies, like 'a band (חבל) of prophets', and notes the Targum reads it as a woman's labor pains. Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra read pangs, and Ibn Ezra says the vowel sets it apart from the 'portions' (חבלי) of Manasseh.

sources.quote: מַחֲנוֹת אוֹיְבִים, כְּמוֹ ״חֶבֶל נְבִיאִים״
sources.says: Rashi says it means camps of enemies, as in 'a band of prophets'.

sources.quote: וְיוֹנָתָן תִּרְגֵּם: ״כְּאִתְּתָא דְּיָתְבָא עַל מַתְבְּרָא״, לְשׁוֹן ״חֶבְלֵי יוֹלֵדָה״
sources.says: Rashi says Targum Jonathan renders it 'like a woman on the birthing stool', the language of birth pangs.

sources.quote: חבלי. מכאובי כמו חבלי יולדה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means pains, as in 'the pangs of a woman in labor'.

sources.quote: אפפוני חבלי מות - כמו צירים וחבלים ועל כן הוא בשלש נקודות להפריש בינו ובין חבלי מנשה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means pangs, and its vowel sets it apart from 'the portions of Manasseh'.

18:5.headline: Torrents of the wicked, or sicknesses?
18:5.body: Rashi reads נחלי as troops sweeping in like a river (נחל), and Radak as troubles flooding in. Radak and Metzudat Zion also read it from 'your wound is sick (נחלה)', meaning illness.

sources.quote: וְנַחֲלֵי בְלִיַּעַל. אַף הוּא לְשׁוֹן גְּיָסוֹת שׁוֹטְפִים כְּנַחַל
sources.says: Rashi says it also means troops sweeping in like a river.

sources.quote: הצרות הן כנחל השוטף
sources.says: Radak says the troubles are like a flooding river.

sources.quote: ואפשר לפרש נחלי מן נחלה מכתך
sources.says: Radak says it can also be read from 'your wound is sick'.

sources.quote: ונחלי. מלשון חולי כמו נחלה מכתך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from the word for illness, as in 'your wound is sick'.

18:5.headline: בליעל: people without a yoke, or 'may he not rise'?
18:5.body: Metzudat Zion reads בליעל as בלי עול, 'without a yoke': people who threw off the yoke of heaven. Ibn Ezra cites Rabbi Yehuda Halevi, who read it as a curse, 'may he not rise' (יעלה).

sources.quote: בליעל. כמו בלי עול שפרקו עול שמים
