34:11.body: The word means young lions, and the Targum says lion cubs. Ibn Ezra notes that some read it as כופרים, deniers of God. He prefers people who grab like young lions and still go hungry.

sources.quote: יש אומרים: הכופרים בעיקר. והנכון בעיני: שהם בני האדם הדומים לכפירים לטרוף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some read it as those who deny God, but he thinks it means people who are like young lions in seizing prey.

sources.quote: בְּנֵי אַרְיְוָן אִתְמַסְכַּנוּ
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'lion cubs became poor'.

sources.quote: גדולים ועשירים
sources.says: Metzudat David says the lions stand for great and wealthy people.

34:22.headline: Which evil kills the wicked: his own, or one blow?
34:22.body: Rashi and Radak say the wicked man is killed by the very evil he does or plans. Ibn Ezra reads it as one disaster, set against the 'many evils' of the righteous in verse 20, who are saved from them all.

sources.quote: תְּמוֹתֵת אֶת הָרָשָׁע הָרָעָה שֶׁהוּא עוֹשֶׂה
sources.says: Rashi says the evil the wicked man does is what kills him.

sources.quote: הרעה שחושב הרשע לעשות לצדיק, אותה רעה תמיתהו
sources.says: Radak says the evil the wicked plans against the righteous is the evil that kills him.

sources.quote: רעה אחת מיד תמותת הרשע, כנגד רבות רעות צדיק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says one evil kills the wicked at once, set against the many evils of the righteous.

34:22.headline: יאשמו: found guilty, or laid waste
34:22.body: The word looks like אשם, guilt, and the Targum reads it that way. Radak and Metzudat Zion say it means ruin, from שממה, desolation.

sources.quote: וענינו מן שממה; וכן (הושע יד א): תאשם שמרון. ואשם ושמם כענין אחד
sources.says: Radak says it means desolation, as in 'Samaria shall be desolate', and that אשם and שמם mean the same.

sources.quote: יאשמו. מל׳ שממה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says יאשמו comes from the word for desolation.

sources.quote: וְסַנְאִי צַדִיקָא יִתְחַיְבוּן
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'those who hate the righteous will be found guilty'.

35:3.headline: וסגר: 'block the way', or the name of a weapon
35:3.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it as shutting the path before the pursuers. Radak and Meiri say it is the name of a weapon, set beside the spear.

sources.quote: הָגֵן בֵּינִי וּבֵינֵיהֶם כִּמְחִיצָּה
sources.says: Rashi says it means shield me from them with a wall between us.

sources.quote: וסגור - לסגור עליהם שלא ישיגוהו ברדפם אחריו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means to shut them in so they cannot catch him as they chase him.

sources.quote: וסגר שם כלי מכלי המלחמה
sources.says: Radak says וסגר is the name of one of the weapons of war.

sources.quote: והסגור שם לכלי מחדד
sources.says: Meiri says הסגור is the name of a sharp weapon.

35:8.headline: שואה: darkness, or sudden disaster
35:8.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion say שואה means darkness, so the trap-setter walks into the dark. Radak says it means a tumult that comes without warning.

sources.quote: שׁוֹאָה. חֹשֶׁךְ, בְּרוּאִינָ״ה בְּלַעַ״ז
sources.says: Rashi says שואה means darkness, and adds a foreign-language word.

sources.quote: שואה. חושך כמו אמש שואה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שואה means darkness, as in 'last night's שואה'.

sources.quote: וענין שואה כמו מהומה הבאה פתאום; וכן: ומשאת רשעים כי תבא
sources.says: Radak says שואה means an uproar that comes suddenly, as in 'the ruin of the wicked when it comes'.

35:13.headline: ותפלתי על חיקי תשוב: a wish, or a posture
35:13.body: Rashi and Radak read it as 'may what I prayed for them come back on me'. Ibn Ezra reports Rabbi Levi's view that he prayed bowed down and crushed, and Meiri reports a view that he kept returning to pray all day.

sources.quote: תְּפִלָּתִי שֶׁהִתְפַּלַּלְתִּי עֲלֵיהֶם תָּשׁוּב עָלַי
sources.says: Rashi says the prayer I prayed for them will come back on me.

sources.quote: כלומר, הטוב שהייתי מבקש עליהם יבוא עלי
sources.says: Radak says the good I asked for them will come to me.

sources.quote: אמר רבי לוי: הטעם שהייתי מתפלל ואני משתחוה ונדכה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports Rabbi Levi's view that I prayed while bowing down and crushed.

sources.quote: וי״מ ותפלתי על חיקי תשוב כלומ׳ שכל היום אני חוזר ומתפלל
sources.says: Meiri reports a view that it means all day long I keep returning to pray.

35:14.headline: Why a mother's mourning, and not a father's
35:14.body: Radak says a person grieves more for his mother, who bore, nursed and raised him. Meiri says a son finds some comfort after his father in the inheritance, but none after his mother.

sources.quote: כי יותר כואב אדם על אמו שנוצר ממנה בבטנה והיניקתו וגמלתו וטפחתו עד שגדל
sources.says: Radak says a person grieves more for his mother, from whose womb he was formed, who nursed, weaned and raised him.

sources.quote: אבלות האב יש לבן קצת נחמה בשמחתו על ירושתו אבל אבילות האם היא בלי שום נחמה
sources.says: Meiri says in mourning a father a son has some comfort in his joy at the inheritance, but mourning a mother has no comfort.

35:14.headline: קדר: a darkened face, or dark clothes
35:14.body: Radak says it may mean a face that grows dark with grief, or the black clothes a mourner wears. Ibn Ezra says mourners put on dark garments, and Metzudat Zion ties it to darkness.

sources.quote: וטעם קדר כי מפני היגון והאנחה ינוס זוהר פני אדם כי יתקדרו פניו. או אמר קדר על המלבוש, כי האבל לובש שחורים
sources.says: Radak says it means the shine of a person's face flees from grief and sighing so his face grows dark, or else it is about clothing, since a mourner wears black.

sources.quote: וטעם קודר – כי מנהג האבל להלביש עצמו קדרות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the custom of a mourner to dress himself in dark clothes.

sources.quote: קודר. ענין חושך כמו שמש וירח קדרו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says קודר means darkness, as in 'sun and moon grew dark'.

35:16.headline: Grinding teeth: glee, or anger
35:16.body: Radak says חרק שן here means glee, the grinding of teeth when seeing revenge on one's enemies. Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David read it as anger.

sources.quote: חרק מקור; וענינו: שמח, שמחרק אדם שניו בראותו נקמה מאיביו
sources.says: Radak says חרק is a verb-noun meaning glad, since a person grinds his teeth on seeing revenge on his enemies.

sources.quote: ענין שחיקת וטחינת השינים אלו באלו בהתקצף
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the grinding of the teeth against each other in anger.

sources.quote: חרק עלי שניו דרך כעס וקצף
sources.says: Metzudat David says each of them ground his teeth at me in anger and rage.

35:27.headline: 'His servant': David, or the whole people
35:27.body: Radak says the servant is David, whose peace God wanted and whom he saved. Meiri says it refers to the whole nation, as in 'Jacob my servant'.

sources.quote: הוא דוד שרצה בשלומו והצילהו משונאיו
sources.says: Radak says the servant is David, whose peace God wanted and whom he saved from his enemies.

sources.quote: ושלום עבדו לשיטתנו נאמ׳ על כלל האומה כמו יעקב עבדי
sources.says: Meiri says that in his reading, 'the peace of his servant' is said of the whole nation, as in 'Jacob my servant'.

35:17.headline: משאיהם: their darkness, or their roar
35:17.body: Rashi and Metzudat David read it as darkness. Radak and Meiri read it as their roaring noise and tumult.

sources.quote: מִשּׁוֹאֵיהֶם. מֵחֹשֶׁךְ שֶׁלָּהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says משואיהם means from their darkness.

sources.quote: הצל נפשי מחשכת הצרות אשר יביאו עלי
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means save my life from the darkness of the troubles they bring on me.

sources.quote: ופרוש משאיהם: משאונם וממהמתם
sources.says: Radak says משאיהם means their roar and their tumult.

sources.quote: ושואיהם שם כמו שאונם והמונם
sources.says: Meiri says שואיהם is a noun like their roar and their noise.

36:2.headline: Here 'sin' is a voice inside, the urge to do wrong
36:2.body: פשע usually means a crime. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion say here it is the evil urge itself, which speaks to the wicked man and tells him to do as he likes.

sources.quote: שֶׁהַפֶּשַׁע, הוּא יֵצֶר הָרָע, אוֹמֵר לָרָשָׁע
sources.says: Rashi says the פשע here is the evil urge, and it speaks to the wicked man.

sources.quote: כי הפשע, והוא יצר הרע, אומר לרשע עשה מה שתרצה. וקראו פשע כמו שקראו חטאת
sources.says: Radak says the פשע is the evil urge telling the wicked to do what he wants, and it is called פשע just as it is called חטאת in Genesis 4:7.

sources.quote: יצה״ר נקרא פשע כמו שנקרא חטאת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the evil urge is called פשע, just as it is called חטאת.

36:3.headline: Who hates whom: God the sinner, or the sinner the good?
36:3.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra say God finds the man's sin and so hates him. Radak gives two other readings: the man does the sin so often he grows sick of it, or he seeks out sin and hates the good way.

sources.quote: כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּמְצָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶת עֲוֹנוֹ, לִשְׂנֹא אוֹתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is so that God will find his sin and hate him.

sources.quote: למצוא השם עונו וישנאהו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God will find his sin and hate him.

sources.quote: מרוב התמדתו יקוץ בעברה וישנאנה
sources.says: Radak says that from doing the sin so often, he grows sick of it and hates it.

sources.quote: יפתנו למצא עונו לשנא להפך, והוא הדרך הטוב
sources.says: Radak also says it can mean sin lures him to hate the opposite, the good way.

36:6.headline: God's kindness reaches the sky, or withdraws to it
36:6.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion say בהשמים means 'up to the heavens', so God's kindness is huge. Rashi reads it the other way: because of the wicked, God takes His kindness away from people up to heaven.

sources.quote: ופרוש בהשמים: עד השמים
sources.says: Radak says בהשמים means up to the heavens.

sources.quote: בהשמים. ר״ל עד השמים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means up to the heavens.

sources.quote: בִּשְׁבִיל רְשָׁעִים הַלָּלוּ אַתָּה מְסַלֵּק חֶסֶד מִן הַתַּחְתּוֹנִים
sources.says: Rashi says that because of these wicked men God removes His kindness from those below.

36:7.headline: 'Mountains of God' means very high mountains
36:7.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion say that adding God's name to a thing is a way of saying it is huge, as with 'cedars of God'. Rashi also reads אל as strength, as in 'the mighty of the land'.

sources.quote: וכן מנהג הלשון כשרוצה להגדיל הדבר סומך אותו אל האל
sources.says: Radak says that when the language wants to make a thing great, it joins it to God's name.

sources.quote: הרוצה להגדיל דבר מה סומכו למלת אל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says one who wants to make a thing great attaches it to the word אל.

sources.quote: אַתָּה מַגְבִּיהוֹ וּמְתַקְּפוֹ כְּהַרְרֵי אֵל, לְשׁוֹן תּוֹקֶף
sources.says: Rashi says God raises up and strengthens the one He favors like mountains of אל, and that אל here is a word for strength.

36:9.headline: A 'river of your delights', and the river out of Eden
36:9.body: עדניך means 'your delights' and has the letters of Eden. Metzudat David pictures a river flowing out of Eden to water the righteous. Radak says the delights will be as many as the waters of a river.

sources.quote: ומימי נחל היוצא מהעדן תשקה אותם
sources.says: Metzudat David says God will give them drink from the waters of a river that flows out of Eden.

sources.quote: שיהיו העדנים לרוב כמו מי הנחל
sources.says: Radak says the delights will be plentiful like the waters of a river.

sources.quote: וּמַבּוּעַ בְּסִימוּתָךְ תַּשְׁקִנוּן
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'from the spring of your sweetness you will give them drink'.

36:13.headline: 'There they fell': in that place, or at that time
36:13.body: Metzudat David reads שם as a place: the wicked fall right where they came to harm him. Ibn Ezra and Meiri say שם can mean 'then'. Meiri also reads it as 'there', in the world to come.

sources.quote: מקום אשר יבואו להצר לי שם נפלו
sources.says: Metzudat David says they fall in the very place where they come to harm him.

sources.quote: ופירוש שם כמו אז
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says שם can mean 'then'.

sources.quote: אבל שם ר״ל לעולם הבא יפלו ונדחו מאין תקומה
sources.says: Meiri says 'there' may mean in the world to come, where they fall and do not rise.

37:1.headline: אל תתחר: 'don't be angry', or 'don't compete'
37:1.body: Ibn Ezra and Meiri say תתחר may come from חרון, anger. Rashi, Radak and Meiri also give 'don't join in', like ואיך תתחרה את הסוסים, 'how will you compete with horses'.

sources.quote: יש אומרים: כי תתחר מבנין התפעל מגזרת חרון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some take תתחר as a reflexive form from the root of anger (חרון).

sources.quote: ומלת תתחר מלשון חרי אף מבנין התפעל מלשון ויתגל. וי״מ אל תתערב מלשון ואיך תתחרה את הסוסים
sources.says: Meiri says תתחר comes from burning anger (חרי אף), and some say it means 'don't mix in', from ואיך תתחרה את הסוסים.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ ״וְאֵיךְ תְּתַחֲרֶה אֶת הַסּוּסִים״ (ירמיה יב:ה) לָרוּץ בִּמְרוּצָתָם
sources.says: Rashi says it is like ואיך תתחרה את הסוסים: to run in their race.

sources.quote: אל תתחר רצונו לומר אל תתערב
sources.says: Radak says אל תתחר means 'do not mix in'.

37:3.headline: 'Tend faithfulness': feed on it, keep it, or teach it
37:3.body: Rashi reads רעה as 'feed': live off the reward of your faith. Ibn Ezra says it means 'keep', as a shepherd keeps a flock, and Radak says it means to shepherd others by teaching.

sources.quote: תֹּאכַל וְתִתְפַּרְנֵס מִשְּׂכַר הָאֱמוּנָה שֶׁהֶאֱמַנְתָּ בְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says you will eat and be fed from the reward of the faith you had in God.

sources.quote: רעה אמונה - כמו: שומר אמונים, כי הרועה כמו שומר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says רעה אמונה is like שומר אמונים, since a shepherd is like a keeper.

sources.quote: והמלמד בני אדם רעה אותם
sources.says: Radak says that one who teaches people is shepherding them.

37:4.headline: והתענג על ה': a command, or a promise?
37:4.body: Radak and Meiri say the command form stands for the future: you will find delight in God. Rashi reads it as enjoying comforts while leaning on God's support.

sources.quote: ובא הצוי (והתענג) במקום אי"תן, כמו: ומת בהר (דברים לב ג) כמו תמות
sources.says: Radak says the command form והתענג stands in place of a future, like ומת בהר, which means 'you will die'.

sources.quote: ובאה מלת התענג צווי במקום עתיד כמו אם בין כוכבים שים קנך
sources.says: Meiri says התענג is a command used in place of the future, like שים קנך.

sources.quote: הִתְעַנֵּג בְּתַפְנוּקִים עַל מִשְׁעַנְתּוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says to enjoy delicacies, resting on the support of God.

37:7.headline: דום: 'wait', or 'be silent'
37:7.body: Rashi says דום means 'wait for His rescue', like Jonathan's דמו, and Metzudat Zion says 'hope'. Menachem, quoted by Rashi, and the Targum read it as 'be silent'.

sources.quote: הַמְתֵּן לִישׁוּעָתוֹ, כְּמוֹ ״אִם כֹּה יֹאמְרוּ אֵלֵינוּ דֹּמּוּ״ דִּיהוֹנָתָן
sources.says: Rashi says דום means 'wait for His rescue', like Jonathan's דמו.

sources.quote: וּמְנַחֵם חִבְּרוֹ לְשׁוֹן דְּמָמָה, כְּמוֹ ״וַיִּדֹּם אַהֲרֹן״
sources.says: Rashi says Menachem tied it to silence (דממה), like וידם אהרן.

sources.quote: דום. קוה כמו לאלהים דומי נפשי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says דום means 'hope', like לאלהים דומי נפשי.

sources.quote: שְׁתוֹק קֳדָם יְיָ
sources.says: The Targum renders it: be silent before the Lord.

37:7.headline: והתחולל: 'hope', or 'writhe like a woman in labor'
37:7.body: Rashi says it means hoping (תוחלת). Ibn Ezra says it comes from חיל כיולדה, the pain of a woman in labor, and that this is the right reading.

sources.quote: וְהִתְחוֹלֵל. לְשׁוֹן ״תּוֹחֶלֶת״
sources.says: Rashi says והתחולל is the language of hoping (תוחלת).

sources.quote: ואחרים אמרו: שהוא מגזרת חיל כיולדה והוא הנכון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says others take it from the pain of a woman in labor, and that this is the right one.

sources.quote: לו רצונו לומר: סבול החיל והכאב בעבורו
sources.says: Radak says לו means: bear the pain and the labor for His sake.

37:14.headline: חרב פתחו: draw the sword, sharpen it, or start a fight
37:14.body: Metzudat David says פתחו means they drew the sword from its sheath. Ibn Ezra gives 'sharpen' as another reading, and Rashi reads it as the wicked starting strife on their own.

sources.quote: הוציאוה מתערה
sources.says: Metzudat David says פתחו means they took the sword out of its sheath.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: כי פתיחת חרב היא הלטישה, וכמוהו והמה פתיחות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some say opening a sword is sharpening it, like והמה פתיחות.

sources.quote: תָּגָר וְחֵרוּם מַתְחִילִים הָרְשָׁעִים מֵאֲלֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the wicked start strife and war on their own.

37:18.headline: 'Forever': the world to come, or this world?
37:18.body: Radak's father reads the whole verse as the world to come. Ibn Ezra reads it as this world, where the inheritance passes to the children.

sources.quote: ואדני אבי, זכרו לברכה, פרש כל הפסוק: לעולם הבא. והחכם רבי אברהם בן עזרא פרשו: לעולם הזה; ופרש נחלתם: שינחילו הטוב לבניהם
sources.says: Radak says his father explained the whole verse as the world to come, while Ibn Ezra explained it as this world, with the inheritance meaning they pass the good to their children.

37:20.headline: 'Consumed, consumed': emphasis, or two different subjects?
37:20.body: Radak says the repeat stresses how complete the ending is. Ibn Ezra says the first כלו is about the glory and the second about the wicked.

sources.quote: וכפל כלו לרוב הכליון
sources.says: Radak says כלו is doubled for the fullness of the ending.

sources.quote: וכלו הראשון על היקר. וכלו השני על הרשעים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the first כלו is about the glory and the second is about the wicked.

37:21.headline: 'The righteous gives': Rashi says this is God
37:21.body: Rashi reads the 'righteous one' as God, the Righteous One of the world, who gives to the lender what the wicked man took. Radak reads it as a righteous person who gives freely.

sources.quote: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, שֶׁהוּא צַדִּיקוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, חוֹנֵן מִשֶּׁלּוֹ וְנוֹתֵן לָזֶה שֶׁהִלְוָה מַה שֶּׁהוּא גּוֹזֵל מִמֶּנּוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it is God, the Righteous One of the world, who gives from His own to the lender what the wicked man takes.

sources.quote: והצדיק בהפך, כי חונן לבני אדם ונותן להם משלו
sources.says: Radak says the righteous man is the opposite: he is kind to people and gives them from his own.

37:22.headline: מברכיו: those God blesses, or those who bless God?
37:22.body: Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read it as those whom God blesses. Radak reads it as those who bless God, the righteous.

sources.quote: טעם מבורכיו ברכת ה' היא תעשיר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says מבורכיו means that God's blessing is what makes rich.

sources.quote: ואת אשר יברכם יירשו הארץ
sources.says: Metzudat David says those whom He blesses will inherit the land.

sources.quote: כי מברכיו מברכי האל, יתברך
sources.says: Radak says מברכיו means those who bless God.

37:23.headline: גבר means a hero, a man of knowledge, or one who strives
37:23.body: Rashi reads גבר as a hero in awe of God, and Ibn Ezra as a man full of knowledge. Radak and Meiri say he is called גבר because he overcomes (מתגבר): the wicked, or his poverty.

sources.quote: מִי שֶׁהוּא גִּבּוֹר בְּיִרְאַת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says גבר is one who is a hero in awe of God.

sources.quote: גבר - בלשוננו הוא מלא דעת, כמו: לכו נא הגברים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says גבר in our language means one full of knowledge, like לכו נא הגברים.

sources.quote: הצדיק שמתגבר במעשיו הטובים על הרשע
sources.says: Radak says it is the righteous man who overcomes the wicked by his good deeds.

sources.quote: וקרא הצדיק גבר על שמתגבר לעבור עתו במעט ממונו
sources.says: Meiri says the righteous man is called גבר because he overcomes, getting through his time on little money.

37:26.headline: 'His seed for blessing': children, or the one who sows charity?
37:26.body: Radak reads זרעו as his children, who learn his ways. Rashi plays on the word: the one who sows (זורע) for charity ends in blessing.

sources.quote: זֶה שֶׁהוּא זוֹרֵעַ לִצְדָקָה, סוֹפוֹ לִבְרָכָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is the one who sows for charity, whose end is blessing.

sources.quote: וזרעו גם כן ילמדו דרכיו
sources.says: Radak says his children will also learn his ways.

37:28.headline: חסידיו: kindness beyond what the law asks
37:28.body: Radak asks why חסידיו follows משפט, since חסד goes past the line of the law. He answers that one who trains in fair dealing will reach kindness, giving even to someone he owes nothing.

sources.quote: ואמר: חסידיו אחר שאמר משפט, והחסד גדול מהמשפט כי הוא לפנים משורת הדין? לפי שכשירגיל אדם את עצמו במעשה היושר והמשפט לא יטה מקו האמת, ועל כל פנים יבא למדת החסידות, שהיא גמילות הטובה אף למי שלא נתחייב לו
sources.says: Radak says חסד is greater than משפט, being beyond the line of the law, and that one trained in fair dealing will come to חסידות, doing good even to one he owes nothing.

37:30.headline: יהגה: 'speaks' aloud, or 'thinks' in the heart first
37:30.body: Metzudat Zion says יהגה means speaks. Rashi says the righteous man first thinks the wisdom in his heart, and only then does his tongue speak.

sources.quote: יהגה. ידבר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says יהגה means 'speaks'.

sources.quote: תְּחִלָּה בְּלִבּוֹ חָכְמָה, לִרְאוֹת דִּין שֶׁפָּסְקָה תּוֹרָה לְכָל דָּבָר, וְאַחַר כָּךְ לְשׁוֹנוֹ תְּדַבֵּר מִשְׁפָּט
sources.says: Rashi says first he thinks wisdom in his heart, to see the law the Torah rules on every matter, and afterward his tongue speaks justice.

37:31.headline: One verb, many steps: not even one slips
37:31.body: תמעד is a singular verb but its subject אשריו, 'his steps', is plural. Radak and Meiri say this means not even one of his steps slips.

sources.quote: לא תמעד אשריו: אפילו אחת מאשריו, ופרושו: רגליו
sources.says: Radak says it means not even one of his steps, which are his feet.

sources.quote: ומלת תמעד באה על אשוריו שהם רבים כלומ׳ לא תמעד אחת מאשוריו
sources.says: Meiri says תמעד is said of his steps, which are many, meaning not one of his steps will slip.

sources.quote: תמעד. ענין החלקה והשמטה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says תמעד means slipping.

37:35.headline: ומתערה: takes root, soaks up water, or shows itself
37:35.body: Rashi says it means taking root, like ערות על יאור. Radak says it soaks up moisture like a fresh tree, and Ibn Ezra says it means the wicked shows himself openly.

sources.quote: מַשְׁרִישׁ, כְּמוֹ ״עָרוֹת עַל יְאוֹר״
sources.says: Rashi says it means taking root, like ערות על יאור.

sources.quote: שפרושו שמתלחלח כמו העץ שהוא רענן ורטוב
sources.says: Radak says it means he becomes moist, like a tree that is fresh and wet.

sources.quote: וטעם מתערה – מתגלה העושה בגלוי כל רע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says מתערה means he reveals himself, one who does all evil in the open.

37:37.headline: שמר תם: 'watch the blameless man', or 'keep wholeness'
37:37.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it as watching the blameless man and learning from him. Metzudat David and the Targum read it as keeping the way of wholeness.

sources.quote: הִסְתַּכְּלוּ בְּדַרְכֵי הַתְּמִימִים, לִלְמֹד מִמַּעֲשֵׂיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says: look at the ways of the blameless, to learn from their deeds.

sources.quote: ועתה שים לבך ושמור איש תם וראה איש ישר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says: now take it to heart and watch a blameless man, and see an upright man.

sources.quote: שמר דרך תם וראה דרך ישר ללכת בה
sources.says: Metzudat David says: keep the way of the blameless, and see the upright way, to walk in it.

sources.quote: נְטַר שְׁלֵימוּתָא וַחֲמֵי תְרִיצוּתָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it: keep wholeness, and see uprightness.

38:10.headline: He puts his hope in God, not in the doctors
38:10.body: Ibn Ezra reads נגדך as 'before you alone'. The sick man longs to live, and he lays that longing before God, not before the doctors. Radak quotes this reading.

sources.quote: אדני נגדך - לבדך כל תאותי, אולי אחיה ולא נגד הרופאים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says all his longing to live is before God alone, not before the doctors.

sources.quote: והחכם רבי אברהם בן עזרא פרש: נגדך לבדך כל תאותי, אולי אחיה מחליי; ולא נגד הרופאים
sources.says: Radak quotes Ibn Ezra's reading.

38:11.headline: A heart that spins in circles
38:11.body: סחרחר is a doubled word, like ירקרק, 'greenish'. Radak links it to the Aramaic סחור סחור, 'all around'. A troubled person's thoughts go round and round.

sources.quote: סְחַרְחַר. מֻקָּף יָגוֹן, וְזֶהוּ מִתֵּיבוֹת הַכְּפוּלוֹת, כְּמוֹ ״יְרַקְרַק אֲדַמְדַּם
sources.says: Rashi says it means surrounded by grief, and is one of the doubled words, like 'greenish, reddish'.

sources.quote: ופרוש סחרחר: סביב; ותרגום סביב (בראשית כג יז ובכל המקומות): סחור סחור
sources.says: Radak says it means 'around', since the Aramaic translation of 'around' is סחור סחור.

sources.quote: ומי שיש לו צרות רבות מחשבותיו הולכות וסובבות אנה ואנה
sources.says: Radak says a person with many troubles has thoughts that go around this way and that.

38:21.headline: Written one way, read another: hated for chasing good
38:21.body: The word is written רדופי but read רדפי. Radak says the written form means good is what he chases. The spoken form means 'my chasing'. Either way, they hate him because he pursues what is good.

sources.quote: ומלת רדפי כתובה רדופי, רוצה לומר: שהטוב רדופי שאני רודף אחריו, וקרי רדפי והוא מקור על הפועל
sources.says: Radak says the word is written רדופי, meaning good is my pursuit that I chase, and read רדפי, the plain verb form.

sources.quote: תַּחַת רָדְפִי טוֹב. בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁאֲנַחְנוּ דְּבֵקִים בַּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וּבְמִצְווֹתָיו
sources.says: Rashi says they hate us because we cling to God and his commandments.

39:2.headline: A muzzle, like the one an ox must not wear
39:2.body: מחסום appears only here. Rashi links it to 'do not muzzle an ox': David puts a muzzle on his own mouth. The Midrash says the Torah is that muzzle, keeping the tongue from evil talk.

sources.quote: מַחְסוֹם. כְּמוֹ ״לֹא תַחְסֹם שׁוֹר״
sources.says: Rashi says מחסום is a muzzle, as in 'do not muzzle an ox'.

sources.quote: ענין דבר ההושם בפי הבהמה שלא תישך ולא תאכל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the thing put in an animal's mouth so it cannot bite or eat.

sources.quote: וכי יש מחסום לפה אמרו הן. (משלי טו ד) מרפא לשון עץ חיים. זו התורה
sources.says: The Midrash asks whether there is a muzzle for the mouth, and answers yes: the Torah.

39:5.headline: חדל is חלד, 'world', with two letters swapped
39:5.body: מה חדל אני can mean 'how short-lived I am'. Metzudat Zion says חדל is חלד, 'the world' or 'lifetime', with letters swapped, as כבש and כשב are the same word. So David asks how long his time in the world will be.

sources.quote: חדל. היא הפוך מן חלד כמו כשב כבש וענינו זמן העולם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חדל is חלד reversed, like כשב and כבש, and means one's time in the world.

sources.quote: ושאדע מה חדל אני כלומ׳ כמה אני חדל ונמנע מזה העולם
sources.says: Meiri reads it as 'how much I cease and am held back from this world'.

39:6.headline: Breath, or trouble?
39:6.body: הבל means a breath or vapor. Radak says 'all הבל' means the tiniest wisp, like 'vanity of vanities'. Metzudat Zion says הבל can also mean troubles.

sources.quote: ואמר: כל הבל רוצה לומר: המעט שבהבל, כאלו אמר: הבל הבלים
sources.says: Radak says 'all הבל' means the smallest bit of vapor, like 'vanity of vanities'.

sources.quote: יש הבל שהוא ענין פורעניות וצרות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says הבל sometimes means calamity and troubles.

39:12.headline: His 'treasure': his body, or his wealth?
39:12.body: חמודו means 'what he holds dear'. Rashi says it is his flesh, melted away like cloth eaten by a moth. Metzudat David reads it as his treasured wealth.

sources.quote: חֲמוּדוֹ. בְּשָׂרוֹ, שֶׁהוּא חֶמְדָּתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says חמודו is his flesh, which is what he treasures.

sources.quote: וגם תמס חמודות עשרו כעש הזה המבלה את הבגד
sources.says: Metzudat David says God melts away the treasures of his wealth, like a moth wears out a garment.

4:1.headline: For the music leader, or for the God who is glad to lose
4:1.body: Rashi reads למנצח as 'for the leader', the Levite who led the Temple music. The Midrash also reads it as 'to the One who is beaten by His creatures', because God is glad when people win an argument with Him.

sources.quote: מִזְמוֹר זֶה יָסַד דָּוִד, שֶׁיֹּאמְרוּהוּ בְּנֵי לֵוִי הַמְנַצְּחִין בִּנְגִינוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says David wrote this psalm for the Levites who led the music on the Temple platform.

sources.quote: דבר אחר למנצח למי שמנוצח מבריותיו
sources.says: The Midrash reads it as 'to the One who is beaten by His creatures', and says a human king gets angry when beaten but God is glad, as when Moses talked Him out of destroying Israel.

4:5.headline: Be silent, or stop what you are doing
4:5.body: Radak says this root can mean silence in speech or a halt in action, and reads it here as 'stop rebelling'. Maimonides reads it as silence: no words can praise God fully, so the wise should know Him in their hearts and be still.

sources.quote: ומזה הענין הוא ודמו סלה, כלומר: חדלו לכם ממעשיכם
sources.says: Radak says the word here means stop your actions, and notes that Maimonides read it differently.

sources.quote: על כן השתיקה עדיפה, ויש להסתפק במה שהשכלים משיגים
sources.says: Maimonides says silence is the best praise of God, and cites this verse as the command to the wise.

4:7.headline: Odd spelling: raise your light over us like a banner
4:7.body: נסה is spelled strangely. Rashi reads it from נס, a banner raised high. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as נשא, 'lift up', with ס in place of ש and ה in place of א.

sources.quote: הָרֵם עָלֵינוּ לְנֵס אֶת אוֹר פָּנֶיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says it means raise the light of your face over us like a banner, and gives a second reading, 'make it shine'.

sources.quote: ובה"א תחת האל"ף, והוא כמו נשא
sources.says: Radak says the word is נשא, lift up, with ס for ש and ה for א.

4:9.headline: Who is alone here: God, or the man who sleeps safe?
4:9.body: Radak reads לבדד with God: 'You alone, LORD, make me dwell safely'. Rashi reads it with the sleeper, as in Deuteronomy 33:28 where Israel dwells safe and alone: so secure he needs no guards.

sources.quote: אתה יי' לבדך תעשה זה ובך בטחוני ולא באחר
sources.says: Radak says it means You, LORD, alone will do this, and my trust is in You and no one else.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן מִבְטָח וָשֶׁקֶט הוּא, שֶׁאֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ לְהוֹשִׁיב גְּיָסוֹת עִמּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi compares Deuteronomy 33:28 and says the word means safety and calm, with no need for troops beside him.

40:2.headline: I hoped and hoped: hope is all Israel has
40:2.body: The verse doubles the verb: 'hoping, I hoped'. The Midrash says Israel has nothing in hand but hope, and God saved David as the reward for hoping, not for sacrifices.

sources.quote: אין ביד ישראל אלא קווי כדי שיגאלו בשכר קוה קויתי
sources.says: The Midrash says Israel has nothing but hope, so that they will be redeemed as the reward for 'I hoped and hoped'.

sources.quote: ולמה עשה לי כך בשכר הקווי. ולא רצה לא זבחים ולא עולות אלא הקווי
sources.says: The Midrash has David say God did this for him as the reward for hoping, and wanted neither sacrifices nor burnt offerings, only the hope.

40:6.headline: Nothing compares to You, or Your wonders cannot be listed
40:6.body: Rashi reads אין ערך אליך as 'nothing can be compared to You', from ערך, value. Radak's first reading is that Your wonders are too many to set out in order, and he gives Rashi's reading second.

sources.quote: אֵין לְדַמּוֹת לְךָ כָּל שַׂר וּמוֹשִׁיעַ, לְשׁוֹן עֵרֶךְ כְּמוֹ ״כְּעֶרְכְּךָ״
sources.says: Rashi says no ruler or savior can be likened to You, from the word for value, as in 'according to your valuation'.

sources.quote: אין לערוך אליך וכנגדך כל הנפלאות שעשית עמנו, כי רבות הן מלערכן ומלספרן
sources.says: Radak says no one can set out before You all the wonders You did for us, because they are too many to list or count.

sources.quote: או אין ערוך כמו: אין כמוך באלהים אדני ואין כמעשיך
sources.says: Radak's second reading: 'there is none like You among the gods'.

40:7.headline: Ears You dug for me: listening over sacrifice
40:7.body: כרה means to dig, as one digs a pit. Rashi says God hollowed out ears so we could hear, and Ibn Ezra says God asked for listening, not offerings, as in 'obeying is better than sacrifice'.

sources.quote: כרית. חפרת כמו בור כרה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says כרית means 'You dug', as in 'he dug a pit'.

sources.quote: כָּרִיתָ. עֲשִׂיתָם חֲלוּלִים לִשְׁמֹעַ
sources.says: Rashi says it means You made them hollow so they could hear.

sources.quote: לא בקשת זבח רק כרית לי אזנים שאשמע בקולך, כמו: הנה שמוע מזבח טוב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God did not ask for sacrifice, only dug ears for him to obey His voice, as in 'obeying is better than sacrifice'.

40:9.headline: Your Torah in my belly: in my heart, or in my food
40:9.body: Radak reads מעי, my insides, as my heart, and Ibn Ezra as hidden within, like the scroll Ezekiel was told to eat. Rashi reads it plainly: even what I eat follows Your Torah.

sources.quote: ותורתך בתוך מעי: בתוך לבי, כי הלב בכלל המעים
sources.says: Radak says 'within my insides' means within my heart, because the heart counts among the insides.

sources.quote: ותורתך בתוך מעי - בסתר על דרך: אכול את המגלה הזאת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means in secret, like 'eat this scroll'.

sources.quote: וְתוֹרָתְךָ בְּתוֹךְ מֵעָי. אַף מַאֲכָלִי, עַל פִּי תוֹרָתְךָ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says even my food is according to Your Torah.

40:10.headline: To 'bring tidings' can mean bad news too
40:10.body: בשר means to bring news to many people. Radak and Ibn Ezra say it is used for bad news as well as good, as with the messenger in 1 Samuel 4 who reported the Ark was taken.

sources.quote: והבא לספר חדשות אם טוב ואם רע יקרא מבשר: על טוב ברוב; ועל רע גם כן, כמו: ויען המבשר
sources.says: Radak says one who tells news, good or bad, is called מבשר: mostly for good, but also for bad, as in 'the messenger answered'.

sources.quote: להגיד דבר חדש טוב או רע, כמו: ויען המבשר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word means telling something new, good or bad, as in 'the messenger answered'.

sources.quote: בשרתי. ענין השמעות חדשות לרבים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means making news heard by many.

40:13.headline: My sins caught up with me: the sins, or their punishment
40:13.body: Ibn Ezra says the harm that comes on a person is also called עון, sin, because the sin caused it, as in Cain's 'my עון is too great'. Radak reads it as the sins themselves, too many for him to see them all.

sources.quote: העונש והרע הבא על האדם יקרא עון, כי הוא היה הסבה לביאת הרעה, כמו: גדול עוני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the punishment and harm that come on a person are called עון, because the sin caused them, as in 'my עון is great'.

sources.quote: לא אוכל לראות עונותי כלם כי רבים המה
sources.says: Radak says I cannot see all my sins, because they are many.

40:18.headline: The evyon is poorer still: he longs for everything
40:18.body: Metzudat Zion says an אביון is poorer than an עני, a poor man. He reads it from תאב, to long: such a person longs for everything, because all of it is out of his reach.

sources.quote: ואביון. הוא דל מעני כי תאב הוא לכל דבר היות הכל נמנע מאתו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the אביון is poorer than the עני, because he longs for everything, since everything is kept from him.

41:2.headline: משכיל: one who looks after the weak, or who thinks it through
41:2.body: Radak says משכיל means one who looks in on a sick man and helps him. Ibn Ezra prefers 'one who understands' what God is doing. He also brings a reading where the visitor makes the sick man wise by comforting him. Metzudat David says it means giving to the poor wisely, so as not to shame them.

sources.quote: ומשכיל: משגיח ומביט, כלומר: שבא לבקרו
sources.says: Radak says משכיל means one who watches over and looks at the sick man, that is, comes to visit him.

sources.quote: והנכון: מגזרת שכל, שישים לבו שישכיל במעשה השם עם החולי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from שכל, understanding: one who sets his mind to understand God's way with the sick.

sources.quote: שמשכיל - פועל יוצא והוא המבקר וידבר על לבו וישכילנו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra adds that some read it as the visitor who speaks to the sick man's heart and makes him understand.

sources.quote: הנותן צדקה לדל בהשכל לבל יכלימו
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means one who gives charity to the poor wisely, so as not to shame him.

41:3.headline: בנפש here means 'to the will of', not 'soul'
41:3.body: נפש usually means soul or life. Maimonides says it can also mean will, and cites this verse: do not hand him over to what his enemies want. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it the same way.

sources.quote: כלומר אל תסגירהו אל רצונם
sources.says: Maimonides lists this verse under נפש meaning will: do not hand him over to their will.

sources.quote: ברצון איביו, כי הם רוצים שימות
sources.says: Radak says it means the will of his enemies, who want him to die.

sources.quote: בנפש. ברצון כמו אם יש את נפשכם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בנפש means 'by the will', as in 'if it is your will' in Genesis 23:8.

41:4.headline: הפכת: God turned his rest to pain, or turns him gently
41:4.body: Radak says God has turned the sick man's bed from a place of rest into trouble. He also reads it as a prayer: turn his bed back to health. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David picture God turning the sick man from side to side, like a nurse.

sources.quote: והנה הפכת משכבו מן המנוחה לצרה
sources.says: Radak says God turned his bed from rest into trouble.

sources.quote: ויש לפרש הפכת: כמו תהפך, והוא דרך תפלה
sources.says: Radak says הפכת can also be read as 'you will turn', as a prayer.

sources.quote: שתהפכהו על משכבו מצד אל צד ותסעדנו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God turns him on his bed from side to side and supports him.

sources.quote: כדרך המשמש את החולה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is like one who tends a sick man.

41:5.headline: 'Heal my soul': the body, or the sin behind the illness
41:5.body: Meiri says it means healing the body from its illness. Radak notes that David did not say 'heal my body', because his sins caused the illness. Metzudat David says sin is the soul's sickness and forgiveness is its cure.

sources.quote: ורפאה נפשי ר״ל רפואת גופו מחליו
sources.says: Meiri says 'heal my soul' means healing his body from its illness.

sources.quote: ולא אמר רפאה גופי, כי סבת חליו הם עונותיו
sources.says: Radak says he did not say 'heal my body', because his sins were the cause of his illness.

sources.quote: כי העון הוא חולי הנפש והמחילה היא הרפואה
sources.says: Metzudat David says sin is the sickness of the soul, and forgiveness is the cure.

41:10.headline: עקב: a lifted heel, or a lying-in-wait
41:10.body: עקב usually means heel. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say here it means an ambush, as in Joshua 8:13. Radak and Ibn Ezra keep the heel: the friend lifts himself over David as if David were under his foot.

sources.quote: הִגְדִּיל עָלַי עָקֵב. מַאֲרָב
sources.says: Rashi says עקב here means an ambush.

sources.quote: עקב. ענין מארב כמו ואת עקבו מים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says עקב means an ambush, as in 'its rear guard west of the city' in Joshua.

sources.quote: כאלו אני מדרך רגלו כך הוא מתגדל עלי
sources.says: Radak says the friend lords it over him as if David were the ground under his foot.

sources.quote: הגדיל עקיבו שלא בא לבקרני, ושם לנפשו מעלה גדולה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the friend raised his heel by not coming to visit, and thought himself important.

41:13.headline: בתמי: my honesty, or my bodily health
41:13.body: תם usually means whole or honest. Radak and Metzudat David read it as David's honesty. Ibn Ezra brings a view that here it means a whole, healthy body, and says that view is right.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: כי תומי - רמז לבריאת הגוף, והוא הנכון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some read תומי as a hint to the body's health, and that this is correct.

sources.quote: ובעבור שהלכתי אני בתמימות
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means because he walked in honesty.

sources.quote: במצאתני זך וישר
sources.says: Radak says it means when God found him pure and upright.

41:14.headline: 'From עולם to עולם': all time, all space, or two worlds
41:14.body: עולם can mean time, the world, or a world. The Targum reads 'from this world to the world to come'. Radak reads 'from the first time to the last'. Metzudat David reads 'from one end of the world to the other'.

sources.quote: מִן עַלְמָא הָדֵין וְעַד עָלְמָא דְאָתִי
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'from this world to the world to come'.

sources.quote: מהזמן הראשון עד הזמן האחרון
sources.says: Radak says it means from the first time to the last.

sources.quote: מקצה העולם עד קצהו
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means from one end of the world to the other.

42:2.headline: A male deer with a female verb: both are meant
42:2.body: איל is the male deer, but the verb תערג beside it is feminine. Rashi and Radak say the verse mixes them on purpose to include both male and female.

sources.quote: כְּאַיֶּלֶת תַּעֲרוֹג לֹא נֶאֱמַר וְכְאַיָּל יַעֲרוֹג לֹא נֶאֱמַר, אֶלָּא כְּאַיָּל תַּעֲרֹג. דִּבֵּר הַכָּתוּב בְּזָכָר וּבִנְקֵבָה
sources.says: Rashi notes the verse uses neither an all-female nor an all-male form, so it speaks of both.

sources.quote: ואמר איל לשון זכר ותערוג לשון נקבה כולל זכרים ונקבות
sources.says: Radak says the male noun and female verb together take in males and females.

sources.quote: ואיל - על לשון נקבה, כמו: עז בת שנתה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra instead says איל here is itself used as a feminine word.

42:3.headline: Thirst here means the soul's need to know God
42:3.body: Maimonides lists this verse where thirst stands for a lack of wisdom and knowing God, not for water. Radak says the thinking soul's thirst for God is stronger than the body's thirst.

sources.quote: נעשה שימוש גם בביטויי הרעב והצמא לציון העדר החכמה וההשגה
sources.says: Maimonides says hunger and thirst are also used for a lack of wisdom and understanding, and cites this verse.

sources.quote: וצמאון הנפש המשכלת אל כבודה יותר מצמאון הגוף אל המים
sources.says: Radak says the thinking soul's thirst for God is greater than the body's thirst for water.

42:5.headline: אדדם: walking slowly with them, or falling silent?
42:5.body: Rashi reads this rare word as 'I walked slowly with them', one word doing the work of two. He reports that Dunash read it from דום, silence, and the midrash reads it that way too.

sources.quote: וְתֵיבָה זוֹ מְשַׁמֶּשֶׁת כִּשְׁתֵּי תֵיבוֹת, אֶדַּדֶּה עִמָּהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says this one word stands for two: 'I will walk slowly with them'.

sources.quote: וְדוֹנָשׁ פָּתַר אֶדַּדֵּם לְשׁוֹן דְּמָמָה
sources.says: Rashi reports that Dunash explained it as silence.

sources.quote: כשהיה בית המקדש קיים האומות דוממין לפני. ועכשיו אני דוממתי
sources.says: The midrash reads it as silence: once the nations were silent before Israel, and now Israel is silent.

42:5.headline: חוגג: pilgrims at a festival, or Greek for pools of water
42:5.body: Rashi and Radak read המון חוגג as the crowd going up for the festival, or dancing for joy. The midrash hears a Greek word for pools of water: the pilgrims were as countless as water.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיוּ הוֹלְכִים לָחֹג
sources.says: Rashi says they were going to keep the festival.

sources.quote: או פי' חוגג מרקד מרוב שמחה
sources.says: Radak also offers 'dancing from great joy'.

sources.quote: לשון יוני הוא חוגים של מים. כשם שלא היה להם לחוגים של מים שיעור
sources.says: The midrash says it is Greek for pools of water, and like water the pilgrims had no limit.

42:11.headline: רצח here is a sword, not a murder
42:11.body: Elsewhere רצח means murder. Radak and Metzudat Zion say here it names the sword used to kill, so the taunts feel like a blade in the bones.

sources.quote: הוא שם תואר לחרב שמרצחין בו
sources.says: Radak says it is a name for the sword one kills with.

sources.quote: ר״ל בחרב שרוצחים בה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means the sword people kill with.

43:1.headline: "Judge me" here means "take my side against them"
43:1.body: שפטני sounds like asking to be put on trial. The commentators read it the other way: the poet asks God to win his case and punish his enemies.

sources.quote: קח נקמתי מהאויבים
sources.says: Radak says it means: take revenge for me on my enemies.

sources.quote: שפוט משפטי לנקום נקמתי
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means: judge my case so as to avenge me.

sources.quote: קח משפטי מאלה המחרפים אותי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means: win my case against those who insult me.

43:3.headline: Why "dwellings" in the plural for one Temple?
43:3.body: Ibn Ezra says the plural means the Temple's courtyards, in the third Temple still to be built. The Aramaic Targum makes them the study halls of God's house.

sources.quote: ומשכנותיך - העזרות העתידות להבנות בבית שלישי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says "your dwellings" are the courtyards that will be built in the third Temple.

sources.quote: וּמֶדְרְשֵׁי בֵּית שְׁכִינְתָּךְ
sources.says: The Targum translates it as "the study halls of the house of your Presence".

43:4.headline: "The joy of my joy": two words for gladness stacked together
43:4.body: שמחת גילי puts one word for joy on top of another. Radak says the pairing marks the highest joy, and Meiri compares it to "Song of Songs", the finest song.

sources.quote: והוא שמחת כל שמחותי, והסמיכות למעלת השמחה
sources.says: Radak says God is the joy of all his joys, and joining the two words shows how great the joy is.

sources.quote: ושמחת גילי רומז להפלגה כמו שיר השירים
sources.says: Meiri says the phrase points to the utmost degree, like "Song of Songs".

45:1.headline: Lilies: a musical instrument, or people who grew among thorns
45:1.body: Radak says שושנים is an instrument named for the lily. Rashi says the lilies are Torah scholars, soft and lovely. The Midrash says Korach's sons were lilies picked from among the thorns before the fire.

sources.quote: שושנים. כלי ניגון ששמו שושנה
sources.says: Radak says שושנים is a musical instrument called shoshana.

sources.quote: לִכְבוֹד תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים יִסְּדוּ הַשִּׁיר הַזֶּה, שֶׁהֵם רַכִּים כְּשׁוֹשַׁנִּים וְנָאִים כְּשׁוֹשַׁנִּים
sources.says: Rashi says the song honors Torah scholars, who are soft and lovely like lilies.

sources.quote: ובני קרח שהיו שושנים נלקטו מבין הקוצים שלא יאכלו עמהם
sources.says: The Midrash says Korach's sons were lilies, picked from among the thorns so they would not burn with them.

45:1.headline: A song said through an interpreter, or one that wakes the mind
45:1.body: משכיל heads many psalms. Rashi says it means the song was said through an interpreter. Meiri says it means a song that stirs a person to pay attention.

sources.quote: עַל יְדֵי תּוּרְגְּמָן
sources.says: Rashi says משכיל means it was said through an interpreter.

sources.quote: ומלת משכיל פירושה מעורר לב האדם להיותו נותן לב על הדבר
sources.says: Meiri says משכיל means a song that wakes a person's heart to pay attention.

45:2.headline: A heart that stirs, like lips that move or a bubbling pan
45:2.body: רחש appears only here. Rashi and Meiri say it means a small stirring, like moving lips. Metzudat Zion links it to the מרחשת, a deep pan whose contents bubble.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן נַעֲנוּעַ, וְכֵן כָּל לְשׁוֹן שִׁירוּץ וְרִיחוּשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says רחש means moving, like all words for swarming and stirring.

sources.quote: ורחש הוא ענין תנועה קלה וקטנה מלשון רחושי מרחשן שפוותיה וכן הרמש נקרא רחש לדקות תנועתו
sources.says: Meiri says רחש is a light, small movement, like moving lips, and small creeping things are called רחש for their tiny movements.

sources.quote: ומזה יאמר מנחת מרחשת (ויקרא ב׳:ז׳) ולפי שמעשיה רוחשים ומנענעים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the deep-pan offering, מרחשת, is named from this, because its contents stir and move.

45:2.headline: A quick scribe, or a skilled one
45:2.body: מהיר usually means quick. Radak reads it so: his tongue speaks as fast as a scribe writes. Rashi cites Rabbi Moshe HaDarshan that in Arabic מהיר means skilled.

sources.quote: לשוני מדבר עליו במהירו' כמו עט סופר מהיר אשר הוא כותב בלא עיכוב
sources.says: Radak says his tongue speaks quickly, like a fast scribe who writes without stopping.

sources.quote: רָאִיתִי בִּיסוֹדוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי מֹשֶׁה הַדַּרְשָׁן: מָהִיר בִּלְשׁוֹן עֲרָבִי בָּקִי
sources.says: Rashi cites Rabbi Moshe HaDarshan that מהיר in Arabic means expert.

45:3.headline: 'Beautiful-beautiful': a doubled word that means more, not less
45:3.body: Ibn Ezra says doubling the last letters weakens a word, as in שחרחרת, 'blackish'. Doubling the first letters, as here, makes it stronger: 'very beautiful'. Meiri reports a reading that the doubling shows beauty that grew little by little.

sources.quote: כי כפל העי"ן והלמ"ד הוא לחסרון רק הפ"א והעי"ן שהם כפולים, הם באים ליתרון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says doubling the last root letters makes a word weaker, but doubling the first letters makes it stronger.

sources.quote: ואמ׳ יפיפית ולא יפית להורות שלא נברא כן מתחלת היצירה רק שהתיפה מעט מעט
sources.says: Meiri reports a reading that it says יפיפית, not יפית, to show the beauty was not there from the start but grew little by little.

45:5.headline: Succeed, or rush ahead like fire?
45:5.body: צלח usually means 'succeed'. Ibn Ezra reports a reading from 'lest He rush like fire'. Radak reads it as 'pass on', riding over your enemies.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: כי צלח הוא מגזרת: פן יצלח כאש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that some read צלח from 'lest He rush like fire'.

sources.quote: וצלח. כמו ועבור ר"ל כשתעבור על אויביך
sources.says: Radak says צלח means 'pass on', as when you ride over your enemies.

45:5.headline: Your right hand will teach you, or shoot for you
45:5.body: ותורך can mean 'will teach you' or 'will shoot'. Rashi reads teaching: the Torah teaches you how to fight. Ibn Ezra reports that Rabbi Yossi read it as shooting, since the next verse speaks of sharp arrows.

sources.quote: הַתּוֹרָה וּדְבַר הָאֱמֶת שֶׁתַּעֲסֹק בּוֹ, הִיא תוֹרֶה אוֹתְךָ טַכְסִיסֵי הַמִּלְחָמָה
sources.says: Rashi says the Torah you study will teach you the ways of battle.

sources.quote: ורבי יוסי אמר: כי ותורך מגזרת ויורם אלהים והאות שאחריו כתוב: חציך שנונים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that Rabbi Yossi read ותורך as 'shoot', with the next verse's sharp arrows as proof.

45:7.headline: Is the king called 'God' here?
45:7.body: כסאך אלהים reads like 'your throne, O God'. Rashi says אלהים here means a ruler or judge, as Moses was made אלהים to Pharaoh. Ibn Ezra reads 'your throne is God's throne'. Maimonides says the word can mean God, angels, or rulers.

sources.quote: כִּסְאֲךָ, שַׂר וְשׁוֹפֵט, לְעוֹלָם וָעֶד; כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״נְתַתִּיךָ אֱלֹהִים לְפַרְעֹה״
sources.says: Rashi reads אלהים as 'prince and judge', as when God made Moses אלהים to Pharaoh.

sources.quote: כסאך כסא אלהים, כמו: וישב שלמה על כסא ה'
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads it as 'your throne is the throne of God', like 'Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD'.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 2
sources.quote: שהמונח 'אלהים' משותף א) לאלוה ב) ולמלאכים ג) ולשופטים מנהיגי המדינות
sources.says: Maimonides says the word אלהים is shared by God, angels, and judges who lead nations.

45:9.headline: Your garments, or your betrayals, smell sweet
45:9.body: בגדותיך means 'your garments', which smell of spices. Rashi cites a Midrash that hears בגידותיך, 'your betrayals', in the same letters: even your wrongs are forgiven and smell sweet.

sources.quote: וּמִדְרָשׁוֹ (ירושלמי פאה א, א): כָּל בְּגִידוֹתֶיךָ וְסִרְחוֹנֶיךָ מִתְכַּפְּרִים וּמְרִיחִים רֵיחַ עָרֵב
sources.says: Rashi cites a Midrash: all your betrayals and sins are forgiven and give off a sweet smell.

45:9.headline: A spice, or the corners of a robe?
45:9.body: קציעות appears only here. Rashi says it is a spice, the one the Targum calls קציעתא. Ibn Ezra prefers 'corners', from מקצועות, describing the robes.

sources.quote: ״קִדָּה״ (שמות ל:כד) מְתַרְגְּמִינָן ״קְצִיעֲתָא״
sources.says: Rashi says קציעות is the spice קדה, which the Targum calls קציעתא.

sources.quote: והנכון שקציעות מגזרת המקצועות והמלה סמוכה אל בגדותיך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says קציעות more likely comes from 'corners' and belongs with 'your garments'.

45:10.headline: Precious women, or royal visitors?
45:10.body: Rashi reads ביקרותיך as 'your visits': kings' daughters will come to visit you. Ibn Ezra reads it from יקר, 'precious': kings' daughters will be among your honored women.

sources.quote: קוֹ״ף דָּגוּשׁ, לְפִי שֶׁהוּא לְשׁוֹן בִּקּוּר
sources.says: Rashi says the word means visiting, which is why the ק has a dot.

sources.quote: מגזרת יקר, ששפחות היקרות שלך עמהם, הן בנות מלכים. והאומר שהוא מגזרת בקורת תהיה לא דיבר נכונה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from יקר, precious, and that reading it as visiting is wrong.

46:1.headline: A musical instrument, young women, or something hidden?
46:1.body: Rashi says עלמות is the name of a musical instrument, and Meiri ties that name to young women and their joyful songs. The Aramaic Targum hears 'hidden': the sons of Korah sang when their father was hidden from them and they were saved.

sources.quote: שֵׁם שֶׁל כְּלִי שִׁיר בְּדִבְרֵי הַיָּמִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is the name of a musical instrument mentioned in Chronicles.

sources.quote: ולכן נתיחס לעלמות להיות כל שמחה גדולה נעדרת כלומ׳ לחשק העלמות ולנעם שיריהם
sources.says: Meiri says the instrument stirs great joy and is named for young women and the sweetness of their songs.

sources.quote: בִּזְמַן דְאִתְכַּסֵי אֲבוּהוֹן מִנְהוֹן וְהִנוּן אִשְׁתֵּזְבוּ וַאֲמַרוּ שִׁירָתָא
sources.says: The Targum says the sons of Korah sang when their father was hidden from them and they were saved.

46:4.headline: Waters throwing up mud, churning, or piling into heaps
46:4.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read יחמרו from חומר, 'clay': the stormy water throws up mud. Menachem, quoted by Rashi, links it to 'my insides churn,' and Radak links it to 'heaps,' meaning high waves.

sources.quote: יְגָרְשׁוּ רֶפֶשׁ וְחֹמֶר וָטִיט (ישעיהו נז:כ) כְּמִשְׁפָּטָם, וּמְנַחֵם חִבְּרוֹ כְּמוֹ ״מֵעַי חֳמַרְמָרוּ״
sources.says: Rashi says the waters throw up mire and clay, and reports that Menachem linked the word to 'my insides churn' in Lamentations 1:20.

sources.quote: מלשון חומר וטיט
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from clay and mud.

sources.quote: מענין חמרים חמרים כלומר יעשו המים הגלים הגבוהים
sources.says: Radak links it to 'heaps upon heaps' and says the waters make high waves.

46:5.headline: Which river makes God's city glad?
46:5.body: Rashi says it is the river of the Garden of Eden, and Ibn Ezra says it is the Gihon, Jerusalem's own spring. Metzudat David points to the water Ezekiel saw flowing out of the Temple.

sources.quote: נָהָר. גַּן עֵדֶן (בראשית ב:י)
sources.says: Rashi says the river is the one in the Garden of Eden, from Genesis 2:10.

sources.quote: נהר ירושלים שהיה גיחון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the river of Jerusalem, the Gihon.

sources.quote: פלגי הנהר היוצא מבה״מ כמ״ש והנה מים יוצאים
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is the river that goes out from the Temple, as in Ezekiel 47.

46:6.headline: The morning here is the rescue after a dark time
46:6.body: Radak says the war is called evening and the rescue is called morning, and Rashi says this morning is the final redemption. The Aramaic Targum ties it to Abraham, who prayed for the city in the mornings.

sources.quote: והעת ההיא תקרא ערב והישועה תקרא בקר
sources.says: Radak says the time of war is called evening and the rescue is called morning.

sources.quote: לִפְנוֹת בֹּקֶר. לְקֵץ הַגְּאֻלָּה
sources.says: Rashi says the turn of morning means the end time of redemption.

sources.quote: בִּזְכוּתֵיהּ דְאַבְרָהָם דְצַלֵי עֲלָה לְעִדָנֵי צַפְרָא
sources.says: The Targum says God helps the city for the sake of Abraham, who prayed for it in the mornings.

46:7.headline: Kingdoms tottered, or kingdoms arrived?
46:7.body: Metzudat David reads מטו as 'tottered,' as kingdoms began to fall. Meiri reports another reading from Aramaic, where the same word means 'reached' or 'arrived.'

sources.quote: והממלכות מטו לפול
sources.says: Metzudat David says the kingdoms tottered and began to fall.

sources.quote: וי״ל מטו מלשון הגיע כמלשון ארמי
sources.says: Meiri reports that some read מטו as 'arrived,' as the word means in Aramaic.

46:7.headline: Does the earth melt or sway at God's voice?
46:7.body: Menachem, quoted by Rashi, reads תמוג as 'melts,' as in 'all the people of Canaan melted away.' Dunash reads the same word as 'shakes' or 'sways.'

sources.quote: תָּמֵס, כֵּן פָּתַר מְנַחֵם (שמות טו:טו) ״נָמֹגוּ כָּל יוֹשְׁבֵי כְנָעַן״, וְכֵן (יחזקאל כא:כ) ״לָמוּג לֵב״, אֲבָל דּוּנָשׁ פָּתַר אוֹתָם לְשׁוֹן הֲנָעָה
sources.says: Rashi says Menachem explained it as melting, while Dunash explained it as moving or shaking.

sources.quote: תמוג - הטעם הפך תולדתם שהיא יבשה מאד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the earth melts, the opposite of its very dry nature.

46:10.headline: Burning war wagons, or round shields?
46:10.body: Rashi reads עגלות as war chariots, and Ibn Ezra as wagons carrying weapons or food. The Aramaic Targum renders it 'round shields.'

sources.quote: עֲגָלוֹת יִשְׂרֹף בָּאֵשׁ. רִכְבֵי מִלְחָמוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says the wagons are chariots of war.

sources.quote: והעגלות שיביאו בהם כלי הנשק, או מזון הנלחמים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are the wagons that bring weapons or food for the fighters.

sources.quote: תְּרֵיסַיָא עֲגִילִין יוֹקִיד בְּנוּרָא
sources.says: The Targum says God will burn round shields in fire.

48:3.headline: יפה נוף: a fair region, a fair branch, or a fair bride?
48:3.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion read נוף as a region: Zion is the fairest place in its land. Rashi also offers a tree branch, or a bride, from the Greek word people on the coast used for a bride.

sources.quote: כַּלַּת שֶׁל יוֹפִי, שֶׁכֵּן קוֹרִין בְּכַרְכֵּי הַיָּם לְכַלָּה נִינְפִי
sources.says: Rashi says it can mean a beautiful bride, since in the coastal cities a bride is called 'ninfi'.

sources.quote: עִיר שֶׁהוּא נוֹף יָפֶה, לְשׁוֹן נוֹף שֶׁל אִילָן
sources.says: Rashi first reads it as a fair branch, like the branch of a tree.

sources.quote: הר ציון הוא יפה המחוז כלומר אין גדול בכל המחוז כמוהו. נוף פירושו מחוז
sources.says: Radak says נוף means a region, and Zion is the finest in its region.

sources.quote: שַׁפִּיר הֵיךְ חֲתָנָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'beautiful as a bridegroom'.

48:3.headline: 'The far north' may be the altar's north side
48:3.body: Radak reads it as place: Zion lay on the north side of Jerusalem. Rashi and the midrash read it as the north side of the altar, where sin offerings were slaughtered, so a sinner went home forgiven and glad.

sources.quote: הר ציון ירכתי צפון. כי ציון בצפון ירושלים
sources.says: Radak says Zion is in the north of Jerusalem.

sources.quote: ״יֶרֶךְ הַמִּזְבֵּחַ צָפוֹנָה״ (ויקרא א:יא) שֶׁשָּׁם שׁוֹחֲטִין חַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it is the north side of the altar, where sin and guilt offerings were slaughtered.

sources.quote: וכי בצפון הוא והלא אינו אלא בדרום. אלא שם הוא נשחט
sources.says: The midrash asks how Zion can be in the north when it is in the south, and answers that this is where the offering is slaughtered.

48:6.headline: נחפזו: they rushed off, or, letters swapped, they turned reckless
48:6.body: Metzudat Zion reads it as panic and haste. Meiri swaps two letters to read נפחזו, 'they became like fools', and Rashi ties it to פחזות, recklessness.

sources.quote: והנכון לפרש נחפזו כמו נפחזו כלומ׳ נעשו כפתאים לרוב בהלתם
sources.says: Meiri says נחפזו should be read as נפחזו: they became like fools from great panic.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ ״וּבְפַחֲזוּתָם״ (ירמיהו כג:לב)
sources.says: Rashi compares it to פחזות, recklessness, in Jeremiah 23:32.

sources.quote: מלשון חפזון ובהלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means haste and panic.

48:10.headline: דמינו: we waited in hope, or we pictured in our minds?
48:10.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as quiet hope, from the word for being still. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as thinking and picturing, and Rashi reports that Menachem did too.

sources.quote: דִּמִּינוּ וְקִוִּינוּ אֶל חַסְדֶּךָ
sources.says: Rashi explains it as 'we hoped for your kindness'.

sources.quote: וּמְנַחֵם פָּתַר אוֹתוֹ לְשׁוֹן מַחֲשָׁבָה
sources.says: Rashi reports that Menachem explained it as thought.

sources.quote: היינו מחשבים בלבינו ומדמים חסדך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says we were thinking in our hearts and picturing your kindness.

sources.quote: ענין תוחלת ותקוה כמו דום לה׳
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means hope, as in 'be still before God'.

48:14.headline: פסגו: a verb made from פסגה, a mountain peak
48:14.body: This verb is very rare. Rashi reads it from פסגה, the peak, so it means 'raise her palaces high', and Ibn Ezra reads 'look at her palaces, tall as a peak'.

sources.quote: הַגְבִּיהוּ בִּירְנִיּוֹתֶיהָ, כְּמוֹ ״אַשְׁדּוֹת הַפִּסְגָּה״
sources.says: Rashi says it means raise her towers high, from 'the slopes of the Pisgah'.

sources.quote: הביטו ארמנותיה שהם פסגה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means look at her palaces, which are like a peak.

48:15.headline: על מות: until death, forever, or as in our youth?
48:15.body: Read as two words, God leads us 'until death'. Read as one word, עלמות, it means 'forever' or 'as in our youth', and the midrash reads 'in two worlds'.

sources.quote: ובעל המסורת אומר: כי הם שתי מלות והטעם עד מותנו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that the Masorah counts two words, meaning 'until our death', while he prefers 'forever'.

sources.quote: כְּאָדָם הַמַּנְהִיג אֶת בְּנוֹ קָטָן לְאַט
sources.says: Rashi reads it from youth: God leads us gently, like a man leading his small son.

sources.quote: יַדְבְּרִינָנָא כְיוֹמֵי טַלְיוּתָנָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it: he will lead us as in the days of our youth.

sources.quote: הוא ינהגנו עלמות. בשני עולמות
sources.says: The midrash reads עלמות as 'in two worlds'.

49:2.headline: חלד: the aging earth, the people of the time, or the חולדה?
49:2.body: Rashi says חלד is the earth, because it grows old and rusts, and quotes the rabbis that it comes from the חולדה, which lives on land and not in the sea. Metzudat Zion says it means the people of the time.

sources.quote: חָלֶד. הִיא הָאָרֶץ, עַל שֵׁם שֶׁהִיא נוֹשֶׁנֶת וַחֲלוּדָה
sources.says: Rashi says חלד is the earth, named for being old and rusty.

sources.quote: עַל שֵׁם הַחוּלְדָּה, שֶׁהִיא בַּיַּבָּשָׁה וְאֵינָהּ בַּיָּם
sources.says: Rashi says our rabbis explained it as named for the חולדה, which is on dry land and not in the sea.

sources.quote: חלד. אנשי הזמן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חלד means the people of the time.

49:3.headline: בני אדם: the common crowd, or the children of Abraham?
49:3.body: Maimonides lists this verse for the third sense of אדם, the common people as against the distinguished, and Metzudat Zion reads it the same way. Rashi instead reads בני אדם as the children of Abraham.

sources.quote: והוא שם להמון, כלומר לפשוטי העם להוציא המיוחדים
sources.says: Maimonides says אדם is also a name for the multitude, meaning the plain people, as against the distinguished ones.

sources.quote: בני אדם. המון העם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בני אדם means the crowd of the people.

sources.quote: בני איש. הגדולים שבהם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בני איש means the great ones among them.

sources.quote: בְּנֵי אַבְרָהָם, שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״הָאָדָם הַגָּדוֹל בָּעֲנָקִים״
sources.says: Rashi says בני אדם are the children of Abraham, who is called the great man among the giants.

49:5.headline: אטה למשל אזני: does the poet speak the parable, or first listen?
49:5.body: Ibn Ezra first reads אטה as speaking this wisdom in a parable, then allows that the poet listens too: 'I also incline my ear to a parable'. Meiri says he listens to the sages' parables first, to correct himself, and only then speaks to others.

sources.quote: אטה - אדבר זאת החכמה בדרך משל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אטה means I will speak this wisdom by way of a parable.

sources.quote: ויתכן להיות טעם אטה, גם אני אטה אזני למשל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is also possible that אטה means: I too will incline my ear to a parable.

sources.quote: לשמוע משלי החכמים וחידותם להוכיח נפשי בהם
sources.says: Meiri says it means to hear the parables and riddles of the wise, to reprove his own soul with them.

49:5.headline: חידתי and אפתח: a riddle is closed, so he must open it
49:5.body: Ibn Ezra says a riddle is closed and sealed, which is why the poet says he will open it. Rashi says the riddle itself is the question in the next verse: why should I fear in evil days?

sources.quote: ובעבור כי החידה סתומה גם סגורה, על כן אפתח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that because the riddle is sealed and also closed, therefore he says אפתח.

sources.quote: וְזוֹ הִיא הַחִידָה: לָמָּה אֲנִי צָרִיךְ לִירָא בִּימֵי רָע בְּיוֹם פְּקֻדַּת עָוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says this is the riddle: why must I fear in evil days, on the day of reckoning for sin?

49:6.headline: עון עקבי: sins under the heel, the end, or my crooked path?
49:6.body: Rashi reads עקבי as the heel: sins I trample under my heel, treating them as light. Radak reads it as the end, because the heel is the end of the body, and Ibn Ezra reads it as walking a crooked path.

sources.quote: עֲוֹנוֹת שֶׁאֲנִי דָּשׁ בֶּעָקֵב, שֶׁאֲנִי מְזַלְזֵל בָּהֶם, שֶׁהֵם בְּעֵינַי עֲבֵרוֹת קַלּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it means sins I tread on with my heel, that I treat lightly, which are light transgressions in my eyes.

sources.quote: ולפי שהעקב הוא סוף כל הגוף נקרא סוף כל דבר עקב
sources.says: Radak says that since the heel is the end of the whole body, the end of every matter is called עקב.

sources.quote: והטעם: שאלך בדרך לא ישרה ואותו העון לעולם סביבי יהיה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the meaning is that I will walk on a crooked path and that sin will always be around me.

49:9.headline: ויקר פדיון: too costly, too rare, or held back?
49:9.body: Metzudat David reads ויקר as 'costly': redeeming a soul costs too much. Metzudat Zion says something hard to find is called יקר, as in ודבר ה' היה יקר, and Menachem, in Rashi, ties it to holding back.

sources.quote: להפדות את הנפש הוא דבר יקר
sources.says: Metzudat David says that to redeem the soul is a precious, costly thing.

sources.quote: דבר אשר תקשה מציאותו קרוי יקר וכן ודבר ה׳ היה יקר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says a thing that is hard to find is called יקר, like ודבר ה׳ היה יקר.

sources.quote: וּמְנַחֵם חִבְּרוֹ לְשׁוֹן מְנִיעָה כְּמוֹ ״אוֹקִיר אֱנוֹשׁ מִפָּז״
sources.says: Rashi says Menachem linked it to the language of holding back, like אוקיר אנוש מפז.

49:11.headline: The wise 'die' but the fool and brute 'perish': why two words?
49:11.body: Rashi says death is said of the wise because only their body dies in this world, while perishing is said of the fool. Meiri says the same, because death points to the body alone.

sources.quote: בַּחֲכָמִים נֶאֱמַר מִיתָה, שֶׁאֵינָם מֵתִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֶלָּא הַגּוּף בִּלְבַד, וּבִכְסִיל וּבַעַר נֶאֱמַר אֲבֵדָה
sources.says: Rashi says death is said of the wise, because only the body dies in this world, and loss is said of the fool and the brute.

sources.quote: וייחס לחכמים מיתה ולכסיל ובער אבדן כי המיתה רומזת על הגוף בלבד
sources.says: Meiri says death is assigned to the wise and loss to the fool and brute, because death points to the body alone.

49:12.headline: קרבם בתימו: their inner thoughts, or their graves?
49:12.body: Rashi reads קרבם as their inner thoughts: they plan houses to last forever. Ibn Ezra reports some who read it as קברם, their grave, 'the house of their eternity', and the Targum also has them dwelling in their burial house.

sources.quote: מַחְשְׁבוֹתָם לִבְנוֹת לָהֶם בָּתִּים שֶׁיִּתְקַיְּמוּ לְעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says it means their thoughts, to build themselves houses that will last forever.

sources.quote: יש אומרים: כי הוא הפוך קברם והוא הבית הנקרא בית עולמו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some say it is a reversal of קברם, their grave, which is the house called a person's house of eternity.

sources.quote: בְּבֵית קְבוּרְתְּהוֹן יִשְׁרוֹן לַעֲלָם
sources.says: The Targum says they will dwell in the house of their burial forever.

49:13.headline: נמשל כבהמות: like the beasts in what way?
49:13.body: Metzudat David says the likeness is in lacking understanding, and Radak says it is in death, when the soul too is cut off. Maimonides uses the verse twice: for Adam after the sin, made like the beasts in his food and most of his state, and for ignorant rebels, counted among the animals.

sources.quote: הבוטח בעשרו הוא נמשל לבהמות ודומים אליהם בחסרון הדעת
sources.says: Metzudat David says one who trusts in his wealth is compared to the beasts and is like them in lacking understanding.

sources.quote: כמו הבהמות שנכרתו במותן כן האדם הרע נכרת במותו שלא תשאר נשמתו אלא תאבד
sources.says: Radak says that as the beasts are cut off in their death, so the wicked man is cut off in his death, and his soul does not remain but is lost.

sources.quote: והשווה אותו לבהמות במזונו וברוב מצביו
sources.says: Maimonides says that Scripture made Adam like the beasts in his food and in most of his conditions, and cites this verse as the Torah's own comment on it.

sources.quote: והם נכללו במערכת של שאר פרטי בעלי החיים
sources.says: Maimonides says the ignorant rebels were counted among the other individual living creatures, and cites נמשל כבהמות נדמו.

49:13.headline: נדמו: 'are like', 'are silenced', or 'are cut off'?
49:13.body: Metzudat Zion reads נדמו as 'are like', the same idea as נמשל. Rashi reads it as silence, and Radak also offers 'cut off'.

sources.quote: נדמו. מלשון דמיון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says נדמו is from the language of likeness.

sources.quote: נִדְמוּ. לְשׁוֹן דְּמָמָה
sources.says: Rashi says נדמו is the language of silence.

sources.quote: הוא עניין דמיון והוא כפל לשון או פי' נדמו נכרתו
sources.says: Radak says it is about likeness and a doubling of language, or it means they were cut off.

49:14.headline: כסל למו: folly, or the fat around the loins?
49:14.body: Metzudat Zion reads כסל as folly, from כסילות. Rashi, quoting the sages, reads it as the loins: fat covers their kidneys, which would advise them to turn back from evil.

sources.quote: כסל. מל׳ כסילות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says כסל is from the language of folly.

sources.quote: חֵלֶב יֵשׁ לָהֶם עַל כִּסְלֵיהֶם וּמְכַסּוֹת אֶת כִּלְיוֹתֵיהֶם וְאֵינָן יוֹעֲצוֹת אוֹתָם לָשׁוּב מֵרָעָתָם
sources.says: Rashi, quoting the sages, says they have fat on their loins that covers their kidneys, and the kidneys do not advise them to turn back from their evil.

49:14.headline: ואחריהם: the people who come after them, or their own end?
49:14.body: Rashi first says it means those who come after, who tell what happened to the first. He also quotes the sages that their final day is always in their mouths, and Meiri reads it as ואחריתם, 'their end'.

sources.quote: וְהַבָּאִים אַחֲרֵיהֶם יְדַבְּרוּ בָהֶם וִיסַפְּרוּ בְּפִיהֶם מַה אֵרַע לָרִאשׁוֹנִים
sources.says: Rashi says those who come after them will speak about them and tell with their mouths what happened to the first.

sources.quote: יוֹם אַחֲרִיתָם תָּמִיד בְּפִיהֶם, וְאֵין חֲרֵדִים מִמֶּנּוּ
sources.says: Rashi says the day of their end is always in their mouths, and they are not afraid of it.

sources.quote: ואחריהם כמו ואחריתם
sources.says: Meiri says ואחריהם is like ואחריתם.

49:15.headline: שתו: 'set' like sheep, or the foundations of Sheol?
49:15.body: Ibn Ezra and Radak read שתו as 'set' or 'placed': they set themselves like sheep. Rashi reads it from שתות, the foundations of Sheol, so the doubled ת stands for a second ת.

sources.quote: כצאן, שתו - כמו: שתו בשמים פיהם. והטעם: שמו עצמם במחשבתם שהם כצאן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says שתו is like שתו בשמים פיהם, and means they set themselves, in their thoughts, as sheep.

sources.quote: שתו. פועל עומד כמו הושתו או הם שתו עצמם בלי תקוה אחר המות
sources.says: Radak says שתו is a passive verb like הושתו, or that they set themselves without hope after death.

sources.quote: דְּגוּשׁוֹת הַתָּי״ו בִּמְקוֹם תָּי״ו שְׁנִיָּה: לִשְׁאוֹל שׁוֹתְתוּ, לְשׁוֹן שְׁתוּתֶיהָ שֶׁל שְׁאוֹל
sources.says: Rashi says the tav is doubled in place of a second tav: they were made foundations for Sheol, from the language of its foundations.

49:15.headline: מות ירעם: Death their shepherd, eating them, or breaking them?
49:15.body: Radak reads ירעם as 'shepherds them': Death is their shepherd. Rashi gives two other readings: the angel of death eats them, or it means breaking, like היורע ברזל.

sources.quote: כמו הרועה שאוסף הצאן כן יהיה הרועה שלהם המות
sources.says: Radak says that as a shepherd gathers the flock, so Death will be their shepherd.

sources.quote: מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת יֹאכְלֵם
sources.says: Rashi says the angel of death will eat them.

sources.quote: לָשׁוֹן אַחֵר: לְשׁוֹן רְצִיצָה
sources.says: Rashi gives another reading: the language of crushing.

49:15.headline: מזבל לו: their dwelling, or the Temple they destroyed?
49:15.body: Metzudat Zion reads זבול as a dwelling, like בית זבול לך. Rashi, quoting our rabbis, reads it as the Temple, which the wicked destroyed.

sources.quote: מזבול. ענין מדור כמו בית זבול לך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says מזבול means a dwelling, like בית זבול לך.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ פֵּרְשׁוּ מִזְּבֻל לוֹ עַל שֶׁפָּשְׁטוּ יְדֵיהֶם בַּזְּבוּל, שֶׁהֶחֱרִיבוּ אֶת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says our rabbis explained מזבל לו as because they stretched out their hands against the Temple and destroyed it.

49:15.headline: לבקר: the morning of redemption, set against 'spending the night'
49:15.body: Rashi says the morning is the day of redemption, when Israel's morning dawns, and Radak says it is the day of judgment. Ibn Ezra says לבקר is set against ילין, 'spends the night', in verse 13.

sources.quote: לְיוֹם הַגְּאֻלָּה, כְּשֶׁיִּזְרַח בָּקְרָם שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says it means the day of redemption, when the morning of Israel dawns.

sources.quote: וקרא יום הדין בקר
sources.says: Radak says he called the day of judgment morning.

sources.quote: טעם לבקר – כנגד ילין
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the meaning of לבקר is against ילין.

49:16.headline: יקחני: taken while alive, dying, or soul joined above?
49:16.body: Rashi reads 'He will take me' as taking him in his lifetime to walk in His ways. Radak reads it as 'He will let me die', and Ibn Ezra reads it as the soul clinging to the upper soul.

sources.quote: כִּי יִקָּחֵנִי בְּחַיַּי לָלֶכֶת בִּדְרָכָיו
sources.says: Rashi says it means that He will take me in my life to walk in His ways.

sources.quote: כי יקחני. כי ימיתני
sources.says: Radak says כי יקחני means that He will let me die.

sources.quote: וזה טעם יקחני, שתדבק נשמתו בנשמה העליונה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the meaning of יקחני is that his soul will cling to the upper soul.

49:18.headline: לא יקח הכל: not everything, or nothing at all?
49:18.body: The words could mean he will not take everything. Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read הכל as 'anything at all': he will take nothing, not even a part.

sources.quote: פי' הכל מאומה ממנו
sources.says: Radak says הכל means anything at all from it.

sources.quote: יקח הכל - אפילו חלק ממנו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says יקח הכל means even a part of it.

sources.quote: הכל. כלל וכלל לא וכן ולרש אין כל
sources.says: Metzudat David says הכל means not at all, like ולרש אין כל.

5:1.headline: הנחילות: an instrument, a swarm of enemies, or an inheritance?
5:1.body: Rashi says הנחילות may name a musical instrument, or mean troops of enemies, like a swarm (נחיל) of bees. Metzudat Zion says it was an instrument that sounded like buzzing bees, and the midrash hears נחלה, inheritance: David's two kingdoms, in this world and the next.

sources.quote: וְיִתָּכֵן לִפְתּוֹר נְחִילוֹת – גְּיָסוֹת, כְּמוֹ נָחִיל שֶׁל דְּבוֹרִים
sources.says: Rashi says נחילות may mean troops, like a swarm of bees.

sources.quote: כֻּלָּם שְׁמוֹת כְּלֵי זֶמֶר הֵם
sources.says: Rashi brings Menachem's view that these words are all names of instruments.

sources.quote: והוא שם כלי זמר אשר קולו נשמע כשריקת הדבורים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is an instrument whose sound was like the buzzing of bees.

sources.quote: על שני נחילות שנחל דוד את המלכות בעולם הזה ולעולם הבא
sources.says: The midrash reads it as the two inheritances of kingship David received, in this world and the next.

5:2.headline: בינה here is a plea, "understand!", not the noun "wisdom"
5:2.body: Elsewhere בינה is usually the noun "understanding." Rashi points out that here the stress falls on the first letter, which marks it as a plea: "understand my thoughts."

sources.quote: כָּל בִּינָה שֶׁבַּמִּקְרָא הַטַּעַם תַּחַת הַנּוּ״ן, חוּץ מִזֶּה וַחֲבֵרוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says every בינה in Scripture is stressed on the נ except this one and one other, which mean "understand."

sources.quote: בינה - לשון ציווי, כמו: שימה נא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בינה here is a command.

5:2.headline: הגיגי: the prayer locked in the heart, too heavy to say
5:2.body: Radak says אמרי is what David says aloud, and הגיגי, from הגה, to murmur, is what he thinks in his heart. Rashi says it is for times when worry is shut inside and he has no strength to pray in words.

sources.quote: מה שאוציא בפי האזינה, ומה שאהגה בלבי בינה
sources.says: Radak says David asks God to hear what he says aloud and to understand what he thinks in his heart.

sources.quote: ואמר הגיגי מן הגה בהכפל
sources.says: Radak says הגיגי comes from the root הגה, with a letter doubled.

sources.quote: וּכְשֶׁאֵין בִּי כֹּחַ לְהִתְפַּלֵּל לְפָנֶיךָ וְהַדְּאָגָה עֲצוּרָה בְּלִבִּי
sources.says: Rashi says it is for when David has no strength to pray and the worry is shut up in his heart.

5:4.headline: Why pray in the morning: judgment time, or before the workday?
5:4.body: Rashi says morning is when God judges the wicked, so David calls out then. Radak says morning is the time to pray, before a person gets busy with the world.

sources.quote: בַּבֹּקֶר אֲנִי קוֹרֵא לְךָ עֲלֵיהֶם, שֶׁהוּא עֵת מִשְׁפָּט בָּרְשָׁעִים
sources.says: Rashi says David calls to God in the morning, the time of judgment for the wicked.

sources.quote: כי בבקר עת התפלה טרם שיעסוק האדם בעסקי העולם
sources.says: Radak says morning is the time for prayer, before a person is busy with worldly matters.

sources.quote: טעם בקר – כל בקר, כמו: חדשים לבקרים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means every morning.

5:6.headline: הוללים: fools, the wicked, or those who bring wailing?
5:6.body: Rashi reads הוללים as fools whose minds are mixed up. Radak says the word means folly at times and wickedness at others, and the midrash also hears יללה, wailing: people who bring wailing into the world.

sources.quote: מִשְׁתַּטִּים, וּבִלְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה מְעֻרְבָּבִין
sources.says: Rashi says it means people acting foolishly, or in the language of the Mishnah, confused.

sources.quote: ענין הוללים הוא פעמים בענין סכלות
sources.says: Radak says the word sometimes means folly and sometimes wickedness.

sources.quote: הוללים אלו שמביאין יללה לעולם
sources.says: The midrash says הוללים are those who bring wailing into the world.

5:9.headline: שוררי: enemies who watch me, waiting for me to fall
5:9.body: Rashi and Radak read שוררי as enemies who watch, from the verb in "I see him, but not near." The Targum instead renders the word "my praise."

sources.quote: עוֹיְנַי הַמְּצַפִּים שֶׁאֶבְגּוֹד בְּךָ וְתַעַזְבֵנִי
sources.says: Rashi says these are enemies waiting for David to betray God so that God will leave him.

sources.quote: והוא מגזרת אשורנו ולא קרוב (במדבר כד יז), לפי שהוא מביט לרעה
