sources.says: Metzudat David says David prayed here about his error of cutting the corner of Saul's robe.

sources.quote: יש מפרשים בו: תענוג, כמו: תשגה תמיד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra notes that some read it as delight, as in 'be always ravished (תשגה) by her love'.

7:1.headline: כוש: why the psalm calls Saul a 'Cushite'
7:1.body: The sages say כוש means Saul: he stood out as a Cushite's skin stands out, or was handsome, or never changed his hatred. Ibn Ezra says Cush was simply a man of that name from the tribe of Benjamin.

sources.quote: מַה כּוּשִׁי מְשֻׁנֶּה בְּעוֹרוֹ, אַף שָׁאוּל מְשֻׁנֶּה בְּמַעֲשָׂיו
sources.says: Rashi says just as a Cushite is different in his skin, so Saul was different in his deeds.

sources.quote: וקראו כוש לפי שהיה יפה, כמו האשה הכשית
sources.says: Radak says the sages called Saul Cush because he was handsome, as with 'the Cushite woman'.

sources.quote: מה כושי זה אינו משתנה בעורו, כך שאול לא היה משתנה בשנאתו אל דוד
sources.says: Radak also cites: as a Cushite does not change his skin, so Saul did not change his hatred of David.

sources.quote: והנכון שזה כוש היה יהודי וככה שמו והוא מבני בנימין
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Cush was a real Israelite with that name, from the tribe of Benjamin.

7:2.headline: בך: 'in you' adds up to 22, the letters of the Torah
7:2.body: The Midrash reads the letters of בך as the number 22, since ב is 2 and ך is 20. So 'in you I trust' becomes trust in the Torah, written with 22 letters.

sources.quote: א"ר יוחנן ב"ך בתורתך בעשרים ושתים אותיות זו אל"ף בי"ת
sources.says: Rabbi Yochanan says בך means in your Torah, with its 22 letters, the alef-bet.

7:3.headline: פרק: the lion tears apart, and breaks the neck
7:3.body: פרק means to tear off or break apart. Ibn Ezra says it suits a lion, which breaks the neck, the מפרקת, a word built from the same letters.

sources.quote: וטעם פורק – כי האריה יפסיק המפרקת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word is פורק because the lion breaks the neck (מפרקת).

sources.quote: פּוֹרֵק. לְשׁוֹן ״פָּרְקוּ נִזְמֵי הַזָּהָב״
sources.says: Rashi says it is the same word as in 'take off the gold rings'.

sources.quote: ופורק הוא ענין שבור והפרדת דבר מדבר וקעקוע אבר מאבר
sources.says: Meiri says it means breaking, pulling one thing from another, tearing limb from limb.

7:5.headline: ואחלצה: did David strip his enemy, or rescue him?
7:5.body: The root חלץ can mean to strip off or to pull out to safety. Rashi says David stripped Saul by cutting his robe; Radak says David rescued Saul from his own men, for nothing in return.

sources.quote: שִׁחַתִּי אֶת חֲלִיצָתוֹ בְּכָרְתִּי אֶת כְּנַף מְעִילוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says David spoiled Saul's garment when he cut the corner of his robe.

sources.quote: וָאֲחַלְּצָה לְשׁוֹן הַפְשָׁטָה
sources.says: Rashi says ואחלצה means stripping off.

sources.quote: אבל חלצתי מי שהיו צוררי ריקם. ובחנם הייתי מציל אותו
sources.says: Radak says David rescued the man who was his enemy for no reason, and saved him for nothing.

sources.quote: ולשון ואחלצה לפי׳ זה הוא ענין הצלה
sources.says: Meiri notes that on this reading ואחלצה means rescue.

7:6.headline: ירדף: a blended verb, chasing David and setting others on him
7:6.body: The form mixes two verb patterns, 'he chases' and 'he makes others chase'. Radak says Saul did both: he hunted David himself and sent Israel after him.

sources.quote: וטעם ההרכבה, כי האויב ירדפהו בעצמו וירדפהו לאחרים, שיאמר לאחרים שירדפוהו. כך שאול היה רודפו ומרדפו לישראל
sources.says: Radak says the word is blended because the enemy chases him himself and makes others chase him; so Saul chased David and set Israel to chase him.

sources.quote: ירדף. הוא לשון מורכב מן יפעול ויפעיל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is a blend of two verb forms.

7:6.headline: וכבודי: 'my glory' means my soul, not my body
7:6.body: Ibn Ezra says כבוד here is the soul, the honored part of a person. He rejects a teacher who read it as the body, and calls 'lies in the dust' a figure of speech.

sources.quote: וכבודי – טעמו הנפש, כמו: בסודם אל תבא נפשי וכנגדה אל תחד כבודי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says כבודי means the soul, as in 'let my soul not enter their council', where 'my glory' stands opposite 'my soul'.

sources.quote: על כן טעה רבי יהודה בן בלעם שאמר שכבודי הוא גופי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Rabbi Yehuda ben Bal'am was wrong to say כבודי is the body.

sources.quote: וכבודי הוא נפשי
sources.says: Radak says כבודי is my soul.

7:6.headline: סלה: a musical sign, 'truly', or 'forever'?
7:6.body: Radak says סלה tells the singer to raise his voice and adds no meaning to the words. Ibn Ezra reads it here as 'truly', and the Targum as 'forever'.

sources.quote: ומלת סלה פרשתיה (תהלים ג ג) שהיא הרמת הקול בנגון, ואין לה טעם בענין שהיא בו
sources.says: Radak says סלה is raising the voice in the melody and has no meaning in the passage it sits in.

sources.quote: וטעם סלה – באמת היה כן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says סלה here means 'truly, it was so'.

sources.quote: וִיקָרִי לְעַפְרָא יַשְׁרֵי לְעָלְמִין
sources.says: The Targum renders סלה as 'forever'.

7:8.headline: לאמים: foreign nations, or the tribes of Israel?
7:8.body: Metzudat David says these nations are the Philistines, Ammon and Moab. Radak says one 'congregation' of them must be Israel's twelve tribes, since many nations are not one congregation.

sources.quote: ואף אם עדת הפלשתים ועמון ומואב תסבב
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means the gathering of the Philistines, Ammon and Moab.

sources.quote: לאמים הם שנים עשר שבטי ישראל
sources.says: Radak says לאמים are the twelve tribes of Israel.

sources.quote: ואלו היה אומר לאמים על אמות העולם לא היה אומר ועדת; כי לא תכלול אותם עדה אחת
sources.says: Radak says that if it meant the nations of the world it would not say 'congregation', because one congregation cannot hold them all.

sources.quote: ור' משה אמר: שעדת לאומים הם ישראל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites Rabbi Moshe that the congregation of peoples is Israel, a reading he rejects.

7:10.headline: יגמר: let evil finish off the wicked, or let their evil end
7:10.body: The words can be read two ways. Radak says the evil the wicked plan will finish them off; others, cited by Ibn Ezra, take it as a prayer that the evil of the wicked stop.

sources.quote: שהרע שחושבים ושעושים הרשעים יגמר אותם ויכלה אותם
sources.says: Radak says the evil the wicked plan and do will finish and destroy them.

sources.quote: יגמר נא רע – הוא הפועל. ורשעים – הם פעולים. ויש אומרים: שיסור רע רשעים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'evil' is the one that acts and 'the wicked' are acted on; others say it means the evil of the wicked should be removed.

sources.quote: יִגְמָר. לְשׁוֹן כִּלָּיוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says יגמר means coming to an end, destruction.

7:10.headline: וכליות: the kidneys stand for what is hidden
7:10.body: God 'tests hearts and kidneys'. Ibn Ezra says the kidneys stand for secret things, because they are hidden deep inside the body.

sources.quote: וטעם כליות כנוי לסתרים כמו הכליות שהם נסתרים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'kidneys' is a name for secret things, as the kidneys are hidden.

sources.quote: הוא שהוא בחן לבות ויודע מחשבות האדם הוא יודע הצדיקים והרשעים
sources.says: Radak says the one who tests hearts knows people's thoughts, and so knows who is righteous and who is wicked.

7:12.headline: זעם: God is angry daily, or Saul angers God daily
7:12.body: Rashi reads it as God being angry each day at what the wicked do. Radak turns it around: God judges the man who angers God every day, and that man is Saul.

sources.quote: זוֹעֵם בְּכָל יוֹם. כְּשֶׁרוֹאֶה אֶת מַעֲשֵׂה הָרְשָׁעִים
sources.says: Rashi says God is angry every day when he sees what the wicked do.

sources.quote: שופט הצדיק, ושופט מי שהוא זעם אל בכל יום, כי לא ישוב מרשעו
sources.says: Radak says God judges the righteous, and judges the one who angers God every day because he does not turn from his wickedness.

sources.quote: ומה היה זעם שאול לאל? שהיה מבזה מעשה האל ודברו
sources.says: Radak asks how Saul angered God, and answers that he scorned God's deeds and word.

7:15.headline: יחבל: labor pains of evil, or simply destroying
7:15.body: Rashi and Radak read יחבל as labor pains: the wicked man is pregnant with trouble and gives birth to lies. Meiri prefers to read it as 'destroys'.

sources.quote: יְחַבֶּל. לְשׁוֹן הֵרָיוֹן וְלֵידָה, כְּמוֹ ״שָׁמָּה חִבְּלַתְךָ אִמֶּךָ״
sources.says: Rashi says יחבל is the language of pregnancy and birth, as in 'there your mother was in labor with you'.

sources.quote: ידמה מחשבות הלב להריון. וכשיוצאין בפה או במעשה דומין לחבלי האשה וללדה
sources.says: Radak says the verse likens thoughts to pregnancy, and speech and deeds to labor pains and birth.

sources.quote: הנה יחבל און כל האיש הרמוז אליו ישחית בחנם ובעול
sources.says: Meiri reads it as: the man spoken of destroys for nothing and unjustly.

7:15.headline: וילד: to 'give birth' to a lie, says Maimonides
7:15.body: Maimonides lists senses of ילד, to give birth, and one is producing new thoughts and opinions; he cites this verse for it. Rashi adds a folk saying: whatever Falsehood gives birth to, Loss takes away.

sources.quote: כן הושאל המונח לחידושי המחשבות, ולדעות ולשיטות שהן מחייבות, כמו שנאמר
sources.says: Maimonides says the word was borrowed for new thoughts, opinions and views, as in 'and gives birth to lies'.

sources.quote: מַתְלָא אָמַר : כָּל מַה דְּשִׁקְרָא מוֹלִיד, פַּחְתָּא נָסְבָא
sources.says: Rashi cites a proverb: whatever Falsehood gives birth to, Loss takes.

sources.quote: אתקון ביניהון דכל מה דשיקרא מכניס פחתא נסבא
sources.says: The Midrash tells that Falsehood and Loss entered Noah's ark as a pair, agreeing that whatever Falsehood brings in, Loss takes.

71:1.headline: לעולם: never ashamed, or not ashamed in the world to come?
71:1.body: The Midrash notes that Israel has been shamed in this world, so it reads לעולם as 'in the world to come'. Meiri joins the word to 'I trust': I will trust you forever.

sources.quote: וכי לא נתביישו ישראל בעולם הזה אלא אינו אומר אלא לעולם הבא
sources.says: The Midrash asks whether Israel was not shamed in this world, and answers that the verse speaks of the world to come.

sources.quote: ומלת לעולם יראה לי שהיא חוזרת למעלה ממנה ר״ל בך ה׳ אחסה לעולם ולא אבוש
sources.says: Meiri says לעולם goes with the words before it: in you, God, I will trust forever, and not be ashamed.

71:4.headline: וחומץ: a robber, spelled with צ instead of ס
71:4.body: This word appears only here. Rashi and Radak read it as חומס, a man of violence, with צ in place of ס; the Targum renders it 'the snatcher'.

sources.quote: וְחוֹמֵץ. כְּמוֹ ״חוֹמֵס״
sources.says: Rashi says וחומץ is like חומס, one who does violence.

sources.quote: וחומץ. בצד"י כמו בסמ"ך
sources.says: Radak says it is spelled with צ but means the same as with ס.

sources.quote: וחומץ. חומס וגוזל כמו אשרו חמוץ
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means one who robs and steals, as in 'relieve the oppressed (חמוץ)'.

sources.quote: מִן יְדָא דְמָרֵי עִילָא וַחֲטוֹף
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'from the hand of the fraud and the snatcher'.

71:6.headline: גוזי: God brought me out of the womb, like the quail
71:6.body: This word appears only here. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it like ויגז שלוים, when God brought the quail in from the sea, so God is the one who brought David out of his mother.

sources.quote: אַתָּה מוֹצִיאִי וּמַעֲבִירִי, כְּמוֹ ״וַיָּגָז שַׂלְוִים״
sources.says: Rashi says it means you bring me out and carry me across, as in 'he brought over quail'.

sources.quote: ענין הוצאה כמו ויגז שלוים (במדבר י״א:ל״א) שהוציאם מן הים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means bringing out, as with the quail God brought out of the sea.

sources.quote: ובמקום אחר נאמ׳ גוחי ר״ל ממשיכי ושניהם ענין הוצאה והעתקה מחשך לאור
sources.says: Meiri says another psalm uses גוחי, and both words mean bringing out and moving from darkness to light.

71:7.headline: כמופת: David as a warning to others, or a wonder?
71:7.body: Rashi and Radak say David's troubles made him a warning sign: people saw he was punished and feared for themselves. Ibn Ezra and the Targum read מופת as a wonder, since God held him up.

sources.quote: רַבִּים רָאוּ צָרוֹתַי וְדָאֲגוּ, פֶּן יִקְרָאֵם דֻּגְמַת צָרָתִי
sources.says: Rashi says many saw his troubles and worried that the same would happen to them.

sources.quote: כי רבים יוסרו בראותם כי נענשתי על העון ואני מופת להם
sources.says: Radak says many will learn a lesson when they see he was punished for his sin, so he is a sign to them.

sources.quote: בעבור שנסמכתי עליך ואתה סמכתני הייתי כמופת לרבים שלא היו מאמינים בך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that because he leaned on God and God held him up, he became a wonder to many who did not believe.

sources.quote: הֵיךְ תָּמְהָא הֲוֵיתִי לְסַגִיעִין
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'I was like a marvel to many'.

71:9.headline: זקנה: old in years, or 'old' in sins?
71:9.body: Radak takes it plainly: David was old when Absalom rebelled. Rashi reads it as 'if I have grown old in sins', and Meiri as troubles that have dragged on a long time.

sources.quote: אִם זָקַנְתִּי בַּחֲטָאִים, כְּלוֹמַר, שֶׁחָטָאתִי הַרְבֵּה
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'if I have grown old in sins', that is, if I have sinned a great deal.

sources.quote: עתה כשאני זקן וכלה כחי
sources.says: Radak says: now, when I am old and my strength is gone.

sources.quote: ר״ל לעת התישנות הצרות ואריכותם
sources.says: Meiri says it means the time when the troubles have grown old and long.

71:15.headline: ספרות: more saving acts than David can count
71:15.body: This word appears only here. Radak and Meiri read it as 'numbers', and it shares its root with יספר, 'will tell', earlier in the verse: David tells of God's help all day because he cannot count it.

sources.quote: עד שלא ידעתי להם ספורות והוא שם כמו מספרים
sources.says: Radak says he does not know their number; ספורות is a noun meaning numbers.

sources.quote: לא ידעתי מספר ידוע לתשועתך לומר אגמור לספר כולם ואחדל
sources.says: Metzudat David says he knows no set number for God's saving acts that would let him finish telling them all and stop.

sources.quote: וספורות שם מספר על משקל בשורות
sources.says: Meiri says ספורות is a word for number, built like בשורות.

sources.quote: אֲרוּם לָא יְדַעִית מִנְיָנֵהוֹן
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'for I do not know their count'.

71:17.headline: למדתני: God taught David, or made him used to it
71:17.body: Radak reads it as teaching: God gave David understanding from his youth. Ibn Ezra reads it as habit, like a wild donkey 'used to' the desert: praising God became David's custom.

sources.quote: שנתת לי לב מבין מנעורי
sources.says: Radak says God gave him an understanding heart from his youth.

sources.quote: כי אתה למדתני כמו רגילות, כמו: פרא למוד מדבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says למדתני here means habit, as in 'a wild donkey used to the desert'.

sources.quote: אַלֵיפְתַּנִי בְּנִסַיָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'you taught me through miracles'.

71:18.headline: ושיבה: a later stage of old age than זקנה
71:18.body: The verse names two kinds of old age. Radak says שיבה is older than זקנה, and Rashi puts them at sixty and seventy.

sources.quote: וְעַד זִקְנָה וְשֵׂיבָה. לִכְשֶׁאַגִּיעַ לְשִׁשִּׁים וְשִׁבְעִים
sources.says: Rashi says it means when I reach sixty and seventy.

sources.quote: והשיבה יותר מהזקנה
sources.says: Radak says שיבה is more than זקנה.

71:20.headline: הראיתנו: written 'us', read 'me', David and the whole exile
71:20.body: The written text says 'you showed us' and 'revive us', but it is read 'me'. Radak says the reading speaks for David alone, while the writing takes in all the exiles, who will return as he returned to Jerusalem.

sources.quote: הראיתנו. כתוב בוי"ו וקרי ביו"ד, והכתיב על כל בני הגלות והקרי מדבר על דרך יחיד
sources.says: Radak says it is written with ו and read with י: the written form is about all the exiles, and the read form speaks of one person.

sources.quote: כי כמו שהיה הוא גולה ואחר כך שב לירושלים כן ישראל ישובו לירושלים
sources.says: Radak says that just as David went into exile and then returned to Jerusalem, so Israel will return to Jerusalem.

72:1.headline: The name Solomon hints at wholeness, and at the Messiah
72:1.body: Rashi says David prayed this for his son Solomon. Meiri says the name hints at שלימות, "wholeness", and Radak and the Targum also read the psalm as about the King Messiah.

sources.quote: עַל שְׁלֹמֹה בְּנוֹ הִתְפַּלֵּל תְּפִלָּה זוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says David prayed this prayer for his son Solomon.

sources.quote: והתיחס לשלמה על רמז שלימות
sources.says: Meiri says the psalm is tied to Solomon as a hint of wholeness.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים על מלך המשיח
sources.says: Radak says some explain the psalm as about the King Messiah.

sources.quote: לְמַלְכָּא מְשִׁיחָא הַב
sources.says: The Targum renders "to the king" as "to the King Messiah".

72:3.headline: The mountains "carry peace": the hills, or the nations?
72:3.body: Rashi takes it literally: the hills bear fruit, so no one envies his neighbor. Radak says the mountains are a figure for the nations, and the Targum has the people who live in the mountains.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁהֵן עוֹשִׂין פֵּרוֹת, אֵין עֵין הַבְּרִיּוֹת צָרָה
sources.says: Rashi says that when the mountains bear fruit, people have no reason to envy each other.

sources.quote: דרך משל על האומות שיצא שלום על ישראל בימיו
sources.says: Radak says the mountains and hills are a figure for the nations, who will make peace with Israel in his days.

sources.quote: יִטְלוּן יָתְבֵי טוּרַיָא שְׁלָמָא
sources.says: The Targum says the people who live in the mountains will carry peace.

72:7.headline: "Until בלי the moon" is "until the moon wears out"
72:7.body: בלי usually means "without". Metzudat Zion ties it here to בליה, wearing out, and Metzudat David reads the phrase as "until the moon wears out", meaning forever.

sources.quote: מל׳ בליה והפסד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בלי comes from the word for wearing out and loss.

sources.quote: עד שיבלה הירח ר״ל עד עולם
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means until the moon wears out, that is, forever.

72:8.headline: וירד looks like "go down" but here means "rule"
72:8.body: The root is רדה, "to rule", as in "rule the fish of the sea". Metzudat Zion and Meiri read it as dominion, and the Targum has וישלוט, "and he will rule".

sources.quote: ענין ממשלה כמו ורדו בדגת הים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means rule, like ורדו בדגת הים.

sources.quote: או הוא ענין ממשלה ושלטנו׳ כמו וירד מים עד ים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is either "going down" or rule, and cites this verse for rule.

sources.quote: וירד ר״ל ימשול
sources.says: Meiri says וירד means he will rule.

sources.quote: וְיִשְׁלוֹט מִן סְטַר יַמָא רַבָּא
sources.says: The Targum renders it as he will rule from one great sea.

72:10.headline: The kings "return" the gift: they bring it again and again
72:10.body: The verse says ישיבו, "return", where "bring" would do. Radak, Metzudat David and Meiri say the word means the gifts came again and again.

sources.quote: לפיכך הוא בלשן השבה כלומר פעם אחר פעם
sources.says: Radak says it uses the language of returning, meaning time after time.

sources.quote: לפי שהיה תמידי פעם אחר פעם לזה אמר לשון השבה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it was constant, time after time, so the verse uses the language of returning.

sources.quote: שלא פעם אחת לבד רק ישובו בזה פעמים רבות
sources.says: Meiri says they bring it not once but many times.

72:14.headline: "From within" is here a wrong: deceit hidden in the heart
72:14.body: מתוך usually means "from inside". Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as a wrong in itself, deceit or an evil plan kept in the heart, beside חמס, open robbery.

sources.quote: הוא מרמה בלא ידיעה, וחמס הוא גזל בידיעה
sources.says: Radak says מתוך is deceit without knowledge, and חמס is robbery that is known.

sources.quote: מחשבה רעה הטמונה בתוך הלב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says מתוך is an evil thought hidden inside the heart.

sources.quote: בַּעֲלֵי מְזִמּוֹת חוֹרְשֵׁי אָוֶן
sources.says: Rashi ties מתוך to the schemers who plow wrongdoing.

72:15.headline: Who lives, and who gives: the king, God, or the poor man?
72:15.body: Rashi says Solomon himself lives, and God gives him the gold of Sheba. Radak and Meiri say the poor man is the one who lives, kept alive by the king's gold.

sources.quote: וִיחִי. שְׁלֹמֹה
sources.says: Rashi says the one who lives is Solomon.

sources.quote: וְיִתֶּן לוֹ. הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says the one who gives to him is the Holy One.

sources.quote: יתן לעני מהונו שיחיה עמו
sources.says: Radak says the king will give the poor man from his wealth so that he lives.

sources.quote: שיחיה העני עמו כלומ׳ עם המלך
sources.says: Meiri says the poor man will live with him, that is, with the king.

72:16.headline: פסת בר: abundance, fine bread, or a handful of grain?
72:16.body: Metzudat Zion says abundance, Rashi cites the sages' fine bread rolls for the days of the Messiah, and Ibn Ezra says a handful, like the פס ידא, the palm of a hand.

sources.quote: ענין רבוי מלשון פשה תפשה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says פסת means abundance, from the word for spreading.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן גְּלוּסְקָאוֹת לִימוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ
sources.says: Rashi says the sages explained it as fine bread rolls for the days of the Messiah.

sources.quote: כמו פס ידא כף זורעת בר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like פס ידא, a palm that sows grain.

72:19.headline: "His glorious name" is the name that is written but not said
72:19.body: Two commentators say שם כבודו is a particular name of God. Radak says it is the Name that is written but not pronounced, and Ibn Ezra says it is the honored Name that names God Himself.

sources.quote: הוא השם הנכתב ולא נקרא שהוא שם הכבוד
sources.says: Radak says it is the Name that is written but not read, the Name of glory.

sources.quote: הוא השם הנכבד שהוא שם העצם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the honored Name, the one that names God's essence.

73:3.headline: People who mix things up, or plain fools?
73:3.body: Rashi reads הוללים as people who mix things up, like wine "mixed (מהול) with water" in Isaiah 1:22. Metzudat Zion reads it as fools, since no one sins unless a spirit of folly enters him.

sources.quote: בַּהוֹלְלִים. מְעַרְבְּבִים, כְּמוֹ (ישעיהו א:כב) ״סָבְאֵךְ מָהוּל בַּמָּיִם״
sources.says: Rashi says הוללים are people who mix things up, like wine mixed with water.

sources.quote: בהוללים. ענין סכלות כמו והתהוללו הרכב (ירמיהו מ״ו:ט׳) ור״ל רשעים כי אין אדם עובר עבירה אא״כ נכנס בו רוח שטות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means folly, and points to the wicked, since no one sins without a spirit of folly.

73:4.headline: No knots at their death, or no fear of dying
73:4.body: Radak says חרצבות are knots: a hard death is like knots that will not come loose, but these men die at ease. Rashi brings the sages, who read the word as a short form of חרדין ועצבין: they do not tremble or grieve over the day of death.

sources.quote: כי פירוש חרצובות קשרים ומי שהוא מת בצער ובקושי הוא כאילו יש לו קשרים בהפרד החיים
sources.says: Radak says חרצבות means knots, and one who dies in pain is like one held by knots as life departs.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ פֵּרְשׁוּ חַרְצֻבּוֹת נוֹטְרִיקוֹן: שֶׁאֵין חֲרֵדִין וְעַצְבִין מִיּוֹם הַמִּיתָה
sources.says: Rashi says the sages read חרצבות as an abbreviation: they do not tremble or grieve over the day of death.

73:4.headline: Is אולם their strength, their hall, or "however"?
73:4.body: Radak reads אולם as their strength, from the phrase יש לאל ידי, "it is in my power." Metzudat Zion reads it as a palace hall. Ibn Ezra rejects reading it as the common word "however," which never ends a sentence.

sources.quote: אולם מן יש לאל ידי, אמר בחייהם כח טבעם בריא וחזק
sources.says: Radak says אולם comes from יש לאל ידי and means their natural strength is healthy and firm.

sources.quote: אולם. ארמון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אולם means a palace.

sources.quote: וזה איננו נכון שתהיה מלת אולם שהיא מלת טעם באחרונה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is wrong to read אולם here as the linking word "however" placed at the end.

73:6.headline: Violence wraps them like a garment, or like fat
73:6.body: Radak reads שית as a garment: they wear violence all day like clothes. Rashi says their violence makes them fat, wrapping their backsides in thick flesh. Meiri reads שית as a foundation: violence is the root of all they do.

sources.quote: יעטפו להם שית החמס וישימוהו תמיד כו שיעטוף האדם מלבושו תמיד כל היום
sources.says: Radak says they wrap themselves in violence as a person wears his garment all day.

sources.quote: הֶחָמָס שֶׁעוֹשִׂין, עוֹשֶׂה אוֹתָם שְׁמֵנִים וְעוֹטֵף אֶת שְׁתוֹתֵיהֶם וַעֲגָבוֹתֵיהֶם בְּעֹבִי שׁוּמָן וּבָשָׂר
sources.says: Rashi says the violence they do makes them fat and wraps their backsides in thick fat and flesh.

sources.quote: ושית פירושו לדעתי כמו יסוד מלשון שתותיה
sources.says: Meiri says in his view שית means a foundation.

73:7.headline: The heart as a lookout: they got more than they pictured
73:7.body: Radak says the heart is called שכוי because it looks ahead in thought, from the Aramaic סכותא, a lookout. Metzudat Zion ties it to Job 38:36. These men get more than their hearts can even picture.

sources.quote: מתרגמינן מנעה סכותא וכן נקרא הלב שכוי, שצופה הדברים במחשבה
sources.says: Radak says the Aramaic renders a lookout as סכותא, and the heart is called שכוי because it looks out in thought.

sources.quote: משכיות. ענין הבטה וכן מי יתן לשכוי בינה (איוב ל״ח:ל״ו) והוא הלב המביט וחושב הנולדות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means looking, as in Job, and refers to the heart that looks ahead.

73:10.headline: Back here, or beaten down?
73:10.body: Rashi reads הלם as "here," as in Judges 18:3. Ibn Ezra cites Rabbi Moshe, who reads it as "struck," like the blow to Sisera. Meiri reads it as a broken heart: God's people keep falling back into this confusion.

sources.quote: הֲלֹם. כְּמוֹ ״מִי הֲבִיאֲךָ הֲלֹם״ (שופטים יח:ג) – פֹּה
sources.says: Rashi says הלם means "here," as in Judges.

sources.quote: אמר רבי משה: הלום תואר מגזרת: והלמה סיסרא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites Rabbi Moshe, who reads הלום as "struck," from the verb used for striking Sisera.

sources.quote: ויראה לי במלת הלום שהוא מענין וילך הלום (ש״א יד טז) ר״ל שבירת הלב
sources.says: Meiri says הלום means a broken heart.

73:17.headline: The sanctuary: the Temple, or a journey of the mind
73:17.body: Rashi says Asaph came to the Temple in Jerusalem and saw what happened to Sennacherib. Radak says he came there in thought, to the world of angels and spirits. Meiri calls it a figure for coming to understand God's ways.

sources.quote: אֲשֶׁר בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם, וְרָאִיתִי מַה שֶּׁאֵרַע בְּסַנְחֵרִיב
sources.says: Rashi says this is the sanctuary in Jerusalem, where Asaph saw what happened to Sennacherib.

sources.quote: עד שבאתי במחשבות לבבי אל מקדשי אל והוא עולם המלאכים והרוחות
sources.says: Radak says he came in his thoughts to God's sanctuaries, the world of angels and spirits.

sources.quote: והוא משל להשגת ידיעת דבריו
sources.says: Meiri says the sanctuary is a figure for grasping knowledge of God's ways.

73:17.headline: Judge a life by how it ends, not how it starts
73:17.body: Maimonides says Asaph thought about the wicked who thrive until he saw that things must be judged by how they end, not how they begin. Ibn Ezra says a person is not put in this world to enjoy it or be rich, but so that his end will be good.

sources.quote: עד שהתברר לו שיש לראות את הדברים לפי אחריתם ולא לפי תחילתם
sources.says: Maimonides says it became clear to the prophet that things must be seen by their end and not their beginning.

sources.quote: כי לא הובא האדם בעולם הזה להתענג בו או להיותו מלך או עשיר, רק שתהיה אחריתו טובה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says people are not brought into this world to enjoy it or to be king or rich, but so that their end will be good.

73:19.headline: בלהות is בהלות, terrors, with two letters swapped
73:19.body: Metzudat Zion says בלהות is the word בהלות, "terrors," with two letters turned around. Rashi reads it as demons.

sources.quote: בלהות. הוא הפוך מן בהלות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בלהות is בהלות with its letters reversed.

sources.quote: מִן בַּלָּהוֹת. מִן שֵׁדִים
sources.says: Rashi says בלהות means demons.

73:20.headline: Waking from a dream, or a sleep that never ends
73:20.body: Radak reads מהקיץ as waking up: the wicked vanish like a dream once you wake. Rashi hears קץ, "end": a sleep with no end, the death that struck Sennacherib's army.

sources.quote: הנה הם כמו החלום שמעת הקיץ לא ימצא דבר ממה שרואה בחלום
sources.says: Radak says the wicked are like a dream, which leaves nothing once the dreamer wakes.

sources.quote: כַּחֲלוֹם מֵהָקִיץ. כְּשֵׁינָה שֶׁאֵין לָהּ קֵץ, שֶׁהוּא שֵׁינַת עוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says it is like a sleep that has no end, an eternal sleep.

73:20.headline: In the city, or when God wakes the dead?
73:20.body: Rashi reads בעיר as "in the city," Jerusalem, where Sennacherib's army fell. Radak gives his father's reading, בהעיר, "when He rouses": when the dead rise, the wicked will be scorned. The Aramaic Targum also reads it as rousing them from their graves.

sources.quote: אֲדֹנָי בָּעִיר צַלְמָם תִּבְזֶה. בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם, שֶׁהֵרֵעוּ עָלֶיהָ
sources.says: Rashi says בעיר means in Jerusalem, the city they harmed.

sources.quote: פירש אדוני אבי ז"ל בעיר כמו בהעיר המתים
sources.says: Radak says his father read בעיר as בהעיר, when the dead are roused.

sources.quote: בְּאִתְּעַר יַתְהוֹן מִן בֵּית קְבוּרְתְּהוֹן
sources.says: The Targum renders it as God rousing them from their graves.

73:20.headline: Their צלם: their bodies, or their souls?
73:20.body: Maimonides says צלם here means the soul, a person's true form, because scorn falls on the soul and not on the shape of the body. Radak allows the body, the spirit, or both, as in "in our image" in Genesis.

sources.quote: כי הבזיון שייך לנפש, שהיא צורת המין, לא לתבנית האברים ומתארם
sources.says: Maimonides says scorn belongs to the soul, the true form of a human, not to the shape of the limbs.

sources.quote: וצלמם תפרש אם תרצה על הגוף או על הרוח כמו בצלמנו כדמותינו או על שניהם
sources.says: Radak says צלמם can be read as the body, the spirit, or both, as in "in our image."

73:21.headline: A heart gone sour like vinegar
73:21.body: Radak takes יתחמץ from vinegar: Asaph found nothing sweet in his heart to rest on. Metzudat Zion says the vinegar is a figure for anger.

sources.quote: מענין חומץ יין כלומר שלא הייתי מוצא דבר מתוק וערב בלבבי
sources.says: Radak says the word comes from vinegar: he found nothing sweet or pleasant in his heart.

sources.quote: יתחמץ. מלשון חומץ ובא בדרך השאלה על הכעס
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says יתחמץ comes from vinegar and is used as a figure for anger.

73:24.headline: "Take me," as God took Enoch
73:24.body: Ibn Ezra says "taking" with nothing added means the righteous soul joining the beings above, who have no body and never die. He compares Enoch, whom God "took."

sources.quote: מלת לקיחה בלא דבר הוא התחברות נשמת הצדיק עם העליונים שאינם גוף ולא ימותו לעולם, על כן בדברי חנוך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word "take" alone means the soul of the righteous joining the bodiless beings above who never die, as with Enoch.

73:26.headline: My flesh longs for God, or my flesh wastes away
73:26.body: Rashi reads כלה as longing, as in "my soul longs (כלתה) for Your help." Radak reads it as ending: when the flesh and the living soul fail, God remains his portion forever.

sources.quote: כָּלָה שְׁאֵרִי. לְשׁוֹן תַּאֲוָה, כְּמוֹ ״כָּלְתָה לִתְשׁוּעָתְךָ נַפְשִׁי״
sources.says: Rashi says כלה means longing, as in "my soul longs for Your salvation."

sources.quote: כשיכלה שארי שהוא הבשר ויכלה לבבי והוא הנפש החיה
sources.says: Radak says it means when the flesh comes to an end and the heart, the living soul, comes to an end.

73:28.headline: Nearness to God means knowing Him, not standing close
73:28.body: Maimonides says "nearness of God" in this verse is nearness of knowledge, coming to grasp Him, not being near in space.

sources.quote: כי כל אלה קרבת ידיעה, כלומר השגה של ידע, לא קרבת מקום
sources.says: Maimonides says all these verses speak of nearness of knowledge, not nearness of place.

73:28.headline: Your works, or Your messages?
73:28.body: Rashi reads מלאכותיך as God's missions, the holy spirit that comes into Asaph's heart. Ibn Ezra reads it as God's works, and says an angel, מלאך, is named for always doing God's work.

sources.quote: מַלְאֲכוֹתֶיךָ. שְׁלִיחוּתֶיךָ, רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ הַבָּא בְּלִבִּי לֵאמֹר
sources.says: Rashi says מלאכותיך means God's missions, the holy spirit that comes to his heart.

sources.quote: מלאכותיך - לשון רבים והיחיד מלאכה ומזאת הגזרה מלאך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word is the plural of מלאכה, work, and מלאך comes from the same root.

74:1.headline: Anger is called 'nose', because it smokes from the nostrils
74:1.body: אפך means both 'your nose' and 'your anger'. Rashi says an angry person's nostrils seem to give off smoke. Meiri says that is why anger is called אף.

sources.quote: כָּל הַכּוֹעֵס, נְחִירָיו מוֹצִיאִין עָשָׁן
sources.says: Rashi says that when anyone is angry, smoke seems to come out of his nostrils.

sources.quote: וגם לעקר הענין הכעס נקרא על זה אף ר״ל על שיראה בנחירים
sources.says: Meiri says anger itself is called אף, 'nose', because it shows in the nostrils.

74:3.headline: Everlasting ruins, or everlasting darkness?
74:3.body: משאות is a rare word. Rashi reads it as ruin, like שאיה, a wasteland. Metzudat Zion reads it as darkness.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן חֻרְבָּן, כְּמוֹ ״שָׁאִיָּה״
sources.says: Rashi says למשאות means ruin, like שאיה, devastation.

sources.quote: למשואות. ענין חושך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means darkness.

74:4.headline: Your 'meeting place': the Temple
74:4.body: מועד often means a set time. Here Rashi says it is the Temple, where God said 'I will meet you there'. Radak says it is where Israel gathered on the festivals.

sources.quote: הוּא בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, אֲשֶׁר נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ ״וְנוֹעַדְתִּי לְךָ שָׁם״
sources.says: Rashi says מועדך is the Temple, of which God said 'I will meet with you there'.

sources.quote: בית המקדש הנקרא מועד לפי שנועדים שם ישראל לרגלים
sources.says: Radak says the Temple is called מועד because Israel gathered there on the pilgrim festivals.

74:6.headline: A one-time word for a tool, read from Arabic
74:6.body: כילפות appears only here. Rashi says Dunash read it from Arabic, as a carpenter's tool. Ibn Ezra reports a reading with כ swapped for ק: tools for peeling, קלף.

sources.quote: כֵּילַפֹּת לְשׁוֹן עֲרָבִי הוּא, כָּךְ פֵּרֵשׁ דּוֹנָשׁ, וְהוּא מִכְּלֵי הַנַּגָּרִים
sources.says: Rashi says כילפות is an Arabic word, as Dunash explained, and is a carpenter's tool.

sources.quote: וכלפות בהתחלף הכ"ף בקו"ף, שהיו מקלפים כמו כובע וקובע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that כלפות swaps כ for ק, meaning they were peeling, just as כובע and קובע are the same word.

74:8.headline: Their rulers, their sons, or 'let us crush them'?
74:8.body: נינם is hard to read. Rashi says it means their rulers, all agreed. Radak reads it as 'let us oppress them'. Meiri reads it as their descendants.

sources.quote: נִינָם מוֹשְׁלֵיהֶם, וְכֵן (תהלים עב:יז) ״יָנוֹן שְׁמוֹ״
sources.says: Rashi says נינם means their rulers, as in 'his name shall rule'.

sources.quote: נינם יחד. נינה אותה רוצה לומר נהרגם כמו חרב היונה
sources.says: Radak says נינם means 'let us oppress them', meaning kill them, like 'the oppressing sword'.

sources.quote: ונינם יראה לי שהוא כמו ניניהם
sources.says: Meiri says נינם seems to mean 'their descendants'.

74:13.headline: The sea crumbled into pieces, a path for each tribe
74:13.body: פוררת means to crumble or break into many pieces. Metzudat Zion compares 'the earth crumbles'. Metzudat David cites the Sages: the sea split into twelve paths, one for each tribe.

sources.quote: פוררת. ענינו הרצוץ לחתיכות רבות כמו פור התפוררה ארץ
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says פוררת means smashed into many pieces, like 'the earth crumbles'.

sources.quote: בכחך פוררת הים לי״‎ב גזרים לכל שבט שביל לעצמו כן ארז״‎ל
sources.says: Metzudat David cites the Sages: God broke the sea into twelve parts, a path for each tribe.

74:15.headline: You split open a spring, named for what the rock became
74:15.body: Springs are not split; rocks are. Radak says the verse calls it a spring for what the split rock turned into. He adds that God turned dry rock to water and the river to dry land.

sources.quote: מעין ונחל. על שם סופו אמר מעיין כי המעיינים לא יבקעו אלא הצור יבקע ויהיה מעיין
sources.says: Radak says it is called a spring for what it became, since springs are not split; the rock was split and became a spring.

sources.quote: אתה הובשת נהרות איתן. דבר והפכו כי הצור החלמיש הפכת למעיין ומקום המים הפכת ליבשה
sources.says: Radak says these are opposites: hard rock turned into a spring, and a place of water turned into dry land.

74:19.headline: A wild beast, or a band of enemies?
74:19.body: חיה usually means a living creature. Ibn Ezra reads it as a wild beast. Rashi reads it as a troop, as in 'the Philistines gathered לחיה', so: do not hand us to the armies of the nations.

sources.quote: והטעם: חית השדה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means the beasts of the field.

sources.quote: לִגְדוּדֵי הָאֻמּוֹת, כְּמוֹ ״וַיֵּאָסְפוּ פְלִשְׁתִּים לַחַיָּה״
sources.says: Rashi says it means the troops of the nations, as in 'the Philistines gathered into a troop'.

74:19.headline: Your turtledove, or those who teach your Torah?
74:19.body: תורך means 'your turtledove'. Rashi says a turtledove never takes a new mate after its mate dies, and Israel never traded God for another. The Targum hears תורה in it: 'the souls of those who teach Your Torah'.

sources.quote: הַתּוֹר הַזֶּה, מִשֶּׁמֵּת הַזָּכָר, בֶּן זוּגָהּ, אֵינָהּ מִזְדַּוֶּגֶת לְאַחֵר. אַף יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא הֶחֱלִיפוּךָ בְּאֵל אַחֵר
sources.says: Rashi says the turtledove never pairs again after its mate dies, and Israel too never exchanged God for another god.

sources.quote: נַפְשָׁת מְאַלְפֵי אוֹרַיְתָךְ
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'the souls of those who teach Your Torah'.

75:1.headline: אל תשחת: a plea not to destroy, or a tune's name?
75:1.body: Rashi reads אל תשחת, "do not destroy," as a plea to spare Israel. Ibn Ezra says it names the tune, a song whose first words were אל תשחת.

sources.quote: אַל תַּשְׁחֵת. אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says it means "do not destroy Israel."

sources.quote: על נועם פיוט תחלתו אל תשחת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the psalm was sung to the tune of a song that began with אל תשחת.

sources.quote: לבל ישחית את ישראל בהיותם בגולה
sources.says: Metzudat David says the psalm asks God not to destroy Israel while they are in exile.

75:4.headline: The earth's pillars: its mountains, or Israel accepting the Torah?
75:4.body: Radak and Ibn Ezra say the earth's pillars are its mountains. Rashi reads the verse as the giving of the Torah: the shaking world was made firm when Israel said "we will do and we will hear."

sources.quote: עמודיה. הם ההרים
sources.says: Radak says the pillars are the mountains.

sources.quote: ועמודיה – הם הריה שלא תמוט
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the pillars are the earth's mountains, which do not shake.

sources.quote: תִּכַּנְתִּי עַמּוּדֶיהָ. כְּשֶׁאָמַרְתִּי: ״נַעֲשֶׂה וְנִשְׁמַע״
sources.says: Rashi says the pillars were made firm when Israel said "we will do and we will hear."

75:6.headline: עתק: arrogant words, or a thick, stiff neck?
75:6.body: Ibn Ezra says עתק may describe the speech, as arrogant words, or the neck itself. Meiri pictures someone who talks big because his neck is fat and strong.

sources.quote: ועתק - תאר, כמו: יצא עתק מפיכם, או יהיה תואר הצואר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says עתק describes either the words, as in "arrogance came out of your mouth," or the neck.

sources.quote: תדברו עתק ודברים חזקים כנגד האל
sources.says: Radak says it means speaking hard, strong words against God.

sources.quote: כמי שידבר גבוהות מצד שרואה צוארו עתק ר״ל שמן ועב וחזק ותקיף
sources.says: Meiri says it is like someone who talks proudly because he sees his neck is fat, thick and strong.

75:7.headline: הרים: mountains, or being raised up?
75:7.body: הרים usually means mountains, and Ibn Ezra reads it that way. Radak and Meiri read it as "raising up": no one is raised by east, west or desert, only by God, as the next verse says.

sources.quote: כי יש במזרח או מערב או במדבר הרים, שהוא נגד ארץ ישראל מי שיושיעכם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads it as the mountain desert near the Land of Israel, where the wicked hoped to find help.

sources.quote: הרים. הוא לשון הרמה והגבהה
sources.says: Radak says הרים here means raising and lifting up.

sources.quote: והרים הוא מקור מן הנוסף מלשון הרמה ומפני זה מלת ממדבר קמוצה
sources.says: Meiri says הרים is a verb meaning raising, and the vowel under ממדבר shows the two words are not joined.

75:7.headline: Meiri hears family, trade and speech in east, west, desert
75:7.body: Meiri reads מוצא, "east," as a person's descent, מערב, "west," as trade, and מדבר, "desert," as speech, the sign of wisdom. None of these, he says, can raise a person up.

sources.quote: והזכיר שלשה דברים שהאדם נערך בהם והוא יחס ועושר וחכמה
sources.says: Meiri says the verse names three things people are valued by: family, wealth and wisdom.

sources.quote: והעושר קרא מערב מלשון סחורה כמו לערוב מערביך (יחזק׳ כז ט) והחכמה קרא מדבר מלשון דבור
sources.says: Meiri says wealth is called מערב, from a word for trade, and wisdom is called מדבר, from דבור, speech.

75:9.headline: חמר: red wine, strong wine, or murky wine?
75:9.body: Radak says חמר means red, as אחמר does in Arabic. Rashi reads it as strong wine, and Ibn Ezra as murky, like churned-up water.

sources.quote: חמר. פועל עבר, ואדום הוא אחמר בערבי
sources.says: Radak says חמר is a verb, and red in Arabic is אחמר.

sources.quote: וְיַיִן חָמַר. חָזָק
sources.says: Rashi says it means strong wine.

sources.quote: פועל עבר מגזרת חומר מים רבים, כמו עכור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a verb from the churning of great waters, meaning murky.

76:3.headline: Shalem, the old name inside the name Jerusalem
76:3.body: Shalem is Jerusalem, as with Melchizedek, “king of Shalem.” Ibn Ezra offers meanings for the name: complete, or meant for peace. Radak gives the midrash: Shem called it Shalem, Abraham called it Yireh, and God joined both into Yerushalayim.

sources.quote: היא ירושלם אולי נקראה כן, כי היא שלימה כנגד שער השמים, או שהיא ראויה להיות בשלום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Jerusalem may be called Shalem because it is complete, facing the gate of heaven, or because it is fit to be at peace.

sources.quote: ואברהם קרא לבית המקדש יראה, אמר הקב"ה אם אקרא אותו כמו שקראו שם אבטל דברי אברהם ואם אקרא אותו כמו שקראו אברהם אבטל דברי שם קרא אותו ירושלים
sources.says: Radak brings the midrash that Abraham named the place Yireh and Shem named it Shalem, so God called it Yerushalayim to keep both.

sources.quote: בשלם. הוא ירושלים כמ״ש ומלכי צדק מלך שלם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says Shalem is Jerusalem, as in “Melchizedek king of Shalem.”

76:5.headline: Full of light, or the One who sweeps enemies away
76:5.body: Radak and Meiri read נאור from אור, light: God is revealed in bright light. Rashi reads it from נאר, to reject and destroy: God sweeps His enemies out of the world.

sources.quote: מְנָאֵר אֶת אוֹיְבֶיךָ וְקָמֶיךָ וּמְטַאטְאָן מִן הָעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says God casts off His enemies and sweeps them from the world.

sources.quote: נאור. הנכון מן אור
sources.says: Radak says the right reading is from אור, light.

sources.quote: ומלת נאור י״א כי הוא תואר בענין נאר מקדשו (איכה ב ז) ועניינו משחית האויבים והעיקר בפירושה שהוא תואר מבנין נפעל מלשון אורה
sources.says: Meiri reports the reading “destroyer of enemies,” but says the main reading is from the word for light.

76:6.headline: The brave became fools, or became plunder
76:6.body: Rashi reads אשתוללו from שולל, confused and led astray: the brave soldiers acted like fools. Radak reads it from שלל, spoil: the strong-hearted became plunder for Israel.

sources.quote: וְנִגְזַר אֶשְׁתּוֹלְלוּ מִגִּזְרַת ״מוֹלִיךְ יוֹעֲצִים שׁוֹלָל״ (איוב יב:יז), וְהוּא לְשׁוֹן מִשְׁגֶּה
sources.says: Rashi says the word comes from “He leads counselors astray” and means confusion.

sources.quote: ואשתוללו מן שלל אומר כי הגוים אבירי לב שנאספו על ירושלים יהיו לשלל לישראל
sources.says: Radak says the word comes from שלל, spoil: the strong nations that gathered against Jerusalem will become spoil for Israel.

76:11.headline: Human anger ends up praising God
76:11.body: The verse says human rage will praise God, which seems strange. Rashi says when God punishes the angry, everyone praises Him, even the angry themselves. Radak says their anger turns, against their will, into thanks.

sources.quote: כַּעֲסָן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים גּוֹרֵם שֶׁהַבְּרִיּוֹת מוֹדִים לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says the anger of the wicked causes people to praise God.

sources.quote: הם יודוך על כרחם כלומר חמתם תשוב הודאה לך
sources.says: Radak says they will praise God against their will, and their anger will turn into thanks.

76:11.headline: Gird on the leftover anger, or hold it back
76:11.body: תחגר usually means to gird or tie on. Rashi reads it from the language of the Mishnah, where it means to catch and stop: God holds back the anger of the rest. Radak and Metzudat David read it as binding up what anger is left.

sources.quote: תַּחְגֹּר לְשׁוֹן עֲכָבָה בִּלְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה
sources.says: Rashi says תחגר means holding back, as the word is used in the Mishnah.

sources.quote: שארית חמות תחגור. כשתעשה הנקמה הגדולה במחנה גוג מגוג תחגור ותאזור שארית חימות
sources.says: Radak says God will gird and bind the remaining anger of the nations.

sources.quote: ובעבור זאת תחגור מסביב לאסור ולקשור שארית החמה
sources.says: Metzudat David says God will wrap around and tie up the rest of the anger.

76:12.headline: Gifts out of fear, or gifts to the Feared One
76:12.body: Ibn Ezra reads למורא as “because of the fear.” He reports Rabbi Moshe, who reads מורא as a name for God, the One to be feared. Meiri also reads it as God’s name, as in Isaiah 8.

sources.quote: למורא - בעבור המורא. ורבי משה אמר: כי הוא תאר, כמו הוא מוראכם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means because of the fear, and reports that Rabbi Moshe reads it as a title, as in “He is your fear.”

sources.quote: כי הוא ית׳ נקרא מורא כאמרו והוא מוראכם
sources.says: Meiri says God is called מורא, “the Feared One,” as in Isaiah.

77:1.headline: ידותון: a singer's name, or the harsh decrees against Israel
77:1.body: Rashi hears ידותון as דתות, the harsh decrees that passed over Israel. Radak and Meiri take it as the name Yedutun, and Metzudat David gives the decrees or a musical instrument.

sources.quote: עַל הַדָּתוֹת וְעַל הַדִּינִין הָעוֹבְרִים עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi explains the word as the decrees and judgments that passed over Israel.

sources.quote: בעבור הדתות והדינין שעברו על ישראל או הוא שם כלי נגון
sources.says: Metzudat David says it refers to the decrees and judgments that passed over Israel, or else it is the name of a musical instrument.

sources.quote: למנצח על ידותון. כמו לידותון
sources.says: Radak says על ידותון means the same as לידותון, 'for Yedutun'.

sources.quote: והוא שנתנו לידותון לשורר
sources.says: Meiri says the psalm was given to Yedutun to sing.

77:2.headline: והאזין: 'and he will hear', or 'so hear me!'
77:2.body: Ibn Ezra lists three readings of the verb form: a past tense, a command, or the plain 'to hear' form. Metzudat David reads it as 'he will listen', and Meiri as a command, 'hear me'.

sources.quote: יש אומרים: והאזין – היה ראוי להיות והאזין כמו לא האמין פועל עבר. ורבי משה אמר: שהוא לשון ציווי. ולפי דעתי: שהוא שם הפועל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a view that it is a past form, Rabbi Moshe's view that it is a command, and his own view that it is the basic verb form.

sources.quote: וכאשר ארים קולי יאזין באזניו לשמוע אלי
sources.says: Metzudat David says that when I raise my voice, God will listen with his ears to hear me.

sources.quote: והאזין אלי כלומ׳ אחר שאני צועק אליך אף ברחמיך האזן אלי
sources.says: Meiri says it means 'since I cry out to you, in your mercy hear me'.

77:3.headline: תפוג: stop, weaken, or cool down
77:3.body: Rashi says the flowing will not go still. Radak and Metzudat Zion say the word means growing weak, as in 'the law grows weak' in Habakkuk, and Meiri says it is a word for cooling.

sources.quote: וְלֹא תִדְמֶה נִגְּרָתָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says its flowing will not go still.

sources.quote: ענין רפיון וחלישות כלומר לא תרפה ותחלוש מכתי אלא תמיד ניגרה
sources.says: Radak says it means slackening and weakness: my wound does not ease or weaken but always flows.

sources.quote: ענין רפיון וחלישות כמו תפוג תורה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means slackening and weakness, as in 'the law grows weak'.

sources.quote: ואמ׳ תפוג שהוא לשון צינון כי חוזק הדבר יקרא חום גדול והשקטו יקרא הצנה
sources.says: Meiri says תפוג is a word for cooling, since the strength of a thing is called great heat and its quieting is called cold.

77:4.headline: אשיחה: tell of his kindnesses, or pour out my troubles
77:4.body: Rashi reads אשיחה as speaking of God's old kindnesses. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as telling of the speaker's troubles.

sources.quote: אָשִׂיחָה. בְּאוֹתָן חֲסָדִים וְטוֹבוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says אשיחה means speaking of those kindnesses and good things.

sources.quote: אשיחה. אדבר ואנוד בצרתי
sources.says: Radak says it means 'I will speak and mourn in my trouble'.

sources.quote: אשיחה. ענין ספור התלאות כמו ישפוך שיחו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means telling of hardships, as in 'he pours out his complaint'.

77:4.headline: ותתעטף: wrapped up in oneself, or fainting
77:4.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as bent over and tormented, as if wrapped up in oneself. Ibn Ezra compares it to people fainting from hunger, and Rashi explains it with a French word.

sources.quote: כי האדם בעת הצרה כפוף ומעונה כאילו מעוטף קצתו בקצתו
sources.says: Radak says a person in trouble is bent and tormented, as if part of him were wrapped in another part.

sources.quote: ותתעטף - כמו העטופים ברעב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like 'those who faint from hunger'.

sources.quote: פַּשְׁמִי״ר בְּלַעַ״ז
sources.says: Rashi explains the word with the foreign-language word פשמיר.

77:5.headline: שמרות עיני: the night watches, or the eyelids
77:5.body: Rashi reads שמרות as the night watches, the hours when a sleeper wakes. Ibn Ezra, quoting Rabbi Moshe, and Metzudat David read it as the eyelids that guard the eyes, held open so he cannot sleep.

sources.quote: שְׁמוּרוֹת לְשׁוֹן אַשְׁמוּרוֹת הַלַּיְלָה
sources.says: Rashi says שמורות is like אשמורות, the watches of the night.

sources.quote: אמר רבי משה: כי שמורות תאר השם, כמו עצומות, כי העפעפים שומרות העינים בהסגרם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports Rabbi Moshe's view that שמורות describes the eyelids, which guard the eyes when they close.

sources.quote: כאלו אחזת מכסי העין השומרים אותם מן האבק
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is as if God held the eyelids that guard the eyes from dust, so I cannot close them.

77:5.headline: נפעמתי: struck and broken, perhaps like a ringing bell
77:5.body: Metzudat Zion says the word means being struck, and ties it to פעמון, a bell that rings by being hit. Meiri says it means being broken, and some read it as panic.

sources.quote: והוא מלשון פעמון שמקשקש ומכה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from the word for a bell, which rattles and strikes.

sources.quote: נפעמתי - כמו ותפעם רוחו, כל כך הוכיתי עד שלא יכלתי לדבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like 'his spirit was troubled': I was struck so hard that I could not speak.

sources.quote: ונפעמתי לשון כתיתה ושבירה מלשון ותפעם רוחו
sources.says: Meiri says נפעמתי means crushing and breaking, from 'and his spirit was troubled'.

sources.quote: וי״מ בשניהם לשון בהלה
sources.says: Meiri reports a view that in both places it means panic.

77:7.headline: נגינתי: my music in the Temple, my prayer, or a sign of rescue
77:7.body: Rashi reads it as the music the speaker played in the Temple long ago. Meiri reads it as 'my prayer', and also as a hint of the prophecy of rescue.

sources.quote: אֲנִי זוֹכֵר אֶת נְגִינוֹתַי שֶׁהָיִיתִי מְנַגֵּן בִּימֵי קֶדֶם בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says I remember the songs I used to play in the days of old in the Temple.

sources.quote: אזכרה נגינתי ר״ל תפלתי בלילה
sources.says: Meiri says 'I will remember my music' means my prayer at night.

sources.quote: ויש לפרש נגינתי רמז על נבואת הישועה
sources.says: Meiri says it can also be explained as a hint of the prophecy of rescue.

77:11.headline: חלותי: my sickness, my trembling, my death, or my plea
77:11.body: Rashi ties it to sickness and trembling, and Metzudat Zion to trembling. Radak and Meiri read it as 'my death', and Ibn Ezra reports a view that it means 'my plea'.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ לְחַלּוֹתִי, לְשׁוֹן חֹלִי וְחִיל
sources.says: Rashi says it is like 'to make me sick', from the words for sickness and trembling.

sources.quote: מלשון חיל ורעדה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from the words for trembling and shaking.

sources.quote: שם על משקל חנות משורש חלל, ופירושו אם אומר מיתתי היא הגלות
sources.says: Radak says it is a noun like חנות from the root חלל, meaning 'my death is this exile'.

sources.quote: וענין ואומר חלותי היא קשה לפרש
sources.says: Meiri says the meaning of חלותי is hard to explain.

sources.quote: ואחרים אומרים: כי חלותי מגזרת רבים יחלו פני נדיב כמו תפלתי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports others who say חלותי comes from 'many seek the favor of a noble', so it means my prayer.

77:11.headline: שנות: years, a change, or sleep
77:11.body: Radak reads שנות as the years that passed, and Rashi and Metzudat Zion as a change in God's right hand. Ibn Ezra reports a view that it comes from the word for sleep, and he rejects it.

sources.quote: אזכור השנים שעברו שעורר האל יתברך ימינו והוציאנו מגלות מצרים
sources.says: Radak says it means the years gone by, when God stirred his right hand and brought us out of Egypt.

sources.quote: אֶת אֲשֶׁר נִשְׁתַּנֵּית יְמִין עֶלְיוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says it means the way the right hand of the Most High has changed.

sources.quote: שנות. השתנות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שנות means a change.

sources.quote: ופירוש שנות מגזרת שנת עולם. וזה רחוק בעיני, כי איך תישן הימין שהיא הזרוע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a view that שנות comes from the word for sleep, and says it is far-fetched, since a right arm cannot sleep.

77:12.headline: Written 'I will mention', read 'I will remember'
77:12.body: The text is written אזכיר but read אזכור. Radak says the written form means telling others, and the read form means remembering, and I find comfort.

sources.quote: כתיב ביו"ד ר"ל אזכיר לאחרים, וקרי אזכור בוי"ו כלומר כשאזכור מעללי יה אנחם
sources.says: Radak says it is written with a yod, meaning 'I will mention to others', and read with a vav, meaning 'when I remember the deeds of God I am comforted'.

77:14.headline: בקדש: in holiness, at Sinai, or in heaven
77:14.body: Rashi reads it as God's way of making his name holy by judging the wicked. Radak says it may mean the gathering at Mount Sinai, and Meiri says it means heaven.

sources.quote: דֶּרֶךְ מִדָּתְךָ לְקַדֵּשׁ אֶת שִׁמְךָ בָּעוֹלָם, לַעֲשׂוֹת דִּין בָּרְשָׁעִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is your way to make your name holy in the world by bringing judgment on the wicked.

sources.quote: יתכן לפרש בקדש על מעמד הר סיני
sources.says: Radak says בקדש may be explained as the gathering at Mount Sinai.

sources.quote: שדרכך בקדש ר״ל בשמים
sources.says: Meiri says your way is בקדש, meaning in heaven.

77:16.headline: Why Joseph is named beside Jacob as father of the people
77:16.body: Radak, Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra say Joseph is named because he fed and kept alive the family in the famine, as if he were their father.

sources.quote: כי בסיבת יוסף ירדו למצרים והוא כלכלם כל ימי חייו כאילו הם בניו
sources.says: Radak says they went down to Egypt because of Joseph, and he supported them all his life as if they were his sons.

sources.quote: כי יעקב ילדם ויוסף כלכלם ברעב לזה נקראים ע״ש שניהם
sources.says: Metzudat David says Jacob fathered them and Joseph fed them in the famine, so they are called by both names.

sources.quote: וטעם להזכיר יוסף עם יעקב כי הוא החיה ישראל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Joseph is named with Jacob because he kept Israel alive.

77:17.headline: יחילו: the waters trembled, or the waters split
77:17.body: Metzudat Zion reads יחילו as shaking and trembling. Meiri reads it as the sea splitting, and Radak joins both: the waters trembled and were split.

sources.quote: יחילו. ירגזו ענין רתת ורעדה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says יחילו means 'they will shake', a word for trembling and shaking.

sources.quote: יחילו ר״ל שיקרעו והוא ענין אף ירגזו תהומות
sources.says: Meiri says יחילו means that they will be torn open, which matches 'the depths also shook'.

sources.quote: ים סוף ראוך וחלו ממך ונבקעו
sources.says: Radak says the Red Sea saw you, trembled before you, and was split.

77:18.headline: חצציך: your arrows of lightning, or small stones
77:18.body: Rashi reads חצציך as חציך, 'your arrows', and Metzudat David says these are the lightning. Radak and Meiri read it as small stones, like gravel.

sources.quote: חֲצָצֶיךָ. כְּמוֹ חִצֶּיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says חצציך means the same as חציך.

sources.quote: חצציך. הם הברקים שהם חציו של מקום
sources.says: Metzudat David says חצציך are the lightning bolts, which are God's arrows.

sources.quote: אף חצציך יתהלכו. אבני הנהר
sources.says: Radak says 'your חצצים go about' means the stones of the stream.

sources.quote: ואף חצציך ר״ל אבנים קטנות כעין חצץ
sources.says: Meiri says חצציך means small stones like gravel.

77:19.headline: גלגל: a chariot wheel, or the rolling sky
77:19.body: Rashi and Metzudat David link גלגל to wheels, and the Egyptian chariots. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as the heavens or the air, which roll.

sources.quote: קוֹל רַעַמְךָ כַּגַּלְגַּל עַל הַיָּם לָהוּם אֶת מַחֲנֵה מִצְרַיִם
sources.says: Rashi reads it as 'the sound of your thunder like a wheel over the sea, to confuse the camp of Egypt'.

sources.quote: קול רעם בא בגלגלי מרכבות פרעה
sources.says: Metzudat David says the sound of thunder came in the wheels of Pharaoh's chariots.

sources.quote: והשמים כל אחד מהתשעה נקרא גלגל לפי שהם מתגלגלים וסובבים תמיד
sources.says: Radak says each of the nine heavens is called a גלגל, because they always roll and turn.

sources.quote: כי בגלגל הם הרעמים, רק בעבור היותו באויר שהוא מתגלגל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says thunder is in the גלגל, because it is in the air, which rolls.

77:20.headline: Written 'paths', read 'path': twelve paths through the sea
77:20.body: The text is written ושביליך, plural, but read ושבילך, singular. Radak and Meiri say the plural fits because the sea was split into twelve parts.

sources.quote: וכתוב ושביליך לשון רבים כי לא היה דרך אחד אלא דרכים הרבה כמו שכתוב לגוזר ים סוף לגזרים
sources.says: Radak says it is written in the plural, since there was not one road but many, as 'who cut the Red Sea into parts' says.

sources.quote: ואמ׳ שביליך לשון רבים כי לשנים עשר קרעים נקרע
sources.says: Meiri says the plural is used because the sea was torn into twelve parts.

sources.quote: ושבילך. ענין מסילה ודרך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שבילך means a road and a way.

78:2.headline: The promised riddles are veiled lines about the manna and the Ark
78:2.body: Asaph says he will speak in riddles. Radak says lines like "bread of the mighty" (the manna) and "He gave His strength into captivity" (the captured Ark) are those riddles.

sources.quote: שהוא אומר על הארון ולא היו מבינים זה לולי שכתב בספר שמואל גלות הארון והדבר הסתום יקרא חידה
sources.says: Radak says the line about God's strength going into captivity means the Ark, which no one would grasp without the book of Samuel, and a hidden matter is called a riddle.

sources.quote: כי לולי שהוא מפורש בספר שמואל שבית הארון היתה החידה קשה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the riddle about the Ark would be hard if the book of Samuel did not spell it out.

78:9.headline: Which Ephraimites fled? An old Egypt story or the men of Shiloh
78:9.body: Rashi reads this as members of Ephraim who left Egypt early, trusting their weapons, and fell in battle. Ibn Ezra's plain reading is the people of Shiloh, the shrine in Ephraim's land.

sources.quote: שֶׁיָּצְאוּ מִמִּצְרַיִם בִּזְרוֹעַ לִפְנֵי הַקֵּץ וּבָטְחוּ בִּגְבוּרָתָם וּבְחִצֵּיהֶם, וְסוֹפָם הָפְכוּ לָנוּס בְּיוֹם קְרָב
sources.says: Rashi says these Ephraimites left Egypt by force before the set time, trusted their own strength and arrows, and in the end turned and fled in battle.

sources.quote: שבט אפרים רומי קשת הם אנשי שילה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the bow-shooting tribe of Ephraim here means the people of Shiloh.

78:20.headline: Here "bread" means meat
78:20.body: The people ask if God can also give לחם. Radak and Ibn Ezra say this לחם is meat, as when sacrifices are called "My bread," since the verse goes on to ask for שאר, flesh.

sources.quote: הגם לחם. הוא בשר כמו את קרבני לחמי
sources.says: Radak says the לחם here is meat, as in "My offering, My bread."

sources.quote: ומלת הגם לחם הוא הבשר, כמו את קרבני לחמי לחם אשה והעד אם יכין שאר לעמו שהטעם כפול, כי שאר כמו בשר.
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says לחם here is meat, and the proof is the next phrase, where שאר also means meat.

78:25.headline: Bread of angels, of the skies, or bread taken into the limbs
78:25.body: Rashi first reads אבירים, "mighty ones," as angels. He also hears איברים, "limbs": the manna was fully taken into the body. Radak says the mighty ones are the skies.

sources.quote: לַחְמָם שֶׁל מַלְאָכִים, דָּבָר אַחֵר: אַבִּירִים אֵיבָרִים, שֶׁהָיָה נִבְלָע בְּכָל הָאֵיבָרִים וְלֹא הָיוּ צְרִיכִים לִנְקָבֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it is the bread of angels, or reads אבירים as איברים, limbs, because the manna was absorbed into all the limbs.

sources.quote: השחקים הם אבירים כמו שנאמר עליהם חזקים כראי מוצק
sources.says: Radak says the mighty ones are the skies, which are called strong as cast metal.

78:39.headline: Is this רוח the breath of life or the urge to sin?
78:39.body: Maimonides reads רוח here as the life force of the body. Rashi says it is the urge to sin, which leaves at death and does not return, and warns that reading it as the breath of life would deny that the dead will rise.

sources.quote: הוא גם שם רוח החיים: "רוּחַ הוֹלֵךְ וְלֹא יָשׁוּב"
sources.says: Maimonides lists this verse under the sense of רוח as the spirit of life.

sources.quote: וְלֹא יִתָּכֵן לְפָרֵשׁ רוּחַ הוֹלֵךְ וְלֹא יָשׁוּב – רוּחָם שֶׁל חַיִּים בָּהֶם, שֶׁאִם אָמַרְתָּ כֵּן, כָּפַרְתָּ בִּתְחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים
sources.says: Rashi says one cannot read "a spirit that goes and does not return" as their life breath, since that would deny the rising of the dead.

78:40.headline: Grieving God here means rebelling against Him
78:40.body: Maimonides says עצב can mean pain, anger, or rebellion, and he lists this verse under rebellion and sin. Ibn Ezra calls it a figure of speech taken from grief.

sources.quote: והוא שמם של המרי והחטא
sources.says: Maimonides says one sense of עצב is rebellion and sin, and cites this verse for it.

sources.quote: יעציבוהו - דרך משל מן עצבון, כטעם מר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says יעציבוהו is a figure of speech taken from grief.

78:41.headline: They drew a line around what God could do
78:41.body: Rashi reads התוו from תו, a mark, as in Ezekiel 9:4: they demanded a sign. Radak says they set a limit on God in their minds: this He can do, that He cannot.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן סִימָן, כְּמוֹ ״וְהִתְוִיתָ תָּו״ (יחזקאל ט:ד). וְסִימָן הוּא לְשׁוֹן מוֹפֵת וְנִסָּיוֹן. בִּקְשׁוּ מִמֶּנּוּ אוֹת וְסִימָן
sources.says: Rashi says התוו means a mark, as in Ezekiel, and that they asked God for a sign.

sources.quote: הגבילו אותו כלומר שמו לו גבול בלבבם זה יכול לעשות אבל זה לא יוכל לעשות
sources.says: Radak says they set a boundary on God in their hearts: this He can do, but that He cannot.

78:47.headline: Is חנמל a locust, a hard frost, or a hailstone?
78:47.body: Rashi calls חנמל a kind of locust, and gives a reading that splits it: it came, camped (חן), and chewed (מל) the leaves. Radak says it is a hard frost, following Saadia's Arabic. Ibn Ezra thinks it is a hailstone.

sources.quote: שֵׁם אַרְבֶּה, וּמִדְרָשׁוֹ : בָּא חָן וּמָל, הָיָה מוֹלֵל אֶת יֶרֶק הָעֵץ וְהָעֵשֶׂב וְאוֹכְלוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is a name for a locust, and the midrash reads it as "it came, camped, and chewed" the green of trees and grass.

sources.quote: הוא מין ממיני הברד ורב סעדיה פירש אותו בלשון ערבי
sources.says: Radak says it is a kind of hail, and that Saadia explained it with an Arabic word.

sources.quote: ולפי דעתי: כי בחנמל – אבן, כמו אבנים גדולות מן השמים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says in his view חנמל is a stone, like the great stones from heaven.

78:48.headline: רשפים: birds that snatched the cattle, or flashes of fire
78:48.body: Rashi gives the sages' story: Egyptians carried slaughtered animals home and birds snatched them, reading רשפים as birds, as in Job 5:7. By the plain meaning, he says, they are sparks of fire within the hail.

sources.quote: וְזֶה וּמִקְנֵיהֶם לָרְשָׁפִים לָעוֹפוֹת, כְּמוֹ ״וּבְנֵי רֶשֶׁף יַגְבִּיהוּ עוּף״ (איוב ה:ז). זֶה מִדְרָשׁוֹ. וּלְפִי פְשׁוּטוֹ: לָרְשָׁפִים רִשְׁפֵּי אֵשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says the midrash reads רשפים as birds, but the plain meaning is sparks of fire.

sources.quote: כמו שכתוב ואש מתלקחת בתוך הברד
sources.says: Radak ties it to the fire that flashed inside the hail in Exodus.

78:50.headline: Their lives, or their livestock?
78:50.body: Rashi reads וחיתם as their bodies and Radak as their souls, which points to the death of the firstborn. Metzudat Zion reads it as their animals, struck by plague.

sources.quote: וְחַיָּתָם. גּוּפָם
sources.says: Rashi says וחיתם means their body.

sources.quote: וחיתם. כמו נפשם ויש מפרשים וחייתם על מות המקנה
sources.says: Radak says it means their souls, and notes others read it as the death of the livestock.

sources.quote: וחיתם. ובהמתם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means their animals.

78:57.headline: A tricky bow: aimed one way, shooting another
78:57.body: Rashi says a רמיה bow does not send the arrow where the archer wants. Radak pictures a sly archer who aims one way and turns at once, like Israel serving God under each judge and turning away when he died.

sources.quote: כְּקֶשֶׁת רְמִיָּה. שֶׁאֵינָהּ זוֹרֶקֶת חֵץ לְמָקוֹם שֶׁהַמּוֹרֶה חָפֵץ
sources.says: Rashi says it is a bow that does not throw the arrow where the archer wants.

sources.quote: המורה הרמאי הערום מראה עצמו מורה לצד אחד והוא מורה לצד אחר
sources.says: Radak says the deceitful archer pretends to aim one way and shoots the other way.

78:61.headline: "His strength" here is the Ark
78:61.body: God gave "His strength" into captivity. Rashi and Radak say this is the Ark, captured by the Philistines, where God's strength and glory were seen.

sources.quote: מָסַר הָאָרוֹן וְהַלּוּחוֹת בְּיַד פְּלִשְׁתִּים
sources.says: Rashi says God handed the Ark and the tablets to the Philistines.

sources.quote: עוזו ותפארתו. הוא הארון כי בו נראה עוז האל ותפארתו
sources.says: Radak says His strength and glory are the Ark, because God's strength and glory were seen through it.

78:65.headline: God pictured as a warrior shouting himself awake from wine
78:65.body: Rashi reads מתרונן from רנה, a shout: the warrior rouses himself with cries to throw off his wine. Ibn Ezra cites others who read it as the drunk man sinking into sleep.

sources.quote: מִתְרוֹנֵן. מִתְעוֹרֵר וּמִתְגַּבֵּר בְּדִבּוּר לְהָקִיץ מִיֵּינוֹ, מִתְרוֹנֵן לְשׁוֹן רִנָּה הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says מתרונן means rousing and strengthening himself with speech to wake from his wine, and it comes from רנה.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: כי המתרונן הוא השכור בנפול התרדמה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some read המתרונן as the drunkard when deep sleep falls on him.

78:71.headline: David tended the nursing ewes before he led Israel
78:71.body: Radak says עלות are nursing ewes, named for their young. Rashi tells how David fed the young ones the soft grass first, and God said such a shepherd should lead His people.

sources.quote: עלות. הנקבות מן הצאן המניקות נקראו עלות על שם בניהן שנקראו עולים
sources.says: Radak says the nursing ewes are called עלות after their young, who are called עולים.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיָה רַחֲמָנִי וּמוֹצִיא הַגְּדָיִּים תְּחִלָּה וּמַאֲכִילָן רָאשֵׁי עֲשָׂבִים הָעֶלְיוֹנִים שֶׁהֵם רַכִּים
sources.says: Rashi says David was kind, letting the young goats out first to eat the soft tops of the grass.

79:1.headline: Why call a poem about the Temple's ruin a song?
79:1.body: The psalm mourns Jerusalem, yet it opens with מזמור, a song. Rashi says it is a song because God poured his anger on wood and stones and spared his people. Meiri says the name comes from the instruments, some of which were played to stir grief.

sources.quote: וּמַהוּ מִזְמוֹר, וַהֲלֹא קִינָה הִיא
sources.says: Rashi asks why it is called a song when it is a lament.

sources.quote: שֶׁשָּׁפַךְ חֲמָתוֹ עַל עֵצִים וְעַל הָאֲבָנִים וְלֹא עָשָׂה כְּלָיָה בְּבָנָיו
sources.says: Rashi answers that God poured out his anger on wood and stones and did not wipe out his children.

sources.quote: כי כלי הניגון מהם שהיה קולם משמח ומהם שהיה מרעיד הלבבות
sources.says: Meiri says some instruments made people glad and some made hearts tremble, and a psalm sung on them was called a song.

79:2.headline: How can the dead of a sinful city be called pious?
79:2.body: The verse calls the slain חסידיך, your pious ones. Rashi asks how, since they were sinners, and answers that once they were punished they count as pious again. Radak, citing his father, says there really were pious people among them.

sources.quote: וַהֲלֹא רְשָׁעִים הָיוּ? אֶלָּא מִשֶּׁקִּבְּלוּ פֻּרְעָנוּתָם, הֲרֵי הֵם חֲסִידִים
sources.says: Rashi says they were wicked, but once they received their punishment they are called pious.

sources.quote: כתב אדוני אבי ז"ל כי היו בהם עובדי האל וחסידים
sources.says: Radak quotes his father that there were servants of God and pious people among them.

8:5.headline: 'You take note of him': just a repeat, or lifelong care?
8:5.body: Metzudat Zion says תפקדנו only repeats 'you remember him'. Radak says it adds that God watches a person's deeds all his life, and Maimonides cites the verse as wonder that God cares for each single person.

sources.quote: תזכרנו וכפל הדבר במ״ש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means 'you remember him', the same idea said twice.

sources.quote: ותפקדנו, כל הימים אשר הוא חי תשגיח עליו ובמעשיו לתת לאיש כדרכיו
sources.says: Radak says it can mean that all his life God watches him and his deeds, to repay each person by his ways.

sources.quote: הנביאים אף התפלאו על היות ההשגחה על פרטי בני האדם
sources.says: Maimonides says the prophets wondered that God watches over each single person, and cites this verse.

8:9.headline: Who crosses the paths of the seas: man, fish, or Leviathan?
8:9.body: Radak says it is man, who builds ships and sails the seas. Ibn Ezra brings a view that it is the fish, and the Targum names Leviathan.

sources.quote: שעושה ספינות ועובר בהם ארחות ימים
sources.says: Radak says man builds ships and crosses the paths of the seas in them.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: כי על הדג ידבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads it as man in ships, and brings others who say it is the fish.

sources.quote: וְלִוְיָתָן דְחָלִיף אִסְרָטֵי יַמָא
sources.says: The Targum translates: and Leviathan, who passes through the paths of the seas.

80:1.headline: שושנים: a name for Israel, or a rose-shaped instrument
80:1.body: Rashi takes אל שושנים as Israel and points to Song of Songs 2:2. Metzudat Zion says it names a musical instrument built in the shape of a rose.

sources.quote: אֶל שׁוֹשַׁנִּים. אֶל יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says אל שושנים means 'to Israel' and cites Song of Songs 2:2.

sources.quote: על שושנים והוא כלי נגון עשוי בצורות שושנה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is a musical instrument made in the shape of a rose.

80:1.headline: עדות: testimony, ornament, or a decree
80:1.body: Rashi reads 'testimony' as a hint of three exiles. Metzudat Zion links it to עדי, ornament, and Meiri also records a view that it means a decree.

sources.quote: מִזְמוֹר שֶׁל עֵדוּת, שֶׁרָמַז לָהֶם בּוֹ שָׁלֹשׁ גָּלֻיּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi calls it a psalm of testimony that hints at three exiles.

sources.quote: מלשון עדי וקשוט וכן את הנזר ואת העדות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from the word for ornament and decoration.

sources.quote: וי״א שהוא כמו חק אולי שם לו חק לזמר זה המזמור
sources.says: Meiri records a view that עדות means a statute, perhaps one set for singing this psalm.

80:2.headline: Why the whole people is called Joseph
80:2.body: Rashi says all Israel carries Joseph's name because he fed and supported them in the famine. Radak says Israel was called Joseph and Ephraim after the kingdom split.

sources.quote: וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים עַל שֵׁם יוֹסֵף, לְפִי שֶׁהוּא פִּרְנְסָם וְכִלְכְּלָם בִּימֵי הָרָעָב
sources.says: Rashi says all Israel is named for Joseph because he fed and supported them in the famine.

sources.quote: מעת שנחלקה מלכות ישראל נקרא ישראל יוסף ואפרים כי הוא הבכור במקום ראובן
sources.says: Radak says that once the kingdom of Israel split, Israel was called Joseph and Ephraim.

80:3.headline: ולכה: 'go before us', or 'it is yours to save us'
80:3.body: Rashi says ולכה is not about walking but is like לך, 'to you'. Radak reads it as 'go before us', and Ibn Ezra reports the first reading but says it is not right in his eyes.

sources.quote: אֵין זֶה לְשׁוֹן הֲלִיכָה, אֶלָּא כְּמוֹ ״לְךָ״
sources.says: Rashi says this is not a word of walking but means the same as לך.

sources.quote: ולכה לישועתה לנו, תלך לפנינו להושיענו
sources.says: Radak reads it as 'go before us to save us'.

sources.quote: והטעם ולכה ועליך הדבר להושיענו וזה הפירוש איננו ישר בעיני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra gives the reading 'saving us is your task' and says this explanation is not right in his eyes.

80:4.headline: השיבנו: bring us back from exile, or turn our hearts back
80:4.body: The Targum reads it as 'bring us back from our exile'. Radak reads it as 'turn our hearts toward you', and Ibn Ezra as 'help us return to him'.

sources.quote: אֱלָהָא אֲתֵיב יָתָנָא מִגָלוּתָנָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'God, bring us back from our exile'.

sources.quote: אלהים השיבנו. כלומר הכון לבבינו אליך
sources.says: Radak says it means 'direct our hearts toward you'.

sources.quote: אלהים השיבנו - שיעזרנו לשוב אליו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it asks that God help us return to him.

80:20.headline: The refrain adds a name of God each time
80:20.body: The same plea appears three times: with אלהים, then אלהים צבאות, then יהוה אלהים צבאות. Rashi and Meiri read the growing names as three exiles of growing weight.

sources.quote: כָּאן נֶאֶמְרוּ שָׁלֹשׁ אַזְכָּרוֹת (שֶׁל שֵׁמוֹת), וּבָאֶמְצָעִי שְׁתֵּי אַזְכָּרוֹת
sources.says: Rashi counts three names of God here, two in the middle refrain, and one in the first.

sources.quote: הַכֹּל לְפִי חֹזֶק הַגָּלֻיּוֹת וְהַצָּרָה וְהַגְּאֻלָּה
sources.says: Rashi says all this follows the strength of the exiles, the distress and the redemption.

sources.quote: ונראה שרמז שלשה גליות וכפי כפל הצרות כפל האזכרות ברוב תפלה ותחנה
sources.says: Meiri says the verse hints at three exiles, and the names multiply as the troubles multiply.

80:5.headline: עשנת: you are angry, or our prayer is like smoke
80:5.body: Metzudat David reads 'smoked' as 'were angry'. Ibn Ezra and Meiri give another reading, where the people's prayer has become like smoke before God.

sources.quote: עשנת. כעסת למאס תפלת עמך
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means 'you were angry and rejected your people's prayer'.

sources.quote: כאילו עלה אליך עשן בעת תפלת עמך והנה היתה התפלה, כמו עשן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is as if smoke rose to God at the time of the people's prayer, so the prayer was like smoke.

sources.quote: מתי עשנת בתפלת עמך עניינו עד מתי תהיה נחשבת לפניך התפלה כעשן
sources.says: Meiri says it means 'how long will the prayer be counted before you as smoke'.

80:6.headline: שליש: a third, a large measure, or three tears
80:6.body: Rashi gives several readings: the 70 years of Babylon as a third of Egypt's 210, a drinking vessel, or the three tears of Esau. Metzudat Zion says it is a large measure.

sources.quote: בְּבָבֶל, שֶׁהָיוּ שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה, שֶׁהוּא שְׁלִישׁ שֶׁל מָאתַיִם וְעֶשֶׂר שֶׁל מִצְרַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says it means Babylon, which lasted 70 years, a third of Egypt's 210.

sources.quote: וּמְנַחֵם פֵּרֵשׁ: שָׁלִישׁ שֵׁם שֶׁל כְּלִי שֶׁשּׁוֹתִין בּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi reports that Menachem explains שליש as the name of a vessel people drink from.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ פֵּרְשׁוּהוּ עַל שָׁלֹשׁ דְּמָעוֹת שֶׁהוֹרִיד עֵשָׂו
sources.says: Rashi reports that our rabbis explained it as the three tears Esau shed.

sources.quote: שם מדה גדולה וכן וכל בשליש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the name of a large measure, as in Isaiah 40:12.

80:7.headline: למו: they mock 'them', or they mock God
80:7.body: Metzudat Zion reads it as 'at them'. Radak says the mockery may be aimed at God, saying he cannot save us, and Ibn Ezra calls it a stand-in word used out of respect for God.

sources.quote: למו. להם ר״ל עליהם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says למו means 'to them', that is, 'at them'.

sources.quote: להם לעצמם או בזו לאל יתברך כלומר ילעגו לך ויאמרו שלא תוכל להושיענו
sources.says: Radak says it means either 'for themselves' or a mockery of God, saying he cannot save us.

sources.quote: כנוי בעבור כבוד השם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra calls it a substitute word, used for the sake of God's honor.

80:9.headline: A word for breaking camp is used for pulling up a vine
80:9.body: Rashi reads תסיע as pulling the vine up and out of Egypt, like Job 19:10. Radak notes the verb of travelling is used for a vine, and Ibn Ezra ties it to Israel's journey in the wilderness.

sources.quote: עָקַרְתָּ מִשָּׁם (חולין צב.), כְּמוֹ ״וַיַּסַּע כָּעֵץ תִּקְוָתִי״
sources.says: Rashi says it means you uprooted the vine from Egypt, like 'he pulled up my hope like a tree'.

sources.quote: ואמר לשון נסיעה על הגפן כמו ויסע כעץ תקותו
sources.says: Radak says the verse uses the language of travelling about a vine, like 'he pulled up my hope like a tree'.

sources.quote: וטעם תסיע – בעבור לכתם במדבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says תסיע refers to their going in the wilderness.

80:14.headline: A raised letter turns 'forest' into 'the Nile'
80:14.body: The letter ע in מיער is written raised above the line. Rashi reads it as if the word were מיאור, 'from the Nile', so Israel's enemy is a harmless river creature if Israel is worthy and a forest boar if not.

sources.quote: הָעַיִ״ן תְּלוּיָה (וכאלו נכתב באל״ף). זָכוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל, הֲרֵי עֵשָׂו אוֹיְבָם כְּחַיַּת הַיְאוֹר
sources.says: Rashi says the ע hangs, as if written with an א, and that if Israel is worthy Esau is like a river animal.

sources.quote: ועי״ן של מיער תלויה לא ידענו הטעם אלא שבדרש אמרו זכו מיאור לא זכו מיער
sources.says: Meiri says the reason for the hanging ע is unknown except for the Midrash: if worthy, 'from the Nile'; if not, 'from the forest'.

80:14.headline: The boar is a nation: Amalek, Esau, or any beast-like nation
