80:14.body: Rashi says the forest boar stands for Amalek, since a pig has some signs of a clean animal and Amalek has the merit of its fathers. Meiri says the rabbis read it as Esau's descendants, and Ibn Ezra reads it as nations that act like beasts.

sources.quote: וַחֲזִיר מִיָּעַר הוּא עֲמָלֵק
sources.says: Rashi says the boar from the forest is Amalek.

sources.quote: וְיֵשׁ לוֹ (לֶחָזִיר) מִקְצָת סִימָנֵי טָהֳרָה. אַף עֲמָלֵק יֵשׁ לוֹ זְכוּת אָבוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says the pig has some signs of a clean animal, and so Amalek has the merit of its fathers.

sources.quote: ורבותי׳ פירשו חזיר מיער על זרעו של עשו
sources.says: Meiri says his teachers explained the boar from the forest as Esau's descendants.

sources.quote: וטעם חזיר - ועוף האומות הדומות לחיות ולעוף הדורס
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the boar and the bird stand for nations that are like beasts and birds of prey.

80:14.headline: זיז: anything that creeps in the field, or a giant bird
80:14.body: Rashi derives זיז from the verb for moving, so it means every creature of the field. Ibn Ezra and Radak say it is a bird, and Radak adds that it is so large its wings cover the sun.

sources.quote: כָּל רֶמֶשׂ הַשָּׂדֶה, וּלְשׁוֹן זִיז – שֶׁהוּא זָז מִמְּקוֹמוֹ וְהוֹלֵךְ
sources.says: Rashi says it means every creeping thing of the field, from the word for something that moves from its place and goes.

sources.quote: וזיז - עוף והוא שם מין
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says זיז is a bird and the name of a kind.

sources.quote: הזיז הזה עוף גדול הוא ובשעה שפורש כנפיו מכסה גלגל חמה
sources.says: Radak quotes the Midrash that זיז is a large bird whose spread wings cover the sun.

80:16.headline: בן: a branch of the vine, Esau, or King Messiah
80:16.body: In a verse about a vine, בן can mean 'son' or 'branch'. Ibn Ezra takes it as a branch, Rashi reads it as Esau, and the Targum reads it as King Messiah.

sources.quote: ומלת בן – סעיף, כמו: בן פורת יוסף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בן means a branch, as in 'a fruitful son, Joseph'.

sources.quote: וְעַל עֵשָׂו, שֶׁהָיָה בֵּן חָבִיב לְאָבִיו
sources.says: Rashi reads it as Esau, who was a son his father loved.

sources.quote: וְעַל מַלְכָּא מְשִׁיחָא דְחַיֵלְתָּא לָךְ
sources.says: The Targum reads it as 'the King Messiah whom you strengthened for yourself'.

80:17.headline: כסוחה means pruned, not uprooted
80:17.body: Rashi ties כסוחה to pruning, the word Onkelos uses for לא תזמור. Meiri says the Midrash notices the verse says pruned, because a pruned vine grows back.

sources.quote: כְּסוּחָה, לְשׁוֹן ״לֹא תִזְמוֹר״ (ויקרא כה:ד), תִּרְגֵּם אוּנְקְלוֹס ״לָא תִכְסַח״
sources.says: Rashi says כסוחה is like לא תזמור, which Onkelos translates לא תכסח.

sources.quote: ובדרש עקירה לא נאמ׳ אלא כסוחה שכל גפן הנכסחת ר״ל נזמרת סופה לעלות שגזעו מחליף
sources.says: Meiri says the Midrash notes the verse says pruned and not uprooted, because a pruned vine's trunk will sprout again.

80:18.headline: Who is 'the man of your right hand'?
80:18.body: Radak says the man is Israel, bought out of slavery. Ibn Ezra says the figure points to Israel or to the Messiah son of Ephraim.

sources.quote: ישראל כי בימינך ובזרועך הגדול קניתם מבית עבדים
sources.says: Radak says the man of your right hand is Israel, whom God acquired from the house of slaves.

sources.quote: והנמשל הוא על ישראל, או משיח בן אפרים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the figure stands for Israel, or for the Messiah son of Ephraim.

81:3.headline: The harp whose name says it outshines all other music
81:3.body: Rashi asks why the instrument is called נבל. He answers with a play on the root: it מנבל, puts to shame, every other kind of music.

sources.quote: לָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמוֹ נֵבֶל? שֶׁהוּא מְנַבֵּל כָּל מִינֵי זֶמֶר
sources.says: Rashi says it is called nevel because it shames all other kinds of music.

81:5.headline: A rule for Israel, judgment from God
81:5.body: משפט can mean a rule or a judgment. Rashi says blowing the shofar is a rule for Israel, and that day is God's day of judgment. Meiri says a command whose reason people cannot see is a חק, a decree, to them, but from God's side it is fair and just.

sources.quote: וְהוּא יוֹם הַמִּשְׁפָּט לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says that day is God's day of judgment.

sources.quote: אע״פ שאין המצוה טעמה נגלית לעם והיא אצלם חק, אצל השם הוא משפט
sources.says: Meiri says that though the reason for the command is hidden from the people, so it is a decree to them, to God it is justice.

81:6.headline: A testimony, or a gold chain on Joseph's neck?
81:6.body: עדות usually means testimony, and Radak reads it as a reminder set in Israel. Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David read it from עדי, jewelry: the gold chain Pharaoh put on Joseph's neck the day he left prison.

sources.quote: כלומר זכר ועדות שם זה החוק שהיא תקיעת שופר ביהוסף
sources.says: Radak says God set the law of blowing the shofar in Joseph as a reminder and a testimony.

sources.quote: עדות. מלשון עדי וקשוט
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from jewelry and ornament.

sources.quote: ביום הזה שמו עדי הזהב על יוסף
sources.says: Metzudat David says on this day they put the gold ornament on Joseph.

81:6.headline: Joseph's name gains a letter from God's name
81:6.body: Joseph is spelled here יהוסף, with an extra ה. Ibn Ezra says the letter is added for honor, taken from God's name. Radak says Joseph here stands for all of Israel.

sources.quote: כי הזכיר יהוסף בתוספת ה"א תפארת, בעבור השם הנכבד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Joseph's name is written with an added letter ה for glory, because of God's honored name.

sources.quote: יהוסף. כמו יוסף וכל ישראל נקרא בשם יוסף
sources.says: Radak says יהוסף is the same as Joseph, and all of Israel is called by Joseph's name.

81:6.headline: Whose language was it that he did not know?
81:6.body: The verse says 'a language I did not know, I hear'. Rashi says this is Joseph, whom the angel Gabriel taught seventy languages. Radak says it is Israel in Egypt, hearing a foreign tongue. Ibn Ezra also suggests Israel hearing God's voice at Sinai.

sources.quote: שֶׁלִּמְּדוֹ גַבְרִיאֵל שִׁבְעִים לָשׁוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says Gabriel taught Joseph seventy languages.

sources.quote: הייתי שומע מדברים לשון אחרת שאינו לשוני
sources.says: Radak says Israel heard people speaking a language that was not their own.

sources.quote: ויתכן: היות שפת לא ידעתי רמז לישראל, ששמעו קול השם בסיני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it may hint at Israel hearing God's voice at Sinai.

81:8.headline: Answered with thunder, or hidden from the thunder?
81:8.body: בסתר רעם means 'in the hiding of thunder'. Rashi reads it as: you called me in secret, and I answered you openly, with thunder. Ibn Ezra and Radak also give another reading: God hid Israel from the thunder that struck Egypt.

sources.quote: אַתָּה קְרָאתַנִי בְּסֵתֶר, בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ, וַאֲנִי עָנִיתִיךָ בְּקוֹל רַעַם
sources.says: Rashi says Israel called God in secret, and God answered with thunder.

sources.quote: וי"מ שהסתרתי ממך הרעם שהכיתי בו מצרים
sources.says: Radak brings another reading: God hid from Israel the thunder he struck Egypt with.

sources.quote: בהסתיר הרעם ממך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads it as God hiding the thunder from Israel.

81:10.headline: A strange god living inside your own body
81:10.body: The verse says there shall be no strange god בך, in you. Meiri brings the sages' reading of 'in you' as inside your body. The strange god inside a person is the urge to do wrong.

sources.quote: בך בגופך איזהו אל זר שהוא בגופו של אדם הוי אומר זה יצר הרע
sources.says: Meiri quotes the sages: 'in you' means in your body, and the strange god in a person's body is the evil urge.

81:13.headline: The hardness of their heart, or what their heart saw?
81:13.body: Ibn Ezra and Radak read שרירות as hardness, from שריר, firm. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as sight, from a root meaning to look. Either way, God let them go their own way.

sources.quote: בחוזק, כמו: שריר וקיים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means strength, as in 'firm and lasting'.

sources.quote: בְּמַרְאִית לִבָּם
sources.says: Rashi says it means what their heart saw.

sources.quote: במראה כמו אשורנו ולא קרוב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means sight, as in 'I behold him, but not near'.

sources.quote: שלחתיהו בחוזק לבם רע
sources.says: Radak says God sent them off in the hardness of their bad heart.

81:16.headline: God's enemies will deny, or will waste away
81:16.body: Radak and Ibn Ezra read יכחשו as 'they will deny': out of fear, the enemies will claim they never harmed Israel. Ibn Ezra adds a second reading from the same root: they will grow thin, as in 'my flesh is lean'.

sources.quote: מרוב פחדם יכחשו שלא מרדו בך, או על דרך ויכחשו אויביך לך, מטעם ובשרי כחש משמן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says out of fear they will deny they rebelled, or it means growing lean, as in 'my flesh is lean'.

sources.quote: בישראל מיראתם אותו ויאמרו שלא הרעו לו
sources.says: Radak says out of fear they will say they did Israel no harm.

81:16.headline: Whose time lasts forever, the enemies' or Israel's?
81:16.body: The verse says 'their time will be forever'. Rashi says it is the enemies' time of punishment. Radak and Metzudat David say it is Israel's time of blessing, which would never end if they listened.

sources.quote: פּוּרְעָנוּתָם לְעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says it means their punishment forever.

sources.quote: עת וזמן ברכתם שהוחל בטוב יהיה לעולם
sources.says: Radak says the time of their blessing, once begun, would last forever.

sources.quote: עת הטובה ההיא היתה לעולם מבלי הפסק
sources.says: Metzudat David says that good time would have lasted forever without a break.

82:1.headline: God does not just stand; He stands ready
82:1.body: Rashi says God stands in the court to see whether the judges rule truly. The Midrash notes the verse says נצב, not the plain word עומד: God stands ready among those who pray, as in 'before they call, I will answer'.

sources.quote: לִרְאוֹת אִם אֱמֶת יִשְׁפֹּטוּ
sources.says: Rashi says God stands there to see whether they judge truly.

sources.quote: רבי חגי בשם רבי יצחק אמר אלקים עומד אין כתיב כאן אלא נצב בעדת
sources.says: Rabbi Chaggai notes the verse does not say עומד but נצב, and links it to 'before they call, I will answer'.

82:1.headline: 'Among the gods': among angels, or among judges?
82:1.body: אלהים usually means God. Radak says the second אלהים here means the judges, and God stands among them. Ibn Ezra says it means the angels, through whom God's justice is done on earth.

sources.quote: בקרב אלהים. בקרב הדיינים
sources.says: Radak says 'among the gods' means among the judges who judge Israel.

sources.quote: בקרב אלהים - הם המלאכים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says these are the angels, since all God's judgment on earth is done through them.

82:6.headline: 'You are gods': deathless like angels, or true judges?
82:6.body: Rashi says God meant 'you are like angels': He gave the Torah so that death would no longer rule them. Radak says judges are called אלהים when they judge truly. Maimonides applies the words to people who give their lives to knowing God.

sources.quote: נְתַתִּיהָ לָכֶם עַל מְנָת שֶׁאֵין מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת שׁוֹלֵט עוֹד בָּכֶם
sources.says: Rashi says 'gods' means angels: God gave the Torah on condition that the angel of death would no longer rule them.

sources.quote: כי השופטים נקראו אלהים כשהם שופטי אמת
sources.says: Radak says judges are called אלהים when they judge truly.

sources.quote: האנשים הללו הם אשר עם ה' תמיד, והם אשר נאמר להם
sources.says: Maimonides says this verse was said to people who keep their bodily drives small and aim at knowing God.

82:7.headline: Die like Adam, like any man, or like the crowd?
82:7.body: Rashi reads אדם as Adam, the first man, who brought death on himself by ruining his deeds. Radak reads it as any human being. Maimonides lists this verse under a third sense of אדם: the common crowd, as against the few who stand out.

sources.quote: אָכֵן כְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן תְּמוּתוּן, אַחֲרֵי שֶׁחִבַּלְתֶּם מַעֲשֵׂיכֶם כְּמוֹהוּ
sources.says: Rashi says you will die like Adam, the first man, since you ruined your deeds as he did.

sources.quote: וכשתמותון תמותון כאחד האדם
sources.says: Radak says when they die they will die like any human, and their souls will not rise with the angels.

sources.quote: ובמשמעות השלישית הזאת
sources.says: Maimonides puts this verse under the third meaning of אדם, which he gives just before as the common crowd, not the distinguished few.

82:8.headline: God takes the nations, or the poor among them?
82:8.body: Radak says God takes as His own portion the oppressed poor in every nation. Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi, quoted by Ibn Ezra, turns it around: God will be the inheritance of those who cry out, in every nation.

sources.quote: אתה תנחל העניים העשוקים באיזה עם שיהיה
sources.says: Radak says God will take as His portion the oppressed poor of whatever nation.

sources.quote: ורבי יהודה הלוי אמר: אתה תהיה נחלה לצועקים בכל הגוים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads the ב as extra, so God inherits all nations, and quotes Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi that God will be the inheritance of those who cry out.

83:2.headline: Two names for God here: אלהים the judge, אל the strong one
83:2.body: Ibn Ezra says אלהים in this verse means 'judge'. He reads אל, at the end of the verse, as the strong one who is able to save.

sources.quote: אלהים - כמו שופט
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אלהים here is like 'judge'.

sources.quote: וטעם אל – שאתה תקיף שתוכל להושיע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אל means You are mighty and able to save.

83:2.headline: דמי: God should not fall silent, like a watchman who keeps calling
83:2.body: Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra say דמי means silence. Meiri says a watchman keeps shouting to warn people, and the psalm asks God to guard like that, never falling quiet.

sources.quote: דמי. ענין שתיקה כמו לך דומיה תהלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says דמי means silence, as in לך דומיה תהלה.

sources.quote: דמי - שתיקה, מגזרת: וידום אהרן, אף על פי שהוא משרש אחר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says דמי means silence, like 'Aaron was silent', even though it is from a different root.

sources.quote: אחר שדרך השומר לצעוק תמיד לעורר האדם להזהר מכל פגע
sources.says: Meiri says the way of a watchman is to shout all the time to warn people against harm, and the psalm uses this as a picture for God's constant guarding.

83:4.headline: They plot in secret against the ones God keeps hidden
83:4.body: The enemies plan a סוד, a secret plot, against God's צפונים, 'hidden ones'. Ibn Ezra sets the two words against each other, Radak says Israel is hidden in God's shelter, and Meiri calls them God's treasure.

sources.quote: וטעם צפוניך – צפונים בסתרך, כנגד סוד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says צפוניך means those hidden in God's shelter, set against the word סוד, secret plot.

sources.quote: צפוניך. ישראל שהם צפונים בסתרך
sources.says: Radak says צפוניך is Israel, who are hidden in God's shelter.

sources.quote: וצפוניך ר״ל סגולתך
sources.says: Meiri says צפוניך means God's treasure.

83:6.headline: A pact against Israel is a pact against God's own name
83:6.body: Rashi says God is called 'the God of Israel', so if Israel's name is wiped out, God's name will no longer be spoken either. That is why the pact is עליך, 'against You'.

sources.quote: שֶׁאֵין אַתָּה קָרוּי אֱלֹהִים אֶלָּא לָנוּ אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁלֹּא יִזָּכֵר שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל אַף שִׁמְךָ הַגָּדוֹל אֵינוֹ נִזְכָּר
sources.says: Rashi says God is called God only by us, 'the God of Israel', so once Israel's name is not remembered, God's great name is not mentioned either.

sources.quote: כי בהכחד שם אומתנו לא יתפרסם שם יחודך בעולם הזה
sources.says: Meiri says that if our nation's name is wiped out, the name of the one God will not be made known in this world.

83:7.headline: The Hagrites: Hagar's sons, named after their mother
83:7.body: Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David say the Hagrites are sons Hagar bore to another husband; Ibn Ezra says they took her name because she had been Abraham's servant. Radak adds they may be Abraham's sons, if Hagar is Keturah.

sources.quote: הם ההגריאים שילדה הגר מבעל אחר, ובעבור שהיתה שפחת אברהם התייחסו הבנים אליה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are the Hagrites whom Hagar bore to another husband, and because she had been Abraham's maid the sons were named after her.

sources.quote: המה בני הגר שילדה מבעל אחר לא מאברהם
sources.says: Metzudat David says they are the sons Hagar bore to another husband, not to Abraham.

sources.quote: שאר בני הגר שהיו מבעל אחר או מאברהם אם היא קטורה
sources.says: Radak says they are Hagar's other sons, from another husband, or from Abraham if she is Keturah.

83:9.headline: Why 'even Assyria'? It once walked away from evil
83:9.body: Rashi, following Bereshit Rabbah, says Assyria had once left Nimrod's plan but now joined the wicked. Radak says 'even' because Assyria is so far away, and his father read it as Assyria forgetting its own defeat.

sources.quote: גַּם זֶה שֶׁהָיָה מְחַבֵּב מִתְּחִלָּתוֹ מַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים שֶׁפֵּרַשׁ מֵעֲצַת נִמְרוֹד
sources.says: Rashi says even this one, who at first loved good deeds and left Nimrod's plan, went back to being wicked.

sources.quote: אמר גם לפי שהוא רחוק מארץ ישראל יותר משאר הגוים הנזכרים, ואדוני אבי ז"ל פי' כי אמר גם כלומר עדיין מחזיק ברשעתו ולא זכר מפלתו
sources.says: Radak says 'even' because Assyria is farther from the land of Israel than the other nations; his father explained that Assyria still held on to its wickedness and did not remember its defeat.

83:11.headline: Which battle was at Ein Dor? Rashi says he does not know
83:11.body: Rashi says he does not know whether the battle at Ein Dor was Gideon's or Barak's. Radak takes it as the war on Midian, and Meiri ties it to Jabin, the king of Canaan.

sources.quote: אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ אֵיזוֹ מִן הַמִּלְחָמוֹת הָיְתָה בְּעֵין דֹּאר
sources.says: Rashi says he does not know which of the wars was at Ein Dor.

sources.quote: על מדין אמר ואף על פי שלא נזכר זה בספר שופטים
sources.says: Radak says it is about Midian, even though the book of Judges does not mention it.

sources.quote: וכן נשמדו בעין דאר נראה שמוסב על יבין מלך כנען
sources.says: Meiri says 'destroyed at Ein Dor' seems to refer to Jabin, king of Canaan.

83:13.headline: נאות: God's dwelling place, or God's best land
83:13.body: Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read נאות as dwelling; Ibn Ezra says it is like נוות, from נוה. The Targum renders it 'all the choice land of God'.

sources.quote: אֶת נְוֵה בֵּית אֱלֹהִים
sources.says: Rashi says it means the dwelling of God's house.

sources.quote: נאות - כמו נוות, כי אותיות אהו"י נראות ונעלמות מתחלפות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says נאות is like נוות, because the letters א, ה, ו, י swap with each other.

sources.quote: נאות. מדור
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says נאות means dwelling.

sources.quote: יַת כָּל עִידִית אֱלֹהִים
sources.says: The Targum says 'all the choice land of God'.

83:14.headline: גלגל: thistle heads that break off and roll in the wind
83:14.body: Rashi says the גלגל is the head of a field thistle, which breaks off in winter and rolls like a wagon wheel in the wind. Radak says it is straw that the wind rolls along.

sources.quote: הוּא רָאשֵׁי קוֹצֵי הַשָּׂדֶה הַקְּרוּיִים קרדנ״ש בְּלַעַ״ז, וּכְשֶׁמַּגִּיעִין יְמֵי הַחֹרֶף נִתָּקִים וְנִשְׁחָתִים מֵאֲלֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it is the heads of field thistles, which break off and fall apart on their own when winter comes.

sources.quote: כגלגל. הוא הגדל בראש הקוצים המתגלגל ע״י הרוח
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is what grows on top of thorns and is rolled by the wind.

sources.quote: כגלגל. הוא הקש המתגלגל מפני הרוח
sources.says: Radak says it is straw that rolls before the wind.

83:17.headline: קלון: shame that burns the face red, or being made light
83:17.body: Metzudat Zion says קלון may come from קלוי באש, 'roasted in fire', because a shamed face turns red as if burned, or from קלות, lightness. Radak gives the fire reading in his father's name.

sources.quote: כי המתבייש פניו מאדימות כאילו נשרף באש, או הוא מל׳ קלות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says a person who is ashamed turns red in the face as if burned in fire, or else the word comes from lightness.

sources.quote: ואדוני אבי ז"ל פירש קלון מן קלוי באש כאלו אמר מלא פניהם בושת כי המתבייש יהיו פניו כאש
sources.says: Radak says his father explained קלון from 'roasted in fire', meaning 'fill their faces with shame', since an ashamed person's face is like fire.

84:4.headline: The bird whose name means freedom
84:4.body: דרור is a bird, and the same word means freedom. Ibn Ezra says it may be named so because it sings only when it is free. Radak says it is called free because it nests among people, in their houses.

sources.quote: שם עוף מנגן, אולי נקרא כן בעבור שאין מנהגו לנגן כל זמן שאיננו חפשי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a singing bird, perhaps named so because it does not sing while it is not free.

sources.quote: שהוא חפשי בין בני אדם שמקנן בבתיהם
sources.says: Radak says the bird is free among people and nests in their houses.

84:4.headline: The chicks are the young priests at the altar
84:4.body: The bird sets its chicks on God's altars. Radak reads the chicks as the young priests, called פרחי כהונה, who stayed by the altar like chicks in a nest. Meiri gives the same reading.

sources.quote: הם פרחי כהונה שהיו עם המזבחות תמיד כמו האפרוחים בקן
sources.says: Radak says the chicks are the young priests, always at the altars like chicks in a nest.

sources.quote: ואפרוחיה על פרחי כהונה
sources.says: Meiri says her chicks stand for the young priests.

84:7.headline: A valley of weeping, of trees, or of springs?
84:7.body: Rashi hears בכא as בכי, weeping: sinners crying in the depths of Gehinnom. Ibn Ezra says it is a place name, or a valley of trees called בכאים. Radak links it to the springs deep in the sea.

sources.quote: בְּעוּמְקָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנֹּם בִּבְכִי וִילָלָה
sources.says: Rashi says they are in the depths of Gehinnom, weeping and wailing.

sources.quote: שם מקום, או עמק שם אילנים הנקראים בכאים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a place name, or a valley with trees called bechaim.

sources.quote: ויהיה בכא מן נבכי ים והוא מקום המבוע
sources.says: Radak says בכא comes from the 'springs of the sea', the place where water flows out.

84:7.headline: A teacher, the early rain, or a place?
84:7.body: מורה can mean a teacher or guide, and Metzudat David reads it that way. Radak reads it as the early rain, as in 'early rain and late rain'. Ibn Ezra brings Rabbi Yehuda, who says it is a place name.

sources.quote: המורה להם את הדרך אשר ילכו בו
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is the one who shows them the way to go.

sources.quote: מורה. כמו מורה ומלקוש
sources.says: Radak says it means the early rain, as in 'early rain and late rain'.

sources.quote: אמר רבי יהודה: כי מורה שם מקום כמו מגבעת המורה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra quotes Rabbi Yehuda that מורה is a place name, like the hill of Moreh.

84:8.headline: From crowd to crowd, or from study house to synagogue?
84:8.body: חיל can mean strength, an army, or a crowd. Radak says the pilgrims moved from one group of travelers to the next. Rashi reads it as going from the study house to the synagogue. The Targum says from the Temple to the study house.

sources.quote: העולים לרגל היו הולכים מצבא אל צבא
sources.says: Radak says the pilgrims went from one company to the next.

sources.quote: מִבֵּית הַמִּדְרָשׁ לְבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת
sources.says: Rashi says it means from the house of study to the synagogue.

sources.quote: מִן בֵּית מַקְדְשָׁא לְבֵית מֶדְרָשָׁא
sources.says: The Targum translates it as from the Temple to the house of study.

84:10.headline: Who is 'our shield': God, the king, or the Temple?
84:10.body: The verse asks God to look at 'our shield'. Rashi says the shield is the Temple. Ibn Ezra says it is the king, who protects the people. Radak reads it as God himself: you who shield us, look.

sources.quote: הוּא בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הַמֵּגִין עָלֵינוּ
sources.says: Rashi says our shield is the Temple, which protects us.

sources.quote: הוא המלך שיגן ביד העם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the king, who protects the people.

sources.quote: שאתה מגן בעדנו ראה
sources.says: Radak reads it as: you who shield us, look.

85:2.headline: "You were pleased with your land": looking back, or ahead?
85:2.body: Ibn Ezra reads the past tense as history, the return from Babylon. Radak reads it as a prophecy of the final redemption, and Rashi reads it as a condition: the land is pleased only when God brings Jacob home.

sources.quote: רצית ה' ארצך - בזמן בית שני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this happened in the time of the Second Temple.

sources.quote: מתנבא על הגאולה בשלשה פסוקים הראשונים
sources.says: Radak says the first three verses prophesy the redemption.

sources.quote: אָז רָצִיתָ אַרְצֶךָ וְעוֹלָמְךָ מִתְרַצֶּה
sources.says: Rashi says that if God brings back Jacob's captives and forgives them, then the land and the world are pleased.

85:2.headline: Did God bring the captives back, or give them rest?
85:2.body: Radak and Meiri read שבת as "you brought back" Jacob's captives. They also cite readers who take it as "you gave rest", from a word for rest and quiet.

sources.quote: פעל ייצא כאילו אמר השיבות ויש מפרשים אותו ענין מנוחה וזהו דעת רבי יהודה חיוג
sources.says: Radak says it works like "you brought back", and that some read it as rest, which is the view of Rabbi Yehuda Chayyuj.

sources.quote: וי״מ כמו הניחות מלשון בשובה ונחת
sources.says: Meiri says some read it as "you gave rest", as in "in returning and rest" (Isaiah 30:15).

85:5.headline: "Return us": or "come back, and bring us back"?
85:5.body: Rashi, following the midrash, hears two returns in שובנו: God comes back, and then brings Israel back. Meiri reads it as "give us rest" from the anger of exile.

sources.quote: שׁוּב אַתָּה וַהֲשִׁיבֵנוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it means: you return, and bring us back.

sources.quote: שובנו ר״ל הניחנו מרוגז זה הגלות
sources.says: Meiri says it means: give us rest from the anger of this exile.

85:10.headline: "Glory" in the land: what the Second Temple lacked
85:10.body: Ibn Ezra and Meiri say this Glory, God's presence, was missing from the Second Temple. Radak says it will dwell there when the redeemer comes.

sources.quote: והנה זה המזמור לעד כי הכבוד לא היה בבית שני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this psalm is a witness that the Glory was not in the Second Temple.

sources.quote: זה הכבוד לא היה בארצנו בבית שני
sources.says: Meiri says this Glory was not in the land in Second Temple times, and lists five things the sages say that Temple lacked.

sources.quote: שבבא הגואל ישכון הכבוד שם
sources.says: Radak says that when the redeemer comes, the Glory will dwell there.

85:11.headline: Righteousness and peace "kiss": one from people, one from God
85:11.body: Rashi says the righteousness is what Israel does and the peace is what God sends, and the two meet like a kiss. Metzudat David says each one depends on the other.

sources.quote: הַצְּדָקָה שֶׁהָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עוֹשִׂים, וְהַשָּׁלוֹם מֵאֵת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says the righteousness Israel does and the peace that comes from God will kiss each other.

sources.quote: תלוים המה זה בזה כשנעשה צדק תבוא השלום
sources.says: Metzudat David says they depend on each other: when we do right, peace comes.

sources.quote: נשקו, כלומר אחים ורעים
sources.says: Radak says they are like brothers and friends.

85:14.headline: Who walks before God: righteousness, or a righteous man?
85:14.body: Ibn Ezra first reads it as a picture: God sends righteousness walking ahead of him. He prefers to supply a missing word: a righteous man walks before God, as Abraham and Isaac did.

sources.quote: והנכון: כי צדק שם דבר ותחסר מלת איש, כאילו כתוב: איש צדק לפניו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word "man" is missing, as if it said "a righteous man before him".

sources.quote: כדרך התהלכו אבותי לפניו אברהם ויצחק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares it to Abraham and Isaac, who walked before God.

sources.quote: כל איש יהלך לפניו צדק
sources.says: Radak says every person will keep righteousness in front of him.

86:1.headline: Answer me, for I am poor: two words that sound alike
86:1.body: David asks God to answer him, עֲנֵנִי, because he is poor, עָנִי. Ibn Ezra says the two words are set side by side on purpose, as a turn of style.

sources.quote: אזנך ענני כי עני - דרך צחות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra calls the pairing of 'answer me' and 'poor' a play of style.

86:2.headline: How could David call himself pious without boasting?
86:2.body: Calling yourself חָסִיד, 'pious', sounds like bragging, and the commentators ask about it. Rashi answers that David heard himself insulted, could have taken revenge, and kept silent.

sources.quote: שֶׁאֲנִי שׁוֹמֵעַ גִּדּוּפִי וְחֶרְפָּתִי, וִיכֹלֶת בְּיָדִי לְהִנָּקֵם, וַאֲנִי שׁוֹתֵק
sources.says: Rashi says David was pious because he heard insults, had the power to take revenge, and stayed silent.

sources.quote: יש תמיהים איך קרא דוד עצמו חסיד
sources.says: Radak notes that some wonder how David could call himself pious, and answers that he did good even to enemies like Saul.

86:3.headline: 'All day long' read as the whole long exile
86:3.body: No one can pray literally all day, the midrash asks. So Rashi reads 'all the day' as the whole exile, a time that is day for the nations and night for Israel.

sources.quote: וכי איפשר לו לאדם להתפלל כל היום
sources.says: The midrash asks how a person could pray all day, and answers that 'day' means this world, day for the nations and night for Israel.

sources.quote: כָּל הַגָּלוּת, שֶׁהוּא יוֹם לָאֻמּוֹת וְלַיְלָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says 'all the day' means the whole exile.

86:4.headline: Lifting my soul: a prayer, a gift, or a hope
86:4.body: 'To you I lift my soul' can mean I pray with my whole heart, I bring my soul as a gift, or I set my hope on you. Radak gives all three; Meiri reads it as a gift, like the portions Joseph sent his brothers.

sources.quote: דרך תחינה בכל לב, או דרך מנחה או דרך תקוה ותוחלת
sources.says: Radak says lifting the soul is either a heartfelt plea, an offering, or hope.

sources.quote: ונפשי אשא הוא לשון מנחה מענין וישא משאת
sources.says: Meiri reads 'I lift' as bringing an offering, from the same word as the portions in Genesis 43:34.

86:12.headline: With all my heart: both the good urge and the bad
86:12.body: The verse uses the fuller word לְבָב for 'heart'. The midrash and Meiri read it as two hearts, the good urge and the bad, both given over to praising God.

sources.quote: אודך ה' אלקי בכל לבבי. ביצר טוב וביצר רע
sources.says: The midrash reads 'with all my heart' as with the good urge and with the bad urge.

sources.quote: רומז לשתי הלבבות יצר הרע ויצר הטוב
sources.says: Meiri says the word hints at the two hearts, the bad urge and the good.

87:1.headline: Whose foundation: this song's, or the whole world's?
87:1.body: This word for 'foundation' appears only here, and it is not clear what 'its' refers to. Rashi says the song itself is founded on Zion, its subject; the midrash says the world stands on the merit of two holy mountains.

sources.quote: יְסוּדַת מִזְמוֹר זֶה; עַל הַר צִיּוֹן וִירוּשָׁלַיִם יְסָדוֹ הַמְשׁוֹרֵר
sources.says: Rashi says the foundation is that of this psalm, which the poet built on Mount Zion and Jerusalem.

sources.quote: יסודתו של עולם בזכות שני הרים של קדושה הר סיני והר המוריה
sources.says: The midrash reads it as the world's foundation, resting on the merit of Sinai and Moriah.

87:2.headline: The gates of Zion heard as gates that stand out
87:2.body: The midrash hears ציון, Zion, as מְצֻיָּנִים, 'marked out'. God loves the gates marked out by their study of law more than every synagogue and house of study.

sources.quote: אוהב אני שערים המצויינין בהלכה מכל בתי כנסיות ובתי מדרשות
sources.says: The midrash has God say he loves the gates distinguished in law more than all synagogues and study houses.

sources.quote: בָּתֵּי מֶדְרָשַׁיָא דִקְבִיעָן בְּצִיוֹן
sources.says: The Targum turns 'the gates of Zion' into the study houses set in Zion.

87:3.headline: Glorious things said of you, or God's glorious name said in you
87:3.body: Rashi reads 'glorious things are spoken of you' as God's praise of Jerusalem. The midrash reads it as the glorious name of God, which was said aloud only in the Temple.

sources.quote: דִּבְרֵי כָבוֹד נִדְבְּרוּ בָּךְ מִפִּי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says words of honor about Jerusalem were spoken by God.

sources.quote: למה אומרים ישראל את השם במקדש בפירוש ובמדינה בכנויו
sources.says: The midrash uses the verse to explain why God's name was pronounced in full in the Temple but by a substitute elsewhere.

87:4.headline: Rahab is a nickname for proud Egypt
87:4.body: רַהַב here is a name for Egypt. Metzudat Zion says Egypt was called this for its arrogance, from the verb for acting brazenly. Ibn Ezra adds it can mean the proud of any nation.

sources.quote: ויקראו כן ע״ש גאותם והוא מל׳ ירהבו הנער בזקן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says Egypt was called Rahab for its pride, from the word in 'the youth will act boldly against the elder'.

sources.quote: הוא מצרים המחצבת רהב, או רהב כל גוי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Rahab is Egypt, or the proud ones of every nation.

87:4.headline: Those who know Zion, or those I love
87:4.body: The word usually means 'those who know me'. Radak reads it as those who know Zion's worth. Metzudat Zion reads it as 'my dear ones', as in 'call understanding your close friend'.

sources.quote: ואמר ליודעי. כמו ליודעי מעלת ציון
sources.says: Radak says it means those who know Zion's high worth.

sources.quote: ליודעי. ענינו אהוב וחביב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means beloved and dear.

87:7.headline: My springs, or my thoughts, are all in you
87:7.body: מַעְיָן is a spring of water, but the commentators also read it as 'my thoughts' or 'my insides'. The midrash keeps the spring: as a well gives fresh water every hour, Israel sings a new song every hour.

sources.quote: או פירוש מעיני עיוני והשגחתי בך
sources.says: Radak offers that it means my thought and attention are on you.

sources.quote: כָּל־מַעְיָנַי. כָּל קְרָבַי
sources.says: Rashi says it means all my insides.

sources.quote: כשם שהבאר נובע מים חדשים בכל שעה כך ישראל אומרים שירה חדשה בכל שעה
sources.says: The midrash compares Israel's new songs to a well that gives fresh water every hour.

88:1.headline: The psalm's heading word means sickness, an instrument, or forgiving
88:1.body: Rashi reads מחלת as sickness: Israel sick with love and suffering in exile. Metzudat Zion says it names a musical instrument, and Midrash Tehillim hears God forgiving (מוחל) David.

sources.quote: עַל חוֹלַת אַהֲבָה וְעִנּוּיָהּ, שֶׁהִיא מְעֻנָּה בְּיִסּוּרֵי הַגָּלוּת
sources.says: Rashi says it means the sickness of love: Israel afflicted by the sufferings of exile.

sources.quote: מחלת. שם כלי נגון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says מחלת is the name of a musical instrument.

sources.quote: ולמי נתן רשות לדוד. שנאמר למנצח על מחלת. שמחל לו הקב"ה
sources.says: Midrash Tehillim ties מחלת to God forgiving (מחל) David.

88:1.headline: לענות can mean 'to sing aloud' or 'for affliction'
88:1.body: Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra read לענות as raising the voice in song, like קול ענות. Midrash Tehillim ties it to David's afflictions (ענותו).

sources.quote: להרים הקול בשיר כמו וענו הלוים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means raising the voice in song, like וענו הלוים.

sources.quote: ומלת לענות – כמו קול ענות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says לענות is like קול ענות.

sources.quote: לענות (תהלים קלב א) זכור ה' לדוד את כל ענותו
sources.says: Midrash Tehillim ties לענות to the verse 'remember for David all his afflictions' (ענותו).

88:1.headline: Rashi: משכיל marks a psalm the prophet spoke through an interpreter
88:1.body: Rashi says that wherever משכיל appears, the words were spoken through an interpreter. Meiri reads it instead as a song that stirs the heart.

sources.quote: כָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר מַשְׂכִּיל, עַל יְדֵי תּוּרְגְּמָן נֶאֱמַר
sources.says: Rashi says that wherever משכיל is said, it was said through an interpreter.

sources.quote: וכן משכיל ר״ל מעורר הלבבות
sources.says: Meiri says משכיל means it stirs the hearts.

88:2.headline: In 'by day I cried', 'day' also covers the night
88:2.body: Radak says night is also called יום, as when God struck the firstborn of Egypt 'on the day', which was at night. Ibn Ezra says יום here just means 'a time'.

sources.quote: הלילה גם כן יקרא יום וכן ביום הכותי כל בכור בארץ מצרים ומכת בכורים בלילה היתה
sources.says: Radak says night is also called יום, like the day the Egyptian firstborn were struck, which was at night.

sources.quote: טעם יום – זמן כמו אתה עובר היום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says יום here means a time.

88:6.headline: 'Free among the dead': free from what?
88:6.body: Ibn Ezra says the dead are free from all the commandments, bodily labor and earthly kings. Radak hears the speaker wishing for that freedom, since now he is a slave.

sources.quote: במתים חפשי - מכל המצות ומכל עבודות הגוף וממלכי האדמה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says חפשי means free from all the commandments, all bodily labor and earthly kings.

sources.quote: טוב לי שאהיה עם המתים שאהיה חפשי ועתה אני עבד
sources.says: Radak says it is good to be with the dead and free, whereas now the speaker is a slave.

sources.quote: הִנְנִי בֵּין הַמֵּתִים חָפְשִׁי מִן הָעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says the speaker is among the dead, free from the world.

88:6.headline: 'Not remembered any more' may mean 'not remembered yet'
88:6.body: Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David read עוד as 'still' (עדיין). Ibn Ezra says the word signals a time when the dead will be remembered.

sources.quote: כמו עדיין וכן עוד היום גדול
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says עוד means 'still' (עדיין).

sources.quote: עדיין לא זכרתם כי לא באה זמן התחיה
sources.says: Metzudat David says you have not remembered them yet, because the time of resurrection has not come.

sources.quote: לאות כי יבוא עת ומועד שיזכרו בו המתים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a sign that a time will come when the dead are remembered.

88:8.headline: סמכה can mean 'leaned on', 'came near' or 'grew strong'
88:8.body: Rashi reads סמכה as 'leaned on me'. Radak says it means near and around, and Meiri adds 'grew strong'.

sources.quote: נִשְׁעֲנָה וְתָלָה עָלַי
sources.says: Rashi says סמכה means it leaned and hung on me.

sources.quote: סמכה. ענין הקרוב והסיבוב
sources.says: Radak says it means nearness and surrounding.

sources.quote: וי״א שהוא כמו התחזקה כדרך סומך ה׳ לכל הנופלים
sources.says: Meiri says some take it as 'grew strong', like סומך ה' לכל הנופלים.

88:9.headline: 'You made me abominations': Ibn Ezra says a letter is missing
88:9.body: The verse says 'you made me abominations (תועבות) to them'. Ibn Ezra and Meiri read it as 'like an abomination': a כ is left out.

sources.quote: הרחקת, תועבות - חסר כ"ף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says a kaf is missing at הרחקת and תועבות.

sources.quote: וכן ענין שתני תועבות למו ר״ל כתועבות
sources.says: Meiri says שתני תועבות למו means 'like abominations' (כתועבות).

88:11.headline: Rashi: 'the dead' here are the wicked, dead even while alive
88:11.body: Rashi reads המתים as the wicked, who are called dead even in life. Radak reads it as people who die in exile.

sources.quote: הֲלָרְשָׁעִים, שֶׁאַף בְּחַיֵּיהֶם קְרוּיִין מֵתִים
sources.says: Rashi says המתים means the wicked, who are called dead even in their lifetime.

sources.quote: אם נמות בגלות תעשה לנו פלא אחר כך
sources.says: Radak says it asks: if we die in exile, will you do a wonder for us afterward?

88:11.headline: Rashi hears 'slackened hands' in רפאים
88:11.body: Radak takes רפאים as the dead. Rashi hears רִפּוּ יְדֵיהֶם, 'they let their hands go slack', and says it means the nations that dropped God's service.

sources.quote: שֶׁמָּא אֵלּוּ הָאֻמּוֹת שֶׁרִפּוּ יְדֵיהֶם מֵעֲבוֹדָתְךָ וּמִתּוֹרָתְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says it may mean the nations who let their hands go slack from God's service and Torah.

sources.quote: רפאים. מל׳ רפיון וחלשות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רפאים comes from slackness and weakness.

sources.quote: והם המתים יקומו מקברם ויודוך
sources.says: Radak says רפאים are the dead who would rise from their graves and praise God.

88:13.headline: 'Darkness' is the grave, or Gehinnom
88:13.body: Metzudat David reads the darkness as the dark of the grave. The Targum calls it the darkness of Gehinnom, and Meiri allows that these names point there.

sources.quote: כשנהיה בחשכת הקבר
sources.says: Metzudat David says the darkness is the darkness of the grave.

sources.quote: תְוַדְעוּ בַּחֲשָׁךְ גֵהִנָם פְּרִישְׁוָתָךְ
sources.says: The Targum renders the darkness as the darkness of Gehinnom.

sources.quote: או איפשר שכלם רמז על גיהנם
sources.says: Meiri allows that all these names for the grave may instead point to Gehinnom.

88:16.headline: מנער: 'from my youth', or 'shaken off' in a sudden death
88:16.body: Radak reads מנער as 'from my youth'. Rashi reads it from נער, 'shake', as in וינער ה': a sudden, choking death.

sources.quote: מימי נעורי אני סובל זה העוני
sources.says: Radak says it means from the days of my youth I have borne this affliction.

sources.quote: מֵת מִתּוֹךְ תִּשְׁנוֹק מִיתָה חֲטוּפָה
sources.says: Rashi says וגוע מנער means dying from choking, a snatched death, from the root of וינער ה'.

88:17.headline: צמתותני is an extra-long verb, and commentators say why
88:17.body: Radak says the lengthened form strengthens the meaning: 'cut me off many times over'. Meiri says the extra letters are there to stress it.

sources.quote: כמו ירקרק שהוא ירוק שבירוקים כן צמתתוני ר"ל כרתו אותי כריתות רבות
sources.says: Radak says it works like ירקרק, 'very green', so צמתתוני means they cut me off many times over.

sources.quote: כי היה ראוי לומר צמתוני ובא כן להפליג כמו יפיפית
sources.says: Meiri says it should have been צמתוני, and the longer form is there to stress it, like יפיפית.

88:19.headline: מחשך: are the friends in darkness, or is the speaker?
88:19.body: Radak says it is as if his friends are in a dark place, so he cannot see them. Rashi and Meiri turn it around: the speaker himself has gone dark.

sources.quote: כאילו מיודעי במקום חשך שלא אראה אותם
sources.says: Radak says it is as if my acquaintances were in a dark place where I cannot see them.

sources.quote: נֶחְשַׁכְתִּי וְנֶחְדַּלְתִּי מֵהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says: I have grown dark and I have ceased from them.

sources.quote: או למיודעי מחשך אני והטעם שחשך תארי מן החולי
sources.says: Meiri says it may mean I am darkness to my acquaintances, because the illness darkened my looks.

89:1.headline: Ezrahite: 'the man from the east', or a son of Zerah?
89:1.body: The Sages read Eitan the Ezrahite as Abraham. They hear אזרחי as 'from the east', from Isaiah's 'who roused one from the east'. Radak's plain reading is Eitan son of Zerah, a wise man of Judah.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ פֵּרְשׁוּהוּ (בבא בתרא טו.) בְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עַל שֵׁם ״מִי הֵעִיר מִמִּזְרָח
sources.says: Rashi reports that the Sages explained Eitan as Abraham, because of the verse 'who roused one from the east'.

sources.quote: והוא איתן בן זרח בן יהודה, והיה מחכמי ישראל
sources.says: Radak says that in the plain sense he is Eitan son of Zerah son of Judah, one of Israel's wise men.

89:3.headline: Kindness builds the world, or kindness is built forever?
89:3.body: עולם can mean 'world' or 'forever'. Maimonides reads 'the world is built by kindness': God making the world at all is kindness. Ibn Ezra objects that עולם in Scripture always means time: God's kindness to David stands forever.

sources.quote: נאמר: "עוֹלָם חֶסֶד יִבָּנֶה" (תהילים פט,ג), כלומר: בנין העולם – חסד הוא
sources.says: Maimonides reads the verse as saying that building the world is itself kindness.

sources.quote: והמפרשים עולם חסד יבנה - כי בחסד נבנה העולם איננו מטעם זה המזמור. ועוד: כי כל עולם בכל המקרא הוא זמן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says reading it as 'the world was built by kindness' does not fit this psalm, and that עולם in Scripture always means time.

sources.quote: כִּי אָמַרְתִּי: עַד עוֹלָם יִבָּנֶה בְחֶסֶד כִּסֵּא דָוִד
sources.says: Rashi's first reading is that David's throne would be built with kindness forever.

89:9.headline: Two names for God: the Strong One, and Yah
89:9.body: חסין appears only here. Maimonides counts it among God's names and derives it from strength, as in Amos, 'strong as the oaks'. He says the short name יה means eternal existence.

sources.quote: וכן השם "חֲסִין" (תהילים פט,ט) נגזר מכוח: "וְחָסֹן הוּא כָּאַלּוֹנִים
sources.says: Maimonides says the name חסין comes from strength, as in Amos 2:9.

sources.quote: וכן לשם "יה" יש משמעות של מציאות נצחית
sources.says: Maimonides says the name יה means eternal existence.

sources.quote: וחסין מורה כי הוא קיום העולם אחר הוויתו
sources.says: Radak says חסין shows that God keeps the world standing after creating it.

89:11.headline: Rahab, 'Arrogance', is a name for Egypt
89:11.body: רהב means 'arrogance'. Rashi and Radak say it is a name for Egypt, crushed at the Red Sea. Ibn Ezra explains the name: the arrogant ones.

sources.quote: רָהַב. מִצְרַיִם (ישעיהו ל:ז
sources.says: Rashi says Rahab is Egypt, as in Isaiah 30:7.

sources.quote: בכל זה הפסוק מוכיח כי על קריעת ים סוף אמר הפסוק אשר לפניו כי רהב הוא מצרים
sources.says: Radak says this verse shows the psalm speaks of the splitting of the sea, since Rahab is Egypt.

sources.quote: וטעם דכאת כחלל רהב – הם מצרים, והטעם אנשי רהב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Rahab is Egypt, meaning the men of arrogance.

89:12.headline: תבל is the part of the earth where people live
89:12.body: The verse uses two words for the earth. Radak and Ibn Ezra explain the difference. ארץ is all land, lived on or not. תבל is only the lived-in part, which is why it comes with 'all that fills it'.

sources.quote: ארץ תקרא המישבת ושאינה מיושבת והמיושבת תקרא תבל לפיכך אמר ומלואה
sources.says: Radak says ארץ means both settled and empty land, and only the settled part is called תבל.

sources.quote: ותבל הוא הנושבת מהארץ, על כן ומלואה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says תבל is the inhabited part of the earth, so the verse adds 'and all that fills it'.

89:16.headline: Which 'shout' do the happy people know?
89:16.body: Rashi says תרועה is the shofar blast of Rosh Hashanah, which wins God's favor. Metzudat Zion reads it as closeness and friendship. Radak reads it as the blast of soldiers winning a battle.

sources.quote: יוֹדְעֵי תְרוּעָה. שֶׁיּוֹדְעִין לְרַצּוֹת אֶת בּוֹרְאָם בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה בִּתְרוּעָה
sources.says: Rashi says these are people who know how to win their Creator's favor with the shofar on Rosh Hashanah.

sources.quote: תרועה. ענין התחברות וריעות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says תרועה here means closeness and friendship.

sources.quote: וטעם התרועה כי המלחמה המתגברים על אשר כנגדם הם תוקעים ומריעים להפחיד אשר כנגדם
sources.says: Radak says the תרועה is the blast that winning soldiers sound to frighten their enemies.

89:23.headline: No enemy will be his creditor, or no enemy will trick him
89:23.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read ישיא from lending: no enemy will press David like a creditor. Ibn Ezra reports another reading, from 'your pride has tricked you': no enemy will deceive him.

sources.quote: לֹא יַשִּׁיא אוֹיֵב בּוֹ. לֹא יִגְבַּר עָלָיו לִהְיוֹת לוֹ כְּנוֹשֶׁה
sources.says: Rashi says the enemy will not overpower him like a creditor.

sources.quote: ישיא. ענין הלואה כמו כי תשה ברעך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is about lending, as in Deuteronomy 24:10.

sources.quote: יש אומרים: כי הוא מגזרת: זדון לבך השיאך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that some derive it from 'the pride of your heart has deceived you'.

89:36.headline: God's promise to David will not run dry
89:36.body: כזב usually means 'lie', and Metzudat Zion reads it so. Rashi links it to Isaiah's spring whose waters 'do not fail'. God's oath to David will not fail him.

sources.quote: אִם לְדָוִד אֲכַזֵּב. לְשׁוֹן ״לֹא יְכַזְּבוּ מֵימָיו
sources.says: Rashi says the word is like 'whose waters do not fail' in Isaiah 58:11.

sources.quote: אכזב. מל׳ כזב ושקר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from the words for lying and falsehood.

89:44.headline: צור, usually 'rock', is the sword's sharp edge
89:44.body: צור usually means 'rock'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it as the edge of the sword, as in the flint knives of Joshua 5. God turned back the edge of the king's sword.

sources.quote: הֲשִׁיבוֹתָ אָחוֹר וְהָפַכְתָּ אֶת חִדּוּד חַרְבּוֹ, כְּמוֹ ״חַרְבוֹת צֻרִים
sources.says: Rashi says God turned back the sharp edge of his sword, as in 'flint knives' in Joshua 5:2.

sources.quote: אף צור חרבו - חידוד חרבו וחרבות צורים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says צור means the sharpness of the sword, as in 'flint knives'.

89:49.headline: Here שאול is the grave, not a place of punishment
89:49.body: Meiri says this verse proves שאול can mean the grave. The verse speaks of every person, and every person dies. So שאול cannot always mean Gehinnom.

sources.quote: וזה ראיה גמורה על מלת שאול שנאמרת לפעמים על הקבר ולא כדעת מי שיחייבה בכל מקום גיהנם
sources.says: Meiri says this verse is full proof that שאול sometimes means the grave, against those who say it always means Gehinnom.

89:52.headline: The Messiah's 'heels': his late coming, or the last days
89:52.body: עקב means 'heel', the back end of the foot. Radak and Ibn Ezra read 'the heels of your anointed' as his delay: enemies mock him for being late. Rashi reads it as the last days before the Messiah.

sources.quote: ומה חרפו עקבות משיחך התאחרות משיחך שמתאחר לבא ואומרים שלא יבא לעולם
sources.says: Radak says the enemies mock the Messiah's delay and say he will never come.

sources.quote: והטעם שאחרו פעמיו לבוא כאומרים נשברו עקביו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says his steps are late in coming, as if people said his heels were broken.

sources.quote: עִקְּבוֹת מְשִׁיחֶךָ. סוֹפֵי מֶלֶךְ הַמָּשִׁיחַ, וּלְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says it means the end times of the Messiah, a phrase also used in the Mishnah.

9:6.headline: Here 'rebuke' means destroy, not just scold
9:6.body: גערת usually means to shout at someone. Radak and Ibn Ezra say that when it has no ב after it, as here, it means to wipe out.

sources.quote: גערה הקשורה בלא בי"ת לשון השחתה
sources.says: Radak says this verb without ב means destruction, as in Malachi 2:3.

sources.quote: בלא בי"ת כדמות כריתה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that without ב it is like cutting off.

sources.quote: ענין זעקת נזיפה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion gives the plain sense, a scolding shout.

9:8.headline: A fully spelled 'throne' answers a shortened one in Exodus
9:8.body: In Exodus 17:16 God's throne and name are both written short, כס יה. Rashi says that once Amalek is wiped out, name and throne are whole again, so here the throne is spelled in full.

sources.quote: שֵׁם שָׁלֵם וְכִסֵּא שָׁלֵם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: כִּסְאוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the name and the throne are now whole, as the full spelling כסאו shows.

sources.quote: כֵּס חָסֵר וְשֵׁם חָלוּק
sources.says: Rashi contrasts Exodus 17:16, where the throne is missing letters and the name is split.

sources.quote: כל זמן שזרעו של עמלק קיים לא השם שלם ולא הכסא שלם
sources.says: The midrash says that while Amalek's line lives, neither God's name nor throne is whole.

9:10.headline: בצרה: a time of trouble, or a time of drought?
9:10.body: Rashi reads it as 'times of trouble'. Ibn Ezra reports that Dunash took it from the word for drought, and rejects that because it does not fit the psalm.

sources.quote: עִתִּים שֶׁל צָרָה
sources.says: Rashi explains it as times of trouble.

sources.quote: ורבי דונש פירש בו: לשון יחיד מן דברי הבצרות. ואין זה מטעם המזמור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Dunash read it as the singular of 'droughts', and that this does not fit the psalm.

9:13.headline: Written 'poor', read 'humble', because the poor are usually humble
9:13.body: The written text has עניים, the poor, but it is read aloud as ענוים, the humble. Radak and Meiri say the two overlap, since most poor people are humble.

sources.quote: כתיב ביו"ד וקרי בוא"ו, כי הענוים הם כמו העניים והחלשים ברוב
sources.says: Radak says it is written with yod and read with vav, because the humble are mostly the poor and the weak.

sources.quote: וצעקת ענוים קרי והכוונה עניים כי על הרוב העניים הם ענוים
sources.says: Meiri says the reading is 'humble' but the meaning is 'poor', since the poor are mostly humble.

9:14.headline: An extra נ in 'be gracious to me', read as three kingdoms
9:14.body: The usual form is חנני, with two נ. Ibn Ezra calls this longer form an odd word, and the midrash reads its three נ letters as three kingdoms.

sources.quote: נמצא שלם והיא מלה זרה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word appears in full form and is an unusual word.

sources.quote: חנני אין כתיב אלא חננני. שלש נוני"ן כנגד שלש מלכיות
sources.says: The midrash says it is written חננני, not חנני, and its three נ stand for three kingdoms.

9:17.headline: הגיון: quiet thought, or a song of praise?
9:17.body: Metzudat Zion reads it as thought, as in 'the meditation of my heart'. Meiri and the Targum take it as praise spoken or sung aloud for the rescue.

sources.quote: ענינו מחשבה כמו והגיון לבי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means thought, as in Psalm 19:15.

sources.quote: היא לנו הגיון ודבור של שבח לעולם
sources.says: Meiri says this rescue is for us words of praise forever.

sources.quote: יְרַנְנוּן צַדִיקַיָא לְעָלְמִין
sources.says: The Targum renders it: the righteous will sing forever.

9:18.headline: Sheol gets two 'to' markers, meaning its very lowest level
9:18.body: Hebrew can say 'toward' with ל at the front or ה at the end, and one is enough. Here both appear, and the sages read the doubling as the lowest level of Sheol.

sources.quote: לַמַּדְרֵגָה הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה שֶׁל שְׁאוֹל
sources.says: Rashi, quoting the Talmud, says the extra marker means the lowest level of Sheol.

sources.quote: כל תיבה שלא נתן למ"ד ברישה ניתן ה"א בסופה
sources.says: The midrash states the rule: a word without ל at the start gets ה at the end, and asks why this one has both.

90:1.headline: Moses is called both "man" and "of God": which is he?
90:1.body: The midrash asks how Moses can be called both איש, a man, and אלהים, God. It answers that he was called God when he stood over Pharaoh, and a man when he fled from him.

sources.quote: אם איש למה אלקים ואם אלקים למה איש. אלא בשעה שהיה עומד לפני פרעה נקרא אלקים
sources.says: The midrash asks why Moses is called both man and God, and answers that before Pharaoh he was called God.

sources.quote: איש האלהים. שהיה נביא
sources.says: Radak says "man of God" means Moses was a prophet.

90:1.headline: God is the world's dwelling place, not the other way round
90:1.body: The sages ask whether God dwells in the world or the world dwells in God. They read מעון, "dwelling," to say God is the world's home, which is why He is also called מקום, "the Place."

sources.quote: מעונו של עולם ואם העולם מעונו. בא משה ופירש
sources.says: The midrash says we would not know whether God is the world's dwelling or the world His, until Moses explained it.

sources.quote: שהוא מקומו של עולם
sources.says: The midrash says God is called "the Place" because He is the place of the world.

sources.quote: הוא מעון עולמו ואין עולמו מעונו
sources.says: Maimonides quotes the sages: He is the dwelling of His world, and His world is not His dwelling.

sources.quote: כי השמים אינה מעונות לנו באמת רק אתה המעון באמת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the heavens are not our true dwelling; only God is.

90:3.headline: שובו: return to the dust, or return to God?
90:3.body: Ibn Ezra reads שובו as "return to the dust you were taken from." Rashi reads it as "turn back from your bad ways," and the midrash learns here that repentance was made before the world.

sources.quote: אל העפר אשר לקחתם ממנה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means return to the dust you were taken from.

sources.quote: שׁוּבוּ בְנֵי אָדָם מִדַּרְכֵיכֶם הָרָעִים
sources.says: Rashi says it means "turn back, people, from your bad ways."

sources.quote: גדולה תשובה שקדמה לבריאת עולם
sources.says: The midrash says repentance is great, because it came before the world was created.

90:4.headline: A thousand years in whose eyes, God's or a person's?
90:4.body: Rashi follows the sages: a thousand human years are one day for God. Radak's plain reading speaks to a person: even if you lived a thousand years, they would feel like yesterday.

sources.quote: אֶלֶף שָׁנִים שֶׁל בְּנֵי אָדָם הֵם כְּיוֹם אֶחָד שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says a thousand human years are like one day of God.

sources.quote: כי אילו יראה בעיניך ותחשב שתחיה אלף שנים מה שלא חיה האדם הראשון כאין הם
sources.says: Radak says that even if a person thought he would live a thousand years, more than Adam did, they would be as nothing.

sources.quote: ורבותינו זכרונם לברכה פירשו בעיניך כנגד האל יתברך
sources.says: Radak notes that the sages read "in your eyes" as God's eyes.

90:5.headline: The sages break זרמתם into "scattered, died, finished"
90:5.body: Rashi says זרמתם comes from זרם, a flood: God sweeps people's years away. The midrash splits the word apart, and Rabbi Yochanan hears זרו מתו תמו, "they scattered, died, were finished."

sources.quote: זְרַמְתָּם. לְשׁוֹן שְׁטִיפָה, כְּמוֹ ״זֶרֶם מַיִם״
sources.says: Rashi says the word means sweeping away, like a flood of water.

sources.quote: זרו מתו תמו שנתם
sources.says: Rabbi Yochanan reads the word as "they scattered, died, their sleep ended."

sources.quote: זרו מתורתך רמה נגעה בהם
sources.says: Resh Lakish reads it as "they strayed from your Torah, and worms touched them."

90:6.headline: חלף: grass that grows fresh, or grass that passes away?
90:6.body: חלף can mean to pass away or to be renewed. Rashi reads it as passing away at once, while Radak and Meiri read it as fresh growth in the morning before the grass withers at night.

sources.quote: בַּבֹּקֶר יָצִיץ. מִיָּד חָלַף
sources.says: Rashi says it sprouts in the morning and passes away at once.

sources.quote: וחלף. זה מן לשון אם יכרת ועוד יחליף יחליפו כח ענין התחדשות
sources.says: Radak says the word means renewal, as in "if it is cut down it will sprout again."

sources.quote: יציץ ויתחדש כמו אם יכרת ועוד יחליף
sources.says: Meiri says it means the grass blooms and renews itself.

90:8.headline: עלמנו: the sins of our youth, or our hidden sins?
90:8.body: Rashi and the Targum read עלמנו as our youth, as in "whose son is this young man (העלם)." Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as hidden things: nothing we hide escapes the light of God's face.

sources.quote: עֲלֻמֵינוּ. נְעוּרֵינוּ, כְּמוֹ (שמואל א יז:נו) ״בֶּן מִי זֶה הָעֶלֶם״
sources.says: Rashi says the word means our youth, as in "whose son is this young man."

sources.quote: עַוְיַת טַלְיוּתָנָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it "the sins of our youth."

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני: שהוא מגזרת תעלומה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from תעלומה, a hidden thing.

sources.quote: ענין הנעלם הוא למאור פניך כי אין נסתר לך
sources.says: Radak says whatever is hidden is in the light of God's face, since nothing is hidden from Him.

90:9.headline: Our years end like הגה, a word spoken and gone
90:9.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra say הגה is a spoken word: it exists for a moment and then is as if it never was. The Targum pictures the breath of the mouth on a winter day.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ הֶגֶה. כְּדִבּוּר הַמְּמַהֵר לִכְלוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it is like speech that quickly ends.

sources.quote: שהדיבור אין לו מעמד, כי ברגע דבור המדבר ימצא ואחר כן כאילו לא היה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says speech has no lasting existence: it is there for a moment, then as if it never was.

sources.quote: הֵיךְ הֲבֵל פּוּמָא דְסִתְוָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it "like the breath of the mouth in winter."

90:10.headline: גז: our days are swept away, or shorn off?
90:10.body: Rashi reads גז as passing away, like the wind that swept in the quail. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it as cutting, like shearing hair (גזי נזרך).

sources.quote: גָּז. לְשׁוֹן הַעֲבָרָה, כְּמוֹ ״נָגֹזּוּ וְעָבָר״
sources.says: Rashi says the word means passing away.

sources.quote: ויגז. וַיַּפְרִיחַ, וְכֵן
sources.says: Rashi says the word for the wind bringing the quail means "made them fly," and cites this verse.

sources.quote: שיכרתו מהרה כמו גזי נזרך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means our days are quickly cut off, like shorn hair.

sources.quote: ענין כריתה ותלישה כמו גזי נזרך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means cutting and plucking, like shorn hair.

90:10.headline: ונעפה: we fly off like birds, or vanish in a blink?
90:10.body: Radak reads ונעפה as flying swiftly to the grave, like a bird. Ibn Ezra adds that it may come from עפעף, the eyelid: our days pass like the blink of an eye.

sources.quote: נעופה. אל הקבר כלומר נלך שם במהרה כעוף
sources.says: Radak says it means we go quickly to the grave, like a bird.

sources.quote: או המלה מגזרת עפעף כמו תעופה כבוקר תהיה התעיף עיניך בו ואיננו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word may come from עפעף, the eyelid, so our days are like the blink of an eye.

90:12.headline: ונבא: we will bring a wise heart, or a prophet?
90:12.body: Rashi reads ונבא as "we will bring" a wise heart. The Targum, the Talmud and Maimonides hear נביא, a prophet: the true prophet is a heart full of wisdom.

sources.quote: וְנָבִיא לְשׁוֹן הֲבָאָה
sources.says: Rashi says the word means bringing.

sources.quote: בְּרַם נְבִיָא דְלִבֵּיהּ מַבַּע חוּכְמָתָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it "but a prophet whose heart pours out wisdom."

sources.quote: כלומר שהנביא באמת הוא לְבַב חָכְמָה
sources.says: Maimonides reads the verse to mean the true prophet is a heart of wisdom.

sources.quote: ובנביאי אלו תלמידי חכמים - שנאמר ונביא לבב חכמה
sources.says: Rashi explains that the Talmud calls Torah scholars "my prophets" from this verse.

90:14.headline: Which morning: each day, our youth, or redemption?
90:14.body: Meiri reads בבקר as every single morning. Ibn Ezra reads it as our youth, and Rashi as the morning of redemption after the long night of trouble.

sources.quote: שבענו בבקר פירושו בכל בקר ובקר
sources.says: Meiri says it means every morning.

sources.quote: אם תעשה עמנו חסד בבחרותינו שתלמדנו הדרך הישרה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the morning is our youth, when God teaches us the right path.

sources.quote: בְּיוֹם הַגְּאֻלָּה וְהַתְּשׁוּעָה, שֶׁהוּא בֹּקֶר לְלֵיל הַצָּרָה
sources.says: Rashi says the morning is the day of redemption, which ends the night of trouble.

91:4.headline: סוחרה is armor that goes all the way round
91:4.body: Rashi ties סוחרה to סחור סחור, "round and round". Meiri says the צנה shields only the front of the body, while the סוחרה wraps the sides too.

sources.quote: סֹחֵרָה לְשׁוֹן סְחוֹר סְחוֹר
sources.says: Rashi says סוחרה is the language of סחור סחור, around.

sources.quote: וסוחרה המקפת פני גוף וצדדיו והצנה מגינה בפני הגוף לבד
sources.says: Meiri says the סוחרה goes around the face of the body and its sides, while the צנה guards only the front.

sources.quote: לבוש מברזל מסבבת הגוף סחור סחור
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is an iron garment that goes around the body.

91:6.headline: ישוד: "plunders", or something to do with demons?
91:6.body: ישוד looks like a verb for robbing. Metzudat Zion says it means plundering, and Ibn Ezra reports some who derive it from שדים, demons.

sources.quote: מל׳ שדידה וגזלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is from the language of plundering and robbing.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: כי ישוד, מגזרת שדים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some say ישוד comes from the root of demons.

91:7.headline: יפול: a thousand fall dead beside you, or camp beside you?
91:7.body: Radak and Metzudat David read it as people falling in war or plague at your side. Rashi reads יפול as "camp", as in Genesis, so a thousand demons camp at your left and cannot touch you.

sources.quote: ותראה שיפלו במלחמה משמאלך ומימינך
sources.says: Radak says you will see them fall in war to your left and right.

sources.quote: אף אם בעת הדבר יפלו אנשים רבים מצדך ומימינך
sources.says: Metzudat David says even if many people fall at your side during the plague, it will not reach you.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן חֲנִיָּה, כְּמוֹ ״עַל פְּנֵי כָל אֶחָיו נָפָל״
sources.says: Rashi says יפול is the language of camping, like על פני כל אחיו נפל.

sources.quote: מִשְּׂמֹאלְךָ יַחֲנוּ אֶלֶף שֵׁדִים
sources.says: Rashi says a thousand demons will camp to your left.

91:8.headline: The wicked get their שלמת: payment, or an ending?
91:8.body: Rashi says שלמת means destruction. Ibn Ezra and Meiri say it is the payment God gives the wicked for what they did.

sources.quote: וְשִׁלֻּמַת. כִּלָּיוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says שלמת means ending.

sources.quote: כי השם הביא עליהם דבר לשלם להם כפעלם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God brought a plague on them to pay them back as they deserve.

sources.quote: העונש שהאל משלם להם תראה
sources.says: Meiri says you will see the punishment God pays them.

91:14.headline: חשק is love so strong that nothing else stays in mind
91:14.body: Maimonides says חשק is more than love: it is love so great that no thought remains for anything else. Meiri says the same: he clings to God and turns away from everything else.

sources.quote: שהאהבה המופלגת עד שלא תישאר מחשבה על דבר אחר מלבד אותו אהוב, היא החשק
sources.says: Maimonides says חשק is love so great that no thought is left for anything but the beloved.

sources.quote: כי נפלאה אהבתו לי לדבקה בי ויגעל בכל זולתי וזהו ענין החשק
sources.says: Meiri says his love for God is wonderful, clinging to Him and rejecting all else, and that this is the meaning of חשק.

91:14.headline: "Knows My name": understanding Him, loving Him, or not forgetting Him?
91:14.body: Maimonides says knowing the Name means grasping who God is. Radak says it is loving God, and Meiri says it means not forgetting Him while living among the nations.

sources.quote: שמשמעות ידיעת השם היא השגתו
sources.says: Maimonides says that knowing the Name means grasping Him.

sources.quote: וידיעת שם המפורש שהוא בן ארבע אותיות היא אהבת האל יתברך
sources.says: Radak says knowing the four-letter Name is loving God.

sources.quote: כי ידע שמי כלו׳ לא שכחו עם התאחרו והשתקעו בין האומות
sources.says: Meiri says knowing His name means they did not forget Him, despite the delay and being sunk among the nations.

92:2.headline: להדות: to give thanks, or to confess?
92:2.body: להדות usually means to give thanks, and Radak says the Sabbath is the best day for it, free of weekday work. The midrash, which says Adam spoke this psalm, reads it as confessing: whoever admits his sins and leaves them is saved.

sources.quote: יום השבת טוב להודות בו לה' משאר ימי השבוע כי האדם פנוי מעסקי העולם
sources.says: Radak says the Sabbath is better than other days for thanking God, because a person is free from worldly work.

sources.quote: שכל מי שמודה על פשעים ועוזב ניצל מדינה של גהינם
sources.says: The midrash says Adam taught that anyone who confesses his sins and leaves them is saved from punishment.

92:4.headline: A ten-string harp, saved for the world to come
92:4.body: Rashi says עשור is a harp with ten strings. The midrash says the harp has seven strings now, eight in the days of the Messiah, and ten in the world to come.

sources.quote: כִּנּוֹר שֶׁל עֲשָׂרָה נִימִין
sources.says: Rashi says עשור is a harp of ten strings.

sources.quote: שבעה נימין בכנור שנאמר (תהלים קיט קסד) שבע ביום הללתיך. ולימות המשיח שמונה שנאמר (שם יב א) למנצח על השמינית. ולעתיד לבוא עשר
sources.says: The midrash says the harp has seven strings in this world, eight in the days of the Messiah, and ten in the world to come.

92:4.headline: הגיון: the sweet tune, or the words of the mouth?
92:4.body: Radak and Ibn Ezra read הגיון as the sweetness of the music, and Ibn Ezra adds it may name an instrument. Metzudat Zion reads it as speech, and the midrash has God say He wants the words of Israel's mouths more than harp music.

sources.quote: והגיון. הוא נועם השיר באומרם אותו על הכינור
sources.says: Radak says הגיון is the sweetness of the song when sung on the harp.

sources.quote: והגיון נועם השיר, או שם כלי הניגון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says הגיון is the sweetness of the song, or the name of an instrument.

sources.quote: הגיון. ענין דבור
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says הגיון means speech.

sources.quote: איני רוצה מישראל זמר בכנור אלא הגיון פיהם
sources.says: The midrash has God say He does not want harp music from Israel, but the words of their mouths.

92:7.headline: בער: a fool as dull as cattle, but still teachable
92:7.body: Metzudat Zion says בער means a fool who is like an animal, from בעיר, cattle. The midrash adds hope: a בער in Israel can still be taught Torah by the sages.

sources.quote: שוטה כבהמה מל׳ אנחנו ובעירנו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a fool like an animal, from the word in "we and our cattle."

sources.quote: אדם שהוא בער מישראל חכמי ישראל ילמדוהו דברי תורה
sources.says: The midrash says the sages of Israel will teach Torah to a בער among Israel.

92:11.headline: The God who is מרום, "on high," raises (ותרם) the psalmist
92:11.body: Ibn Ezra notes that ותרם, "you raised," answers ואתה מרום, "you are on high," two verses earlier. The God who is high lifts up the speaker's horn.

sources.quote: אמר: ותרם כנגד ואתה מרום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ותרם is said to match "and you are on high."

92:13.headline: Why a palm tree? Its fruit, and its far-falling shade
92:13.body: Rashi says the righteous are like a palm because it bears fruit, and like a cedar because its stump grows back. The midrash adds that a palm's shade falls far from it, as the reward of the righteous comes far off, in the world to come.

sources.quote: כַּתָּמָר – לַעֲשׂוֹת פֵּרוֹת, וּכְאֶרֶז בַּלְּבָנוֹן – לְהַחֲלִיף גִּזְעוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the palm stands for bearing fruit and the cedar for regrowing its trunk.

sources.quote: מה התמרה הזאת צלה רחוק ממנה כך מתן שכרן של צדיקים רחוק מהן עד עולם הבא
sources.says: The midrash says that as a palm's shade is far from it, the reward of the righteous is far off, in the world to come.

92:15.headline: The righteous keep growing after trees and animals stop
92:15.body: ינובון means to sprout and bear fruit, from תנובה, produce. Meiri notes that trees and animals stop growing at some age, but the righteous keep growing even when old.

sources.quote: ינובון. מל׳ תנובה והצמחה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from produce and growth.

sources.quote: שגדול האלנות ובעלי חיים יש זמן לתכלית גדולם שלא יגדלו עוד אבל הצדיקים ינובון ר״ל יגדלו ויצמחו לעולם אף בשיבתם
sources.says: Meiri says trees and animals reach an age when they stop growing, but the righteous keep growing even in old age.

93:1.headline: God reigned at creation, or will reign at the end?
93:1.body: Meiri reads 'God reigned' as looking back to creation, when God made the world. Rashi and others read it as what people will say in the future, with the past tense standing for what is to come.

sources.quote: גם זה המזמור נראה לי שרומז על חדוש העולם
sources.says: Meiri says he thinks this psalm points to the creation of the world.

sources.quote: ה׳ מָלַךְ. יֹאמְרוּ לֶעָתִיד
sources.says: Rashi says people will say 'God reigns' in the future.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים שזה המזמור על זמן המשיח וה׳ מלך עבר במקום עתיד
sources.says: Meiri reports that some read the psalm about the time of the Messiah, with 'reigned' as a past tense used for the future.

93:1.headline: Pride is a fault in people but fits God
93:1.body: גאות often means human arrogance. Radak says in the end only God will wear this majesty, and Meiri says pride suits God alone: human pride tears things down, but God's holds the world up.

sources.quote: ואז יכירו הכל כי לא ילבש מלכות גאות כי אם האל לבדו
sources.says: Radak says that then everyone will know that only God wears the majesty of kingship.

sources.quote: ויש לפרש דרך צחות שהאל מתלבש בגאות כלומ׳ שהולמו והולמתו ולא שאר הנבראים
sources.says: Meiri says, as a play on the words, that God wears pride because it fits God and fits no other creature.

sources.quote: כי כל גאות סבה לכל הריסת מצב אבל [גאות] האל היא הנותנת והמעמדת תבל בקיומו
sources.says: Meiri says all other pride leads to ruin, but God's majesty is what keeps the world standing.

93:3.headline: Rising rivers: creation, enemy armies, or a song?
93:3.body: Meiri reads the rivers as the waters gathered together at creation. Radak reads them as a picture of the armies of Gog and Magog, and the Aramaic Targum has the rivers raising their voice in song.

sources.quote: נשאו נהרות קולם רומז אל הקוות המים
sources.says: Meiri says the raised voice of the rivers points to the gathering of the waters at creation.

sources.quote: הוא משל על גוג ומגוג ועל המלכים כשיתקבצו להלחם על ירושלים כנהרות חזקים
sources.says: Radak says the rivers are a picture of Gog and Magog and the kings who will gather to fight Jerusalem.

sources.quote: זְקִיפִין נַהַרְוָתָא קָלְהוֹן בְּשִׁירְתָא
sources.says: The Targum says the rivers raise their voice in song.

93:3.headline: A word found only here for crashing waves
93:3.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion read דכים from דכא, 'crush': the waves that break, also called משברים, 'breakers.' The Aramaic Targum reads the line very differently: the rivers will receive the reward of their praise.

sources.quote: ופירוש דכים. ענין שבר כמו תגלנה עצמות דכית
sources.says: Radak says the word means breaking, as in 'the bones you have crushed will rejoice.'

sources.quote: מלשון דכא ושברון והם הגלים הקרואים משברים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from crushing and breaking, and means the waves called breakers.

sources.quote: יְקַבְּלוּן נַהַרְוָתָא אֲגַר שְׁבָחֵיהוֹן
sources.says: The Targum says the rivers will receive the reward of their praises.

94:2.headline: God is 'lifted up' in greatness, not in place
94:2.body: הנשא literally means 'be lifted up'. Maimonides says that when lifting is said of God, it means greatness and power, not rising to a higher place.

sources.quote: וכל לשון נשיאה המיוחסת לו יתעלה היא מן המשמעות האחרונה הזו
sources.says: Maimonides says every use of 'lifting' said of God has this last sense.

sources.quote: רוממות וגדולה ועוז, לא עילוי מקום
sources.says: Maimonides says it means exaltation, greatness and power, not being higher in place.

94:4.headline: The wicked boast, rising like the top of a tree
94:4.body: יתאמרו is a rare form. Rashi says it means they praise themselves, like האמרת in Deuteronomy. Ibn Ezra says they raise themselves up, like the אמיר, the highest branch of a tree.

sources.quote: יִתְאַמְּרוּ. יִשְׁתַּבְּחוּ
sources.says: Rashi says יתאמרו means they praise themselves.

sources.quote: יתרוממו, כנגד: את ה' האמרת בראש אמיר שהוא הסעיף הגבוה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means they raise themselves up, from אמיר, the high branch.

94:6.headline: The stranger is a Jew far from his family
94:6.body: Who is the stranger the wicked kill? Radak says it is an Israelite who moved to a town where he has no family. No one will demand justice for him, so the killers are not afraid. Meiri also reads the stranger as Israel living among the nations.

sources.quote: הוא ישראל שבא להתגורר בעיר אחרת שלא גרו שם אבותיו והוא שאין לו שם מכירים וקרובים
sources.says: Radak says the stranger is an Israelite who came to live in a town where his fathers did not live, with no friends or relatives there.

sources.quote: ויהרגו אלמנה וגר ר״ל ישראל הבא להתגורר עליהם
sources.says: Meiri says the stranger means Israel, who came to live among them.

94:9.headline: Why the ear is planted and the eye is formed
94:9.body: The verse says God 'planted' the ear and 'formed' the eye. Ibn Ezra says ears sit in the head like two planted points. The eye is 'formed' because pictures are formed in it all the time.

sources.quote: והזכיר נטיעה עם האזנים, שהם נטועים כשתי נקודות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the verse uses 'planting' for ears because they are set like two points.

sources.quote: ועם העין הזכיר יצירה, כי הצורות נוצרות בכל עת בעין
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it uses 'forming' for the eye because images are formed in the eye all the time.

94:10.headline: The one who punished nations, or who taught his people?
94:10.body: היסר can mean to punish or to teach. Ibn Ezra says God punished whole nations: the Flood, the tower of Babel, Sodom. The Targum reads it as teaching: God gave the Torah to his people, so he will surely correct them when they sin.

sources.quote: שיסר אנשי המבול ודור הפלגה ואנשי סדום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God punished the people of the Flood, the generation of the tower, and the people of Sodom.

sources.quote: הַאֶפְשַׁר דִיהַב אוֹרַיְתָא לְעַמֵיהּ וְכַד יְחוֹבוּן הֲלָא יִתְוַכְּחוּן
sources.says: The Targum asks: is it possible that he who gave the Torah to his people will not rebuke them when they sin?

94:13.headline: Until the pit is dug, or while it is dug?
94:13.body: עד usually means 'until'. Rashi reads it that way: the sufferer is spared until he sees a pit dug for the wicked. Radak and Meiri say here it means 'while': the righteous rests even as the pit is being dug.

sources.quote: עַד שֶׁיִּרְאֶה שֶׁיִּכָּרֶה לָרָשָׁע שַׁחַת
sources.says: Rashi says: until he sees a pit dug for the wicked.

sources.quote: עד. פירושו כמו בעוד
sources.says: Radak says עד here means 'while'.

sources.quote: ועד במקום ועוד כמו עד זה מדבר
sources.says: Meiri says עד stands for 'while', as in Job.

94:17.headline: The land of silence, or the place of the cut off?
94:17.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read דומה as silence: my soul would have dwelt in silence. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as being cut off, and say the place is the grave.

sources.quote: דּוּמָה. ״דּוּמִיָּה״
sources.says: Rashi says דומה is the same as דומיה, silence.

sources.quote: ענין שתיקה כמו נאלמתי דומיה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means silence, as in 'I was mute in silence'.

sources.quote: מקום הכריתות, כמו ודמיתי אמך והוא הקבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the place of being cut off, as in 'I will cut off your mother', which is the grave.

sources.quote: דומה, כמו כרותה, או הוא שם
sources.says: Radak says דומה means cut off, or is a name for that place.

94:21.headline: They band together, or they cut a death sentence
94:21.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra read יגודו from גדוד, a troop: they gather in bands against the righteous. Radak brings another reading, from the words 'cut down the tree': they cut a verdict against him.

sources.quote: יֵאָסְפוּ גְדוּדִים עַל נֶפֶשׁ צַדִּיק לַהֲרֹג
sources.says: Rashi says troops gather against the righteous one to kill him.

sources.quote: יגודו - מגזרת גדוד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says יגודו comes from גדוד, a troop.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים יגודו מן גודו אילנא כלומר יפסקו הדין עליו
sources.says: Radak says some read it from 'cut down the tree', meaning they cut off a verdict against him.

94:23.headline: Their wickedness, their strength, or their violence?
94:23.body: און can mean wrongdoing or strength. Radak reads אונם as their wickedness. Metzudat Zion reads it as their strength. Rashi reads it as their violence, the force they used.

sources.quote: ואונם. מן עמל ואון
sources.says: Radak says the word comes from 'trouble and wickedness'.

sources.quote: ענין כח כמו מצאתי און לי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means strength, as in 'I have found strength'.

sources.quote: אוֹנָם. אוֹנְסָם
sources.says: Rashi says it means their violence.

95:3.headline: King over all 'gods': which gods does the verse mean?
95:3.body: אלהים can mean God, gods, or higher powers, and Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David say that here it means the angels. The Midrash asks how there can be other gods at all.

sources.quote: ומלך על כל - מלאכי שמים, כי מלאכיו הם
